title: French A1
description: French from your first word to CEFR level A1, the level of the DELF A1. Grammar lessons cover sounds, spelling and accents, liaison and elision, greetings, être and avoir, numbers (with soixante-dix and quatre-vingts), gender and the three articles (definite, indefinite, partitive), adjective agreement, the present tense of regular and key irregular verbs, negation, three ways to ask a question, the near future with aller, reflexive verbs for your daily routine, the time and the date, the imperative for directions, and the passé composé with avoir and être. About 675 everyday words are learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pronunciation, conjugation drills practise the present, the imperative and the passé composé, optional honors lessons explore French culture and the French-speaking world, and a reading list points to graded readers and free resources you can try on your own. The standard is the French of France; Belgian, Swiss and Québec usage is noted where it differs.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Sounds, letters and accents
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French spelling looks strange at first: silent letters, marks over vowels, words that run
into each other. But it follows rules, and once you know them you can read a new word aloud.
This lesson gives you the alphabet, the accents, silent letters, letter groups, nasal vowels,
the French *r*, stress, and how words join, plus the survival phrases every learner needs.

Read every example aloud: pronunciation is learned with your mouth, not your eyes.

## The alphabet and spelling your name

French uses the same 26 letters as English, with different names. You'll need them to spell
your name at a desk or on the phone. The respellings are rough English sounds.

| Letter | Name | Letter | Name | Letter | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | ah | J | zhee | S | ess |
| B | bay | K | kah | T | tay |
| C | say | L | ell | U | ü (see below) |
| D | day | M | emm | V | vay |
| E | uh (as in *the*) | N | enn | W | doobl-vay |
| F | eff | O | oh | X | eeks |
| G | zhay | P | pay | Y | ee-grek |
| H | ash | Q | kü | Z | zed |
| I | ee | R | air (French r) | | |

The traps for English speakers are E (uh), I (ee), G (zhay) and J (zhee): French G and J
sound almost like English J and G swapped. *Zh* is the sound in the middle of English
*measure*.

To ask how a word is spelled, say *Comment ça s'écrit ?* (literally "How does that write
itself?"). The verb for "to spell" is *épeler*: *Vous pouvez épeler, s'il vous plaît ?* When
you spell, add the accent after the letter (*e accent aigu*) and say double letters as *deux*
(two) + the letter: *Pellerin* is *P, E, deux L, E, R, I, N*.

French writes a space before *?*, *!*, *:* and *;* (*Comment ça s'écrit ?*). You don't need to
type it in the app.

## Accents

French has five accent marks. They are part of the spelling: a word without its accent is
misspelled, and sometimes it becomes a different word.

| Mark | Name | On | What it does | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ´ | **[[acute accent]]** (*accent aigu*) | é | a closed "ay", short and tense | *épeler*, *café* |
| ` | **[[grave accent]]** (*accent grave*) | è, à, ù | on *e*: an open "eh"; on *a*, *u*: tells words apart | *très*, *voilà*, *où* (where) |
| ^ | **[[circumflex]]** (*accent circonflexe*) | â, ê, î, ô, û | *ê* = open "eh"; often marks a lost *s* | *s'il vous plaît*, *hôtel* |
| ¨ | **[[diaeresis]]** (*tréma*) | ë, ï | say this vowel separately | *Noël* (Christmas), *naïf* |
| ¸ | **[[cedilla]]** (*cédille*) | ç | *c* sounds like *s* before *a, o, u* | *ça*, *français* |

![A chart of the five French accents. The acute accent on é, as in épeler. The grave accent on è, à and ù, as in très, voilà and où. The circumflex on â, ê, î, ô and û, as in hôtel and s'il vous plaît. The diaeresis on ë and ï, as in Noël and naïf. The cedilla on ç, as in ça and français.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Some useful facts:

- *-ez* at the end of a word, and *-er* at the end of a verb, sound like *é*: *répéter* and
  *excusez* end in "ay". (In short words such as *la mer*, sea, and *cher*, dear, the *r* is said.)
- The grave accent on *à* and *ù* changes no sound. It keeps short words apart: *a* (has) /
  *à* (to, at), *ou* (or) / *où* (where), *la* (the) / *là* (there). *Où* is the only word
  with *ù*.
- The circumflex often marks an *s* that was dropped centuries ago, and English kept it:
  *hôpital* (hospital), *forêt* (forest), *île* (isle). That's a handy hook for guessing
  meanings.
- Accents are written on capital letters too (*À bientôt*, *École*). You'll often see them
  left off on signs, but the Académie française recommends keeping them.

Typing accents. In this app, use the buttons under the answer box. On a Mac, press
Option+e then the letter for *é*, Option+` then the letter for *è à ù*, Option+i for *ê â î ô
û*, Option+u for *ë ï*, and Option+c for *ç*. On Windows, add the US-International keyboard
and type ' then e for *é*, ` then e for *è*, ^ then e for *ê*, " then e for *ë*, and ' then c
for *ç*; or hold Alt and type 0233 (é), 0232 (è), 0234 (ê), 0224 (à), 0231 (ç) on the number
pad. On a phone, press and hold the letter. The app also has *œ* (as in *sœur*, sister) and
the French quotation marks *« »*.

## Silent letters

Most final consonants in French are **[[silent letters]]**: you write them and don't say them.

- *petit* (small) is "puh-TEE", *vous* is "voo", *beaucoup* is "boh-KOO", *d'accord* is
  "dah-KOR".
- A final *-e* without an accent is silent too: *une* is one syllable, "ün".
- The *-ent* at the end of a verb is completely silent: *ils parlent* (they speak) sounds just
  like *il parle*. In words that are not verbs, *-ent* is a nasal "ahn": *lentement* (slowly) is
  "lahnt-MAHN".
- *h* is never pronounced: *l'hôtel* is "lo-TEL". Most words have a **[[mute h]]**, which acts
  like a vowel (*l'homme*, the man).

The CaReFuL rule. Four final consonants are usually said: c, r, f, l, the consonants of
the English word *careful*. So *avec* (with), *bonjour*, *neuf* (nine), *il* (he). The big
exception: *-er* at the end of a verb is "ay", with no *r*: *épeler* ends like *é*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Is the last consonant said?
  accDescr: To decide whether to say a consonant at the end of a French word, first check whether it is c, r, f or l, the letters of careful. If it is, it is usually said, as in avec, bonjour, neuf and il, except for -er at the end of a verb, which sounds like é, as in épeler. If it is any other consonant, it is usually silent, as in petit, vous and beaucoup, unless a liaison joins it to a following vowel, as in vous avez.
  A["A word ends in a consonant"] --> B{"Is it c, r, f or l?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Usually said: avec, bonjour, neuf, il"]
  C --> D["Except verbs in -er: épeler ends in é"]
  B -- "no" --> E["Usually silent: petit, vous, beaucoup"]
  E --> F["Unless a liaison joins it to a vowel: vous avez"]
```

## Letter groups

French spells many sounds with two or three letters. Learn these and you can read almost
anything.

| Spelling | Sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *ou* | "oo" | *vous*, *oui*, *bonjour* |
| *u* | "ü": say "ee" with rounded lips | *tu* (you), *une* |
| *eau*, *au*, *o* | "oh" | *beaucoup*, *au revoir*, *le mot* |
| *ai*, *ei*, *è*, *ê* | "eh" | *s'il vous plaît*, *très* |
| *oi* | "wah" | *voilà*, *moi* (me) |
| *eu* | like "uh" with rounded lips | *deux* (two), *neuf* |
| *gn* | "ny" as in *canyon* | *l'Espagne* (Spain) |
| *ch* | "sh" | *le chat* (the cat) |
| *qu* | "k" | *Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?*, *quatre* (four) |
| *-ille* | "eey" | *la famille* (family) — but *ville* and *mille* say "eel" |
| *c*, *g* before *e*, *i* | soft: "s", "zh" | *merci*, *l'âge* (age) |
| *c*, *g* before *a*, *o*, *u* | hard: "k", "g" | *le café*, *le garçon* (the boy) |

The pair that matters most is *u* and *ou*. *Tu* (you) and *tout* (all) are different words. For both sounds your lips are rounded
and pushed forward. The difference is the tongue: for *ou* it is pulled back, as in English
*food*; for *u* it stays forward, exactly where it is for "ee". Say "ee", hold your tongue
still, and round your lips: that's *u*.

![Two simplified side views of the mouth. On the left, u as in tu: the lips are rounded and the tongue is raised high at the front, as for ee. On the right, ou as in tout: the lips are rounded and the tongue is raised high at the back.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Nasal vowels

A **[[nasal vowel]]** lets air out through the nose as well as the mouth. French has four, each
spelled with a vowel + *n* or *m*. The *n* or *m* itself is not pronounced: it only tells you
the vowel is nasal.

| Spelling | Rough sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *an, am, en, em* | "ahn" from the back of the mouth | *la France*, *lentement*, *encore* |
| *in, im, ain, ein* | "an" as in *bank*, without the *k* | *le vin* (wine), *le pain* (bread) |
| *on, om* | "ohn", lips rounded | *bonjour*, *non*, *le nom*, *le prénom* |
| *un, um* | like *in*, with rounded lips | *un* (one) |

Many speakers in France now say *un* exactly like *in*, so don't worry if you can't hear the
difference. What matters is the rule for when the vowel is not nasal: when a vowel or a
second *n*/*m* follows. *Bon* (good) is nasal, *bonne* is "bun" with a real *n*; *fin* (end) is
nasal, *fine* is "feen".

## The French r

The French *r* is made at the back of the throat, close to where you gargle. It is never
rolled with the tip of the tongue and never the English *r*. Think of the *ch* of Scottish
*loch*, made softer and with your voice: *merci*, *très*, *au revoir*, *prénom*.

## Stress: always at the end

English stresses one syllable in each word (*PHO-to-graph*, *pho-TO-gra-phy*). French gives
every syllable about the same weight and puts a light stress on the last syllable of each
**[[rhythm group]]**, a short group of words said together. So:

- *merCI*, *parDON*, *d'acCORD*, *lenteMENT*;
- inside a group, the stress moves to the end of the group: *merci beauCOUP*, *s'il vous
  PLAÎT*, *Je ne comprends PAS*.

Keep the syllables even, like a ticking clock, and lengthen the last one slightly.

## Elision: j', l', d', n', qu'

French doesn't like two vowels meeting across a word boundary. When a short word ending in a
vowel comes before a word starting with a vowel or mute *h*, it drops its vowel and takes an
apostrophe. This is **[[elision]]**, and it's compulsory.

| Short word | Before a vowel | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *je* (I) | *j'* | *j'épelle* (I spell), *j'habite* (I live) |
| *le*, *la* (the) | *l'* | *l'accent*, *l'hôtel* |
| *de* (of) | *d'* | *d'accord* (literally "of agreement") |
| *ne* (not) | *n'* | *Ce n'est pas ça.* (That's not it.) |
| *que* (that, what) | *qu'* | *Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?* |

*Si* (if) elides only before *il* and *ils*: *si il* becomes *s'il*, as in *s'il vous plaît*
(literally "if it pleases you"). Elision is written as well as said: *je habite* is wrong.

## Liaison: words that join

A silent final consonant can come back to life when the next word starts with a vowel or mute
*h*. This is **[[liaison]]**: the consonant is said at the start of the next word. Final *s* and
*x* sound like "z", *t* and *d* like "t", *n* like "n".

![Liaison arcs joining words. Les amis is said lé-za-mi. Vous avez is said vou-za-vé. Un ami is said un-na-mi. Ils ont is said il-zon.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For now, make the liaison in these places, where it is always made:

- after *les*, *des*, *un*, *mon* before a noun: *les amis* (the friends), *des hôtels*, *un
  ami*, *mon ami* (my friend);
- after *nous*, *vous*, *ils*, *elles* before a verb: *nous avons* (we have), *vous avez*,
  *ils ont*, *elles ont*.

Never make a liaison after *et* (and): *et il* is "ay eel". Honors lesson 04h1 goes through
the full rules.

## Survival phrases

| Phrase | Meaning | When |
|---|---|---|
| *oui*, *non* | yes, no | |
| *merci (beaucoup)* | thank you (very much) | the answer is *de rien* (you're welcome) |
| *s'il vous plaît* / *s'il te plaît* | please | *vous* for strangers and groups, *te* for a friend (Lesson 2) |
| *pardon*, *excusez-moi* | excuse me, sorry | to get past, get attention or apologize; *Pardon ?* = sorry, what? |
| *d'accord* | OK, agreed | |
| *voilà* | here it is, there you go | handing something over, or finishing |
| *Je ne comprends pas.* | I don't understand. | |
| *Vous pouvez répéter ?* | Can you repeat that? | add *encore une fois* (once more) or *lentement* (slowly) |
| *Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?* | What does that mean? | |

## Dialogue: at a language school

Sam arrives at a language school in Lyon to sign up. The secretary is Mme Roux.

> Mme Roux : Bonjour, monsieur. Votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
>
> Sam : Bonjour. Okafor.
>
> Mme Roux : Pardon ? Vous pouvez répéter ?
>
> Sam : Okafor. O, K, A, F, O, R.
>
> Mme Roux : O, K, A… Lentement, s'il vous plaît !
>
> Sam : Excusez-moi. O… K… A… F… O… R.
>
> Mme Roux : Merci. Et votre prénom ?
>
> Sam : Samuel. S, A, M, U, E, L.
>
> Mme Roux : Avec un accent ?
>
> Sam : Non. Euh… « accent », qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?
>
> Mme Roux : Un accent, c'est é, è, ê…
>
> Sam : Ah, d'accord ! Non, pas d'accent.
>
> Mme Roux : Voilà. Merci beaucoup, monsieur Okafor.
>
> Sam : Merci, madame. — Mme Roux : De rien !

Hello, sir. Your name, please? — Hello. Okafor. — Sorry? Can you repeat that? — Okafor.
O-K-A-F-O-R. — O, K, A… Slowly, please! — Sorry. O… K… A… F… O… R. — Thank you. And your
first name? — Samuel. S-A-M-U-E-L. — With an accent? — No. Um… "accent", what does that
mean? — An accent is é, è, ê… — Oh, OK! No, no accent. — There we are. Thank you very much,
Mr Okafor. — Thank you, madam. — You're welcome!

(*Bonjour* is hello, *monsieur* and *madame* sir and madam, *votre* your, *avec* with; they
come back in later lessons.) *Le nom* is a name, and on a form your surname, also called *le nom
de famille*; *le prénom* is your first name. *L'accent* is a written accent and also a way of
speaking: *un accent anglais* (an English accent).

## Pronunciation

- *s'il vous plaît*: "seel voo PLEH"; the *t* and the *s* of *vous* are silent.
- *excusez-moi*: "ex-kü-zay-MWAH"; *s* between vowels = "z".
- *Je ne comprends pas*: "zhuh nuh kohm-prahn PAH"; two nasal vowels, no *d* or *s* said.
- *Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?*: "kess-kuh sah vuh DEER".

## Common mistakes

- Pronouncing final letters: *petit* is not "peh-tit", *vous* is not "voos".
- Saying the *-ent* of verbs: *ils parlent* is "eel parl".
- Saying *u* as "oo". *Tu* and *tout* are different words; keep your tongue forward for *u*.
- Rolling the *r*, or using an English *r*. Make it at the back of the throat.
- Leaving out accents or elision: write *épeler*, not *epeler*, and *j'habite*, not *je habite*.
- Spelling with English letter names: practise E = uh, I = ee, G = zhay, J = zhee.

## Key points

- Letter names: E = uh, I = ee, G = zhay, J = zhee. *Comment ça s'écrit ?* asks for a spelling.
- Five accents (*é; è à ù; â ê î ô û; ë ï; ç*) are part of the spelling.
- Final consonants are usually silent, except c, r, f, l (CaReFuL); verb *-ent* and *h* are
  silent.
- *ou* = "oo", *u* = "ee" with round lips, *oi* = "wah", *eau/au* = "oh", *gn* = "ny".
- Four nasal vowels (*an/en, in/ain, on, un*); the *r* is at the back of the throat; stress is
  on the last syllable of a group.
- Elision: *j', l', d', n', qu'*. Liaison after *les, des, un, mon, nous, vous, ils, elles*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Bonjour ! Greetings, tu and vous
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In France, a conversation never starts without a greeting. You say *bonjour* when you walk
into a shop, a bakery, a doctor's waiting room, even a lift with people in it, and leaving it
out sounds rude. This lesson teaches the greetings and goodbyes for each time of day, how to
ask *Ça va ?* and answer it, how to give your name, and the most important social choice in
French: *tu* or *vous*. It builds on Lesson 1's survival phrases (*merci, s'il vous plaît,
pardon*), which you'll use alongside these.

## Hello and goodbye through the day

| When | Hello | Goodbye |
|---|---|---|
| morning and afternoon | *bonjour* | *au revoir*, *bonne journée* (have a good day) |
| evening (from about 6 p.m.) | *bonsoir* | *au revoir*, *bonne soirée* (have a good evening) |
| going to bed | — | *bonne nuit* (good night) |
| with friends, any time | *salut* | *salut* |

- *Bonjour* (literally "good day") is the all-purpose hello until the evening. There is no
  separate "good morning" or "good afternoon".
- *Bonsoir* takes over in the evening. The switch is loose, roughly between 6 and 7 p.m.;
  nobody will mind if you're half an hour early or late.
- *Bonne nuit* is only for someone going to bed. To greet someone at 9 p.m., say *bonsoir*.
- *Bonne journée* and *bonne soirée* are said when you leave, often with *au revoir*: *Au
  revoir, bonne journée !* Shop staff say it to you, and you can say it back: *Merci, vous
  aussi !* (Thanks, you too!)
- *Salut* is informal: hi and bye between friends, family and young people. Don't use it with
  a shop assistant or your boss.

![A timeline of the day from 6:00 to 24:00. Bonjour covers the morning and afternoon until about 18:00, bonsoir covers the evening, and bonne nuit is shown on a bed with a moon, only for going to bed. Below, the goodbyes: bonne journée during the day, bonne soirée in the evening.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To say when you'll meet again:

- *À bientôt !* — See you soon!
- *À demain !* — See you tomorrow!
- *À plus tard !* — See you later! (Friends shorten it to *À plus !*, said "a-PLUSS".)

## Ça va ? Asking how someone is

The everyday question is *Ça va ?* (literally "It goes?"), with a rising voice. The answer
uses the same words with a falling voice: *Ça va.* (I'm fine.) That's why *ça va* means both
"how are you?" and "I'm fine".

| Question | Register | Typical answer |
|---|---|---|
| *Ça va ?* | casual, very common | *Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ?* |
| *Comment vas-tu ?* | friendly but a bit careful | *Très bien, merci. Et toi ?* |
| *Comment allez-vous ?* | polite, formal | *Bien, merci. Et vous ?* |

The answers go from good to bad: *très bien* (very well), *bien* (well), *ça va* (fine), *pas
mal* (not bad), *pas très bien* (not very well), *mal* (badly). *Très* (very) goes before the
word it strengthens. Just as in English, *Ça va ?* is usually a ritual, not a real question:
the expected answer is *Ça va, et toi ?* even on a so-so day. Answering *Mal* invites a
conversation about what's wrong.

These three questions show the difference in **[[register]]**, how formal a way of speaking is.
French marks register more clearly than English, and the biggest marker is the word for
"you".

## Tu or vous?

French has two words for "you" talking to one person.

- *tu* is informal: for family, friends, children, pets, and usually classmates and young
  people of your own age in a relaxed setting.
- *vous* is polite: for adults you don't know, shop and office staff, older people, your
  boss, a teacher. When in doubt, use *vous*.
- *vous* is also the only plural: talking to two friends or a group, you always say *vous*,
  however well you know them.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing tu or vous
  accDescr: To choose between tu and vous, first count how many people you are talking to. If it is more than one, always use vous. If it is one person, ask whether they are family, a friend, a child or a pet. If yes, use tu. If not, ask whether they have suggested tu, for example by saying on se tutoie or by using tu with you. If yes, use tu. If not, or if you are not sure, use vous.
  A["Talking to how many people?"] -- "two or more" --> V1["vous"]
  A -- "one" --> B{"Family, a friend, a child or a pet?"}
  B -- "yes" --> T1["tu"]
  B -- "no" --> C{"Have they suggested tu?"}
  C -- "yes" --> T2["tu"]
  C -- "no, or not sure" --> V2["vous"]
```

Switching from *vous* to *tu* is a small event. Usually the older or more senior person
suggests it, often with *On se tutoie ?* (Shall we say *tu*?). Using *tu* too soon with a
stranger can sound rude or overfamiliar; using *vous* with a child sounds odd. Many workplaces
and most young people switch to *tu* quickly, so take your cue from the people around you.

The choice changes other words too: *s'il te plaît* goes with *tu*, *s'il vous plaît* with
*vous*; *Comment vas-tu ?* with *tu*, *Comment allez-vous ?* with *vous*.

## Giving your name

Learn these three as fixed phrases for now. (The verb behind them, *s'appeler*, is taught in
full in Lesson 17.)

- *Je m'appelle Léa.* — My name is Léa. (Literally "I call myself Léa".)
- *Comment tu t'appelles ?* — What's your name? (informal)
- *Comment vous appelez-vous ?* — What's your name? (formal)

*Je* is "I". It is always written in small letters (unless it starts a sentence) and becomes
*j'* before a vowel, as you saw in Lesson 1.

When you meet someone, you can say *Enchanté !* (Pleased to meet you!). It's an adjective,
so a woman writes *Enchantée*, with an extra *e*; both are said the same.

## Moi, toi: short answers

*Je* and *tu* can only be used with a verb. To say "me" or "you" on their own, French uses
the **[[stressed pronouns]]** *moi* and *toi* (and *vous*, which is the same word).

- *Et toi ?* — And you? (*Et* means and.)
- *Et vous ?* — And you? (polite)
- *Qui est Léa ? — Moi !* — Who is Léa? — Me!
- *Moi, je m'appelle Léa.* — Me, I'm Léa. (For emphasis, as in a group introduction.)

You'll answer *Ça va, et toi ?* hundreds of times. Never say *Et tu ?*: *tu* can't stand
alone.

## Monsieur, madame

To be polite in France, add *monsieur* (to a man) or *madame* (to a woman) after a greeting:
*Bonjour, monsieur. Merci, madame. Au revoir, madame !* In everyday speech you don't need the
surname. Written short, they are *M.* (*M. Martin*) and *Mme* (*Mme Roux*, no full stop).

*Mademoiselle* (miss) used to be said to young or unmarried women. In 2012 a circular from the
French Prime Minister removed *Mademoiselle* from official forms, and today *madame* is the
safe choice for any adult woman; some people find *mademoiselle* old-fashioned or
condescending.

Greeting friends usually comes with *la bise*, a light kiss on each cheek; honors lesson 93
explains how it works.

## Dialogue 1: at the office

It's 9 a.m. Paul Mercier arrives for a meeting at a company in Toulouse.

> M. Mercier : Bonjour, madame.
>
> Mme Diallo : Bonjour, monsieur. Comment vous appelez-vous ?
>
> M. Mercier : Je m'appelle Paul Mercier.
>
> Mme Diallo : Ah, monsieur Mercier ! Enchantée. Je m'appelle Awa Diallo.
>
> M. Mercier : Enchanté, madame. Comment allez-vous ?
>
> Mme Diallo : Très bien, merci. Et vous ?
>
> M. Mercier : Bien, merci.
>
> Mme Diallo : Voilà, le bureau est ici. À demain, monsieur Mercier ! Bonne journée !
>
> M. Mercier : Merci, vous aussi. Au revoir, madame.

Hello, madam. — Hello, sir. What's your name? — My name is Paul Mercier. — Ah, Mr Mercier!
Pleased to meet you. My name is Awa Diallo. — Pleased to meet you, madam. How are you? — Very
well, thank you. And you? — Well, thank you. — There we are, the office is here. See you
tomorrow, Mr Mercier! Have a good day! — Thank you, you too. Goodbye, madam.

(*Le bureau est ici* means "the office is here".) Notice *Enchantée* with an *e*: Mme Diallo
is a woman.

## Dialogue 2: at a party

Inès and Hugo are students at a friend's party in the evening.

> Inès : Salut ! Je m'appelle Inès. Et toi ? Comment tu t'appelles ?
>
> Hugo : Moi ? Hugo. Salut, Inès !
>
> Inès : Ça va, Hugo ?
>
> Hugo : Pas mal, et toi ?
>
> Inès : Ça va bien. Tu es étudiant ?
>
> Hugo : Oui.
>
> … (later) …
>
> Hugo : Bon, bonne soirée, Inès ! À bientôt !
>
> Inès : Salut, Hugo ! À plus tard !

Hi! I'm Inès. And you? What's your name? — Me? Hugo. Hi, Inès! — How are you, Hugo? — Not
bad, and you? — I'm fine. Are you a student? — Yes. … Right, have a good evening, Inès! See
you soon! — Bye, Hugo! See you later!

(*Tu es étudiant ?* means "Are you a student?". *Bon* here means "right, well then".) Inès and
Hugo use *tu* at once: they're young and at a party. Compare Mme Diallo and M. Mercier, who
stay with *vous*.

## Pronunciation

- *bonjour*: "bohn-ZHOOR", nasal *on*, *j* = zh, French *r*.
- *bonsoir*: "bohn-SWAHR"; *oi* = "wah".
- *au revoir*: "oh-ruh-VWAHR"; in fast speech the *e* nearly vanishes: "or-VWAHR".
- *salut*: "sa-LÜ"; final *t* silent, *u* with rounded lips.
- *Comment allez-vous ?*: "ko-mahn-ta-lay-VOO". The *t* of *comment* is said here because
  *allez* starts with a vowel; this phrase is one of the few places *comment* links.
- *Comment vous appelez-vous ?*: "ko-mahn voo-za-play-VOO"; liaison after *vous*.
- *enchanté*: "ahn-shahn-TAY", two nasal *an* sounds.
- *monsieur*: "muh-SYUH". The spelling is misleading: there is no "mon" sound, and the *r* is
  silent.
- *madame*: "ma-DAM".

## Common mistakes

- Walking into a shop without *bonjour*. Say *Bonjour, madame* or *Bonjour, monsieur* first,
  then ask your question.
- Using *bonne nuit* as an evening greeting. It means good night at bedtime; say *bonsoir*.
- Saying *salut* to staff or older strangers. Use *bonjour* and *au revoir*.
- Using *tu* with someone you don't know. Start with *vous* and wait to be offered *tu*.
- *Et tu ?* Say *Et toi ?* (or *Et vous ?*).
- Forgetting that *vous* is the only plural: to two friends, say *Salut ! Ça va ? … Et vous ?*
- Pronouncing *monsieur* as "mon-sewer". It's "muh-SYUH".

## Key points

- *Bonjour* until evening, *bonsoir* in the evening, *bonne nuit* only at bedtime; *salut* is
  informal hi and bye.
- When leaving: *au revoir*, *bonne journée*, *bonne soirée*, *à bientôt*, *à demain*, *à
  plus tard*.
- *Ça va ?* — *Ça va (bien), et toi ?* Formal: *Comment allez-vous ? — Très bien, merci. Et
  vous ?* Answers: *très bien, bien, pas mal, mal*.
- *Tu* for family, friends and children; *vous* for strangers, staff and anyone you're not
  sure about; *vous* for any group.
- *Je m'appelle …*; *Comment tu t'appelles ?* (informal); *Comment vous appelez-vous ?*
  (formal); *Enchanté(e)*.
- Stressed pronouns stand alone: *Et toi ? Moi !*
- *Bonjour, monsieur / madame*: always polite. *Madame* is the safe choice for any woman.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Être: who you are and where you're from
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've used fixed phrases. Now you meet your first verb: *être* (to be), the most
important and the most irregular verb in French. With it you can say who you are, what
nationality you are and where you're from. You'll also learn all the subject pronouns, the
names of ten countries with their gender, and the small words that say "in" or "to" a city or
a country (*à Paris, en France, au Canada*), which English speakers get wrong for years
unless they learn them early.

## Subject pronouns

A **[[subject pronoun]]** stands for the person doing the action. French always uses one: you
can't drop it as you can in Spanish or Italian.

| | singular | | plural | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | *je* (*j'*) | I | *nous* | we |
| 2nd | *tu* | you (informal) | *vous* | you (formal, or more than one) |
| 3rd | *il* / *elle* / *on* | he, it / she, it / we, people | *ils* / *elles* | they |

- *il* and *elle* are also "it": every French noun is masculine or feminine (this is
  **[[grammatical gender]]**), so a thing is *il* or *elle* depending on its gender. *La France ?
  Elle est belle.* (France? It's beautiful.)
- *ils* is for a group of men, of masculine things, or a mixed group. *Elles* is only for
  a group that is all women or all feminine things. Ten women and one man are *ils*.
- *on* takes the same verb form as *il*. In everyday speech it usually means "we": *On est
  canadiens.* (We're Canadian.) It also means "people, one" in general: *Au Québec, on parle
  français.* (In Québec, people speak French.) In writing and formal speech, use *nous* for
  "we".

## Être: to be

*Être* is the **[[infinitive]]**, the form in the dictionary. Changing a verb to match its
subject is called **[[conjugation]]**. *Être* is an **[[irregular verb]]**: its forms don't follow a
pattern, so learn them by heart.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *je suis* | I am | "zhuh swee" |
| *tu es* | you are | "tü eh" |
| *il / elle / on est* | he / she / we is, are | "eel eh" |
| *nous sommes* | we are | "noo som" |
| *vous êtes* | you are | "voo-ZET" (liaison) |
| *ils / elles sont* | they are | "eel sohn" |

- *es* and *est* sound exactly the same, "eh"; the *s* and *t* are silent.
- *vous êtes* always has a liaison: "voo-zet". *On est* too: "oh-neh".
- *ils sont* (they are) and *ils ont* (they have, Lesson 6) are a classic pair: *sont* has an
  "s" sound, *ont* has a "z" sound from the liaison: "eel SOHN" / "eel ZOHN".

*Je suis Inès. Tu es Hugo ? Elle est à Lyon. Nous sommes à Paris. Vous êtes français ? Ils
sont belges.*

## Nationalities: masculine and feminine

Nationality words can be nouns or adjectives. An adjective changes to match the person it describes. This is called
**[[agreement]]**. For a woman, most nationality adjectives add *-e*, and you can hear the
difference because the final consonant comes back.

| Man | Woman | | Sound |
|---|---|---|---|
| *français* | *française* | French | "frahn-SEH" / "frahn-SEZ" |
| *anglais* | *anglaise* | English | "ahn-GLEH" / "ahn-GLEZ" |
| *américain* | *américaine* | American | nasal "-KAN" / "-KEN" with a real *n* |
| *canadien* | *canadienne* | Canadian | nasal "-DYAN" / "-DYEN", doubled *n* |
| *belge* | *belge* | Belgian | the same |
| *suisse* | *suisse* | Swiss | the same |

Adjectives already ending in *-e* (*belge*, *suisse*) don't change. *Canadien* doubles its *n*
before the *-e*: *canadienne*. For several people add a silent *-s*: *Ils sont américains.
Elles sont canadiennes.* (*Français* and *anglais* already end in *s*, so the masculine plural
doesn't change.) *Anglais* means English (from England); "British" is *britannique*.

Two rules that differ from English:

- No capital letter for the adjective: *Je suis canadien.* The capital appears only when
  the word is a noun for a person: *un Canadien* (a Canadian), as in *C'est un Canadien.*
- For the adjective after *être*, use no article: *Elle est suisse.* A nationality can also be a noun after *être*: *Elle est Suisse.* Both sentences can describe the same person.

## C'est or il est?

Both translate "he is" or "it is", but they're used differently.

- *C'est* + a name, or + *un/une* + noun: *C'est Marc. C'est un ami.* (He's a friend.)
- *Il est / elle est* + an adjective on its own: *Il est canadien. Elle est belge.*

*C'est Marc. Il est canadien. Il est de Montréal.* — This is Marc. He's Canadian. He's from
Montréal. In the plural, *c'est* becomes *ce sont* (Lesson 5).

## Countries have a gender

Countries are nouns, so they're masculine or feminine and normally take an article.

| Feminine | | Masculine | | Plural | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *la France* | France | *le Canada* | Canada | *les États-Unis* | the United States |
| *la Belgique* | Belgium | *le Maroc* | Morocco | | |
| *la Suisse* | Switzerland | | | | |
| *l'Angleterre* | England | | | | |
| *l'Allemagne* | Germany | | | | |
| *l'Espagne* | Spain | | | | |
| *l'Italie* | Italy | | | | |

A memory hook: country names ending in *-e* are usually feminine; the rest are usually
masculine. (There are a few exceptions, such as *le Mexique*, Mexico.) *L'* hides the gender
before a vowel, so learn *l'Allemagne* as feminine.

![A map of France and its neighbours. Belgium is to the north-east, Germany to the east, Switzerland and Italy to the south-east, Spain to the south-west across the Pyrenees, England to the north across the Channel, and Morocco to the south across the Mediterranean.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The picture is a sketch of positions, not shapes. Here is the real map:

```map
base: world
title: France, its neighbours and Morocco
view: 30, -12 to 56, 18
region: France | France
region: Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, United Kingdom | Neighbours in this lesson
region: Morocco | Across the Mediterranean
caption: England is part of the United Kingdom. Canada and the United States, the other countries in this lesson, are across the Atlantic.
```

## In, at and to: à, en, au, aux

French uses different small words for "in" and "to" depending on what follows. The same word
works for both "in" and "to": *J'habite en France* (I live in France), *Je vais en France* (I'm
going to France).

| Place | Word | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| a city or town | *à* | *à Paris, à Lyon, à Montréal* |
| a feminine country | *en* (no article) | *en France, en Belgique, en Suisse, en Italie* |
| a masculine country | *au* | *au Canada, au Maroc* |
| a plural country | *aux* | *aux États-Unis* |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing à, en, au or aux for a place
  accDescr: To say in or to a place, first ask whether it is a city or a country. For a city, use à, as in à Paris or à Montréal. For a country, look at its gender and number. A feminine country takes en with no article, as in en France and en Italie. A masculine country takes au, as in au Canada and au Maroc. A plural country takes aux, as in aux États-Unis.
  A["In or to a place"] --> B{"City or country?"}
  B -- "city" --> C["à: à Paris, à Montréal"]
  B -- "country" --> D{"Which kind of country?"}
  D -- "feminine: la France" --> E["en: en France, en Italie"]
  D -- "masculine: le Canada" --> F["au: au Canada, au Maroc"]
  D -- "plural: les États-Unis" --> G["aux: aux États-Unis"]
```

Learn *au* and *aux* as fixed pairs for now (*au Canada, aux États-Unis*); Lesson 12 shows
where they come from. A masculine country starting with a vowel takes *en* too (*en Iran*),
but none of this lesson's countries does. *En* has another common meaning, "by" with
transport: *en train* (by train), which comes back in Lesson 14.

To say where you're from, use *de* (from, of), which becomes *d'* before a vowel: *Je suis de
Lyon. Il est d'Ottawa.* To say where you live, use *habiter* (to live) with *à* or *en/au*:

| | |
|---|---|
| *j'habite* | *nous habitons* |
| *tu habites* | *vous habitez* |
| *il / elle / on habite* | *ils / elles habitent* |

*Habiter* starts with a mute *h*, so *je* becomes *j'* and there is a liaison after *nous,
vous, ils, elles*: "noo-za-bee-TOHN". Four of the six forms sound the same, "a-BEET". The
pattern is the regular *-er* verb you'll study in Lesson 7.

To ask: *Où habitez-vous ?* or, more casually, *Tu habites où ?* (Where do you live?) Write
*où* (where) with its accent; *ou* without it means "or". *La ville* is the city or town, *le
pays* the country: *Montréal est une ville, le Canada est un pays.*

## Dialogue: a language exchange in Montréal

Julia and Marc meet at a French–English conversation evening.

> Marc : Bonsoir ! Je m'appelle Marc. Et toi ?
>
> Julia : Julia. Enchantée !
>
> Marc : Tu es américaine ?
>
> Julia : Non, je suis allemande. Je suis de Hambourg, mais j'habite à Montréal.
>
> Marc : Ah, Hambourg, c'est une belle ville !
>
> Julia : Et toi, tu es d'où ?
>
> Marc : Moi, je suis canadien. Je suis de Québec, la ville. Et voilà Sofia et Luca. Ils sont
> italiens.
>
> Julia : Ils habitent au Canada ?
>
> Marc : Non, ils habitent en France, à Lyon. Ils sont ici en vacances.
>
> Julia : Et vous, Sofia, vous êtes de Rome ?
>
> Sofia : Non, de Milan ! Mais on habite à Lyon. On est très contents d'être ici.

Good evening! My name's Marc. And you? — Julia. Nice to meet you! — Are you American? — No, I'm
German. I'm from Hamburg, but I live in Montréal. — Oh, Hamburg is a beautiful city! — And you,
where are you from? — Me, I'm Canadian. I'm from Québec City. And here are Sofia and Luca.
They're Italian. — Do they live in Canada? — No, they live in France, in Lyon. They're here on
holiday. — And you, Sofia, are you from Rome? — No, from Milan! But we live in Lyon. We're very
happy to be here.

(*Allemand(e)* means German and *italien(ne)* Italian; both work like the table above. *Mais*
is "but", *belle* "beautiful", *en vacances* "on holiday", *contents* "happy".) Notice *je suis
de Québec* (the city) but *au Québec* (the province); honors lesson 04h2 has more on that.
Julia says *vous* to Sofia because she's talking to Sofia and Luca together.

## Pronunciation

- *je suis*: "zhuh SWEE"; in fast speech "shwee".
- *nous sommes*: "noo SOM", with a short open *o*.
- *vous êtes*: "voo-ZET", always with the liaison.
- *les États-Unis*: "lay-zay-ta-zü-NEE", two liaisons.
- *l'Allemagne*: "lal-MANY", ending in the "ny" of *canyon*; the final *e* is silent.
- *le pays*: "luh pay-EE", two syllables.
- *suisse*: "swees"; *belge*: "belzh".

## Common mistakes

- Keep the noun and adjective distinct: *une Française* names a person; *Je suis française* uses the adjective. *Je suis Française* is possible with a noun reading.
- Forgetting agreement: a woman says *Je suis canadienne*, *Je suis américaine*.
- *Il est un ami*. With a noun, use *c'est*: *C'est un ami.*
- *dans France* or *à France*. Say *en France*; and *au Canada*, *aux États-Unis*, *à Paris*.
- *J'habite en Paris*. Cities take *à*: *J'habite à Paris.*
- Mixing up *ils sont* (they are) and *ils ont* (they have): listen for "s" or "z".
- Writing *ou* for "where". "Where" is *où*, with the accent.

## Key points

- Subject pronouns: *je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles*. *On* = we in speech;
  *ils* for any mixed group.
- *Être*: *je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont*.
- Nationality adjectives agree (*français/française, canadien/canadienne*), take no capital and
  no article after *être*; *belge* and *suisse* don't change.
- *C'est* + name or *un/une* + noun; *il/elle est* + adjective.
- Countries have a gender: *la France, le Canada, les États-Unis*.
- *à* + city, *en* + feminine country, *au* + masculine country, *aux* + plural country.
- *Je suis de Lyon. J'habite à Montréal, au Canada.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers, age and phone numbers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Numbers are everywhere: prices, ages, times, phone numbers, addresses. French numbers start
simply, then do something unusual between 70 and 99, where they count in twenties. This lesson
takes you from *zéro* to *cent* (100), shows how the final consonants of some numbers change
sound, and puts the numbers to work: saying your age, giving a phone number the French way (in
pairs) and spelling out an e-mail address, with the letter names from Lesson 1.

## 0 to 16: learn by heart

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 *zéro* | 5 *cinq* | 10 *dix* | 15 *quinze* |
| 1 *un* | 6 *six* | 11 *onze* | 16 *seize* |
| 2 *deux* | 7 *sept* | 12 *douze* | |
| 3 *trois* | 8 *huit* | 13 *treize* | |
| 4 *quatre* | 9 *neuf* | 14 *quatorze* | |

- *Un* becomes *une* before a feminine noun: *une adresse* (one address, an address).
- 11 to 16 have their own names, all ending in *-ze*. Say the *z* as in *zoo*: "ohnz, dooz,
  trez, ka-TORZ, kanz (nasal, like *cinq*), sez".
- The *p* of *sept* is silent: "set". The *q* of *cinq* is a "k": "sank".

## 17 to 69: patterns

From 17, numbers are built from parts you know.

- 17, 18, 19 are 10 + 7, 10 + 8, 10 + 9: *dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf*.
- The tens: 20 *vingt*, 30 *trente*, 40 *quarante*, 50 *cinquante*, 60 *soixante*.
- After each ten, add the unit with a hyphen: *vingt-deux* (22), *trente-cinq* (35),
  *quarante-huit* (48), *soixante-neuf* (69).
- For 1, use *et* (and) with no hyphens: *vingt et un* (21), *trente et un*, *quarante et un*,
  *cinquante et un*, *soixante et un*.

*Vingt* alone is "van", but in 21 to 29 its *t* is said: *vingt-deux* is "vant-DEUH". *Soixante*
is "swa-SAHNT": the *x* sounds like *s*.

Since the 1990 spelling reform you may also hyphenate every number (*vingt-et-un,
soixante-et-un*). Both spellings are correct and the app accepts both.

## 70 to 99: counting in twenties

Here French switches to counting in twenties, the **[[vigesimal]]** system. There is no single
word for 70, 80 or 90 in the French of France: you build them.

- 70 = 60 + 10: *soixante-dix*. Carry on with 60 + 11, 60 + 12 …: *soixante et onze* (71),
  *soixante-douze* (72), up to *soixante-dix-neuf* (79).
- 80 = 4 × 20: *quatre-vingts*. Then 4 × 20 + 1 …: *quatre-vingt-un* (81, with no *et*),
  *quatre-vingt-deux* (82) …
- 90 = 4 × 20 + 10: *quatre-vingt-dix*. Then *quatre-vingt-onze* (91, no *et*),
  *quatre-vingt-douze* (92), up to *quatre-vingt-dix-neuf* (99).
- 100 is *cent* (no *un* before it).

![The number 97 split into its parts: quatre-vingt-dix-sept means four times twenty, plus ten, plus seven: 80 + 10 + 7 = 97. Below, the patterns: 70 is soixante-dix, sixty plus ten; 80 is quatre-vingts, four twenties; 90 is quatre-vingt-dix, four twenties plus ten.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Quatre-vingts* has an *s* because there are four twenties. It loses the *s* as soon as
another number follows: *quatre-vingts* but *quatre-vingt-trois*, *quatre-vingt-dix*. And the
*t* of *vingt* is not said in 81 and 91: *quatre-vingt-un* is "katr-van-UN", *quatre-vingt-onze*
"katr-van-OHNZ".

To say a number in the 70s or 90s, think "sixty-something" or "eighty-something" first, then
add 10 to 19: 76 = 60 + 16 = *soixante-seize*; 93 = 80 + 13 = *quatre-vingt-treize*.

Belgium and Switzerland say *septante* (70) and *nonante* (90), and parts of Switzerland say
*huitante* (80). You'll be understood in France if you use them, but in France they are rarely
heard; honors lesson 04h2 has the details.

## Numbers that change sound: six, huit, dix

*Six*, *huit* and *dix* have three pronunciations, depending on what follows.

| | Alone (counting) | Before a consonant | Before a vowel or mute h |
|---|---|---|---|
| *six* | "sees" | "see": *six mots* | "seez": *six ans* |
| *huit* | "weet" | "wee": *huit jours* (days) | "weet": *huit ans* |
| *dix* | "dees" | "dee": *dix mots* | "deez": *dix ans* |

The same happens with other numbers before a vowel: *deux ans* ("deuh-ZAHN"), *trois ans*
("trwah-ZAHN"), *un an* ("uh-NAHN"), *vingt ans* ("van-TAHN"), and *neuf* becomes "neuv"
before *ans*: *neuf ans* ("neuh-VAHN"). This **[[liaison]]** is why ages sound so different from
the numbers you count with. *Sept* always keeps its *t* (*sept ans*, "set-AHN"), and in today's speech *cinq*
usually keeps its *k*, even before a consonant (*cinq mots*).

## Your age: J'ai … ans

French says "I have 30 years", using *avoir* (to have), which you'll learn in full in
Lesson 6. Learn these as chunks:

- *Quel âge avez-vous ?* — How old are you? (formal; literally "What age have you?")
- *Tu as quel âge ?* — How old are you? (informal)
- *J'ai trente ans.* — I'm thirty. *Il a sept ans.* — He's seven.

Never say *je suis trente*: that means nothing in French. And always say *ans* (years): *J'ai
vingt ans*, not *J'ai vingt*. *L'an* is the word for "year" when you count years like this.

## Numbers: phone, house, room

*Le numéro* is a number that labels something: a phone number, a house number, a room. (A
number as a quantity is a different word.)

- *Votre numéro de téléphone, s'il vous plaît ?* — Your phone number, please?
- *J'habite au numéro 12.* — I live at number 12.
- *Vous êtes dans la chambre numéro 8.* — You're in room 8.

Phone numbers in France have ten digits, and French speakers read them in pairs:

![The French mobile number 06 12 45 78 97 split into five pairs. Each pair is read as one number: zéro six, douze, quarante-cinq, soixante-dix-huit, quatre-vingt-dix-sept.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Zéro six, douze, quarante-cinq, soixante-dix-huit, quatre-vingt-dix-sept.* Mobile numbers
start with *06* or *07*. A pair beginning with zero is read *zéro* + the digit: *01* is *zéro
un*, *05* is *zéro cinq*. That's why you need 70 to 99 early: almost a third of all pairs (30 of
the 100, from 70 to 99) are in that range.

## Addresses and e-mail

*L'adresse* (feminine) is both a postal address and an e-mail address. In a French postal
address the number comes first: *12, rue de la Paix* (12 Peace Street).

To say an e-mail address, spell the unusual parts and use these words:

| Symbol | Said |
|---|---|
| @ | *arobase* |
| . | *point* |
| - | *tiret* |
| _ | *tiret bas* |

*lea.martin@exemple.fr* is said "*Léa point Martin arobase exemple point F R*". If the name is
unusual, spell it with the letter names: *Martin, M-A-R-T-I-N*.

## Dialogue: joining a sports club

Tom, who is English, signs up at a sports club in Nantes.

> L'employée : Bonjour, monsieur. Votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
>
> Tom : Bonjour. Tom Wright. W, R, I, G, H, T.
>
> L'employée : Merci. Quel âge avez-vous ?
>
> Tom : J'ai trente-quatre ans.
>
> L'employée : Et votre adresse ?
>
> Tom : J'habite au numéro 71, rue Victor-Hugo, à Nantes.
>
> L'employée : Soixante et onze… d'accord. Votre numéro de téléphone ?
>
> Tom : C'est le 07 15 92 36 80.
>
> L'employée : Zéro sept, quinze, quatre-vingt-douze, trente-six… ?
>
> Tom : Quatre-vingts.
>
> L'employée : Merci. Et votre adresse e-mail ?
>
> Tom : tom.wright@exemple.co.uk. Tom, point, Wright, arobase, exemple, point, C O, point, U K.
>
> L'employée : Parfait. Voilà, monsieur, merci !

Hello, sir. Your name, please? — Hello. Tom Wright. W-R-I-G-H-T. — Thank you. How old are you?
— I'm thirty-four. — And your address? — I live at number 71, rue Victor-Hugo, in Nantes. —
Seventy-one… OK. Your phone number? — It's 07 15 92 36 80. — Zero seven, fifteen,
ninety-two, thirty-six…? — Eighty. — Thank you. And your e-mail address? — tom.wright@
exemple.co.uk. — Perfect. There you are, sir, thank you!

(*L'employée* is the (female) employee and *parfait* means perfect.) Notice that *quatre-vingts* is
written with an *s* when nothing follows it, but *quatre-vingt-douze* without one.

## Pronunciation

- *cinq*: "sank"; *sept*: "set"; *neuf*: "neuf" with a rounded "euh".
- *quatre*: "katr"; in fast speech the final *r* nearly disappears: "kat".
- *onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize*: each ends in a buzzing *z*.
- *vingt*: "van"; *vingt et un*: "van-tay-UN"; *quatre-vingts*: "katr-VAN".
- *soixante-dix*: "swa-sahnt-DEES"; *soixante et onze*: "swa-sahn-tay-OHNZ".
- *Quel âge avez-vous ?*: "kel-AHZH a-vay-VOO", linked from *quel* to *âge*.

## Common mistakes

- *Je suis 25.* Say *J'ai vingt-cinq ans.*
- *quatre-vingts-trois*. The *s* goes when another number follows: *quatre-vingt-trois*.
- *soixante-onze* or *quatre-vingt et un*. It's *soixante et onze* but *quatre-vingt-un*.
- Reading a phone number digit by digit. Read it in pairs: *zéro six, douze …*
- Saying the *x* of *six* and *dix* before a consonant: *six mots* is "see moh".
- Saying the *p* of *sept*: it's "set".

## Key points

- 0–16 are single words; 17–19 are *dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf*.
- 21–69: ten + unit with a hyphen; *et* for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 (and 71).
- 70 = *soixante-dix* (60 + 10), 80 = *quatre-vingts* (4 × 20), 90 = *quatre-vingt-dix* (4 × 20
  + 10); *quatre-vingts* loses its *s* before another number; 81 and 91 have no *et*.
- *six, huit, dix* sound different alone, before a consonant and before a vowel.
- Age: *J'ai trente ans. Quel âge avez-vous ?* Never *je suis* + age.
- Phone numbers are read in pairs; *le numéro* is a phone, house or room number.
- E-mail: *arobase* (@), *point* (.).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Sounds in depth: liaison, the mute e and sentence melody
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 gave you the sounds of French letters and two ways words join: elision (*j'habite*)
and the most basic liaisons (*les amis, vous avez*). This honors lesson goes further, into what
makes French sound like French: which liaisons you must make, which you must never make and
which are up to you; how a final consonant glides into the next word; the *e* that French
speakers swallow; the *h* that blocks everything; the difference between open and closed
vowels; and the melody of statements and questions.

Some words for talking about la prononciation (pronunciation): *prononcer* (to pronounce),
*le son* (a sound), *la voyelle* (vowel), *la consonne* (consonant), *la syllabe* (syllable)
and *muet* (silent; feminine *muette*). *On ne prononce pas le h* — you don't pronounce the h.

## Three kinds of liaison

A liaison (Lesson 1) brings back a silent final consonant when the next word starts with a
vowel or mute *h*. French speakers don't make it everywhere. Grammar books sort liaisons into
three groups. The lists below are the core of each, simplified. In the examples, _ marks a
liaison and | a place where none is made.

**[[Compulsory liaison]]**: every speaker makes it, in every style.

| Where | Examples |
|---|---|
| a determiner + its noun or adjective | *les_amis, des_hôtels, un_ami, mon_ami, deux_ans, trois_enfants* |
| a pronoun + its verb, both ways | *nous_avons, vous_êtes, ils_habitent, on_est; sont-ils, vont-elles* |
| a short adjective before its noun | *un petit_ami, un grand_homme* ("gran-TOM") |
| one-syllable prepositions | *chez_elle, dans_un café, en_avion* |
| fixed phrases | *les États_Unis, tout_à fait* (quite), *Comment_allez-vous ?* |

**[[Forbidden liaison]]**: no one makes it; making it sounds wrong.

| Where | Examples |
|---|---|
| after *et* (and) | *Marc et | Inès* |
| after a singular noun | *un étudiant | anglais* (an English student) |
| before an aspirated *h* (below) | *les | héros, les | haricots* |
| before *onze*, *oui* and *huit* | *les | onze joueurs* (the eleven players), *mais | oui* |
| after a pronoun after its verb, before something else | *Sont-ils | arrivés ?* (Have they arrived?) |

**[[Optional liaison]]**: correct either way. Careful or formal speech (news readers, speeches,
poetry) makes more; everyday conversation makes fewer. After a verb (*c'est_un ami*, *je
suis_allé*), after a plural noun (*des amis_anglais*), after *pas* (*pas_encore*, not yet). If
you're unsure, leave an optional liaison out: a missing optional liaison sounds natural; a
forbidden one sounds odd.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Liaison or not?
  accDescr: To decide whether to make a liaison, first check whether the next word starts with a vowel or a mute h. If not, there is no liaison. If it does, check whether the next word starts with an aspirated h, or is onze, oui or huit, or whether the first word is et or a singular noun. If so, the liaison is forbidden. If not, check whether the two words are a determiner and its noun, a pronoun and its verb, a short adjective and its noun, a one-syllable preposition and what follows, or a fixed phrase. If so, the liaison is compulsory. Otherwise it is optional, made more often in careful speech.
  A["Next word starts with a vowel or mute h?"] -- "no" --> N["No liaison"]
  A -- "yes" --> B{"Aspirated h, onze, oui, huit? Or after et or a singular noun?"}
  B -- "yes" --> F["Forbidden"]
  B -- "no" --> C{"Determiner + noun, pronoun + verb, short adjective + noun, short preposition, fixed phrase?"}
  C -- "yes" --> M["Compulsory"]
  C -- "no" --> O["Optional: more in careful speech"]
```

How a liaison sounds. The consonant moves to the next word, and some letters change sound:
*s*, *x* and *z* become "z" (*deux_ans*, "deuh-ZAHN"); *d* becomes "t" (*grand_homme*,
"gran-TOM"); *t* stays "t" and *n* stays "n" (*petit_ami*, *on_a*); *f* becomes "v" in *neuf
ans* and *neuf heures*.

## Enchaînement: consonants that slide

Liaison brings back a silent consonant. **[[Enchaînement]]** is something else: a consonant
that is always pronounced slides over to start the next syllable when a vowel follows.

- *il est* is said "ee-LEH", not "eel | eh";
- *elle a* (she has) is "eh-LAH";
- *avec elle* (with her) is "a-veh-KEL";
- *une amie* (a friend) is "ü-na-MEE";
- *sept ans* is "seh-TAHN".

The result is that French speech is a stream of syllables, each starting with a consonant where
possible, with no breaks between words. This is why English speakers often say they can't tell
where one French word ends and the next begins. Practise saying short groups as if they were
one long word: *il-est-à-Lyon* = "ee-leh-ta-lee-OHN".

### Example 1: Marking a sentence for liaison and enchaînement

*Nous habitons aux États-Unis avec un ami anglais.* (We live in the United States with an
English friend.) Go word by word.

1. *nous | habitons*: pronoun + verb, and *habitons* starts with a mute *h*: compulsory
   liaison, "noo-za-bee-TOHN".
2. *habitons | aux*: after a verb: optional. In everyday speech, leave it out.
3. *aux | États-Unis*: determiner + noun: compulsory, "o-ZAY-ta". Inside *États-Unis*, the
   fixed liaison gives "ay-ta-zü-NEE".
4. *avec | un*: *c* is always said (CaReFuL), so it slides over: enchaînement, "a-veh-KUN".
5. *un | ami*: determiner + noun: compulsory, "uh-na-MEE".
6. *ami | anglais*: the final *i* is a vowel, so there is nothing to link. (With a singular
   noun ending in a consonant, as in *étudiant | anglais*, the liaison would be forbidden.)

Result, with _ for liaison and ‿ for enchaînement: *Nous_habitons aux_États_Unis avec‿un_ami
anglais.*

## The mute e

The **[[mute e]]** is the weak *e* with no accent in *je, le, de, ne, que, petit, samedi*. In
careful speech it sounds like a short "uh". In everyday speech it is often dropped:

| Written | Careful speech | Everyday speech |
|---|---|---|
| *petit* | "puh-TEE" | "ptee" |
| *samedi* (Saturday) | "sa-muh-DEE" | "sam-DEE" |
| *lentement* | "lahn-tuh-MAHN" | "lahnt-MAHN" |
| *Je ne sais pas.* (I don't know.) | "zhuh nuh seh PAH" | "zhuh n'seh PAH" or "sheh PAH" |
| *Qu'est-ce que c'est ?* | "kess-kuh-SEH" | "kess-k'SEH" |

A simplified rule: the *e* drops when only one consonant is said before it, and stays when
dropping it would crush three consonants together. *Samedi* can lose it ("sam-di", two
consonants meet); *vendredi* (Friday) keeps it ("vahn-druh-DEE"), because "vahndrdi" is
unsayable. At the end of a word (*porte, table, une*), the *e* is silent in normal speech; you
hear it in songs and poetry.

Two things never change: the *e* is always written, and you should understand both
versions. Speak carefully at first; the shortened forms will come as you listen.

## The aspirated h

Lesson 1 said French *h* is never pronounced, and that most *h* words act as if they started
with a vowel: *l'homme, les_hommes, j'habite*. A few hundred words, many of them borrowed from
Germanic languages, have an **[[aspirated h]]**. It is still silent, but it blocks elision and
liaison, as if a consonant were there.

| Mute h | Aspirated h |
|---|---|
| *l'homme* (the man) | *le haricot* (the bean) |
| *les_hommes* ("lay-ZOM") | *les | haricots* ("lay a-ree-KOH") |
| *l'hôtel*, *les_hôtels* | *la hauteur* (height), *les | hauteurs* |
| *l'héroïne* (the heroine) | *le héros* (the hero), *les | héros* |

*Le héros* is a famous case: with a liaison, *les héros* would sound like *les zéros* (the
zeros). You can't see an aspirated *h* in the spelling; good dictionaries mark it, for
example with an asterisk or the words *h aspiré*. Other common ones: *le hockey*, *le
hamburger*, *la honte* (shame), *le haut* (the top).

### Example 2: Mute or aspirated?

Decide how to say each phrase, using the table above.

1. *les hôtels*: mute *h*, so liaison: "lay-zo-TEL".
2. *le héros*: aspirated *h*, so no elision (*le*, not *l'*) and the vowel stays: "luh ay-ROH".
3. *les héros*: aspirated *h*, no liaison: "lay ay-ROH". (With a liaison it would sound like
   *les zéros*.)
4. *j'habite*: mute *h*, so elision: "zha-BEET".
5. *la hauteur*: aspirated *h*, so *la* keeps its *a*: "la o-TEUR".

## Open and closed vowels

Some French vowels come in pairs: the same vowel said with the mouth more closed or more
open. These are the **[[open vowel]]** / closed vowel pairs.

| Closed | Open |
|---|---|
| *é*, *-er*, *-ez*, *et*: "ay" without a glide (*été*, *épeler*, *et*) | *è*, *ê*, usually *ai*: "eh" (*très*, *fête*, *mais*) |
| *o* as the last sound of a word, *ô*, *au*, *eau*, *o* before a "z" sound: "oh" (*mot*, *hôtel*, *beau*, *rose*) | *o* before another pronounced consonant: as in British *hot* (*porte*, *bonne*, *homme*) |

Words that differ in one sound like this are a **[[minimal pair]]**: *et* (and) / *est* (is),
*les* / *lait* (milk) in careful speech, *paume* (palm) / *pomme* (apple). Train your ear with
them. Usage varies by region: in the south of France, for example, many speakers say *rose*
with an open *o*, and the *é/è* difference at the end of words is weaker in much of France. Aim
for the standard, but don't worry if you hear differences.

## Rhythm and intonation

French rhythm is even: every syllable gets about the same length, and only the last syllable of
each rhythm group is a little longer and higher (Lesson 1). **[[Intonation]]** is the melody of the
whole sentence.

- Statements: each group rises a little at its end, and the last group falls. *Je m'appelle
  Léa ↗, j'habite à Lyon ↘.*
- Yes/no questions asked with the voice alone rise at the end: *Tu es français ↗ ?* This
  is the most common way to ask a question in conversation, and the rise is the only thing that
  makes it a question.
- Questions with a question word (*où, comment, qu'est-ce que*) usually fall, because the
  question word already does the job: *Où habitez-vous ↘ ?* In relaxed speech, a question word
  at the end often comes with a rise: *Tu habites où ↗ ?*

![Three French sentences with melody arrows. Tu es français, as a statement: the voice falls at the end. Tu es français?, as a question: the voice rises at the end. Où habitez-vous?: the voice starts high on où and falls at the end.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 3: Same words, two meanings

*Vous êtes canadien.* and *Vous êtes canadien ?* have the same words, the same liaison
("voo-zet") and the same rhythm: five even syllables, "voo-zet-ka-na-dyan". The only
difference is the end. For the statement, your voice falls on *-dien*; for the question, it
rises on *-dien*. Try both aloud, then try *Où êtes-vous ?* with a high start on *où* and a fall.

## Reading: a voice message

Daniel, who is learning French in Montréal, leaves a message for his tutor, Claire.

> Bonjour Claire, c'est Daniel. Merci pour le cours ! J'ai un problème avec la prononciation
> du mot « héros ». Je dis « les zéros »… Et le son « u » est difficile, mais j'écoute et je
> répète. Les liaisons, ça va : « les amis », « vous êtes »… Mais « un étudiant anglais », c'est
> une liaison interdite, d'accord ? À jeudi !

Hello Claire, it's Daniel. Thanks for the lesson! I have a problem with the pronunciation of
the word *héros*. I say *les zéros*… And the sound *u* is difficult, but I listen and repeat.
Liaisons are OK: *les amis*, *vous êtes*… But *un étudiant anglais* is a forbidden liaison,
right? See you Thursday!

(*Le cours* is the lesson, *un problème* a problem, *je dis* I say, *difficile* difficult,
*j'écoute et je répète* I listen and repeat, *interdite* forbidden, *jeudi* Thursday.)

## Common mistakes

- Making a liaison after *et*: *et_il* is wrong; say "ay eel".
- Linking into an aspirated *h*: *les_héros* sounds like "the zeros". Say "lay ay-ROH".
- Writing what you hear: *p'tit* and *j'sais pas* are spoken forms; write *petit* and *je ne
  sais pas*.
- Pausing between words. Slide final consonants into the next vowel: *il est* = "ee-LEH".
- Stressing every word. Keep syllables even and lengthen only the last one in each group.
- Using a falling voice for a yes/no question without *est-ce que* or inversion: without the
  rise, *Tu es français.* is a statement.

## Key points

- Compulsory liaison: determiner + noun, pronoun + verb (both ways), short adjective + noun,
  short prepositions, fixed phrases. Forbidden: after *et* and singular nouns, before aspirated
  *h*, *onze*, *oui*, *huit*. Everything else is optional.
- In liaison *s/x/z* = "z", *d* = "t", *f* = "v" in *neuf ans*.
- Enchaînement slides an always-pronounced consonant into the next vowel: *il est*, *une amie*.
- The mute *e* is often dropped in speech (*p'tit*, *sam'di*) but always written.
- An aspirated *h* is silent but blocks elision and liaison: *le héros, les | haricots*.
- Closed *é* vs open *è*; closed *o* (*beau*) vs open *o* (*porte*).
- Statements fall at the end, yes/no questions rise, question-word questions usually fall.
