lessons.title: Le monde francophone: French around the world
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Lesson 3 you learned to say where you're from with *à, en, au, aux*, and in Lesson 4 you
met the French way of counting to 99. Both work differently once you leave France. French is
spoken on five continents, and this course teaches the French of France, but you will meet
people from Brussels, Geneva, Montréal, Dakar and Abidjan. This lesson shows you where French
is spoken, how to say "in" or "to" those places, and the most common differences you'll hear:
Belgian and Swiss numbers, meal names, and some Québec usage.

## Where French is spoken

All the people and places that speak French make up **[[la francophonie]]** (the French-speaking
world). With a capital F, *la Francophonie* is the Organisation internationale de la
Francophonie (OIF), an organization of states and governments that share the language. In its
2026 report the OIF counted about 396 million French speakers; most of them live in Africa.
(Counts like this depend on how well someone must speak to be included, so other estimates are
lower.)

French is an **[[official language]]**, used by law in government and schools, in many countries,
often alongside other languages:

- Europe: France; Belgium (with Dutch and German); Switzerland (with German, Italian and
  Romansh); Luxembourg (with Luxembourgish and German); Monaco.
- North America: Canada (with English), where most French speakers live in Québec, the only
  province whose sole official language is French.
- The Caribbean: Haiti (with Haitian Creole), and the French overseas departments of
  Guadeloupe and Martinique.
- Africa: many countries, among them Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon (with English), the
  Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar (with Malagasy). In Morocco, Algeria and
  Tunisia, French is not an official language but is widely used in business and education.
- The Indian Ocean and the Pacific: Réunion (France), and New Caledonia and French
  Polynesia (both French territories), among others.

```map
base: world
title: Some countries where French is an official language
view: -30, -100 to 60, 60
region: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg | Europe
region: Canada, Haiti | The Americas
region: Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madagascar | Africa
region: Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia | Widely used, but not official
caption: A selection, not a complete list. In Canada, most French speakers live in the province of Québec.
```

## Saying where: the same rules, new places

The rules from Lesson 3 work everywhere:

| Kind of place | Word | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| city | *à* | *à Dakar, à Genève, à Bruxelles, à Abidjan* |
| feminine country or region | *en* | *en Belgique, en Suisse, en Côte d'Ivoire, en Afrique* |
| masculine country or province | *au* | *au Sénégal, au Cameroun, au Luxembourg, au Québec* |
| plural country | *aux* | *aux États-Unis* |

Some cases to watch:

- Québec is both a province and a city. The province is masculine with an article: *le
  Québec, au Québec* (in Québec province). The city has no article: *à Québec* (in Québec
  City). So *J'habite au Québec, à Montréal.*
- Luxembourg works the same way: *au Luxembourg* (the country), *à Luxembourg* (the city).
- Islands without an article take *à*: *à Madagascar*, *à Cuba*. Haiti is the classic
  hesitation: Québec's language office says both *en Haïti* and *à Haïti* are correct, and *en
  Haïti* has become the usual choice. The *h* is mute: *d'Haïti*.
- Continents are feminine and take *en*: *en Afrique, en Europe, en Amérique*.

### Example 1: Choosing the little word

Fill in *à, en* or *au*, and say why.

1. Awa habite ___ Sénégal. → *au*: *le Sénégal* is masculine (it ends in *-al*, not *-e*).
2. Elle travaille ___ Dakar. → *à*: Dakar is a city. (*Travailler* is to work.)
3. Kofi est ___ Côte d'Ivoire. → *en*: *la Côte d'Ivoire* is feminine.
4. Mes amis sont ___ Québec, ___ Québec. → *au Québec, à Québec*: the province, then the
   city.
5. On va ___ Haïti. → *en* (the usual choice; *à* is also correct). (*On va* means we're
   going.)

## Numbers in Belgium and Switzerland

Lesson 4 built 70, 80 and 90 from twenties. Belgium and Switzerland use simpler words: these
are **[[regional variants]]**, correct where they are used.

| | France | Belgium | Switzerland |
|---|---|---|---|
| 70 | *soixante-dix* | *septante* | *septante* |
| 71 | *soixante et onze* | *septante et un* | *septante et un* |
| 80 | *quatre-vingts* | *quatre-vingts* | *huitante* (Vaud, Valais, Fribourg) or *quatre-vingts* |
| 90 | *quatre-vingt-dix* | *nonante* | *nonante* |
| 99 | *quatre-vingt-dix-neuf* | *nonante-neuf* | *nonante-neuf* |

The new words simply continue the pattern of *trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante*:
*septante* comes from *sept*, *huitante* from *huit*, *nonante* from *neuf*. They work exactly
like *soixante*: *septante-deux* (72), *nonante-cinq* (95), with *et* for 1 (*septante et
un*).

![A comparison chart of words that differ between France, Belgium, Switzerland and Québec. 70 is soixante-dix in France and Québec, septante in Belgium and Switzerland. 90 is quatre-vingt-dix in France and Québec, nonante in Belgium and Switzerland. 80 is quatre-vingts everywhere except parts of Switzerland, which say huitante. The morning meal is le petit-déjeuner in France and le déjeuner elsewhere; the midday meal is le déjeuner in France and le dîner elsewhere; the evening meal is le dîner in France and le souper elsewhere. The weekend is le week-end in France, Belgium and Switzerland and usually la fin de semaine in Québec.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: Converting numbers

After a card game, a Swiss friend from Lausanne reads out the points: *Moi, nonante-deux ;
Léa, huitante ; Marc, quarante et un ; et toi, septante-neuf !* Write the scores down.

1. *nonante-deux*: nonante (90) + deux = 92.
2. *huitante*: 80 (she's from Vaud).
3. *quarante et un*: 41, as in France.
4. *septante-neuf*: septante (70) + neuf = 79.

Result: she has 92, Léa 80, Marc 41 and you 79. In France she would say *quatre-vingt-douze,
quatre-vingts, quarante et un, soixante-dix-neuf*. (*Moi* is me, *toi* you.)

## Meals: same words, different times

This is the difference that catches visitors most often.

| | France | Belgium, Switzerland, Québec |
|---|---|---|
| breakfast | *le petit-déjeuner* | *le déjeuner* |
| lunch | *le déjeuner* | *le dîner* |
| dinner, evening meal | *le dîner* | *le souper* |

So if a friend in Montréal invites you *pour dîner*, come at midday, not in the evening. In
France, *le souper* usually means a late meal after a show, though some regions still use it
for the evening meal.

## Québec French

Québec French has its own standard, with its own dictionaries and its own language office (the
Office québécois de la langue française, OQLF), which recommends French words where France often
uses English ones:

- *la fin de semaine* for the weekend (France: *le week-end*). *Bonne fin de semaine !* — Have a
  good weekend!
- *le courriel* for e-mail. France's official terminology has recommended *courriel* too since
  2003, but people in France mostly say *e-mail* or *mail*.
- *tu* is used more widely than in France, including with people you don't know well in many
  everyday situations. Still start with *vous* and follow the other person's lead.

Pronunciation differs as well: for example, *t* and *d* before *i* and *u* sound close to "ts"
and "dz" in Québec: *tu* is "tsü", *dire* is "dzeer". You'll understand it after a little
listening.

Two more everyday words: a mobile phone is *un portable* in France, *un GSM* in Belgium (and
Luxembourg), and *un natel* in Switzerland (originally a brand name).

### Example 3: Reading a message from Montréal

> Salut ! Bonne fin de semaine ! Samedi, on dîne à midi chez mes parents, et le soir, on soupe
> au restaurant. Mon courriel : marc.tremblay@exemple.ca. À bientôt !

Read it as someone from France would need to:

1. *Bonne fin de semaine* = *Bon week-end* in France.
2. *On dîne à midi* = we have lunch at noon (in France: *on déjeune*).
3. *Le soir, on soupe* = in the evening we have dinner (in France: *on dîne*).
4. *Mon courriel* = my e-mail address (in France usually *mon e-mail* or *mon adresse mail*).

(*Samedi* is Saturday, *chez mes parents* at my parents' place, *le soir* in the evening.)

## Reading: an e-mail from Brussels

Élise writes to her new pen friend, Hannah, in England.

> Bonjour Hannah !
>
> Je m'appelle Élise. Je suis belge et j'habite à Bruxelles, en Belgique. J'ai vingt-sept ans.
> En Belgique, on parle français, néerlandais et allemand. Moi, je parle français. Ma mère est
> suisse, de Lausanne. Chez nous, on dit « septante » et « nonante », mais ma mère dit aussi
> « huitante » ! Et toi, tu es anglaise ? Tu habites où ?
>
> À bientôt,
>
> Élise

Hello Hannah! My name is Élise. I'm Belgian and I live in Brussels, in Belgium. I'm
twenty-seven. In Belgium, people speak French, Dutch and German. I speak French. My mother is
Swiss, from Lausanne. At home we say *septante* and *nonante*, but my mother also says
*huitante*! And you, are you English? Where do you live? See you soon, Élise.

(*Parler* is to speak, *néerlandais* Dutch, *allemand* German, *ma mère* my mother, *chez nous*
at home, *on dit* we say.)

## Common mistakes

- *à Sénégal* or *en Sénégal*: *le Sénégal* is masculine, so *au Sénégal*.
- *au Québec* for the city: the city is *à Québec*.
- Correcting a Belgian or Swiss speaker's *septante*: it isn't a mistake. Use the forms of France
  yourself, but understand the others.
- Arriving in the evening for a Québec *dîner*: it's lunch.
- Thinking French is "really" only French from France. Every French-speaking region has its own
  correct usage; this course follows France's.

## Key points

- *La francophonie* is the French-speaking world; *la Francophonie* (OIF) is the organization.
  French is an official language in Europe, Canada, the Caribbean and many African countries.
- Same rules as Lesson 3: *à Dakar, en Côte d'Ivoire, au Sénégal, au Québec* (province), *à
  Québec* (city); *en Haïti* is usual.
- Belgium and Switzerland: *septante* (70), *nonante* (90); parts of Switzerland: *huitante*
  (80).
- Belgium, Switzerland and Québec: *déjeuner* = breakfast, *dîner* = lunch, *souper* = dinner.
- Québec: *la fin de semaine*, *le courriel*, *tu* more widely used.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers in everyday life: sums, marks and handwriting
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 4 took you from *zéro* to *cent*. Knowing the words is one thing; using them at
conversation speed is another. This honors lesson gives you more practice with numbers up to
100 in real situations: where *soixante-dix* and *quatre-vingts* come from, how to do sums out
loud, how French schools give marks, how French people write their digits, and how to catch a
phone number said at full speed.

## Why does French count in twenties?

The short answer: nobody knows for sure. Here is the history in a simplified form, following
the Académie française's own account.

- In the Middle Ages, people in France often counted in twenties for larger numbers: *vint et
  dis* (30), *deux vins* (40), *trois vins* (60), *six vins* (120) and so on. Where this habit
  came from is debated; a Celtic or a Norman (Viking) influence has been suggested, but neither
  is proven.
- A trace survives in Paris: the *Hôpital des Quinze-Vingts*, today an eye hospital, was
  founded by King Louis IX (Saint Louis) around 1260 as a home for 300 blind people: 15 × 20 =
  300.
- From the late Middle Ages, *trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante* replaced most of the
  twenties, perhaps because they made sums easier. *Septante, octante* and *nonante* existed
  too.
- In the 17th century, grammarians and the Académie française settled on *soixante-dix,
  quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix* for standard French. Belgium and Switzerland kept *septante*
  and *nonante* (honors lesson 04h2), and the Académie's dictionary still lists them.

So *quatre-vingts* (four twenties) is a fossil of an old way of counting, like English "four
score and seven years" (87).

## Doing sums out loud

French children learn to say sums like this:

| Sign | Word | Example | Said |
|---|---|---|---|
| + | *plus* (the *s* is said: "plüss") | 2 + 3 = 5 | *Deux plus trois égale cinq.* |
| − | *moins* ("mwan") | 10 − 4 = 6 | *Dix moins quatre égale six.* |
| × | *fois* (times) | 3 × 4 = 12 | *Trois fois quatre égale douze.* |
| ÷ | *divisé par* | 20 ÷ 4 = 5 | *Vingt divisé par quatre égale cinq.* |
| = | *égale* | | |

Instead of *égale* (equals), you can say *font* (make) or *ça fait* (that makes), which is the
usual way in conversation and in shops: *Huit et deux, ça fait dix.* *Et* (and) often replaces
*plus* in speech, as in English. You'll meet *moins* again with the time in Lesson 18. To
*compter* is to count, and to *calculer* is to calculate or work something out.

*La fois* also means "time" in the sense of "occasion": *une fois* (once), *deux fois* (twice),
*encore une fois* (once more, Lesson 1). That's where *fois* = × comes from: three times four.

### Example 1: Reading sums aloud

Say each sum in French, then check.

1. 15 + 60 = 75 → *Quinze plus soixante égale soixante-quinze.* (75 = 60 + 15.)
2. 100 − 9 = 91 → *Cent moins neuf égale quatre-vingt-onze.* (91 = 80 + 11, no *et*.)
3. 4 × 20 = 80 → *Quatre fois vingt égale quatre-vingts.* (The name of 80 *is* the sum.)
4. 90 ÷ 2 = 45 → *Quatre-vingt-dix divisé par deux égale quarante-cinq.*
5. 7 + 70 = 77 → *Sept plus soixante-dix, ça fait soixante-dix-sept.*

## Marks out of 20

French schools usually give marks out of 20, especially from secondary school on (primary
schools often use other scales): *une note sur vingt*. *J'ai quinze sur vingt*
(15/20) is a good mark. *La moyenne*, 10 out of 20, is the pass mark: *avoir la moyenne* means
to get at least 10. Very few students get 20/20, and 16 or more is excellent.

The final exam at the end of secondary school, *le baccalauréat* (*le bac*), is also marked out
of 20. An average of 10 passes, 12 gives the distinction *assez bien* (quite good), 14 *bien*
(good) and 16 *très bien* (very good); 18 or more brings the jury's congratulations.

![A scale of school marks from 0 to 20. Below 10 is below the pass mark. 10 is la moyenne, the pass mark, and 10 to 12 is a pass with no distinction. 12 to 14 is assez bien, 14 to 16 is bien, 16 to 18 is très bien, and 18 to 20 is très bien with the jury's congratulations, as at the baccalauréat.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A 15/20 might look like 75% to you, but in France it's a very good mark, not an average one.
Don't convert French marks to percentages and judge them by your own school's standards.

### Example 2: Good news or bad?

Read each message and decide.

1. *J'ai huit sur vingt en maths.* → 8/20: below the pass mark. Bad news. (*En maths* = in
   maths.)
2. *Lucas a la moyenne en anglais : dix sur vingt.* → He passed, just. (*En anglais* = in
   English.)
3. *Dix-sept sur vingt, c'est génial !* → 17/20: excellent. (*Génial* = great.)
4. *Elle a eu quatorze au bac, mention bien !* → An average of 14: the distinction *bien*.
   (*Elle a eu* = she got.)

## How French people write numbers

French handwriting differs from American handwriting in two digits, and a misread digit can
cost you a train or a phone call.

- 1 is written with a long upstroke (a "flag"), so it can look a little like an
  upside-down V. An American reader can take it for a 7.
- 7 is therefore written with a bar across the middle, so it can't be confused with 1.

Many other Europeans write them the same way. On computers and printed timetables, digits look
the same everywhere.

![Handwritten 1 and 7 in two styles. In the French style, the 1 has a long sloping upstroke and the 7 has a bar across its middle. In the typical American style, the 1 is a single straight line and the 7 has no bar.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Un chiffre* is a digit (0 to 9), *un nombre* is a number as a quantity (*un grand nombre*, a
large number), and *un numéro* (Lesson 4) is a number that labels something, like a phone or
house number. A French phone number has *dix chiffres* (ten digits).

## Phone numbers at full speed

Lesson 4 showed that phone numbers are read in pairs. At speed, use the structure of the
words to stay ahead:

- Wait for the end of the pair. *Soixante…* could be 60 to 79; *quatre-vingt…* could be 80
  to 99. Don't write 6 or 8 too early: write the pair only when you hear the whole number.
- **Listen for *dix* or a *-ze* number after *soixante* or *quatre-vingt*.** *Soixante-douze*
  is 72, not 60 + 2; *quatre-vingt-seize* is 96.
- Pairs that start with 0 are read *zéro* + digit: *zéro neuf* = 09.
- Ask for a repeat with the numbers you have: *Zéro six, douze, et après ?* (… and then?)
  or *Vous pouvez répéter plus lentement ?* (*plus lentement* = more slowly.)

### Example 3: Catching a number

You hear: *Zéro sept, soixante-quatorze, quatre-vingt-un, dix-neuf, quatre-vingt-dix-huit.*

1. *zéro sept* → 07 (a mobile number).
2. *soixante-quatorze*: *soixante* … wait … *quatorze* → 60 + 14 = 74.
3. *quatre-vingt-un*: 80 + 1 = 81 (no *et*).
4. *dix-neuf* → 19.
5. *quatre-vingt-dix-huit*: *quatre-vingt* … wait … *dix-huit* → 80 + 18 = 98.

Result: 07 74 81 19 98. The trap is in pairs 2 and 5: writing 6 or 8 after the first word.

## Reading: homework in the kitchen

Chloé, who is nine, does her homework with her father.

> Le père : Alors, Chloé, les maths ?
>
> Chloé : Trois fois vingt… soixante. Quatre fois vingt… quatre-vingts !
>
> Le père : Très bien ! Et quatre-vingts plus dix-sept ?
>
> Chloé : Quatre-vingt-dix-sept.
>
> Le père : Bravo ! Et ta note en maths, c'est combien ?
>
> Chloé : Dix-huit sur vingt !
>
> Le père : Dix-huit ? C'est génial !
>
> Chloé : Et toi, papa, tu as quelle note ?
>
> Le père : Moi ? Je n'ai pas de notes. Je calcule le prix du dîner !

So, Chloé, maths? — Three times twenty… sixty. Four times twenty… eighty! — Very good! And eighty
plus seventeen? — Ninety-seven. — Well done! And your mark in maths, how much is it? — Eighteen
out of twenty! — Eighteen? That's great! — And you, Dad, what mark do you have? — Me? I don't
have marks. I'm working out the price of dinner!

(*Alors* = so, *ta note* = your mark, *c'est combien ?* = how much is it?, *quelle* = which or
what, *le prix* = the price.)

## Common mistakes

- Writing the first part of a 70s or 90s number too soon: *soixante-quinze* is 75, not 6 and
  then 15.
- *quatre-vingts-deux*: the *s* goes when a number follows (Lesson 4).
- Not saying the *s* of *plus* in sums: in arithmetic it's "plüss".
- Judging French marks like percentages: 14/20 is a good mark.
- Writing a 7 without its bar in France: it's a habit worth getting into, and it makes your 1
  safe too.
- Mixing up *le chiffre* (a digit), *le nombre* (a quantity) and *le numéro* (a phone or house
  number).

## Key points

- French counted in twenties in the Middle Ages; *soixante-dix, quatre-vingts,
  quatre-vingt-dix* were fixed as standard in the 17th century, while Belgium and Switzerland
  kept *septante, nonante*. (Simplified: the origin of the twenties is debated.)
- Sums: *plus*, *moins*, *fois*, *divisé par*, *égale* (or *font*, *ça fait*).
- Marks are out of 20; 10 is *la moyenne* (the pass mark); 16+ is excellent.
- French handwriting: a 1 with a long upstroke, a crossed 7.
- *Le chiffre* (digit), *le nombre* (quantity), *le numéro* (label).
- At speed, wait for the whole pair before writing a phone number down.

lessons.title: Nouns, gender and articles: at home
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Module 1 you learned to greet people, say who you are and where you're from, and count.
Now you start talking about *things*: the keys on the table, the bag under the chair, the
rooms in a flat. To do that in French you need to know two facts about every noun: whether it
is masculine or feminine, and which little word goes in front of it.

By the end of this lesson you can say what something is (*C'est une clé*), say what there is
in a room (*Il y a un lit et une table*) and say where things are (*Le livre est sur la
table*).

## Every noun is masculine or feminine

Every French noun belongs to one of two groups called **[[gender]]**: **[[masculine]]** or
**[[feminine]]**. There is no third group: everything, from a table to a computer, is one or the
other, and "the" changes with it.

| Gender | "the" | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | le | *le livre* (the book), *le lit* (the bed), *le sac* (the bag) |
| feminine | la | *la table* (the table), *la chaise* (the chair), *la porte* (the door) |

Grammatical gender is a label on the word, not a fact about the object. A bed isn't male and
a door isn't female; *le* and *la* simply tell you which group the word is in. Other words
follow the label: the article now, adjectives and possessives later.

The golden rule: never learn a noun without its article. Don't learn *table = table*;
learn *la table*. Say it aloud as one unit, *latable, lelit*, until the article feels like
part of the word. Your vocabulary cards always show nouns with an article, and you type it.

You can sometimes guess. Many nouns ending in *-e* are feminine (*la table, la chaise, la
porte, la fenêtre*), but plenty are not: *le livre, le téléphone*. Treat endings as a hint,
never as a rule; the honors lesson "Guessing gender" (08h1) shows the endings that really
work.

## The: le, la, l', les

The **[[definite article]]** means "the". It has four forms:

| | before a consonant | before a vowel or mute h |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *le salon* | *l'ordinateur* |
| feminine | *la cuisine* | *l'adresse* |
| plural (both genders) | *les salons, les cuisines* | *les ordinateurs* |

- Before a vowel or a mute h, *le* and *la* both shorten to *l'*. This is the elision
  you met in lesson 1: French avoids two vowels bumping into each other, so *le ordinateur*
  becomes *l'ordinateur*, *la adresse* becomes *l'adresse*.
- *L'* hides the gender. For these nouns, learn the gender with *un* or *une*: *un
  appartement* (masculine), *une adresse* (feminine). Your vocabulary list says "masculine"
  or "feminine" for every *l'* noun.
- In the plural, there's only one word: *les*, for masculine and feminine alike.

French uses *le, la, les* in many places where English has no article at all, for example for
things in general: *J'adore les livres.* (I love books.) You'll practise this in lesson 7.

## A, an, some: un, une, des

The **[[indefinite article]]** means "a" or "an":

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *un lit* (a bed) | *des lits* (beds, some beds) |
| feminine | *une chaise* (a chair) | *des chaises* (chairs, some chairs) |

- *Un* goes with masculine nouns, *une* with feminine ones. Unlike *le* and *la*, they never
  shorten: *un ordinateur*, *une adresse*.
- English has no plural "a". French does: *des*. English often says nothing (*There are
  books on the table*), but French needs *des*: *Il y a des livres sur la table.* A French
  noun almost never stands alone.
- *Un* is also the number one, so *un livre* can mean "a book" or "one book".

The picture shows the rooms of a small flat. The labels are coloured by gender: blue for
masculine, pink for feminine.

![The floor plan of a small flat with four rooms. La cuisine (kitchen) with la table and two chaises (chairs); le salon (living room) with a sofa and la fenêtre (window); la chambre (bedroom) with le lit (bed); la salle de bains (bathroom) with a bath. La porte (the front door) opens into the living room. Masculine labels are blue, feminine labels pink.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Here is the way to choose the article when you meet a noun:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing le, la, l' or les
  accDescr: First ask how many things there are. For more than one, use les for "the" and des for "a" or "some". For one thing, ask whether the noun starts with a vowel or mute h. If it does, "the" is l', and "a" is un or une according to its gender, as in l'ordinateur, un ordinateur. If it doesn't, ask the gender: masculine nouns take le and un, as in le livre, un livre; feminine nouns take la and une, as in la table, une table.
  A{"One thing or more than one?"} -- "more than one" --> P["les (the) / des (a, some): les livres, des livres"]
  A -- "one" --> B{"Starts with a vowel or mute h?"}
  B -- "yes" --> L["l' (the), un or une (a): l'ordinateur, un ordinateur"]
  B -- "no" --> G{"Masculine or feminine?"}
  G -- "masculine" --> M["le / un: le livre, un livre"]
  G -- "feminine" --> F["la / une: la table, une table"]
```

## Plurals: you see the -s but hear the article

To make a noun plural, add *-s*, just as in English: *le livre → les livres, la chaise → les
chaises*. But in French the *-s* is silent. *Livre* and *livres* sound exactly the same, so you
hear the difference only in the article:

| one | more than one | what you hear |
|---|---|---|
| *le livre* | *les livres* | luh / lay |
| *la porte* | *les portes* | la / lay |
| *un sac* | *des sacs* | uh(n) / day |

So listen for the article: *le, la, un, une* mean one; *les, des* more than one.

Before a vowel, *les* and *des* do something extra: their silent *s* is spoken as a *z* and
joins the next word. This is liaison (lesson 1): *les_ordinateurs* (lay-zor-dee-na-teur),
*des_appartements* (day-za-par-tuh-mahn). *Un* links too: *un_ordinateur* (uh-nor-dee-na-teur).

Four patterns for spelling the plural:

| Pattern | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| most nouns: add *-s* | *la clé, le téléphone* | *les clés, les téléphones* |
| *-eau*: add *-x* | *le bureau* (office, lesson 7) | *les bureaux* |
| *-al*: change to *-aux* | *le journal* (newspaper) | *les journaux* |
| already ends in *-s, -x* or *-z*: no change | *le cours* (class, lesson 7), *le prix* (price) | *les cours, les prix* |

The *-x* is silent, but *-al → -aux* changes the sound: *journal* (zhoor-NAL), *journaux*
(zhoor-NOH).

## C'est … and ce sont …: what is it?

To say what something is, use *c'est* (it is, that is, this is) with one thing and *ce sont*
(they are, those are) with several:

- *C'est un stylo.* — It's a pen.
- *C'est la chambre de Paul.* — It's Paul's room (literally "the room of Paul").
- *Ce sont des clés.* — They're keys.
- *Qu'est-ce que c'est ?* — *C'est un ordinateur.* — What is it? — It's a computer.
  (*Qu'est-ce que c'est ?* is taught in lesson 11; use it now as a fixed question.)

*C'est* never changes for gender: *C'est un lit. C'est une table.* In everyday speech many
French people say *c'est* for plurals too (*C'est des clés*); you'll hear it, but write *ce
sont*.

In lesson 3 you saw that *c'est* comes before a name or a noun with an article, and *il est /
elle est* before an adjective such as a nationality: *C'est Marc. Il est canadien.* The same
works for things. For a thing that has already been named, French uses *il* for a masculine
noun and *elle* for a feminine one. Both mean "it":

- *Où est le téléphone ? — Il est sur la table.* — Where's the phone? — It's on the table.
- *Où est la clé ? — Elle est dans le sac.* — Where's the key? — It's in the bag.
- *Où sont les livres ? — Ils sont ici.* — Where are the books? — They're here.

## Il y a: there is, there are

*Il y a* means both "there is" and "there are". It never changes:

- *Il y a une table dans la cuisine.* — There's a table in the kitchen.
- *Il y a deux chambres.* — There are two bedrooms.
- *Il y a des livres sous le lit.* — There are books under the bed.
- *Il y a un lit ?* — Is there a bed? (A question with just a rising voice; more in lesson 11.)

The three words run together: *ee-lee-ah*, often just *ya* in fast speech.

(*Il y a* + a time means "ago": *il y a deux ans*, two years ago. You'll use that in lesson 21.)

## Where is it? sur, sous, dans, devant, derrière

These five **[[prepositions]]** say where something is. They go before the noun with its article:

| French | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *sur* | on | *Le livre est sur la table.* |
| *sous* | under | *Le chat est sous la table.* (*le chat*, the cat, lesson 6) |
| *dans* | in, inside | *Le téléphone est dans le sac.* |
| *devant* | in front of | *Le sac est devant la table.* |
| *derrière* | behind | *La chaise est derrière la table.* |

![A table seen from the front. A book lies on the table, a cat sits under it, a bag stands on the floor in front of it with a phone sticking out of the bag, and a chair stands behind the table, only its back showing above the tabletop.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Sur* (on) has the French *u* (round your lips and say "ee"); *sous* (under) has *ou* as in
"soup". To tell *devant* from *derrière*, think of *der-* = "rear".

*Ici* means "here" and *là* means "there": *Le sac est ici. La clé est là.* In everyday
speech *là* is also used for "here", and *là-bas* means "over there" (*La gare est là-bas.* — The station is over there.).
Don't confuse *là* (there, with an accent) with the article *la* (no accent).

## Dialogue: the new flat

Nora visits her friend Thomas, who has just moved into a flat in Lyon.

> Thomas : *Bonjour Nora ! Entre ! Voilà l'appartement.*
>
> Nora : *Merci ! Il y a deux chambres ?*
>
> Thomas : *Oui, il y a deux chambres et une salle de bains. Ici, c'est le salon.*
>
> Nora : *Et là, c'est la cuisine ?*
>
> Thomas : *Oui. Il y a une table et quatre chaises.*
>
> Nora : *Et ça, qu'est-ce que c'est ? Un ordinateur sous le lit ?*
>
> Thomas : *Euh… oui. Et il y a des livres sous le lit aussi.*
>
> Nora : *Où sont les clés ?*
>
> Thomas : *Elles sont sur la table, devant la fenêtre. Voilà !*

Translation:

> Thomas: Hello Nora! Come in! Here's the flat.
>
> Nora: Thanks! Are there two bedrooms?
>
> Thomas: Yes, there are two bedrooms and a bathroom. Here, this is the living room.
>
> Nora: And there, is that the kitchen?
>
> Thomas: Yes. There's a table and four chairs.
>
> Nora: And that, what is it? A computer under the bed?
>
> Thomas: Er… yes. And there are books under the bed too.
>
> Nora: Where are the keys?
>
> Thomas: They're on the table, in front of the window. There you go!

(*Entre !* = come in, *ça* = that, *aussi* = too, lesson 7. *Elles* stands for *les clés*,
which is feminine plural.)

## Pronunciation

- *le* sounds like "luh" (a short, relaxed vowel), *les* like "lay". This is the difference
  between one and several, so make it clear.
- *un* is a nasal vowel, roughly "uh" said through the nose with no *n* sound; *une* has the
  French *u* and a clear *n*: "ewn".
- *la clé* and *la clef* are two spellings of one word, both said "clay".
- *la fenêtre*: fuh-NEH-truh; *derrière*: deh-RYAIR.
- *la salle de bains*: sal-duh-BAN (nasal *in*). You'll often see *salle de bain* without *s*;
  dictionaries give *salle de bains*.
- *l'ordinateur*: lor-dee-na-TEUR, stressed on the last syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Using a noun without an article. "There are books on the table" is *Il y a des livres sur
  la table*.
- Guessing the gender from the object or from English. Learn *la table, le lit*; don't
  reason about it.
- Writing *le ordinateur* or *la appartement*. Before a vowel it's always *l'ordinateur,
  l'appartement*.
- Shortening *un* or *une*: *une adresse*, never ~~un' adresse~~.
- Pronouncing the plural *-s*. *les chaises* is "lay shez", not "lay shez-ss".
- Saying ~~il est~~ or ~~là est~~ for "there is". It's *il y a*.
- Mixing up *sur* and *sous*: *sur la table* is on top of it, *sous la table* under it.

## Key points

- Every noun is masculine or feminine. Learn each one with its article.
- "The": *le* (masculine), *la* (feminine), *l'* (before a vowel or mute h), *les* (plural).
- "A": *un* (masculine), *une* (feminine); plural *des*, which English often leaves out.
- The plural *-s* is silent; listen for *les* and *des*. *-eau → -eaux*, *-al → -aux*.
- *C'est* + one thing, *ce sont* + several; *il* or *elle* for "it", by gender.
- *Il y a* = there is, there are.
- Where: *sur, sous, dans, devant, derrière*; *ici* (here), *là* (there).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Family, avoir and possessives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 5 you learned that every noun is masculine or feminine and takes *le, la* or *un,
une*. Now you'll use that to talk about the people closest to you: *ma mère, mon frère, mes
enfants*. You'll learn the second most important verb in French, *avoir* (to have), and the
words for "my, your, his, her, our, their".

By the end of this lesson you can say who is in your family (*J'ai deux sœurs et un frère*),
ask about someone else's (*Tu as des enfants ?*) and point at a photo: *Qui est-ce ? — C'est
mon père.*

## Avoir: to have

You met *avoir* in lesson 4 for your age: *J'ai trente ans.* Here is the whole verb. Like
*être*, it is irregular: its forms don't follow a pattern, so learn them by heart.

| | avoir | English |
|---|---|---|
| je | *j'ai* | I have |
| tu | *tu as* | you have (informal) |
| il / elle / on | *il a, elle a, on a* | he / she has, we have |
| nous | *nous avons* | we have |
| vous | *vous avez* | you have (formal or plural) |
| ils / elles | *ils ont, elles ont* | they have |

- *Je* becomes *j'* before the vowel: *j'ai* (said "zhay"), never ~~je ai~~.
- *Nous avons, vous avez, ils ont, elles ont*: the *s* of the pronoun links to the verb with
  a *z* sound: *nou-za-von, vou-za-vay, eel-zon*.
- *Ils ont* (they have) and *ils sont* (they are) sound different only in that one sound:
  *eel-ZON* with a *z* is "they have", *eel-SON* with an *s* is "they are". Listen carefully;
  it's one of the most useful sounds in French.

Examples:

- *J'ai un frère et une sœur.* — I have a brother and a sister.
- *Tu as un chien ?* — Do you have a dog?
- *Elle a deux enfants.* — She has two children.
- *Nous avons un chat.* — We have a cat.
- *Vous avez des enfants ?* — Do you have (any) children?
- *Ils ont trois filles.* — They have three daughters.

English needs "do" in the question; French doesn't. *Tu as un chien ?* is just the statement
*Tu as un chien* said with a rising voice. And as you saw in lesson 4, French uses *avoir*,
not *être*, for age: *Mon fils a dix ans* (my son is ten).

## The family

| masculine | feminine | English |
|---|---|---|
| *le père* | *la mère* | father, mother |
| *le fils* | *la fille* | son, daughter |
| *le frère* | *la sœur* | brother, sister |
| *le mari* | *la femme* | husband, wife |
| *le grand-père* | *la grand-mère* | grandfather, grandmother |
| *l'ami* | *l'amie* | friend (male), friend (female) |

- *Les parents* means "the parents"; it can also mean "relatives" in general (*des parents
  à Lyon*, relatives in Lyon). For now, use it for your mother and father.
- *La fille* means both "daughter" and "girl". *La femme* means both "wife" and "woman". The
  context tells you which: *ma fille* is my daughter; *Il y a une fille de dix ans dans le
  salon* is about a ten-year-old girl.
- *L'enfant* (child) can be masculine or feminine: *un enfant* (a boy, or any child) or *une
  enfant* (a girl). In the plural, *des enfants* covers both.
- *Le grand-père, la grand-mère* have a hyphen, and both parts take *-s* in the plural: *les
  grands-pères, les grands-mères*.
- *Marié* means "married". A married woman is *mariée*, with an extra *e* that you don't hear:
  *Il est marié. Elle est mariée.* Lesson 8 explains this agreement.
- Pets are part of the family too: *le chien* (dog), *le chat* (cat).

This is Léa's family. She is the girl in the middle of the bottom row, so everyone is shown
from her point of view.

![Léa's family tree. Top row: Pierre, mon grand-père, and Monique, ma grand-mère. Middle row: their son Marc, mon père, and his wife Sophie, ma mère. Bottom row: their children Hugo, mon frère; Léa, moi; and Chloé, ma sœur. The family dog, Max, mon chien, sits next to Chloé.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## My, your, his, her: possessives

The words for "my, your, his, her, our, their" are **[[possessives]]**. In French they come in
three forms, like the articles: masculine, feminine and plural.

| owner | masculine noun | feminine noun | plural noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | *mon père* | *ma mère* | *mes parents* |
| tu | *ton père* | *ta mère* | *tes parents* |
| il / elle / on | *son père* | *sa mère* | *ses parents* |
| nous | *notre père* | *notre mère* | *nos parents* |
| vous | *votre père* | *votre mère* | *vos parents* |
| ils / elles | *leur père* | *leur mère* | *leurs parents* |

Two decisions, in this order:

1. *Who owns it?* That chooses the row: me → *mon/ma/mes*, you (*tu*) → *ton/ta/tes*, and
   so on.
2. *What is owned?* That chooses the form: masculine noun → *mon*, feminine → *ma*, plural
   → *mes*.

### The possessive agrees with the thing, not the owner

This is the big surprise for English speakers. *Son, sa, ses* all mean "his" or "her".
The form depends on the noun that follows, not on whether the owner is a man or a woman:

- *Paul et sa mère* — Paul and his mother (*mère* is feminine, so *sa*)
- *Julie et sa mère* — Julie and her mother
- *Paul et son père* — Paul and his father (*père* is masculine, so *son*)
- *Julie et son père* — Julie and her father

![A chart with two rows, Paul and Julie. Both rows read the same: son père (le père), sa mère (la mère), ses parents (les parents). The possessive changes with the thing owned, not with the owner.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If it's not clear whose it is, French adds *à lui* (his) or *à elle* (hers): *C'est sa
voiture à elle* (it's her car; *la voiture*, lesson 14). You won't need this often; the context usually makes it clear.

### mon amie, not ma amie

Before a feminine noun that starts with a vowel or mute h, *ma, ta, sa* would bump into the
vowel, but they can't shorten like *la* does (no ~~m'amie~~). Instead French uses *mon, ton,
son*:

- *mon amie* (my friend, female), *ton amie, son amie*
- *mon adresse* (my address; *l'adresse* is feminine), *son école* (his or her school;
  *l'école*, lesson 7)

The noun is still feminine; only the possessive changes its form. The *n* links to the vowel:
*mon_amie* (mo-na-mee). So *mon ami* and *mon amie* sound the same; the spelling shows the
difference.

### notre, votre, leur

These three don't change between masculine and feminine, only for the plural:

- *notre fils, notre fille, nos enfants* — our son, our daughter, our children
- *votre mari, votre femme, vos amis* — your husband, your wife, your friends
- *leur chien, leur maison, leurs chats* — their dog, their house, their cats

*Leur* takes *-s* only when there are several things: *leur fille* (their daughter, one),
*leurs filles* (their daughters).

*Ton, ta, tes* go with *tu*; *votre, vos* go with *vous*. Use the one that matches how you
address the person: *Tu as ton téléphone ? Vous avez votre téléphone ?*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a possessive
  accDescr: First find the owner; that gives the set of words, for example mon, ma, mes for "my" or son, sa, ses for "his" or "her". Then look at the noun that follows. If it is plural, use the plural form, such as mes, ses, nos or leurs. If it is masculine, use the masculine form, such as mon or son. If it is feminine and starts with a vowel or mute h, use the masculine-looking form mon, ton or son, as in mon amie. Otherwise use the feminine form, such as ma or sa. Notre, votre and leur are the same for masculine and feminine.
  A["1. Who owns it? (je → mon / ma / mes, il or elle → son / sa / ses …)"] --> B{"2. What follows?"}
  B -- "a plural noun" --> P["mes, tes, ses, nos, vos, leurs"]
  B -- "a masculine noun" --> M["mon, ton, son, notre, votre, leur"]
  B -- "a feminine noun" --> V{"Starts with a vowel or mute h?"}
  V -- "yes" --> MV["mon, ton, son: mon amie"]
  V -- "no" --> F["ma, ta, sa, notre, votre, leur"]
```

## Qui est-ce ? C'est …

To ask who someone is, say *Qui est-ce ?* (Who is it? Who's that? *qui* = who, lesson 11).
Answer with *c'est* + one person or *ce sont* + several, just as for things in lesson 5:

- *Qui est-ce ? — C'est ma sœur, Chloé.* — Who's that? — It's my sister, Chloé.
- *Et là ? — Ce sont mes grands-parents.* — And there? — Those are my grandparents (*les grands-parents*).
- *C'est ton ami ? — Non, c'est mon frère !* — Is that your friend? — No, it's my brother!

## Dialogue: photos on the phone

Inès shows her new colleague Karim photos of her family.

> Karim : *Qui est-ce ?*
>
> Inès : *C'est ma sœur, Sarah. Elle a vingt-cinq ans. Elle est mariée et elle a un fils.*
>
> Karim : *Et là, c'est son mari ?*
>
> Inès : *Oui, c'est Julien, son mari. Il est belge.*
>
> Karim : *Et le chien ?*
>
> Inès : *C'est leur chien, Biscotte ! Et voilà mes parents, à Marseille.*
>
> Karim : *Tu as des frères ?*
>
> Inès : *Oui, j'ai un frère. Et toi ?*
>
> Karim : *Moi, j'ai trois sœurs. Nous avons une grande famille !*

Translation:

> Karim: Who's that?
>
> Inès: It's my sister, Sarah. She's twenty-five. She's married and she has a son.
>
> Karim: And there, is that her husband?
>
> Inès: Yes, that's Julien, her husband. He's Belgian.
>
> Karim: And the dog?
>
> Inès: That's their dog, Biscotte! And here are my parents, in Marseille.
>
> Karim: Do you have brothers?
>
> Inès: Yes, I have a brother. And you?
>
> Karim: Me, I have three sisters. We have a big family!

(*grande* = big, lesson 8. Notice *son mari*, "her husband": *mari* is masculine, so *son*,
even though Sarah is a woman.)

## Pronunciation

- *le fils* (son) is said "feess": the *l* is silent and the *s* is spoken. Don't confuse it
  with *la fille* (daughter), said "fee-y", where *-ille* sounds like the *y* in "yes".
- *la femme* is said "fam", like the start of English "family": the *e* sounds like *a*.
- *la sœur*: the *œu* is like the vowel in "her" said with rounded lips; the *r* is the French
  *r*.
- *le frère, le père, la mère* all rhyme: *-ère* sounds like "air".
- *mon, ton, son* are nasal: "mohn" with no real *n*, except before a vowel, where the *n*
  links (*mon_ami*).
- *eu* in *leur* sounds like the vowel in *sœur*; *leur* and *leurs* sound the same, except before a vowel,
  where the *s* of *leurs* links as a *z* (*leurs_enfants*).

## Common mistakes

- Choosing *son* or *sa* by the owner. "Her father" is *son père* (*père* is masculine), and
  "his mother" is *sa mère*.
- Writing ~~ma amie~~ or ~~ma école~~. Before a vowel: *mon amie, mon école*.
- Using *être* for age or for having: *J'ai vingt ans* (I'm twenty), never ~~je suis vingt~~.
- Mixing up *ils ont* (they have, with *z*) and *ils sont* (they are, with *s*).
- Forgetting the plural possessive: *mes parents*, not ~~mon parents~~.
- Adding *-s* to *leur* for one thing: *leur fils* (their son) needs no *s*, even though
  *fils* ends in *-s* and "they" are several people.

## Key points

- *avoir*: *j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont*. Use it for having and for age.
- *la fille* = daughter or girl; *la femme* = wife or woman; *l'enfant* can be either gender.
- Possessives: the owner picks the word (*mon / ton / son …*), the noun picks the form
  (masculine, feminine, plural).
- *son, sa, ses* = his or her.
- Before a feminine vowel noun: *mon, ton, son* (*mon amie*).
- *notre / nos, votre / vos, leur / leurs* change only for the plural.
- *Qui est-ce ? — C'est ma sœur. Ce sont mes parents.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Work, study and languages: the present of -er verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you have two verbs in full, *être* and *avoir*, and both are irregular. This lesson
gives you hundreds of verbs at once. Most French verbs end in *-er* (*parler, travailler,
aimer*), and almost all of them follow one pattern. Learn it with one verb and you can use
every other.

You'll use the pattern to talk about work, study and languages: *Je travaille dans un
bureau. Elle est médecin. Nous parlons français et un peu anglais. J'adore chanter.*

## Infinitive, stem and ending

The form of a verb you find in a dictionary is the **[[infinitive]]**: *parler* (to speak),
*travailler* (to work). For the present tense you take off the *-er*; what's left is the
**[[stem]]**: *parl-*, *travaill-*. Then you add an **[[ending]]** for each person:

| | ending | parler (to speak) | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | *-e* | *je parle* | I speak, I'm speaking |
| tu | *-es* | *tu parles* | you speak (informal) |
| il / elle / on | *-e* | *il parle, elle parle, on parle* | he / she speaks, we speak |
| nous | *-ons* | *nous parlons* | we speak |
| vous | *-ez* | *vous parlez* | you speak (formal or plural) |
| ils / elles | *-ent* | *ils parlent, elles parlent* | they speak |

![The present of parler. Six rows: je parle, tu parles, il / elle / on parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils / elles parlent. The stem parl- is the same in every row. The rows for je, tu, il and ils are shaded together with the note "these four sound the same: parl"; nous parlons and vous parlez have endings you can hear.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The French present covers three English forms: *je parle* is "I speak", "I'm speaking" and
"I do speak". There is no separate "-ing" tense.

### Four forms, one sound

Look at the shaded rows. *Parle, parles, parle, parlent* are spelled differently but sound
exactly the same: "parl". The endings *-e, -es* and *-ent* are all silent. Yes, *-ent* too:
*ils parlent* is "eel parl", never "parl-ent". Only *nous parlons* (par-LON) and *vous parlez*
(par-LAY) have an ending you can hear.

That's good news for speaking: you mostly say the stem. In writing, you need the right
ending for each person.

### j' and the linking z

When the verb starts with a vowel or mute h, two things happen (you met both in lesson 1):

- *Je* becomes *j'*: *j'aime* (I like), *j'adore* (I love), *j'étudie* (I study),
  *j'écoute* (I listen), *j'habite* (I live).
- After *nous, vous, ils, elles*, the silent *s* is spoken as *z* and joins the verb:
  *nous_aimons* (nou-zé-MON), *vous_étudiez* (vou-zé-tu-DYAY), *ils_écoutent* (eel-zé-KOOT).

So *ils écoutent* (they listen) has a *z*, but *ils parlent* (they speak) has none.

### The other verbs in this lesson

All of these follow *parler* exactly:

| infinitive | English | je | nous |
|---|---|---|---|
| *travailler* | to work | *je travaille* | *nous travaillons* |
| *aimer* | to like, to love | *j'aime* | *nous aimons* |
| *adorer* | to love, to adore | *j'adore* | *nous adorons* |
| *détester* | to hate | *je déteste* | *nous détestons* |
| *étudier* | to study | *j'étudie* | *nous étudions* |
| *écouter* | to listen (to) | *j'écoute* | *nous écoutons* |
| *regarder* | to watch, to look at | *je regarde* | *nous regardons* |
| *chercher* | to look for | *je cherche* | *nous cherchons* |
| *jouer* | to play | *je joue* | *nous jouons* |
| *danser* | to dance | *je danse* | *nous dansons* |
| *chanter* | to sing | *je chante* | *nous chantons* |

Two details:

- *Étudier* keeps the *i* of its stem: *étudi- + -ons = nous étudions*, *vous étudiez*.
- *Écouter, regarder* and *chercher* need no word for "to", "at" or "for": *J'écoute la
  radio* (I listen to the radio), *Je regarde la télé* (I'm watching TV), *Je cherche mon
  stylo* (I'm looking for my pen). Adding ~~pour~~ or ~~à~~ is a classic mistake.

*Habiter* from lesson 3 is an *-er* verb too: *j'habite, nous habitons, ils habitent*.

## Jobs: Elle est médecin

When you say what someone's job is with *être*, French uses no article:

- *Je suis professeur.* — I'm a teacher.
- *Elle est médecin.* — She's a doctor.
- *Il est ingénieur.* — He's an engineer.
- *Nous sommes étudiants.* — We're students.

This is the same rule as for nationalities in lesson 3 (*Il est canadien*). Job names also
take no capital letter. But with *c'est*, you need the article: *C'est un médecin.* (He's a
doctor / She's a doctor; literally "it's a doctor".) *C'est* needs a noun with an article
after it, as you saw in lesson 5.

Many job words have a masculine and a feminine form:

| for a man | for a woman | English |
|---|---|---|
| *l'étudiant* | *l'étudiante* | student |
| *l'infirmier* | *l'infirmière* | nurse |
| *le professeur* | *la professeure* (or *le professeur*) | teacher |
| *le médecin* | *le médecin* (also *la médecin*) | doctor |
| *l'ingénieur* | *l'ingénieure* (or *l'ingénieur*) | engineer |

*Étudiante* adds an *e*, and the *t* is now spoken (étu-DYAHNT). *Infirmière* changes *-ier*
to *-ière*. For *professeur, médecin, ingénieur*, the feminine forms have become standard in
France in recent decades; you'll see both, and the honors lesson "Guessing gender" (08h1)
tells that story. In everyday speech, a teacher is *le prof* or *la prof*.

![Five numbered pictures: a doctor with a stethoscope, a teacher pointing at a board, an engineer in a hard hat holding a plan, a student with a backpack and books, and an office desk with a computer. Labels: le médecin, le professeur, l'ingénieur, l'étudiant, le bureau.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Where people work or study: *le bureau* (office, and also desk), *l'école* (school),
*l'université* (university), *le cours* (class, lesson, course). For now, use them as chunks:
*Je travaille dans un bureau. J'étudie à l'université. J'ai un cours de français.* (*Au
bureau*, "at the office", is explained in lesson 12.) *Le travail* means "work" or "job":
*J'aime mon travail.*

## Languages: le français, parler français

Language names are masculine nouns, written with a small letter. They look like the
masculine nationality adjective from lesson 3:

- *le français* (French), *l'anglais* (English), *l'espagnol* (Spanish)
- *l'allemand* (German), *l'italien* (Italian), *l'arabe* (Arabic), *le chinois* (Chinese)

Compare: *Il est français* (adjective: he is French) and *Il parle français* (the language).
Both small letters. Only a person from France takes a capital: *un Français*.

With *parler*, you usually leave out the article: *Je parle français. Tu parles anglais ?*
With other verbs, keep it: *J'étudie le français. J'adore l'espagnol.*

*La langue* means "language" (and also "tongue"): *Tu parles quelles langues ?* — Which
languages do you speak? (*quelles* = which, lesson 11.)

## Likes and dislikes: aimer, adorer, détester

These three verbs take either a noun with *le, la, les* or an infinitive:

- *J'aime le café.* — I like coffee. (*le café*, lesson 9)
- *J'adore la musique.* — I love music.
- *Je déteste les chats.* — I hate cats.
- *J'aime danser.* — I like dancing. (Literally "I like to dance".)
- *Elle adore chanter.* — She loves singing.

Two things to notice:

- With likes and dislikes, French uses the definite article for things in general, where
  English uses no article: *J'aime le café*, never ~~j'aime café~~. (Lesson 9 explains this
  further.)
- The verb after *aimer* stays in the infinitive, just like "to dance" in English: *J'aime
  danser*, not ~~j'aime danse~~.

*Aimer* with a person means "to love": *J'aime Paul* is a declaration. For "I like Paul",
French says *J'aime bien Paul*. With things, *aimer* is simply "to like", and *adorer* is the
stronger "to love": *J'adore le chocolat.*

## How much: beaucoup, un peu, aussi

These go straight after the verb:

- *Je travaille beaucoup.* — I work a lot.
- *Elle parle un peu espagnol.* — She speaks a little Spanish.
- *J'aime beaucoup danser.* — I really like dancing.
- *Il chante aussi.* — He sings too.
- *Moi aussi !* — Me too!

## Dialogue: the first evening class

At a language school in Toulouse, two students meet before their Spanish class.

> Camille : *Bonsoir ! Tu étudies l'espagnol aussi ?*
>
> Hugo : *Oui. Je parle un peu espagnol, mais pas beaucoup. Et toi ?*
>
> Camille : *Moi, je parle anglais et j'étudie l'espagnol pour le travail.*
>
> Hugo : *Tu travailles où ?*
>
> Camille : *Je travaille dans un bureau, à Toulouse. Je suis ingénieure. Et toi ?*
>
> Hugo : *Je suis infirmier. Je travaille beaucoup, et le soir, j'écoute des chansons en
> espagnol.*
>
> Camille : *Tu aimes chanter ?*
>
> Hugo : *J'adore chanter ! Mais je déteste danser.*
>
> Camille : *Moi, j'adore danser. Bon, le cours commence !*

Translation:

> Camille: Good evening! Are you studying Spanish too?
>
> Hugo: Yes. I speak a little Spanish, but not much. And you?
>
> Camille: I speak English and I'm studying Spanish for work.
>
> Hugo: Where do you work?
>
> Camille: I work in an office, in Toulouse. I'm an engineer. And you?
>
> Hugo: I'm a nurse. I work a lot, and in the evening I listen to songs in Spanish.
>
> Camille: Do you like singing?
>
> Hugo: I love singing! But I hate dancing.
>
> Camille: I love dancing. Right, the class is starting!

(*mais* = but, lesson 8; *pas beaucoup* = not much, a short answer; *pour* = for, lesson 11;
*le soir* = in the evening, lesson 17; *des chansons* = songs; *commence* = is starting,
lesson 15.)

## Pronunciation

- Never pronounce *-ent* in a verb: *ils parlent, elles travaillent, ils chantent* all end in
  a consonant sound, not in "-ent".
- *travailler*: tra-va-YAY. *-ill-* sounds like the *y* in "yes": *je travaille* is
  "zhuh tra-VYE".
- *-er* at the end of an infinitive sounds like *-ez*: *parler* and *parlez* both end in
  "-ay".
- *le professeur, l'ingénieur*: *-eur* is the rounded vowel of *sœur* plus *r*.
- *l'infirmier* (an-feer-MYAY), *l'infirmière* (an-feer-MYAIR): the feminine ends in a sound
  like "air".
- *le médecin*: mayd-SAN, with a nasal *in* at the end; the middle *e* is usually dropped.

## Common mistakes

- Pronouncing *-ent*: *ils dansent* is "eel dahns".
- Adding an article to a job after *être*: *Je suis ingénieur*, not ~~je suis un ingénieur~~.
  (With *c'est*, the article is needed: *C'est un ingénieur.*)
- Capital letters: *le français, l'anglais*, and *je parle anglais*. Only the people take a
  capital (*les Français*).
- Leaving out the article with likes: *J'aime le thé*, not ~~j'aime thé~~.
- Translating "to", "at", "for" after *écouter, regarder, chercher*: *J'écoute la radio*,
  *Je cherche la clé*.
- Conjugating a second verb: *J'aime chanter*, not ~~j'aime chante~~.
- Saying ~~je étudie~~ or ~~je aime~~: before a vowel, always *j'*.

## Key points

- Regular *-er* verbs: stem + *-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent*.
- *Je, tu, il, ils* forms sound the same; only *nous* (*-ons*) and *vous* (*-ez*) are heard.
- *J'* before a vowel; liaison *z* in *nous_aimons, ils_écoutent*.
- Jobs after *être*: no article (*Elle est médecin*). With *c'est*: *C'est un médecin.*
- Languages: masculine, small letter; *parler français*, but *étudier le français*.
- *Aimer, adorer, détester* + *le / la / les* + noun, or + infinitive.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Describing people and things: adjectives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now name things (*la maison*), people (*mon frère*) and what they do (*il travaille*).
This lesson lets you describe them: a *small* flat, a *red* door, a *kind* brother, *nice*
people. In English, "small" never changes. In French, a describing word changes its ending to
match the noun, and it can come before or after it.

You've already seen the idea twice: *canadien / canadienne* in lesson 3 and *marié / mariée*
in lesson 6. Now you'll learn the whole system.

## Agreement: the adjective follows the noun

A word that describes a noun is an **[[adjective]]**: *petit* (small), *rouge* (red), *gentil*
(kind). In French, an adjective takes the gender and number of its noun. This matching is
called **[[agreement]]**. The dictionary gives the masculine singular; you add endings:

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *un sac noir* | *des sacs noirs* (+ *s*) |
| feminine | *une porte noire* (+ *e*) | *des portes noires* (+ *es*) |

- Feminine: add *-e*. Plural: add *-s*. Feminine plural: add both, *-es*.
- An adjective that already ends in *-e* doesn't add another one: *un livre facile, une langue
  facile*; *un sac rouge, une chaise rouge*. In the plural it just adds *-s*: *des livres
  faciles*.
- An adjective that already ends in *-s* or *-x* doesn't add another *-s* in the masculine
  plural: *un chat gris, des chats gris*; *un homme heureux, des hommes heureux*.
- Agreement works after *être* too: *Le sac est noir. La porte est noire. Les chaises sont
  noires.*
- A mixed group (masculine + feminine) takes the masculine plural: *Paul et Julie sont
  gentils.* *Le lit et la table sont noirs.*

### Can you hear it?

The plural *-s* is silent, as with nouns. The feminine *-e* is silent too, but it often makes
you *hear* the consonant before it, which is silent in the masculine:

| masculine | feminine | what changes in speech |
|---|---|---|
| *petit* | *petite* | puh-TEE → puh-TEET: the *t* is heard |
| *grand* | *grande* | grahn → grahnd: the *d* is heard |
| *mauvais* | *mauvaise* | mo-VAY → mo-VEZ: a *z* sound |
| *gris* | *grise* | gree → greez |
| *vert* | *verte* | vair → vairt |
| *intéressant* | *intéressante* | -SAHN → -SAHNT |
| *joli, bleu, noir* | *jolie, bleue, noire* | no change: they sound the same |

So when you speak, the feminine is often the masculine plus a consonant sound. When you
listen, a final consonant you can hear is a clue that the noun is feminine.

### Irregular feminines

A few common adjectives change more than an *-e*:

| masculine | feminine | English |
|---|---|---|
| *bon* | *bonne* | good (double *n*) |
| *gentil* | *gentille* | kind (double *l*) |
| *blanc* | *blanche* | white |
| *heureux* | *heureuse* | happy (*-eux → -euse*) |
| *long* | *longue* | long (lesson 15) |

*Sympa* (nice, friendly; short for *sympathique*) ends in *-a* but works like an *-e*
adjective: *un homme sympa, une femme sympa*. In the plural it's usually written *sympas*:
*des gens sympas*.

### Invariable adjectives

Some adjectives never change. They are **[[invariable]]**. At this level, the main ones are
*marron* (brown) and *super* (great, lesson 21): *des sacs marron* (brown bags), *une fille super* (a great girl).
*Marron* means "chestnut", and colours named after things usually don't change. *Rose* (pink)
is an exception: it agrees in the plural (*des portes roses*).

## Colours

| French | English | feminine | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *rouge* | red | *rouge* | *une porte rouge* |
| *bleu* | blue | *bleue* | *une chaise bleue* |
| *vert* | green | *verte* | *une table verte* |
| *jaune* | yellow | *jaune* | *une fenêtre jaune* |
| *noir* | black | *noire* | *une porte noire* |
| *blanc* | white | *blanche* | *une maison blanche* |
| *gris* | grey | *grise* | *une table grise* |
| *marron* | brown | *marron* | *une chaise marron* |
| *rose* | pink | *rose* | *une chambre rose* |

*La couleur* (colour) is feminine: *De quelle couleur est le sac ?* — What colour is the bag?
(*quelle*, lesson 11.)

![Nine colour swatches in three rows, each labeled: rouge, bleu, vert; jaune, noir, blanc; gris, marron, rose.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Where the adjective goes

Most French adjectives come *after* the noun, the opposite of English:

- *un livre intéressant* — an interesting book
- *une langue difficile* — a difficult language
- *un sac rouge* — a red bag (colours always go after)
- *une amie canadienne* — a Canadian friend (nationalities always go after)

A short list of very common adjectives comes *before* the noun. A memory hook many
learners use is BAGS: Beauty, Age, Good and bad, Size.

| B: beauty | A: age | G: good and bad | S: size |
|---|---|---|---|
| *beau, joli* | *jeune, vieux, nouveau* | *bon, mauvais* | *grand, petit* |

- *une jolie maison* — a pretty house
- *un jeune homme* — a young man
- *un bon livre* — a good book
- *une petite chambre* — a small bedroom
- *un grand appartement* — a big flat

![A chart with a noun in the middle. Before the noun: the BAGS adjectives, beau and joli (beauty), jeune, vieux and nouveau (age), bon and mauvais (good and bad), grand and petit (size), with the example une petite maison. After the noun: colours, nationalities and most other adjectives, with the examples une maison blanche and un livre intéressant. Both together: une petite maison blanche.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

You can use both at once: *une petite maison blanche* (a small white house), *un bon film
français* (a good French film).

After *être*, the position question disappears: *La maison est petite. Le film est bon.*

### beau, vieux, nouveau: three special forms

*Beau* (beautiful, handsome), *vieux* (old) and *nouveau* (new) have a second masculine form
for nouns that start with a vowel or mute h, so the sounds run smoothly:

| | masculine | masculine before a vowel | feminine | masculine plural | feminine plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| beautiful | *un beau livre* | *un bel appartement* | *une belle maison* | *de beaux livres* | *de belles maisons* |
| old | *un vieux lit* | *un vieil homme* | *une vieille porte* | *de vieux lits* | *de vieilles portes* |
| new | *un nouveau sac* | *un nouvel ordinateur* | *une nouvelle chaise* | *de nouveaux sacs* | *de nouvelles chaises* |

*Bel, vieil, nouvel* sound exactly like *belle, vieille, nouvelle*. In the plural, *-eau*
adds *-x* (*beaux, nouveaux*), like the nouns in lesson 5, and *vieux* doesn't change.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing beau, bel, belle, beaux or belles
  accDescr: If the noun is plural, use beaux for masculine nouns and belles for feminine ones. If it is singular and feminine, use belle. If it is singular and masculine, use bel before a vowel or mute h, as in un bel appartement, and beau otherwise, as in un beau livre. Vieux and nouveau work the same way, with vieil and nouvel before a vowel.
  A{"Plural noun?"} -- "yes" --> P{"Masculine or feminine?"}
  P -- "masculine" --> P1["beaux: de beaux livres"]
  P -- "feminine" --> P2["belles: de belles maisons"]
  A -- "no" --> S{"Masculine or feminine?"}
  S -- "feminine" --> S1["belle: une belle maison"]
  S -- "masculine" --> V{"Starts with a vowel or mute h?"}
  V -- "yes" --> V1["bel: un bel appartement"]
  V -- "no" --> V2["beau: un beau livre"]
```

### des becomes de before an adjective

You may have noticed *de beaux livres* above. In careful writing, *des* becomes *de* when a
plural adjective comes before the noun: *de petites chambres, de bons amis*. In everyday
speech many people keep *des* (*des petites chambres*), and you will hear both. After the
noun, nothing changes: *des chambres bleues*.

## Very, quite, too: très, assez, trop

These go before the adjective:

- *très* (very): *La cuisine est très petite.*
- *assez* (quite, fairly): *Le français est assez facile.*
- *trop* (too): *La chambre est trop petite.* (*trop* means "too much", not "very"; it's a
  complaint.)

*Assez* also means "enough": *C'est assez grand pour nous* (it's big enough for us). Context
tells you which.

*Mais* (but) joins two ideas: *L'appartement est petit, mais il est joli.*

## People: l'homme, le garçon, les gens

- *l'homme* (man; masculine, mute *h*: *un homme, les_hommes*), and *la femme* (woman, from
  lesson 6)
- *le garçon* (boy), and *la fille* (girl, from lesson 6)
- *les gens* (people): always plural, and the adjectives with it are masculine plural:
  *Les gens sont gentils.*

*Garçon* can also mean "waiter" in a café, but calling out *Garçon !* now sounds old-fashioned
and many people find it rude; call a waiter *Monsieur* (lesson 11 has the usual word for
waiter).

## Reading: Léa's message

Léa has just moved to Nantes. She writes to her friend Max.

> Salut Max !
>
> Mon nouvel appartement est petit, mais il est très joli. Il y a une grande fenêtre dans le salon et une cuisine jaune. La chambre est assez petite et le lit est trop vieux ! Mes voisins sont sympas : il y a une vieille dame très gentille et un jeune homme, Malik. Il est étudiant et il chante beaucoup, mais il chante bien ! À Nantes, les gens sont gentils et la ville est belle. Je suis heureuse ici.
>
> Bises, Léa

Translation:

> Hi Max!
>
> My new flat is small, but it's very pretty. There's a big window in the living room and a
> yellow kitchen. The bedroom is quite small and the bed is too old! My neighbours are nice:
> there's a very kind old lady and a young man, Malik. He's a student and he sings a lot, but
> he sings well! In Nantes, people are kind and the city is beautiful. I'm happy here.
>
> Love, Léa

(*les voisins* = neighbours; *une dame* = a lady; *Bises* = love, at the end of a message,
lesson 23. Notice *nouvel appartement*, *heureuse* because Léa is a woman, and *gentils* for
*les gens*.)

## Pronunciation

- *blanc / blanche*: "blahn" (nasal, no *c* sound) / "blahnsh".
- *bon / bonne*: "bohn" is nasal; *bonne* is "bun" with a clear *n* and no nasal.
- *gentil / gentille*: zhahn-TEE / zhahn-TEE-y. The *l* of *gentil* is silent.
- *vieux / vieille*: vyuh / vyay. *Vieil* also sounds like "vyay".
- *heureux*: ur-RUH, with two rounded vowels; *heureuse*: ur-RUHZ.
- Liaison after a BAGS adjective: *un petit_ami* (puh-tee-ta-MEE), *un grand_homme*
  (grahn-TOM: the *d* links as a *t*), *un bon_ami* (bo-na-MEE: the vowel loses its nasal).

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the feminine: *une petite maison*, not ~~une petit maison~~; *Elle est
  heureuse*, not ~~elle est heureux~~.
- Putting colours before the noun: *une porte rouge*, never ~~une rouge porte~~.
- Putting BAGS adjectives after: *un petit sac* is normal; *un sac petit* sounds odd.
- Writing ~~un beau appartement~~ or ~~un nouveau ordinateur~~: before a vowel, *bel, nouvel,
  vieil*.
- Adding *-s* to *marron*: *des sacs marron*.
- Using *trop* for "very": *très bon* is a compliment, *trop bon* is "too good" (though young
  people say *trop bien* for "really great" in slang).
- Treating *les gens* as singular: *Les gens sont sympas*, with *sont*.

## Key points

- Adjectives agree: + *e* (feminine), + *s* (plural), + *es* (feminine plural). Adjectives in
  *-e* don't add another *e*.
- You often hear the feminine: *petit / petite, grand / grande*.
- Irregular: *bon → bonne, gentil → gentille, blanc → blanche, heureux → heureuse*. *Marron*
  never changes.
- Most adjectives, and all colours and nationalities, go after the noun. BAGS go before:
  *beau, joli, jeune, vieux, nouveau, bon, mauvais, grand, petit*.
- *bel, vieil, nouvel* before a masculine vowel noun.
- *très* (very), *assez* (quite, enough), *trop* (too); *mais* (but).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Guessing gender: endings and feminine job titles
lessons.body:
## Can you guess the gender?

In lesson 5 you learned the golden rule: learn every noun with its article, because the
object itself doesn't tell you whether the word is masculine or feminine. That rule still
holds. But French isn't completely random. The *end* of a noun is often a strong clue to its
gender, much stronger than its meaning. Once you know a handful of endings, you can make a
good guess about a word you've never seen, and you'll remember the genders of new words more
easily because they fit a pattern.

This honors lesson teaches the endings that work best, the famous exceptions, and then the
other side of gender: words for people, where grammar meets real life. How do you say "a
female engineer" or "a female author"? The answer has changed in recent decades, and French
speakers don't all agree on it, so this part of the lesson presents current usage and labels
what is still debated.

## Endings that point to feminine

| ending | examples | main exceptions (masculine) |
|---|---|---|
| *-tion, -sion* | *la solution, la question, la télévision* | almost none with *-tion* (rare *le bastion*); *-ion* in general: *l'avion, le camion* (lorry), *le million* |
| *-té* | *la liberté, l'université, la beauté* (beauty) | *l'été* (summer), *le côté* (side), *le comité* |
| *-ette* | *la baguette, la chaussette* (sock), *la fourchette* (fork) | *le squelette* (skeleton) |
| *-ure* | *la voiture* (car), *la culture, la nature* | a few rare words (*le murmure*, murmur) |
| *-ée* | *l'année* (year), *l'entrée* (entrance), *l'idée* (idea) | *le musée* (museum), *le lycée* (secondary school) |

These are very reliable, especially *-tion* and *-té*. The one exception list worth learning
by heart is the short one for *-ée*: *le musée* and *le lycée* are everyday words.

## Endings that point to masculine

| ending | examples | main exceptions (feminine) |
|---|---|---|
| *-ment* | *le bâtiment* (building), *l'appartement, le moment* | *la jument* (mare) |
| *-age* | *le fromage* (cheese), *le voyage* (trip), *le garage* | *la page, la plage* (beach), *l'image, la cage* |
| *-eau* | *le bureau, le gâteau* (cake), *le chapeau* (hat) | *l'eau* (water), *la peau* (skin) |
| *-isme* | *le tourisme, le journalisme* | hardly any |

The *-age* exceptions are the famous ones, and French children learn them too: *la page, la
plage, l'image, la cage, la nage* (swimming). Remember them as a little rhyme: *la page, la
plage, l'image*.

*L'eau* (water) is the most important exception of all: it's feminine (*une eau minérale*,
lesson 9), even though *-eau* words are masculine.

![A chart in two columns. Feminine endings, with an example and an exception: -tion, la solution; -té, la liberté (but l'été); -ette, la baguette; -ure, la voiture; -ée, l'idée (but le musée). Masculine endings: -ment, le bâtiment; -age, le fromage (but la page, la plage, l'image); -eau, le bureau (but l'eau); -isme, le tourisme.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## What about -e?

You may have noticed that many feminine nouns end in *-e*: *la table, la chaise, la porte*.
That's true, but far too many masculine nouns end in *-e* as well for it to be a rule: *le
livre, le téléphone, le problème, le groupe*. Nouns ending in *-ème* or *-me* from Greek are
usually masculine: *le problème, le système, le thème*.

The ending *-e* after a doubled consonant is a better clue: *-elle, -enne, -esse, -ette,
-onne* are mostly feminine (*la vaisselle*, the dishes; *la jeunesse*, youth). And nouns ending
in a consonant or in a vowel other than *-e* lean masculine: *le lit, le sac, le stylo, le
vélo*. But there are many exceptions (*la clé, la main*), so use these as weak hints only.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Guessing the gender of a new noun
  accDescr: First, if you already know the noun with its article, use that. If not, look at the ending. -tion, -sion, -té, -ette, -ure and -ée point to feminine, with exceptions such as l'été and le musée. -ment, -age, -eau and -isme point to masculine, with exceptions such as la page, la plage, l'image and l'eau. A plain -e, or any other ending, is only a weak hint, so look the word up and learn it with un or une.
  A{"Do you know it with un or une?"} -- "yes" --> K["Use that gender"]
  A -- "no" --> B{"What is the ending?"}
  B -- "-tion, -té, -ette, -ure, -ée" --> F["Probably feminine (but l'été, le musée)"]
  B -- "-ment, -age, -eau, -isme" --> M["Probably masculine (but la page, la plage, l'image, l'eau)"]
  B -- "-e or anything else" --> L["Weak hint only: look it up, learn it with un or une"]
```

### Example 1: guessing four new words

You read a sign: *Réservation obligatoire*. A friend mentions *le stationnement* and *la
facture*, and a menu offers *un potage*. What gender is each noun, and how sure can you be?

1. *réservation* ends in *-tion*: feminine, and almost certain. *La réservation* (booking).
2. *stationnement* ends in *-ment*: masculine. *Le stationnement* (parking).
3. *facture* ends in *-ure*: feminine. *La facture* (bill, invoice).
4. *potage* ends in *-age*, and it isn't *page, plage, image, cage* or *nage*: masculine. *Le
   potage* (soup).

All four guesses are right, and the article you heard (*le stationnement, la facture, un
potage*) confirms three of them. When an article is there, it always beats the ending.

### Example 2: spotting the exception

Which is the odd one out: *le garage, le message, la plage, le village*? All four end in *-age*,
so they "should" be masculine, but *la plage* (the beach) is on the list of exceptions. Its
article *la* tells you so. This is why the endings are hints and the article is the fact.

## Words for people: two genders that match

For things, gender is just a label. For people, the grammatical gender usually matches the
person: *le père, la mère; le frère, la sœur*. And many job words have two forms, as you saw
in lesson 7 with *l'étudiant / l'étudiante* and *l'infirmier / l'infirmière*. Here are the
patterns for making the feminine:

| pattern | masculine | feminine | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| same word, only the article changes | *le journaliste, le dentiste* | *la journaliste, la dentiste* | journalist, dentist |
| *-ier → -ière* | *l'infirmier* | *l'infirmière* | nurse |
| *-ien → -ienne* | *le musicien* | *la musicienne* | musician |
| *-eur → -euse* (a verb behind it) | *le chanteur* (*chanter*), *le serveur* | *la chanteuse, la serveuse* | singer, waiter / waitress |
| *-teur → -trice* | *l'acteur, le directeur* | *l'actrice, la directrice* | actor / actress, director, head |
| *-eur → -eure* (no verb behind it) | *le professeur, l'ingénieur* | *la professeure, l'ingénieure* | teacher, engineer |

The *-eur → -euse* pattern goes with nouns made from a French verb you can recognise:
*chanter → le chanteur → la chanteuse*. The *-teur → -trice* pattern is old: it comes from Latin
*-tor / -trix*, which English keeps in rare words such as *aviator / aviatrix*. The last line is the newest, and the one
that was debated.

### Example 3: making female job titles

How do you say each of these about a woman: *le chanteur, le directeur, le journaliste, le
professeur*?

1. *chanteur* comes from the verb *chanter*: *-eur → -euse*. *Elle est chanteuse.*
2. *directeur* ends in *-teur*: *-trice*. *C'est la directrice de l'école.*
3. *journaliste* ends in *-e*: only the article changes. *C'est une journaliste.*
4. *professeur* has no verb *professer* in everyday French: *-eure*. *Elle est professeure.*
   You'll also hear *Elle est prof*, which avoids the question.

Remember the rule from lesson 7: after *être*, no article (*Elle est chanteuse*); after
*c'est*, an article (*C'est une chanteuse*).

## Current usage: how French changed

For a long time, many jobs, especially prestigious ones, had only a masculine name: a woman
was *le professeur*, *le ministre*, *l'auteur*, sometimes with *femme* added (*une femme
médecin*). That has changed:

- Québec led the way: the Office québécois de la langue française recommended feminine job
  titles in 1979. Belgium and Switzerland have their own official guides.
- France: government circulars in 1986 and 1998 asked for feminine titles in official
  texts, and a 1999 government-sponsored guide, *Femme, j'écris ton nom…*, listed them. The
  Académie française, which long preferred *Madame le ministre*, adopted a report on 28
  February 2019 saying there was no obstacle in principle to feminine job names.
- Today *la ministre, la professeure, la directrice, l'ingénieure, la juge* are normal in
  France, in newspapers and official texts alike. Schools are told to use the feminine title
  for a woman who holds a post.

Some forms are still in competition. These are labelled here as "usage varies":

- *l'auteure* or *l'autrice* (author)? *Autrice* follows the *-teur → -trice* pattern and is
  an old word that has come back; *auteure* became common later. In 2019 the Académie noted
  that *auteure* was the more frequent, but *autrice* has been gaining ground since. Both are
  correct.
- *la médecin* or *une femme médecin*? *Elle est médecin* (no article) avoids the choice and
  is the most common. *Une médecin* is increasingly used; *la doctoresse* is old-fashioned.
- Some people, especially older speakers, still say *le professeur* for a woman.

A separate, more heated debate is about **[[écriture inclusive]]** (inclusive writing): ways of
writing both genders in one word with a dot in the middle, as in *les étudiant·es* (male and
female students). Supporters say it makes women visible; opponents say it makes texts hard to
read and pronounce. In France a 2017 government circular excluded these shortened forms from
official texts, and a 2021 circular told schools not to use them, while also requiring
feminine job titles. Many universities, associations and some media do use them. As a
learner, recognise the dot form when you read it; in your own writing, the safe choice is
both words in full: *les étudiants et les étudiantes*.

## Reading: a jobs day at a school

> Vendredi, c'est la journée des métiers au collège Jean Moulin. La directrice, Madame Benali, présente les invités. Il y a une ingénieure, Claire, et un infirmier, Paul. Il y a aussi une chanteuse et un acteur du théâtre de la ville. Le père de Lucas est journaliste et la mère d'Emma est autrice : elle écrit des livres pour les enfants. Les élèves adorent la chanteuse !

Translation:

> On Friday, it's jobs day at Jean Moulin secondary school. The head, Mrs Benali, introduces the guests. There's an engineer, Claire, and a nurse, Paul. There's also a singer and an actor from the town theatre. Lucas's father is a journalist and Emma's mother is an author: she writes books for children. The pupils love the singer!

(*la journée des métiers* = jobs day; *le collège* = secondary school for ages 11–15; *présente
les invités* = introduces the guests; *écrit* = writes, lesson 23; *les élèves* = the pupils.)

## Common mistakes

- Trusting the ending over the article. If you hear *la plage*, it's feminine, whatever the
  *-age* rule says.
- Forgetting that *l'eau* is feminine: *l'eau est froide* (the water is cold).
- Thinking every *-e* noun is feminine: *le livre, le problème, le musée*.
- Making *-euse* from every *-eur*: *le directeur → la directrice*, not ~~la directeuse~~;
  *le professeur → la professeure*, not ~~la professeuse~~.
- Adding an article after *être*: *Elle est actrice*, not ~~elle est une actrice~~.

## Key points

- Feminine endings: *-tion, -té, -ette, -ure, -ée* (but *l'été, le musée, le lycée*).
- Masculine endings: *-ment, -age, -eau, -isme* (but *la page, la plage, l'image, l'eau*).
- *-e* alone is a weak hint: *le livre, le problème*.
- Feminine job titles: same word (*la journaliste*), *-ière, -ienne, -euse, -trice, -eure*.
- Feminine titles are standard in France today (*la ministre, la professeure*); *auteure* and
  *autrice* are both used; the dot of *écriture inclusive* is debated.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Portraits: describing looks and character
lessons.body:
## From adjectives to portraits

In lesson 8 you learned how adjectives agree and where they go: *une petite maison blanche,
un homme heureux, une femme heureuse*. In this honors lesson you put them to work on the
thing people describe most: other people. You'll learn how French talks about hair and eyes
(with a surprise: it uses *avoir* and *les*), some words for character, more irregular
feminine endings, and three adjectives whose meaning changes depending on whether they come
before or after the noun. At the end there's a longer text describing a family photo.

## Hair and eyes: avoir + les

English says "She has long hair" or "He has blue eyes". French uses *avoir* too, but with the
definite article *les*, and the adjective after the noun:
