- *Elle a les cheveux longs.* — She has long hair.
- *Il a les cheveux courts.* — He has short hair.
- *Tu as les yeux bleus.* — You have blue eyes.
- *Mon père a les yeux marron.* — My father has brown eyes.

Some notes:

- *Les cheveux* (hair) is plural in French: one hair is *un cheveu*, and your hair is all the
  *cheveux* together. So the adjective is masculine plural: *longs, courts, blonds*.
- *Les yeux* (eyes) is the plural of *l'œil* (eye), which you'll learn properly in lesson 16.
  The adjective is masculine plural too: *les yeux verts*, but *les yeux marron* (*marron*
  never changes).
- *Court* (short) and *long* (long) come in lesson 15; here they are just for hair.
- The colour words for hair are partly special: *blond* (blond), *brun* (dark brown or
  black), *roux* (red, ginger), *gris* (grey), *blanc* (white). English "red hair" is never
  ~~rouge~~ in French: it's *roux*.
- *Frisé* means curly: *Elle a les cheveux frisés.* Straight hair is *les cheveux raides*.

You can also describe the person directly with *être*: *Elle est blonde* (she's blond, she has
blond hair), *Il est brun* (he has dark hair), *Elle est rousse* (she has red hair). Here the
adjective agrees with the person.

For a beard and glasses, use *avoir* with *une* or *des*: *Il a une barbe* (he has a beard),
*Elle a des lunettes* (she wears glasses). *Les lunettes* is plural only, like English
"glasses".

For build: *grand* (tall), *petit* (short, small), *mince* (slim). French speakers are often
careful with words for weight; *mince* is a compliment, and a polite description often just
avoids the topic.

![A family photo of five people standing in a row. From left to right: a grandfather with grey hair, a beard and glasses; a mother with long curly hair; a father with short dark hair; a girl with red hair in a ponytail; and a small boy with short blond hair. Labels: la barbe, les lunettes, les cheveux longs et frisés, les cheveux courts et bruns, les cheveux roux, les cheveux blonds.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Character: le caractère

*Le caractère* means personality, character. To talk about it, use *être* + adjective:

| French | English | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| *gentil* | kind | *gentille* |
| *sympa* | nice, friendly | *sympa* |
| *drôle* | funny | *drôle* |
| *timide* | shy | *timide* |
| *sportif* | sporty | *sportive* |
| *mignon* | cute, sweet | *mignonne* |
| *intéressant* | interesting | *intéressante* |

- *Ma sœur est drôle et très sportive.* — My sister is funny and very sporty.
- *Mon frère est timide, mais il est gentil.* — My brother is shy, but he's kind.
- *Le bébé est mignon !* — The baby is cute! (*le bébé* is masculine for a girl too.)

*Drôle* comes before the noun with a different meaning: *un drôle de film* is a strange film.
After *être*, it simply means "funny".

## More irregular feminines

Lesson 8 gave you *bon → bonne, gentil → gentille, blanc → blanche, heureux → heureuse*. Most
other irregular feminines follow a few patterns, based on the last letters:

| masculine ending | feminine | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-if* | *-ive* | *sportif → sportive, actif → active* (active) |
| *-er* | *-ère* | *cher → chère* (dear, expensive), *fier → fière* (proud), *premier → première* (first, lesson 19) |
| *-on* | *-onne* | *bon → bonne, mignon → mignonne* |
| *-el* | *-elle* | *naturel → naturelle* (natural), *culturel → culturelle* |
| *-en* | *-enne* | *canadien → canadienne* (lesson 3), *ancien → ancienne* |
| *-eux* | *-euse* | *heureux → heureuse, sérieux → sérieuse* (serious) |

Two traps:

- *roux* (red-haired) becomes *rousse*, with a double *s*, not ~~rouse~~.
- In *-er → -ère*, the feminine always has a spoken *r*. In *cher* and *fier* the *r* is
  already spoken in the masculine, so *cher* and *chère* sound the same (both "shair"); in
  *premier* it is silent, so *premier* (pruh-MYAY) and *première* (pruh-MYAIR) don't.

The doubled *n* (*-onne, -enne*) has a purpose: it tells you that the vowel
before it is no longer nasal. *Bon* is nasal, *bonne* is "bun"; *canadien* ends in a nasal,
*canadienne* in a clear *n*.

### Example 1: describing a person

Describe Sophie: long curly hair, green eyes, slim, funny and sporty.

1. Hair and eyes with *avoir* + *les*, adjectives masculine plural: *Elle a les cheveux longs
   et frisés et les yeux verts.*
2. Build with *être*, adjective feminine: *Elle est mince.* (*mince* ends in *-e*: no change.)
3. Character with *être*: *drôle* ends in *-e* (no change); *sportif → sportive*: *Elle est
   drôle et sportive.*

Full portrait: *Sophie a les cheveux longs et frisés et les yeux verts. Elle est mince, drôle
et sportive.*

### Example 2: two people at once

Now say that Paul and Sophie are both sporty and funny. A mixed group takes the masculine
plural (lesson 8): *sportif → sportifs*; *drôle → drôles*. *Paul et Sophie sont sportifs et
drôles.* If it were Sophie and her sister: *Elles sont sportives et drôles.*

## Adjectives that change meaning with their position

Lesson 8 said that the BAGS adjectives go before the noun and the rest go after. A few
adjectives can go in both places, with a different meaning in each:

| before the noun | after the noun |
|---|---|
| *un grand homme* — a great man | *un homme grand* — a tall man |
| *mon ancien professeur* — my former teacher | *une maison ancienne* — an old house (of historical value) |
| *ma chère amie* — my dear friend | *un restaurant cher* — an expensive restaurant |

The pattern: before the noun the meaning is more figurative (great, former, dear); after the
noun it is literal and describes the thing itself (tall, old, expensive).

- *Victor Hugo est un grand homme.* — Victor Hugo is a great man (his height doesn't matter).
- *Mon frère est un homme grand : il fait deux mètres !* — My brother is a tall man: he's two
  metres tall! (*il fait* = he measures, from *faire*, lesson 13.)
- *C'est mon ancienne école.* — That's my old (former) school.
- *Chère Julie,* — Dear Julie, (the start of a letter; lesson 23.)

Note that *grand* used alone about a person, after *être*, means "tall": *Il est grand.*
Only the position before *homme* gives "great" (*une grande femme* is usually just a tall
woman).

### Example 3: which meaning?

What do these mean? *une ancienne église; une église ancienne; un cher ami; un appartement
cher.*

1. *une ancienne église*: before the noun, "former": a former church (today a museum,
   perhaps).
2. *une église ancienne*: after, "old": an old church, from centuries ago.
3. *un cher ami*: before, "dear": a dear friend.
4. *un appartement cher*: after, "expensive": an expensive flat.

## Reading: the family photo

Inès describes a photo from her grandparents' fiftieth wedding anniversary.

> Voici une photo de ma famille, chez mes grands-parents. À gauche, c'est mon grand-père, Jacques. Il a soixante-quinze ans. Il a les cheveux gris, une barbe et des lunettes. C'est un homme très drôle. À côté de lui, c'est ma mère. Elle a les cheveux longs et frisés et les yeux verts. Elle est professeure et elle est très sportive. Mon père a les cheveux courts et bruns. Il est assez timide, mais il est gentil. À côté de mon père, la fille aux cheveux roux, c'est moi ! Le petit garçon blond, c'est mon frère, Théo. Il a cinq ans et il est très mignon. Ma grand-mère n'est pas sur la photo : c'est la photographe !

Translation:

> Here's a photo of my family, at my grandparents' house. On the left, that's my grandfather,
> Jacques. He's seventy-five. He has grey hair, a beard and glasses. He's a very funny man.
> Next to him, that's my mother. She has long curly hair and green eyes. She's a teacher and
> she's very sporty. My father has short dark hair. He's quite shy, but he's kind. Next to
> my father, the girl with red hair, that's me! The little blond boy is my brother, Théo.
> He's five and he's very cute. My grandmother isn't in the photo: she's the photographer!

(*voici* = here is; *chez* = at the home of, lesson 12; *à gauche* = on the left, lesson 20;
*à côté de lui* = next to him; *la fille aux cheveux roux* = the girl with red hair; *n'est
pas* = isn't, lesson 10; *la photographe* = the photographer.)

## Common mistakes

- Using *des* with hair and eyes: the basic pattern is *Elle a les yeux bleus*. (*Des* or
  *de* appears only when you add more, as in *Elle a de beaux yeux bleus*.)
- Treating *cheveux* as singular: *les cheveux longs*, with plural *-s* on the adjective.
- Saying ~~les cheveux rouges~~ for red hair: it's *les cheveux roux*.
- Forgetting the double letter: *mignonne, naturelle, ancienne, rousse*.
- Mixing up the two meanings: *mon ancien appartement* is the flat you used to live in, not
  an old building.
- Saying ~~un grand homme~~ to mean "a tall man": say *un homme grand*, or *Il est grand*.

## Key points

- Hair and eyes: *avoir* + *les* + noun + adjective (*Il a les yeux bleus*); masculine plural
  adjectives.
- *roux* = red-haired (feminine *rousse*); *brun* = dark-haired; *frisé* = curly.
- *Il a une barbe. Elle a des lunettes.*
- Feminine patterns: *-if → -ive, -er → -ère, -on → -onne, -el → -elle, -en → -enne, -eux →
  -euse*.
- Position changes meaning: *un grand homme / un homme grand; mon ancien prof / une maison
  ancienne; mon cher ami / un restaurant cher*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Food and drink: the partitive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In module 2 you met two kinds of article: *le, la, les* (the) and *un, une, des* (a, some). Food brings a problem neither of them solves. When you say "I eat bread" or "I'd like some water", you don't mean all the bread in the world, and you can't count water. French has a third article for exactly this: the **[[partitive article]]**, *du, de la, de l'*.

You will also learn the two verbs you need at every meal, *manger* (to eat) and *boire* (to drink), the polite chunk *je voudrais* (I would like), and the names of the three meals. By the end you can say what you eat for breakfast and order a drink.

## Food and drink

Learn every word with its article. With *l'*, the gender is hidden, so learn it separately: *l'eau* is feminine (*de l'eau fraîche*, cool water), *l'œuf* is masculine.

| masculine (le) | feminine (la) | l' or plural |
|---|---|---|
| le pain — bread | la viande — meat | l'eau (f) — water |
| le beurre — butter | la bière — beer | l'orange (f) — orange (the fruit) |
| le fromage — cheese | la pomme — apple | l'œuf (m) — egg |
| le lait — milk | | les pâtes — pasta (always plural) |
| le café — coffee; café | | |
| le thé — tea | | |
| le vin — wine | | |
| le jus — juice | | |
| le poulet — chicken | | |
| le poisson — fish | | |
| le légume — vegetable | | |
| le fruit — fruit | | |
| le gâteau — cake | | |
| le chocolat — chocolate | | |

A few notes:

- *le jus d'orange* is orange juice: French builds "orange juice" as "juice of orange".
- *le café* is both the drink and the place where you drink it.
- *les pâtes* is plural in French, so *Les pâtes sont bonnes* — the pasta is good.
- *le légume* and *le fruit* are countable, like *vegetable* in English: *un légume, des légumes*.
- *orange* the colour is invariable: *des chaussures orange* (orange shoes), never *oranges*. Only the fruit takes an *s*.

The three meals are all masculine:

| French | English | Roughly when (in France) |
|---|---|---|
| le petit-déjeuner | breakfast | before work or school |
| le déjeuner | lunch | about 12:00–14:00 |
| le dîner | dinner, evening meal | about 19:30–21:00 |

*Petit-déjeuner* is literally "small lunch"; you will also see it written *petit déjeuner* without the hyphen. Belgium, Switzerland and Québec use the words differently: there *le déjeuner* is breakfast, *le dîner* is lunch and *le souper* is the evening meal. In France, *souper* is old-fashioned or means a late supper.

Here is a French breakfast table, with the words you would use to say "some":

![A breakfast table with six things on it, each labeled: a glass carafe of water (de l'eau), a white jug of milk (du lait), a cup of coffee on a saucer (du café), a baguette on a board (du pain), a block of butter on a dish (du beurre) and a boiled egg in an egg cup (un œuf).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The partitive article: du, de la, de l'

Use the partitive for an amount of something you don't count: some bread, some water, some cheese. English often says "some" or nothing at all; French always needs the article.

| before a | partitive | example |
|---|---|---|
| masculine noun | du | *Je mange du pain.* — I eat (some) bread. |
| feminine noun | de la | *Tu manges de la viande ?* — Do you eat meat? |
| noun starting with a vowel or mute h | de l' | *Elle boit de l'eau.* — She drinks water. |
| plural noun | des | *On mange des pâtes.* — We're eating pasta. |

*Du* is *de + le* squeezed into one word, which French does automatically (you'll see the same thing with *à + le = au* in lesson 12). *De la* and *de l'* never squeeze. In the plural the partitive is the same word as the plural of *un*: *des*.

More examples:

- *Il y a du fromage ?* — Is there any cheese?
- *Le matin, je bois du thé et je mange du pain avec du beurre.* — In the morning I drink tea and eat bread and butter.
- *Les enfants boivent du lait.* — The children drink milk.
- *Nous mangeons du poisson le vendredi.* — We eat fish on Fridays.

### Partitive or un / une?

The question is: are you counting it, or talking about an amount?

- *un œuf* (one egg), *des œufs* (eggs): you count eggs.
- *du pain* (some bread) but *un pain* (a loaf of bread).
- *du café* (coffee, an amount) but *un café* (a coffee: one cup). In a café you order *un café*, *une bière*, *un thé*: one serving each.
- *du gâteau* (some cake, a piece of it) but *un gâteau* (a whole cake).

## Talking about food in general: le, la, les

After verbs of liking and disliking, *aimer, adorer, détester* (lesson 7), you are talking about a food in general, as a category. Then French uses the definite article *le, la, les*, not the partitive:

- *J'aime le fromage.* — I like cheese (cheese in general).
- *J'adore le chocolat.* — I love chocolate.
- *Mon frère déteste les légumes.* — My brother hates vegetables.

Compare the two in one sentence: *J'aime le café, alors je bois du café le matin.* — I like coffee (in general), so I drink coffee (some) in the morning. English says "coffee" both times; French needs *le* for the category and *du* for the amount.

This chart sums up which article to choose for a food:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing le, un, du or de for a food
  accDescr: Start with a food in your sentence. If the verb is a liking verb such as aimer, adorer or détester, use le, la or les. If not, ask whether the sentence is negative; if it is, use de or d', which lesson 10 explains. If it is not negative, ask whether you are counting the food, one or two of them; if yes, use un, une or des. If not, it is an amount, so use du, de la or de l'.
  A["A food in your sentence"] --> B{"Liking verb? aimer, adorer, détester"}
  B -- yes --> LE["le, la, les: J'aime le pain."]
  B -- no --> C{"Negative sentence?"}
  C -- yes --> DE["de, d': lesson 10"]
  C -- no --> D{"Counting it? one, two..."}
  D -- yes --> UN["un, une, des: un œuf"]
  D -- no --> DU["du, de la, de l': du pain"]
```

## manger and boire

*Manger* (to eat) is a regular *-er* verb with one spelling change: in the *nous* form it keeps an *e* after the *g*, *nous mangeons*. Without the *e*, *mangons* would be read with a hard "g" as in *go*; the *e* keeps the soft "zh" sound of *manger*.

*Boire* (to drink) is irregular and worth learning by heart. It has two stems: *boi-* and *buv-*.

| | manger | boire |
|---|---|---|
| je | mange | bois |
| tu | manges | bois |
| il / elle / on | mange | boit |
| nous | mangeons | buvons |
| vous | mangez | buvez |
| ils / elles | mangent | boivent |

- *Qu'est-ce que tu manges ?* — What are you eating? (a question pattern from lesson 11; take it as a chunk for now)
- *Nous buvons de l'eau.* — We're drinking water.
- *Ils boivent du vin rouge.* — They're drinking red wine.
- *On mange à midi.* — We eat at noon. (*on* = we, in everyday speech)

## Ordering politely: je voudrais

*Je voudrais* means "I would like". It is the polite way to ask for something in a shop, café or restaurant. Learn it as a chunk now; the verb it comes from, *vouloir* (to want), is in lesson 19. *Je veux* (I want) exists, but from an adult to a waiter it sounds like a child's demand.

- *Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.* — I'd like a coffee, please.
- *Je voudrais de l'eau, s'il vous plaît.* — I'd like some water, please.
- *Je voudrais du pain avec la soupe.* — I'd like some bread with the soup.

You can also put a verb after it: *Je voudrais manger.* — I'd like to eat.

## Dialogue: Le petit-déjeuner à l'hôtel

Tom is staying in a small hotel. The owner, Madame Roux, serves breakfast. (*Bien sûr* = of course, *frais* = fresh, *Bon appétit !* = enjoy your meal.)

> Madame Roux : Bonjour, monsieur ! Vous voulez du café ou du thé ?
>
> Tom : Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais du café, s'il vous plaît.
>
> Madame Roux : Avec du lait ?
>
> Tom : Oui, un peu. Merci. Il y a aussi du jus d'orange ?
>
> Madame Roux : Bien sûr. Et voilà du pain, du beurre et du fromage.
>
> Tom : Merci beaucoup. J'adore le fromage français !
>
> Madame Roux : Vous mangez des œufs ? Les œufs sont très frais.
>
> Tom : Oui, deux œufs, s'il vous plaît. Le matin, je mange beaucoup !
>
> Madame Roux : Très bien. Bon appétit !

In English:

> Madame Roux: Good morning! Would you like coffee or tea?
>
> Tom: Good morning. I'd like coffee, please.
>
> Madame Roux: With milk?
>
> Tom: Yes, a little. Thank you. Is there orange juice too?
>
> Madame Roux: Of course. And here's some bread, butter and cheese.
>
> Tom: Thank you very much. I love French cheese!
>
> Madame Roux: Do you eat eggs? The eggs are very fresh.
>
> Tom: Yes, two eggs, please. In the morning I eat a lot!
>
> Madame Roux: Very good. Enjoy your meal!

Notice the pattern: *du café, du lait, du pain, du beurre, du fromage* are amounts; *deux œufs* are counted; *J'adore le fromage* is cheese in general. (*Vous voulez* is the *vous* form of *vouloir*: here, "would you like".)

## Pronunciation

- *du* has the French *u* (lips rounded, tongue forward); *de* has a short, relaxed *e*. Keep them apart: *du pain*, *de la viande*.
- *un œuf* ends in a clear *f*: "un-NUF". In the plural the *f* is silent and the vowel closes: *des œufs* sounds like "day-ZUH".
- *le poisson* (fish) has a hard *ss* sound; *le poison* (poison) has a *z* sound. Say *poisson* carefully!
- *le lait* rhymes with *mais*; the *t* is silent. *Le thé* is said "tay": *th* is just *t*.
- *l'eau* sounds exactly like the letter *o*.
- *boivent* ends in a *v* sound: "bwav". *Bois* and *boit* sound the same: "bwa".
- *la viande* has a nasal vowel at the end: "vyahnd". *le pain* is nasal too.

## Common mistakes

- *Je mange pain.* — French needs an article: *Je mange du pain.*
- *J'aime du chocolat.* — After liking verbs, use *le*: *J'aime le chocolat.*
- *Je bois du eau.* — Before a vowel, *de l'*: *Je bois de l'eau.*
- *nous mangons* — Keep the *e*: *nous mangeons.*
- *il bois, ils boient* — *il boit, ils boivent.*
- *Je veux un café.* — Correct French, but blunt. Say *Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.*
- *Un café* when you mean a lot of coffee: *un café* is one cup. *Je bois du café le matin* is the general habit.

## Key points

- The partitive *du, de la, de l', des* means "some" for an amount you don't count: *du pain, de la viande, de l'eau, des pâtes*.
- *du* = *de + le*; *de la* and *de l'* don't change.
- Count it with *un, une, des*: *un œuf, un café* (one cup).
- Liking verbs take *le, la, les*: *J'aime le fromage.*
- *manger*: *nous mangeons*. *boire*: *bois, bois, boit, buvons, buvez, boivent*.
- Order with *je voudrais*: *Je voudrais un thé, s'il vous plaît.*
- Meals in France: *le petit-déjeuner, le déjeuner, le dîner*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Shopping, prices and ne … pas
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you learned to say what you eat and drink. Now you go out and buy it. Shopping needs three new tools: saying no (*Je n'ai pas de lait*), understanding prices (*trois euros cinquante*) and asking for amounts (*un kilo de tomates*). You'll also meet *acheter* (to buy) and the words of the market and the bakery.

## Saying no: ne … pas

To make a French sentence negative, put *ne* before the verb and *pas* after it. This is **[[negation]]**, and the two words wrap around the verb like the bread of a sandwich:

![Two sentences built from word boxes. Je, ne, mange, pas, de viande: the boxes ne and pas are the same colour and a bracket joins them around the verb mange. Below, Il, n', aime, pas, le fromage: ne has become n' before the vowel of aime.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Positive | Negative |
|---|---|
| *Je parle espagnol.* | *Je ne parle pas espagnol.* — I don't speak Spanish. |
| *Elle mange de la viande.* | *Elle ne mange pas de viande.* — She doesn't eat meat. |
| *C'est cher.* | *Ce n'est pas cher.* — It isn't expensive. |
| *Nous avons le temps.* | *Nous n'avons pas le temps.* — We don't have time. |

Before a vowel or a mute *h*, *ne* becomes *n'*: *je n'aime pas, il n'habite pas, ce n'est pas*.

Notice that French has no helper verb like English *do*: *Je ne parle pas* is literally "I not speak not". Never try to translate *don't*.

### ne … jamais: never

Swap *pas* for *jamais* and you get "never": *ne* still goes before the verb.

- *Je ne bois jamais de café le soir.* — I never drink coffee in the evening.
- *Il n'achète jamais de vin.* — He never buys wine.

### What happens to un, une, du, de la after a negative

After a negative, *un, une, des, du, de la* and *de l'* all become plain *de* (*d'* before a vowel). Think of it as "not any": the amount is zero, so there is nothing to count or measure.

| Positive | Negative |
|---|---|
| *J'ai un sac.* | *Je n'ai pas de sac.* — I don't have a bag. |
| *Il y a du lait.* | *Il n'y a pas de lait.* — There's no milk. |
| *Je mange de la viande.* | *Je ne mange pas de viande.* — I don't eat meat. |
| *Elle boit de l'eau.* | *Elle ne boit pas d'eau.* — She doesn't drink water. |
| *J'ai des œufs.* | *Je n'ai pas d'œufs.* — I haven't got any eggs. |

Two things do not change:

1. *le, la, les*: *J'aime le lait → Je n'aime pas le lait.* (You still dislike milk in general.)
2. Anything after *être*: *C'est un livre → Ce n'est pas un livre.* *Ce sont des pommes → Ce ne sont pas des pommes.* Nothing is being counted or measured here; you're just saying what something is.

### In everyday speech: dropping ne

In relaxed conversation, French people very often drop *ne*: *C'est pas cher. J'ai pas de monnaie. Je sais pas.* (*la monnaie* = change, coins; *je sais* = I know.) You need to understand this, because you'll hear it all the time, but write and say *ne* yourself until you're sure of the situation. *Pas* is the word that really carries the "not" in speech.

## Numbers from 100 to 10 000

You know 0–100 from lesson 4. The rest is mostly building blocks:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 cent | 101 cent un | 110 cent dix | 199 cent quatre-vingt-dix-neuf |
| 200 deux cents | 201 deux cent un | 250 deux cent cinquante | 500 cinq cents |
| 1 000 mille | 1 200 mille deux cents | 2 000 deux mille | 10 000 dix mille |

Three spelling rules:

- *cent* takes an *s* when it is multiplied and no other number follows it: *deux cents, cinq cents, deux cents euros*. When another number follows, the *s* goes: *deux cent un, cinq cent vingt*. (*quatre-vingts* in lesson 4 works the same way.)
- *mille* never takes an *s*: *deux mille, dix mille*. And no *un* before it: 1 000 is just *mille*.
- Since the spelling reform of 1990 you may also join every part of a number with hyphens: *deux-cent-cinquante, mille-deux-cents*. Both spellings are correct.

French writes big numbers with a space, not a comma: *10 000* (ten thousand). The comma is the decimal point, which brings us to prices.

## Prices: euros and centimes

A euro (*l'euro*, masculine) has 100 cents (*le centime*). Prices are written with a comma, and the euro sign usually comes after the number with a space: *3,50 €*.

You say the euros, then the word *euros*, then the cents, without the word *centimes*:

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| 3,50 € | trois euros cinquante |
| 1,20 € | un euro vingt |
| 12,99 € | douze euros quatre-vingt-dix-neuf |
| 0,80 € | quatre-vingts centimes |
| 250 € | deux cent cinquante euros |

At a till you will often hear just *trois cinquante* for 3,50 €: when everyone knows it's euros, the word drops. *Euro* starts with a vowel, so the number links to it: *deux_euros, trois_euros, six_euros, dix_euros, vingt_euros, cent_euros*.

To ask the price:

- *C'est combien ?* — How much is it?
- *Ça coûte combien ?* — How much does it cost?
- *Les tomates coûtent combien ?* — How much are the tomatoes?

The answer is usually *C'est 4 euros* or *Ça fait 4 euros* (that comes to 4 euros). *Ça fait* is a chunk here; its verb, *faire*, is in lesson 13. And the reaction: *C'est cher !* (That's expensive!) or *Ce n'est pas cher.* *Cher* has the feminine *chère*: *une boîte chère*. (*Cher* also means "dear", as in *Cher Paul* at the start of a letter.)

## Amounts: un kilo de, une bouteille de

To ask for an amount, use a quantity word + *de* + the noun. The *de* never changes, whatever the gender or number: no *du*, no *des*.

| Amount | Example |
|---|---|
| un kilo de | *un kilo de tomates* — a kilo of tomatoes |
| 500 grammes de | *500 grammes de fromage* — 500 grams of cheese |
| une bouteille de | *une bouteille d'eau* — a bottle of water |
| un paquet de | *un paquet de pâtes* — a packet of pasta |
| une boîte de | *une boîte de chocolats* — a box of chocolates |
| un morceau de | *un morceau de gâteau* — a piece of cake |
| beaucoup de | *beaucoup de sucre* — a lot of sugar |
| un peu de | *un peu de lait* — a little milk |
| combien de | *Combien de pommes ?* — How many apples? |

*Une boîte* is a box, and also a tin or can: *une boîte de tomates* (a can of tomatoes). The 1990 spelling *boite* without the circumflex is also correct. Half a kilo is *un demi-kilo* or *une livre* (a pound, 500 g), which you'll hear at markets.

## acheter: to buy

*Acheter* is an *-er* verb with a twist: when the ending is silent (je, tu, il, ils), the *e* before the *t* gets a grave accent and sounds like *è*. In *nous* and *vous*, where you hear the ending, it stays plain. Lesson 15 explains this pattern fully; for now, learn the forms.

| je | tu | il / elle / on | nous | vous | ils / elles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| achète | achètes | achète | achetons | achetez | achètent |

*J'achète du pain à la boulangerie.* — I buy bread at the bakery. *Vous achetez des fruits au marché ?* — Do you buy fruit at the market?

## Where to shop

- *le marché* — the market: fruit, vegetables, cheese, fish, often outdoors one or two mornings a week.
- *la boulangerie* — the bakery: bread and croissants.
- *le supermarché* — the supermarket.
- *le magasin* — a shop (any shop). *Un magasin de vêtements* is a clothes shop.

At a market stall, the price signs look like this:

![A market stall under a striped awning with five crates. Each crate has a price sign: tomatoes 3,20 € le kilo, apples 2,50 € le kilo, potatoes 1,80 € le kilo, oranges 2,90 € le kilo, and eggs 3,60 € la boîte de 6. The names are written under the crates: les tomates, les pommes, les pommes de terre, les oranges, les œufs.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La pomme de terre* (potato) is literally "apple of the earth"; its plural is *les pommes de terre*. Note *le kilo* on the signs: "per kilo" in French is *le kilo*, with the definite article.

## Dialogue: Au marché

Léa buys fruit and vegetables at another stall. (*Bonne journée* = have a nice day.)

> Le vendeur : Bonjour, madame ! Vous désirez ?
>
> Léa : Bonjour ! Je voudrais un kilo de tomates, s'il vous plaît.
>
> Le vendeur : Voilà. Et avec ça ?
>
> Léa : Les pommes coûtent combien ?
>
> Le vendeur : Deux euros cinquante le kilo.
>
> Léa : Alors deux kilos de pommes. Vous avez des oranges ?
>
> Le vendeur : Ah non, désolé, aujourd'hui je n'ai pas d'oranges.
>
> Léa : Ce n'est pas grave. C'est tout, merci. C'est combien ?
>
> Le vendeur : Ça fait huit euros vingt. … Merci, madame. Bonne journée !

In English:

> Stallholder: Good morning! What would you like?
>
> Léa: Good morning! I'd like a kilo of tomatoes, please.
>
> Stallholder: There you are. Anything else?
>
> Léa: How much are the apples?
>
> Stallholder: Two euros fifty a kilo.
>
> Léa: Then two kilos of apples. Do you have oranges?
>
> Stallholder: Oh no, sorry, I haven't got any oranges today.
>
> Léa: Never mind. That's all, thanks. How much is it?
>
> Stallholder: That comes to eight euros twenty. … Thank you. Have a nice day!

Check the sum: tomatoes 3,20 € + two kilos of apples 5,00 € = 8,20 €. *Vous désirez ?* is a shopkeeper's set phrase for "What would you like?". *Et avec ça ?* (literally "and with that?") means "anything else?", and *C'est tout* (that's all) is how you finish. *Ce n'est pas grave* means "it doesn't matter". Notice *je n'ai pas d'oranges*: *des oranges* became *d'oranges* after the negative.

To pay by card, you can simply ask *Par carte, c'est possible ?* (By card, is that possible?). *La carte* is any card, and also a map and a restaurant menu (lesson 11). *L'argent* is money; it also means silver. *Je n'ai pas d'argent* — I don't have any money.

## Pronunciation

- *cent* sounds exactly like *sans* (without) and *sang* (blood): a nasal "sahn". The *t* is silent except in liaison: *cent_euros*.
- *mille* is "meel": the double *l* is a plain *l*, not the "y" sound of *fille*.
- *le prix* is "pree": the *x* is silent. *Le marché* ends in "shay".
- *combien* is "kom-byan", with two nasal vowels.
- *la boîte* is "bwat"; *la bouteille* is "boo-tay" with a *y* glide at the end.
- *achète* has an open *è*; *achetons* has a weak, almost silent *e*: "ash-TON".
- In speech, *ne* often disappears and *je* shrinks: *Je ne sais pas* can sound like "shay pa".

## Common mistakes

- *Je ne ai pas …* — Elide: *Je n'ai pas …*
- *Je pas mange …* / *Je ne mange …* — You need both parts, around the verb: *Je ne mange pas …*
- *Je n'ai pas du lait.* — After a negative: *Je n'ai pas de lait.*
- *Ce n'est pas de livre.* — After *être*, nothing changes: *Ce n'est pas un livre.*
- *un kilo des tomates* / *une bouteille de l'eau* — After a quantity, just *de*: *un kilo de tomates, une bouteille d'eau*.
- *deux milles, un mille* — *deux mille, mille*.
- *deux cents cinquante* — *deux cent cinquante* (the *s* goes when a number follows).
- *3.50 €* — French writes *3,50 €*, with a comma.

## Key points

- Negation: *ne* + verb + *pas* (*n'* before a vowel). *ne … jamais* = never.
- After a negative, *un, une, des, du, de la, de l'* → *de / d'*; *le, la, les* and anything after *être* don't change.
- In casual speech *ne* is often dropped; keep it in writing.
- *cent* takes *s* only when multiplied with no number after it (*deux cents* but *deux cent un*); *mille* never does.
- Prices: *3,50 €* = *trois euros cinquante*.
- Quantity + *de*: *un kilo de tomates, une bouteille d'eau, beaucoup de sucre*.
- *acheter*: *j'achète, nous achetons, ils achètent*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: At the café and restaurant: asking questions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can already ask a few questions as fixed chunks: *Ça va ?*, *Comment tu t'appelles ?*, *C'est combien ?*. In a café or restaurant you need many more: *Do you have a table? What's the dish of the day? Why not?* This lesson shows the three ways French builds a question, the question words, and everything you need to sit down, order and pay.

## Three ways to ask a yes/no question

French gives you three ways to ask the same question. They mean exactly the same; they differ in how casual or formal they sound.

![Three columns showing the same question, Do you have a table? Intonation: Vous avez une table ? with an arrow showing the voice going up, casual and spoken. Est-ce que: Est-ce que vous avez une table ?, everywhere and safe. Inversion: Avez-vous une table ?, verb then pronoun, written and formal. An arrow along the bottom runs from more casual to more formal.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 1. Intonation

Say the statement and let your voice rise at the end. In writing, add a question mark (French puts a space before it). This is the most common way in conversation.

- *Vous avez une table ?* — Do you have a table?
- *Tu as faim ?* — Are you hungry?

### 2. Est-ce que

Put *est-ce que* (literally "is it that") in front of the statement. The word order doesn't change, so this is the easiest way to ask clearly. It works everywhere, in speech and in writing. Before a vowel it becomes *est-ce qu'*.

- *Est-ce que vous avez une table ?*
- *Est-ce qu'il y a du poisson ?* — Is there any fish?

### 3. Inversion

Swap the subject pronoun and the verb, and join them with a hyphen: this is called **[[inversion]]**. This is the most formal way: you'll see it in writing and hear it in polite set phrases.

- *Avez-vous une table ?*
- *Parlez-vous anglais ?* — Do you speak English?

When the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun is *il, elle* or *on*, French adds a *-t-* between them so the two vowels don't collide: this is the **[[linking t]]**.

- *A-t-il faim ?* — Is he hungry?
- *Mange-t-elle de la viande ?* — Does she eat meat?
- *Parle-t-on français ici ?* — Is French spoken here?

Verbs that already end in *-t* or *-d* don't need it, because their last letter is pronounced in inversion: *Est-il libre ?* (Is he free?) Avoid inversion with *je* at this level (it is rare and often odd); use *est-ce que* instead: *Est-ce que je commande ?* — Shall I order? Inversion with a noun subject (*Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ?*) is in the honors lesson on registers.

## Answering: oui, non and si

*Oui* answers a normal question. But when the question is negative, French uses *si* to say "yes, it is so" and contradict it:

- *Tu n'as pas faim ?* — *Si, j'ai très faim !* — Aren't you hungry? — Yes, I'm very hungry!
- *Vous ne buvez pas de vin ?* — *Non, je ne bois pas d'alcool.* — You don't drink wine? — No, I don't drink alcohol.

Answering *oui* to a negative question sounds wrong to French ears.

## Question words

Most question words can be used in all three styles. *Est-ce que* goes straight after the question word; in inversion the verb and pronoun swap after it; in casual speech the question word often comes at the end.

| | Intonation (casual) | est-ce que | Inversion (formal) |
|---|---|---|---|
| où — where | *Tu vas où ?* | *Où est-ce que tu vas ?* | *Où vas-tu ?* |
| quand — when | *Vous arrivez quand ?* | *Quand est-ce que vous arrivez ?* | *Quand arrivez-vous ?* |
| comment — how | *Tu t'appelles comment ?* | *Comment est-ce que tu t'appelles ?* | *Comment t'appelles-tu ?* |
| pourquoi — why | *Pourquoi tu ne manges pas ?* | *Pourquoi est-ce que tu ne manges pas ?* | *Pourquoi ne manges-tu pas ?* |
| combien — how much | *Ça coûte combien ?* | *Combien est-ce que ça coûte ?* | *Combien coûte le menu ?* |

(*Tu vas* is "you go", from *aller*, the verb of lesson 12; *arriver* is "to arrive".) *Pourquoi* doesn't usually go at the end the way the others do; in casual speech it normally stays at the front. The answer to *pourquoi* starts with *parce que* (because), *parce qu'* before a vowel: *Pourquoi tu ne bois pas de café ? — Parce que je n'aime pas le café.*

### What? qu'est-ce que

For "what" as the object of a verb, use *qu'est-ce que* + statement:

- *Qu'est-ce que vous prenez ?* — What are you having? (*prendre* = to take, to have: lesson 14)
- *Qu'est-ce qu'il mange ?* — What is he eating?
- *Qu'est-ce que c'est ?* — What is it? What's that?

In casual speech you'll hear *quoi* at the end instead: *Tu manges quoi ?* The honors lesson after this module looks at *que* and *quoi* in detail.

### Who? qui

*Qui* asks about people. When "who" is the subject, it is followed straight by the verb in the *il* form: *Qui veut un café ?* — Who wants a coffee? *Qui est-ce ?* — Who is it? Don't mix up the two "what/who" words: *qu'est-ce que* is for things, *qui* is for people.

### Which? What? quel

*Quel* means "which" or "what" before a noun, and it agrees with that noun like an adjective. All four forms sound the same ("kel").

| masculine | feminine | masculine plural | feminine plural |
|---|---|---|---|
| quel | quelle | quels | quelles |

- *Quel vin est-ce que vous avez ?* — Which wine do you have?
- *Quelle boisson ?* — Which drink?
- *Quels desserts aimez-vous ?* — Which desserts do you like?
- *Quel est le plat du jour ?* — What's the dish of the day?

With *être*, *quel* asks "what is …?" and agrees with the noun after the verb: *Quelle est votre adresse ?* — What's your address?

## At the restaurant

| French | English |
|---|---|
| le restaurant | restaurant |
| le serveur / la serveuse | waiter / waitress |
| la carte | the menu (the list of dishes) |
| le menu | the set menu (a fixed-price meal) |
| l'entrée (f) | starter; also entrance |
| le plat | dish; main course |
| le dessert | dessert |
| la boisson | drink |
| l'addition (f) | the bill |
| le verre / la tasse | glass / cup |

Watch the false friend: in France *le menu* is a set meal at a fixed price (for example starter + main course), not the list of everything. The list is *la carte*. If you want to see it, ask *La carte, s'il vous plaît.* And *l'entrée* is the starter, not the main course as in American English.

Useful phrases:

- *Vous avez une table pour deux ?* — Do you have a table for two?
- *Je voudrais réserver une table pour ce soir.* — I'd like to book a table for this evening.
- *La table est libre ?* — Is the table free?
- *Vous avez choisi ?* — Have you chosen? (the waiter, in the past tense of lesson 21)
- *On peut commander ?* — Can we order?
- *Pour moi, une salade, s'il vous plaît.* — For me, a salad, please.
- *Un thé sans sucre.* — A tea without sugar.
- *Un verre de vin rouge / une tasse de café* — a glass of red wine / a cup of coffee
- *J'ai soif. J'ai faim.* — I'm thirsty. I'm hungry.
- *Bon appétit !* — Enjoy your meal!
- *L'addition, s'il vous plaît.* — The bill, please.

*Avoir faim* and *avoir soif* use *avoir*, with no article: French says "I have hunger". *Je suis faim* is a common beginner's mistake. To call the waiter, say *S'il vous plaît !* or *Monsieur ! / Madame !*; *Garçon !* is old-fashioned and rude today.

Here is a café menu. Notice the sections in the order of a meal, and the set menu at the bottom:

![A menu card titled Café du Marché, La carte. Entrées: salade verte 5,00 €, soupe de légumes 6,50 €, œuf mayonnaise 5,50 €. Plats: poulet frites 14,00 €, poisson du jour 16,00 €, pâtes au fromage 12,50 €. Desserts: gâteau au chocolat 6,00 €, tarte aux pommes 6,50 €, assiette de fromages 7,00 €. Boissons: café 2,00 €, thé 3,00 €, jus d'orange 4,00 €, eau minérale 3,50 €, bière 4,50 €, verre de vin 5,00 €. A box at the bottom: Menu du jour, entrée + plat ou plat + dessert 18,50 €, entrée + plat + dessert 23,00 €. At the very bottom: Service compris.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(*la salade verte* = green salad, *la soupe* = soup, *les frites* = chips, fries, *la tarte* = tart, *l'assiette* = plate, *minéral* = mineral.) *Poulet frites* is chicken with chips; *pâtes au fromage* is pasta with cheese.

A meal in a restaurant usually follows these steps:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The steps of a restaurant visit
  accDescr: You arrive and ask for a table with Vous avez une table pour deux. You ask for the menu card with La carte, s'il vous plaît. The waiter asks Vous avez choisi, and you order with Pour moi ... You eat, and people say Bon appétit. You ask for the bill with L'addition, s'il vous plaît. You pay and leave with Merci, au revoir.
  A["Arrive: Vous avez une table pour deux ?"] --> B["Ask for the menu: La carte, s'il vous plaît."]
  B --> C["Order: Pour moi, le menu du jour."]
  C --> D["Eat: Bon appétit !"]
  D --> E["Ask for the bill: L'addition, s'il vous plaît."]
  E --> F["Pay and leave: Merci, au revoir !"]
```

## Dialogue: Au restaurant

Julie and her friend Karim have lunch at the Café du Marché.

> Le serveur : Bonjour ! Vous êtes combien ?
>
> Julie : Deux. Est-ce que la table près de la fenêtre est libre ?
>
> Le serveur : Oui, bien sûr. Voilà la carte. Qu'est-ce que vous buvez ?
>
> Karim : Une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît. J'ai très soif.
>
> Julie : Et pour moi, un jus d'orange. Quel est le poisson du jour ?
>
> Le serveur : C'est du saumon. … Vous avez choisi ?
>
> Julie : Oui. Pour moi, le menu : la soupe et le poisson du jour.
>
> Karim : Moi, je voudrais les pâtes au fromage. Elles sont sans viande ?
>
> Le serveur : Oui, sans viande. Et comme dessert ?
>
> Karim : Pas de dessert pour moi, merci.
>
> Julie : Pourquoi ? Tu n'as pas faim ?
>
> Karim : Non, parce que les pâtes, c'est beaucoup !
>
> Julie : Moi, si ! Un gâteau au chocolat, s'il vous plaît. … Et l'addition, s'il vous plaît.

In English:

> Waiter: Hello! How many are you?
>
> Julie: Two. Is the table by the window free?
>
> Waiter: Yes, of course. Here's the menu. What are you drinking?
>
> Karim: A jug of water, please. I'm very thirsty.
>
> Julie: And for me, an orange juice. What's the fish of the day?
>
> Waiter: It's salmon. … Have you chosen?
>
> Julie: Yes. For me, the set menu: the soup and the fish of the day.
>
> Karim: I'd like the pasta with cheese. Is it without meat?
>
> Waiter: Yes, without meat. And for dessert?
>
> Karim: No dessert for me, thanks.
>
> Julie: Why? Aren't you hungry?
>
> Karim: No, because the pasta is a lot!
>
> Julie: Well, I am! A chocolate cake, please. … And the bill, please.

(*près de* = near, *le saumon* = salmon, *comme dessert* = for dessert.) Julie's *menu* gives her a starter and a main course for 18,50 €; with the juice (4,00 €) and the cake (6,00 €, not part of her menu), she pays 28,50 €. (The three-course *menu* at 23,00 € would have been 1,50 € cheaper, but Julie only decided on dessert at the end.) Karim's pasta (12,50 €) is from the *carte*. Look at the end: Julie asks a negative question, *Tu n'as pas faim ?*, and Karim agrees with *non* (no, I'm not). Then Julie says *Moi, si !*: she contradicts the negative with *si* (I am hungry).

## Pronunciation

- *qu* is always a plain "k": *qui* "kee", *quand* "kahn", *quel* "kel", *qu'est-ce que* "kess-kuh".
- *est-ce que* is said as one word: "ess-kuh".
- In *a-t-il* the *t* links everything: "a-teel". *Mange-t-elle* is "mahnzh-tel".
- *quel, quelle, quels, quelles* all sound the same, except that *quels* and *quelles* link to a following vowel: *quels_enfants* "kel-zahn-fahn".
- *le dessert* has *ss*: "day-SAIR". *Le désert* (desert) has a *z* sound.
- *l'addition* sounds like "la-dee-syon".

## Common mistakes

- *Est-ce que il …* — Elide: *Est-ce qu'il …*
- *A-il faim ? Parle-il ?* — Add the linking *-t-*: *A-t-il faim ? Parle-t-il ?*
- *Oui* to a negative question — use *si*: *Tu ne viens pas ? — Si !*
- *Je suis faim.* — *J'ai faim.* (*avoir*, no article)
- *Qu'est-ce que* for people: *Qu'est-ce que tu cherches ?* asks what; for who, *Qui est-ce que tu cherches ?*
- *Quel* not agreeing: *Quel boisson ?* → *Quelle boisson ?* (*la boisson* is feminine)
- *Le menu, s'il vous plaît* when you want the list of dishes: ask for *la carte*.

## Key points

- Three yes/no questions: intonation (*Vous avez … ?*), *est-ce que* (*Est-ce que vous avez … ?*), inversion (*Avez-vous … ?*).
- Inversion adds *-t-* between a vowel and *il, elle, on*: *a-t-il, parle-t-elle*.
- Answer a negative question with *si* to say yes.
- Question words: *où, quand, comment, pourquoi (→ parce que), combien, qui, qu'est-ce que*; *quel/quelle/quels/quelles* + noun.
- *la carte* = the menu card; *le menu* = the set menu; *l'entrée* = starter.
- *avoir faim, avoir soif*; *L'addition, s'il vous plaît.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: In town: aller, au/à la and the near future
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can buy food and order in a café. Now you leave the café and go into town: to the bank, the museum, the cinema. This lesson gives you the verb *aller* (to go), the small words *au* and *aux* that appear when you say where you're going, and a big reward: with *aller* you can talk about the future, *Je vais visiter le musée* — I'm going to visit the museum.

## aller: to go

*Aller* is the most irregular verb in French, and one of the most frequent. Learn it as a block:

| je | tu | il / elle / on | nous | vous | ils / elles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| vais | vas | va | allons | allez | vont |

- *Je vais à la banque.* — I'm going to the bank.
- *On va au cinéma ce soir ?* — Shall we go to the cinema tonight?
- *Nous allons en France.* — We're going to France.
- *Ils vont où ?* — Where are they going?

Notice the liaison in *nous_allons* and *vous_allez* ("noo-za-lon", "voo-za-lay"). *Vont* rhymes with *sont* and *ont*: *ils sont, ils ont, ils vont* (and *ils font*, lesson 13) — only these very irregular verbs end in *-ont*.

French also uses *aller* for health: *Comment allez-vous ? Ça va ?* (lesson 2) both come from it.

## à + the article: au, à la, à l', aux

To say "to the" or "at the" with a place, French uses *à* + the definite article. Two of the four combinations squeeze into one word. This is called **[[contraction]]**, and you've already met it with *de + le = du* in lesson 9.

![A chart of à plus the article. à + le becomes au (Je vais au cinéma). à + la stays à la (Je vais à la banque). à + l' stays à l' (Je vais à l'hôtel). à + les becomes aux (Je vais aux États-Unis). The two rows that change, au and aux, are shaded. Below: only le and les join with à, the same idea as de + le = du.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Place | Gender | "to the / at the" |
|---|---|---|
| le cinéma | masculine | *Je vais au cinéma.* |
| la banque | feminine | *Je vais à la banque.* |
| l'hôpital | starts with a vowel or mute h | *Je vais à l'hôpital.* |
| les toilettes (the toilets) | plural | *Je vais aux toilettes.* |

So the gender of every place matters: *au musée, au parc, au centre-ville, au marché* but *à la poste, à la pharmacie, à la mairie, à la bibliothèque*, and *à l'église, à l'hôtel, à l'école*. *À la* and *à l'* never contract. The same *au* and *aux* appear with masculine and plural countries (lesson 3): *au Canada, aux États-Unis*.

*À* means "at" as well as "to", so the same forms answer "where are you?": *Je suis au musée.* — I'm at the museum. *Elle travaille à la banque.* — She works at the bank.

### chez: at someone's place

For people, French doesn't use *à*. It uses *chez*, "at the home or shop of":

- *Je vais chez Paul.* — I'm going to Paul's (place).
- *Je suis chez moi.* — I'm at home.
- *Je vais chez le médecin.* — I'm going to the doctor's.

So *à la boulangerie* (to the bakery: a place) but *chez le boulanger* (to the baker's: a person). Never *chez la banque*.

## After a preposition: moi, toi, lui, eux

After *chez, avec, pour, sans* and other prepositions, French uses a special set of pronouns. You know *moi* and *toi* from lesson 2 (*Et toi ?*). These are the **[[stressed pronouns]]**:

| subject | je | tu | il | elle | on | nous | vous | ils | elles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| stressed | moi | toi | lui | elle | nous | nous | vous | eux | elles |

- *Tu viens avec moi ?* — Are you coming with me?
- *Je vais au cinéma avec lui.* — I'm going to the cinema with him.
- *Le gâteau, c'est pour eux.* — The cake is for them.
- *Ce soir, on mange chez elle.* — Tonight we're eating at her place.

When *on* means "we", its stressed form is *nous*: *On va chez nous ?* — Shall we go to our place? *Elle, nous, vous* and *elles* look the same as the subject pronouns; only *moi, toi, lui* and *eux* are new forms. For a group of men or a mixed group, use *eux*; for a group of women, *elles*. Never *avec il* or *pour ils*.

## The near future: aller + infinitive

To say what you're going to do, put the present of *aller* before an infinitive. This is the **[[futur proche]]** (near future), and it's exactly like English "I'm going to …":

![A timeline running from left to right. Maintenant (now) is marked with a red dot and the sentence Je visite le musée. Further right are ce soir, demain and le week-end, with the sentence Je vais visiter le musée above them. Below, the formula: je vais, tu vas, il va … + infinitive.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Je vais visiter le musée.* — I'm going to visit the museum.
- *Demain, nous allons voir un film.* — Tomorrow we're going to see a film.
- *Ce soir, elle va manger au restaurant.* — Tonight she's going to eat at the restaurant.
- *Vous allez acheter du pain ?* — Are you going to buy some bread?

Only *aller* changes; the second verb stays in the infinitive. In the negative, *ne … pas* wraps around *aller*, not the infinitive:

- *Je ne vais pas travailler demain.* — I'm not going to work tomorrow.
- *Ils ne vont pas venir.* — They're not going to come.

Questions work in all three styles of lesson 11: *Tu vas venir ? Est-ce que tu vas venir ? Vas-tu venir ?*

Time words for plans usually go at the start or the end of the sentence:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| maintenant | now |
| aujourd'hui | today |
| ce soir | this evening, tonight |
| demain | tomorrow |
| le week-end | the weekend; at weekends |

*Ce week-end* means "this weekend"; *le week-end* on its own often means "at weekends" in general: *Le week-end, je vais au marché.* *Week-end* can also be written *weekend*.

*Aller* + *aller* is fine too: *Je vais aller à la banque* (I'm going to go to the bank), though *Je vais à la banque* often says the same thing.

## voir and visiter

*Voir* (to see) is irregular:

| je | tu | il / elle / on | nous | vous | ils / elles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| vois | vois | voit | voyons | voyez | voient |

*Je vois l'église.* — I can see the church. *On va voir un film.* — We're going to see a film.

*Visiter* means to visit a place: *visiter un musée, visiter Paris*. For a person, French says *aller voir* (go and see): *Je vais voir ma grand-mère.* — I'm going to visit my grandmother. *Visiter ma grand-mère* sounds like you're touring her like a monument.

## The town

![A map of a town centre with two streets, rue de la République and rue du Marché. Top row: l'église, la mairie with a French flag, le musée with a framed painting, le cinéma with a film strip. Middle row: la banque with a euro sign, la place with a fountain, la pharmacie with a green cross, la poste with an envelope. Bottom row: l'hôpital with an H, le parc with trees, la bibliothèque with books, l'hôtel with a bed.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| French | English |
|---|---|
| la ville / le centre-ville | the town, city / the town centre, downtown |
| le quartier | the neighbourhood, district |
| la rue / la place | the street / the square |
| la banque / la poste | the bank / the post office |
| la pharmacie / l'hôpital (m) | the chemist's, pharmacy / the hospital |
| l'hôtel (m) / le musée | the hotel / the museum |
| l'église (f) / la mairie | the church / the town hall |
| le parc / le cinéma | the park / the cinema |
| la bibliothèque | the library |

Two traps for English speakers. *La bibliothèque* is a library; a bookshop is *la librairie*. And in big cities the town hall is often called *l'hôtel de ville*, which is not a hotel at all. *La place* also means a seat or a parking space: *Il y a une place ?* — Is there a seat?

## Dialogue: Le programme du week-end

Sophie and her neighbour Marc meet in the street on Friday evening. (*le programme* = plan.)

> Marc : Salut, Sophie ! Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce week-end ?
>
> Sophie : Demain matin, je vais au marché, et l'après-midi, je vais visiter le musée d'art. Et toi ?
>
> Marc : Moi, je vais travailler. Mais ce soir, je vais au cinéma avec Lucas et Inès. Tu viens avec nous ?
>
> Sophie : Ce soir ? Non, je ne vais pas sortir. Je suis fatiguée !
>
> Marc : Dommage ! Et dimanche ?
>
> Sophie : Dimanche, je vais voir mes parents. Ils habitent dans le quartier de la gare.
>
> Marc : Ah, chez eux, c'est près de la bibliothèque, non ?
>
> Sophie : Oui, c'est ça. Bon, je vais à la banque maintenant. À demain !

In English:

> Marc: Hi, Sophie! What are you going to do this weekend?
>
> Sophie: Tomorrow morning I'm going to the market, and in the afternoon I'm going to visit the art museum. And you?
>
> Marc: Me, I'm going to work. But this evening I'm going to the cinema with Lucas and Inès. Are you coming with us?
>
> Sophie: Tonight? No, I'm not going to go out. I'm tired!
>
> Marc: Too bad! And Sunday?
>
> Sophie: On Sunday I'm going to see my parents. They live in the station neighbourhood.
>
> Marc: Oh, their place is near the library, isn't it?
>
> Sophie: Yes, that's right. Right, I'm going to the bank now. See you tomorrow!

(*faire* = to do, *sortir* = to go out, *fatigué(e)* = tired, *dommage* = too bad, *la gare* = the station, *près de* = near. *Demain matin* = tomorrow morning; *dimanche* = Sunday, used without an article.) Find the futur proche (*je vais visiter, je vais travailler, je ne vais pas sortir, je vais voir*), *au* and *à la* (*au marché, au cinéma, à la banque*), and the stressed pronouns (*avec nous, chez eux*).

## Pronunciation

- *aujourd'hui*: "oh-zhoor-dwee".
- *la ville* is "veel" (*ll* = *l*, as in *mille*), but *la fille* is "fee-y".
- *eux* is the closed "uh" sound of *deux* without the *d*. *Lui* is "lwee", one quick syllable.
- *l'hôpital, l'hôtel*: the *h* is silent, so the article is *l'* and the liaison is made: *les_hôtels*.
- *la bibliothèque*: *th* is just *t*: "bee-blee-oh-tek".
- *le quartier*: "kar-tyay". *L'église*: "lay-gleez".
- *ils vont* sounds like "eel von"; don't add an *s* sound.

## Common mistakes

- *Je vais à le cinéma. Je vais à les toilettes.* — Contract: *au cinéma, aux toilettes*.
- *Je vais au banque.* — *La banque* is feminine: *à la banque*.
- *Je vais à Paul. Je vais chez la poste.* — People take *chez* (*chez Paul*); places take *à* (*à la poste*).
- *avec il, pour ils* — Use the stressed pronouns: *avec lui, pour eux*.
- *Je vais à visiter …* — No *à* in the futur proche: *Je vais visiter …*
- *Je vais ne pas travailler. Je ne vais travailler pas.* — Wrap *aller*: *Je ne vais pas travailler.*
- *Je vais visiter mes amis.* — For people, *aller voir*: *Je vais voir mes amis.*

## Key points

- *aller*: *vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont*.
- *à + le = au*, *à + les = aux*; *à la* and *à l'* don't change. *Chez* + person.
- Stressed pronouns after prepositions: *moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles*.
- Futur proche: *aller* + infinitive (*Je vais visiter le musée*); negative *Je ne vais pas travailler*.
- *voir*: *vois, vois, voit, voyons, voyez, voient*. *Visiter* is for places, *aller voir* for people.
- Time words: *maintenant, aujourd'hui, ce soir, demain, le week-end*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: À table — eating and ordering the French way
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 9 to 11 you learned the words and grammar for food, shopping and restaurants. This honors lesson looks at the culture around them: when people in France eat, in what order a meal comes, what you actually get when you ask for *un café*, which small shop sells what, and how paying and tipping work. You'll also learn two more ways to order politely, *je vais prendre* and *j'aimerais*.

Everything said here about habits is a generalization: France is a country of 68 million people, and families, regions and generations differ.

## A day of meals

A traditional day in France has three meals at fairly fixed times, plus a snack for children.

| Meal | Typical time | What it often is (simplified) |
|---|---|---|
| le petit-déjeuner | 7:00–8:30 | light and sweet: bread with butter and jam (*une tartine*), a croissant at the weekend, coffee, tea or hot chocolate |
| le déjeuner | 12:00–14:00 | a hot meal; at work or school often in a canteen (*la cantine*) |
| le goûter | about 16:30 | a sweet snack for children after school: bread and chocolate, a biscuit, fruit |
| le dîner | 19:30–21:00 | the family meal of the evening |

The times really are shared. A national time-use survey by INSEE, the French statistics office, found that in 2010 almost half of adults (48 %) were eating at 13:00, and that adults in France spent on average 2 hours 22 minutes a day eating and drinking. The peak for dinner was around 20:15.

*Une tartine* is a slice of bread (often half a baguette cut lengthways) with butter or jam on it. A French breakfast is rarely salty: eggs and bacon belong to hotels for tourists.

## The order of a meal

A full French meal comes in a fixed order. At home on a weekday it may be just a main course and a yoghurt; at a restaurant or a family Sunday lunch you'll see the whole sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The order of a full French meal
  accDescr: A full meal goes in this order. First l'entrée, the starter, such as a salad or soup. Then le plat, the main course of meat or fish with vegetables. Then le fromage, a cheese course with bread. Then le dessert. Last, un café, a small black coffee. The cheese comes before the dessert, not after it.
  A["l'entrée: starter, e.g. salad or soup"] --> B["le plat: main course"]
  B --> C["le fromage: cheese, with bread"]
  C --> D["le dessert"]
  D --> E["le café: a small black coffee"]
```

Two things surprise English speakers. The cheese comes before the dessert, not at the end with crackers. And bread is on the table all through the meal, usually without butter, and is eaten with the food.

In a restaurant you choose either from the *carte* (lesson 11), paying for each dish, or a fixed-price *menu*. Many restaurants also offer *la formule*: a short set menu, typically starter + main course or main course + dessert, especially at lunchtime. *Le plat du jour* (the dish of the day) changes every day and is often the best value.

## Ordering coffee

In France, *un café* is a small, strong black coffee: an espresso. If you want something more like a big coffee with milk, you need another word.

![Four cups side by side. Un café: a small cup of black coffee, a small espresso. Une noisette: a small cup of black coffee with a spot of milk foam, espresso plus a dash of milk. Un café crème: a large cup of light brown coffee, coffee with hot milk. Un chocolat chaud: a large cup of dark brown hot chocolate.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| You say | You get |
|---|---|
| un café (also *un express* or *un expresso*) | a small black espresso |
| un déca | a decaffeinated espresso |
| un café allongé | an espresso with extra water: longer and milder |
| une noisette | an espresso with a dash of milk or foam; *noisette* means hazelnut, for its colour |
| un café crème, or just un crème | a large coffee with hot, frothy milk |
| un chocolat chaud | a hot chocolate |

*Un café au lait* (coffee with milk) is what many people drink at home, often in a bowl; in a café the usual word is *un crème*. Coffee with milk after lunch or dinner is unusual: after a meal, French people take *un café*, black.

## The small shops: les petits commerces

Supermarkets sell everything, but many people still buy some food in small specialist shops. Each shop name is built from the food or the trade, and the shopkeeper's name is related to it:

![Five shop fronts in a row with striped awnings and a window each. La boulangerie shows baguettes and a round loaf. La pâtisserie shows a slice of layer cake and a strawberry tart. La boucherie shows a leg of meat and hanging sausages. La fromagerie shows a wheel of cheese and a wedge. L'épicerie shows jars, a tin, a bottle and some fruit.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Shop | It sells | The person | You go … |
|---|---|---|---|
| la boulangerie | bread, croissants | le boulanger / la boulangère | à la boulangerie, chez le boulanger |
| la pâtisserie | cakes, tarts, pastries | le pâtissier / la pâtissière | à la pâtisserie |
| la boucherie | meat | le boucher / la bouchère | à la boucherie, chez le boucher |
| la charcuterie | ham, sausages, pâté | le charcutier / la charcutière | à la charcuterie |
| la fromagerie | cheese | le fromager / la fromagère | à la fromagerie |
| l'épicerie (f) | groceries: tins, pasta, drinks, some fruit | l'épicier / l'épicière | à l'épicerie |

Many bakeries are also *pâtisseries* (the sign says *boulangerie-pâtisserie*), and a butcher is often a *boucherie-charcuterie*. Remember *à* + place but *chez* + person (lesson 12).

## The baguette

The long, thin loaf called *la baguette* (literally "stick") is the symbol of French bread. On 30 November 2022, UNESCO added "the artisanal know-how and culture of baguette bread" to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. What is protected is not one recipe but a practice: the bakers' skill and the daily habit of buying fresh bread. A basic baguette has only four ingredients: flour, water, salt and yeast (or sourdough).

In a bakery you'll also see *une tradition* or *une baguette tradition*. Since a decree of 1993, bread sold as *pain de tradition française* must be made without additives and must never be frozen during production. It usually costs a little more and has a crunchier crust. You can ask for *une demi-baguette* (half a baguette) or say how you like it: *bien cuite* (well baked) or *pas trop cuite* (not too well baked).

## Polite orders: three levels

You know *je voudrais* (lesson 9). Two more chunks are just as common when ordering:

- *je vais prendre* — "I'm going to have", "I'll have". This is the futur proche of lesson 12 with *prendre* (to take, to have), the verb of lesson 14. It's neutral and very natural with a waiter: *Je vais prendre le plat du jour.*
- *j'aimerais* — "I would like", from *aimer*. It's slightly warmer and more personal than *je voudrais*: *J'aimerais une table près de la fenêtre.*

*Je voudrais* and *j'aimerais* are in the **[[conditional]]**, the "would" form of the verb. At A1 you only need these two forms as fixed chunks.

Roughly, from blunt to most polite (this is a feeling, not a rule):

| Blunt | Neutral | Polite |
|---|---|---|
| *Je veux un café.* | *Un café, s'il vous plaît.* / *Je prends un café.* / *Je vais prendre un café.* | *Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.* / *J'aimerais un café.* |

With all of them, *s'il vous plaît* and a *bonjour* when you arrive matter more than the verb you choose. Lesson 93 says more about *bonjour* in shops.

### Example 1: making an order polite

You are with a friend who doesn't speak French. You want two crème coffees, one croissant and a glass of water. A blunt first try: *Je veux deux crèmes et un croissant et de l'eau.* Let's improve it step by step.

1. Start with a greeting: *Bonjour !*
2. Choose a polite verb: *Je voudrais …* or *Nous allons prendre …* (we're going to have).
3. Count what you can count: *deux cafés crème* (two cups: only *café* takes the *s*; in speech you'll also hear *deux crèmes*), *un croissant*.
4. For tap water, ask for a jug: *une carafe d'eau*. It's tap water, and in a restaurant it normally comes free with a meal. In a café, *un verre d'eau* (a glass of water) is fine.
5. Finish with *s'il vous plaît*.

Result: *Bonjour ! Nous allons prendre deux cafés crème, un croissant et un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.*

### Example 2: working out the bill

At lunch, three colleagues use this board: *Formule entrée + plat 15,50 € — Formule plat + dessert 14,50 € — Plat du jour seul 11,00 € — Café 2,00 €*. (*seul* = on its own.)

- Anna takes the *formule entrée + plat*: 15,50 €.
- Malik takes the *plat du jour* alone and a coffee: 11,00 + 2,00 = 13,00 €.
- Chloé takes the *formule plat + dessert* and a coffee: 14,50 + 2,00 = 16,50 €.

The total is 15,50 + 13,00 + 16,50 = 45,00 €: *quarante-cinq euros*. Malik asks: *L'addition, s'il vous plaît !*

## Paying and tipping

In France, service is included in the price. Since 1987, the prices on a menu must include service, and you'll often see *service compris* (service included) at the bottom of the menu or on the bill. So a tip (*le pourboire*, literally "for drinking") is never required.

What people actually do (a generalization): many leave nothing at a café counter; at a table they often round up or leave a few coins for good service; in a nice restaurant some leave a little more, but well below the 15–20 % usual in the United States. Card payment has made small tips less common. If you hand over a note and want the waiter to keep the change, say *Gardez la monnaie* (keep the change) or *C'est bon, merci.*

To pay for everyone, say *C'est pour moi* (it's on me).

### Example 3: which shop?

Your list for Sunday lunch: *un poulet, une baguette, du fromage, une tarte aux pommes, deux boîtes de tomates*. Where do you go?

- *un poulet*: meat, so *à la boucherie* (chez le boucher).
- *une baguette*: *à la boulangerie*.
- *du fromage*: *à la fromagerie*.
- *une tarte aux pommes*: a cake shop, *à la pâtisserie* (or the *boulangerie-pâtisserie*).
- *deux boîtes de tomates*: tins, *à l'épicerie*.

Five shops, or one supermarket: *Je vais au supermarché !*

## Reading: Le dimanche chez Mamie

> Le dimanche, nous allons chez ma grand-mère. Elle habite dans un petit village près de Lyon. À midi, la table est prête : il y a du pain, de l'eau et du vin rouge pour les grands. D'abord, on mange l'entrée, souvent une salade de tomates. Ensuite, Mamie apporte le plat : du poulet avec des pommes de terre. Après, il y a le fromage. Mon frère adore le fromage, mais moi, je préfère le dessert ! Mamie va toujours chez le pâtissier le samedi : le dimanche, il y a une tarte aux pommes ou un gâteau au chocolat. Enfin, les adultes boivent un café. Le repas dure trois heures. L'après-midi, nous allons au parc… et le soir, on ne va pas manger beaucoup !

In English: On Sundays we go to my grandmother's. She lives in a small village near Lyon. At noon the table is ready: there's bread, water and red wine for the grown-ups. First we eat the starter, often a tomato salad. Next, Granny brings the main course: chicken with potatoes. After that there's the cheese. My brother loves cheese, but I prefer dessert! Granny always goes to the pastry cook's on Saturday: on Sunday there's an apple tart or a chocolate cake. Finally, the adults have a coffee. The meal lasts three hours. In the afternoon we go to the park … and in the evening we're not going to eat much!

(*Mamie* = Granny, *prêt(e)* = ready, *apporter* = to bring, *je préfère* = I prefer, *durer* = to last. *D'abord, ensuite, après, enfin* = first, next, after that, finally: you'll learn them in lesson 17.)

## Dialogue: En terrasse à Lyon

Emma and her colleague Hugo sit on a café terrace at 10 o'clock.

> Le serveur : Bonjour ! Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
>
> Emma : Bonjour. J'aimerais un crème, s'il vous plaît. Et vous avez des croissants ?
>
> Le serveur : Ah non, désolé, nous n'avons pas de croissants. La boulangerie est à côté.
>
> Emma : Ce n'est pas grave. Alors juste un crème.
>
> Hugo : Pour moi, je vais prendre une noisette.
>
> Le serveur : Un crème et une noisette. Très bien. … Voilà !
>
> Hugo : C'est combien ?
>
> Le serveur : Ça fait six euros vingt.
>
> Hugo : Voilà sept euros. Gardez la monnaie.
>
> Le serveur : Merci beaucoup, bonne journée !

In English:

> Waiter: Hello! What can I get you?
>
> Emma: Hello. I'd like a white coffee, please. And do you have croissants?
>
> Waiter: Oh no, sorry, we don't have croissants. The bakery is next door.
>
> Emma: Never mind. Just a white coffee, then.
>
> Hugo: For me, I'll have a noisette.
>
> Waiter: A white coffee and a noisette. Very good. … Here you are!
>
> Hugo: How much is it?
>
> Waiter: That's six euros twenty.
>
> Hugo: Here's seven euros. Keep the change.
>
> Waiter: Thank you very much, have a nice day!

(*Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?* = what can I serve you?, *à côté* = next door.) Hugo's tip is 80 centimes. Not every café sells croissants; when one doesn't, the bakery next door is the usual answer.

## Common mistakes

- Ordering *un café* and expecting a large filter coffee: you'll get an espresso. Ask for *un café allongé* or *un crème*.
- Thinking *l'entrée* is the main course: it's the starter. The main course is *le plat*.
- Waiting for the cheese after the dessert: it comes before.
- *Je vais à la boucher.* — The shop is *la boucherie*; the person is *le boucher*, with *chez*: *chez le boucher*.
- Leaving a 20 % tip out of habit: service is already included, so a small tip is plenty.
- *Je veux …* to a waiter: grammatical but blunt. Use *je voudrais, j'aimerais* or *je vais prendre*.

## Key points

- Meal times in France are fairly fixed: lunch around 12–14 h, dinner around 19:30–21 h, and *le goûter* for children about 16:30.
- Order of a meal: *entrée → plat → fromage → dessert → café*.
- *un café* = an espresso; *une noisette* = with a dash of milk; *un (café) crème* = large with milk.
- Specialist shops: *boulangerie, pâtisserie, boucherie, charcuterie, fromagerie, épicerie*; the people are *boulanger, boucher, fromager …* with *chez*.
- The baguette's know-how and culture joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list on 30 November 2022.
- *Service compris*: service is included; a tip (*le pourboire*) is optional and small.
- Polite orders: *je voudrais, j'aimerais* (conditional), *je vais prendre*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Asking questions in three registers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 showed three ways to ask a question: intonation, *est-ce que* and inversion. They mean the same thing, so why does French keep all three? Because each belongs to a different situation. This honors lesson shows you which to use where, how to make the most formal kind of question (with a noun subject: *Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ?*), and how to choose between *quel, qu'est-ce que, que* and *quoi*.

## What a register is

A **[[register]]** is the level of language that fits a situation: the same meaning can be said in a relaxed way to a friend or in a careful way in a letter. English has registers too: "Gonna grab a coffee?" and "Would you care for a coffee?" ask the same thing. In French, questions are one of the places where registers show most clearly.

![Three stacked bands, each showing the same two questions. Formal, written: Où allez-vous ? Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ? Use: formal letters and e-mails, polite requests to strangers. Standard, safe: Où est-ce que vous allez ? Est-ce que votre fils parle anglais ? Use: everywhere, spoken or written. Casual, spoken: Tu vas où ? Ton fils parle anglais ? Use: friends, family, text messages.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

None of these is "wrong". A French teacher writing to a parent uses inversion; the same teacher texting her sister uses intonation. Using the formal style with a friend sounds stiff; using the casual style in a formal letter sounds careless.

## Casual: intonation and the question word at the end

In everyday speech most questions are statements with a rising voice. When there's a question word, it usually goes at the end, where the information would be in the answer:

- *Tu vas où ?* — Where are you going? (*Je vais à la gare.*)
- *Il arrive quand ?* — When is he arriving?
- *C'est combien ?* — How much is it?
- *Tu fais quoi ce soir ?* — What are you doing tonight? (*faire* = to do)
- *Vous êtes d'où ?* — Where are you from?

Notice *quoi*: in casual speech, "what" at the end of a question is *quoi*, never *que*. *Quoi ?* on its own also means "What?" when you didn't hear; it's casual, and *Pardon ?* or *Comment ?* is politer.

You'll also hear the question word at the front with no inversion: *Où tu vas ? Pourquoi tu ris ?* (*rire* = to laugh). This is very common in speech but avoided in writing. *Pourquoi* is the exception to the "at the end" habit: it usually stays at the front, *Pourquoi tu ne viens pas ?*

Two little tags turn a statement into a check question:

- *n'est-ce pas ?* — isn't it?, right? (neutral to formal): *Vous êtes français, n'est-ce pas ?*
- *hein ?* — eh?, right? (very casual): *C'est bon, hein ?*

## Standard: est-ce que

*Est-ce que* works everywhere: in speech, in e-mails, with your boss, at the doctor's. Put it after the question word and keep normal word order:

- *Où est-ce que vous habitez ?*
- *Qu'est-ce que vous prenez ?* (*que* + *est-ce que*)
- *Est-ce que le musée est ouvert ?* (*ouvert* = open)

If you're unsure which register to use, *est-ce que* with *vous* is never a mistake. It's the best default for a learner.

## Formal: inversion

### With a pronoun

You know this from lesson 11: verb and pronoun swap and are joined by a hyphen, with *-t-* between a vowel and *il, elle, on*:

- *Où allez-vous ?* — Where are you going?
- *Va-t-il au marché ?* — Is he going to the market?
- *A-t-elle une voiture ?* — Does she have a car?
- *Y a-t-il une pharmacie près d'ici ?* — Is there a pharmacy near here? (*Y a-t-il* is the inversion of *il y a*.)

*Pourriez-vous* (could you) is a very common polite inversion: *Pourriez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?* — Could you repeat that, please? Like *je voudrais*, it's a conditional, so treat it as a chunk.

### With a noun subject: complex inversion

When the subject is a noun (*votre fils, le train, Marie*), you can't simply swap it with the verb. Instead the noun stays in front, and a pronoun that repeats it goes after the verb. This is **[[complex inversion]]**:

| Statement | Complex inversion |
|---|---|
| *Votre fils parle anglais.* | *Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ?* — Does your son speak English? |
| *Marie a faim.* | *Marie a-t-elle faim ?* — Is Marie hungry? |
| *Les enfants sont à l'école.* | *Les enfants sont-ils à l'école ?* — Are the children at school? |
| *Le train arrive à 8 heures.* | *Le train arrive-t-il à 8 heures ?* — Does the train arrive at 8? |

The pronoun matches the noun: *fils → il*, *Marie → elle*, *les enfants → ils*. You'll meet this in formal writing, in the news and in official letters; you'll rarely hear it in conversation.

### Simple inversion with a noun: after où, quand, comment, combien, que

After some question words, French also lets you just swap the noun and the verb, with no extra pronoun:

- *Où habite votre fils ?* — Where does your son live?
- *Quand arrive le train ?* — When does the train arrive?
- *Combien coûte le menu ?* — How much is the set menu?
- *Que fait Paul ?* — What is Paul doing?

This is correct and quite common, even in speech, especially when the noun is short. It does not work after *pourquoi* or in a yes/no question: say *Pourquoi Paul part-il ?* (complex inversion), not *Pourquoi part Paul ?*

### Example 1: one question, every register

"When does the train arrive?" (*le train* = the train, *arriver* = to arrive)

1. Casual: start from the statement *Le train arrive* and add the question word at the end: *Le train arrive quand ?*
2. Standard: question word + *est-ce que* + statement: *Quand est-ce que le train arrive ?*
3. Formal with simple inversion (allowed after *quand*): *Quand arrive le train ?*
4. Formal with complex inversion: keep *le train*, put the verb and a matching pronoun after it: *Quand le train arrive-t-il ?* (*arrive* ends in a vowel, so *-t-*.)

All four are correct. Sentences 1 and 2 are what you'll mostly say; 3 and 4 are what you'll mostly read.

### Example 2: building complex inversion step by step

"Do your parents like fish?"

1. Write the statement: *Vos parents aiment le poisson.*
2. Find the verb: *aiment*.
3. Choose the pronoun for the subject: *vos parents* → *ils*.
4. Put the pronoun after the verb with a hyphen: *aiment-ils*. The verb ends in *-t*, so no extra *-t-* is needed (the *t* of *aiment* is pronounced here: "em-teel").
5. Result: *Vos parents aiment-ils le poisson ?*

Now "Does your sister eat meat?": *Votre sœur mange de la viande* → *mange* ends in *-e* → *Votre sœur mange-t-elle de la viande ?*

## What? quel, qu'est-ce que, que or quoi

Four words translate English "what", and the choice depends on grammar and on register.

| Word | When | Example |
|---|---|---|
| quel (quelle, quels, quelles) | before a noun, or before *être* + noun | *Quel vin aimez-vous ? Quelle est votre adresse ?* |
| qu'est-ce que | before a subject and verb (standard) | *Qu'est-ce que vous voulez ?* |
| que | before an inverted verb (formal) | *Que voulez-vous ?* |
| quoi | at the end, or alone (casual) | *Vous voulez quoi ? Quoi ?* |

So "What do you want?" goes *Vous voulez quoi ?* (casual) → *Qu'est-ce que vous voulez ?* (standard) → *Que voulez-vous ?* (formal). *Que* must always be followed by inversion: *Que tu veux ?* is wrong.

*Quel* asks "which one / what" about a noun: *Quel est votre plat préféré ?* (What's your favourite dish?). Don't use *qu'est-ce que* there: *Qu'est-ce que est votre nom ?* is wrong; say *Quel est votre nom ?*

### Example 3: choosing the register

Which question fits each situation?

1. You text a friend to ask whether she's coming tonight. Casual: *Tu viens ce soir ?* (*venir* = to come)
2. You write to a hotel to ask whether breakfast is included. Formal or standard with *vous*: *Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ?* or *Est-ce que le petit-déjeuner est compris ?* (*compris* = included)
3. You stop a stranger in the street. Polite but spoken: *Excusez-moi, madame, est-ce qu'il y a une banque près d'ici ?*, or with the polite inversion *Y a-t-il une banque près d'ici ?*

This chart sums up the choice:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which kind of question to use
  accDescr: Ask who you are talking or writing to. With a friend, family member or in a text message, use intonation, for example Tu vas où ? With someone you don't know, or at work, when speaking, use est-ce que with vous. In formal writing, such as a letter or an e-mail to a company, use inversion, for example Où allez-vous ? If you are not sure, est-ce que with vous is always safe.
  A{"Who is it for?"} -- "friend, family, text" --> B["Intonation: Tu vas où ?"]
  A -- "stranger or work, speaking" --> C["est-ce que + vous: Où est-ce que vous allez ?"]
  A -- "formal letter or e-mail" --> D["Inversion: Où allez-vous ?"]
  A -- "not sure" --> C
```

## Questions in the DELF A1

In the speaking part of the DELF A1, you talk with an examiner you don't know, and one task asks you to put questions to them (lesson 24 describes the whole exam). Use *vous* unless the examiner invites you to say *tu*. Questions with *est-ce que* are correct and natural there; a few inversions with *vous* (*Avez-vous … ? Aimez-vous … ?*) are fine too. What matters most is that each question is clear and correct, not that it's formal.

## Reading: two messages

An e-mail to a hotel:

> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> Je voudrais réserver une chambre pour deux personnes, du 12 au 14 mai. Avez-vous une chambre libre ? Quel est le prix pour une nuit ? Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ? Y a-t-il un parking ?
>
