> Merci d'avance. Cordialement,
>
> Anne Martin

A text message from Anne to her friend:

> Salut Léo ! Tu fais quoi samedi ? On va au musée avec Lisa, tu viens ? On mange où après ? Il y a une pizzeria sympa à côté, hein ?

In English. The e-mail: "Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to book a room for two people, from 12 to 14 May. Do you have a room available? What is the price for one night? Is breakfast included? Is there a car park? Thank you in advance. Kind regards, Anne Martin." The text: "Hi Léo! What are you doing on Saturday? We're going to the museum with Lisa, are you coming? Where shall we eat afterwards? There's a nice pizzeria next door, right?"

(*la nuit* = night, *le parking* = car park, *merci d'avance* = thanks in advance, *cordialement* = kind regards, *samedi* = Saturday.) The same writer uses pronoun inversion (*Avez-vous*), complex inversion (*Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris*) and *Y a-t-il* in the e-mail, and intonation, *quoi* and *où* at the end, and *hein* in the text.

## Common mistakes

- *Votre fils parle-il anglais ?* — Add *-t-*: *parle-t-il*.
- *Parle votre fils anglais ?* — In a yes/no question, keep the noun first: *Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ?*
- *Est-ce que tu vas où ?* — Don't mix styles: *Où est-ce que tu vas ?* or *Tu vas où ?*
- *Que tu fais ?* / *Tu fais que ?* — *Que* needs inversion (*Que fais-tu ?*); at the end, use *quoi* (*Tu fais quoi ?*).
- *Pourquoi part Paul ?* — After *pourquoi*, use complex inversion: *Pourquoi Paul part-il ?*
- *Qu'est-ce que est ton adresse ?* — Use *quel*: *Quelle est ton adresse ?*
- Using *hein* or *quoi ?* with a stranger: they're casual. Say *n'est-ce pas ?* and *Pardon ?*

## Key points

- Casual: intonation, question word at the end, *quoi* (*Tu fais quoi ?*), tags *hein* and *n'est-ce pas*.
- Standard and always safe: *est-ce que* (*Où est-ce que vous allez ?*).
- Formal: inversion with a pronoun (*Où allez-vous ? Y a-t-il … ?*) or complex inversion with a noun (*Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ?*).
- Simple inversion with a noun works after *où, quand, comment, combien, que* (*Où habite votre fils ?*), not after *pourquoi*.
- "What": *quel* + noun or *être*; *qu'est-ce que* (standard); *que* + inversion (formal); *quoi* (casual, at the end).
- Texts and friends: casual. Strangers and the DELF oral: *est-ce que* with *vous*. Formal letters: inversion.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Free time and weather: faire and jouer
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 took you to the café, the market and around town. Module 4 is about free time and
getting around. This first lesson gives you what you need to talk about your hobbies (*les
loisirs*) and the weather, two of the most common small-talk topics in any language.

Two verbs do most of the work. *Faire* (to do, to make) is one of the five or six most
frequent verbs in French, and it is irregular. *Jouer* (to play) you met in lesson 7; here you
learn the two little words that follow it, *à* for games and *de* for instruments. On the way
you meet *lire* (to read) and *nager* (to swim), the weather (*il fait beau, il pleut*) and the
seasons.

## The verb faire

| | faire (to do, to make) |
|---|---|
| je | fais |
| tu | fais |
| il / elle / on | fait |
| nous | faisons |
| vous | faites |
| ils / elles | font |

Three things to notice:

- *fais, fais, fait* all sound the same: "feh". The *s* and the *t* are silent.
- *Nous faisons* is said "fuh-ZON": the *ai* here sounds like the *e* in *le*, not like *fais*.
- *Vous faites* is one of only three *vous* forms that end in *-tes* (with *vous êtes* and
  *vous dites*). ~~Vous faisez~~ doesn't exist.

*Faire* covers both English "do" and "make":

- *Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?* — What are you doing? / What do you do?
- *Je fais un gâteau.* — I'm making a cake.
- *Qu'est-ce que vous faites ce week-end ?* — What are you doing this weekend?
- *Ils font les courses.* — They're doing the shopping. (*les courses* = the shopping)

## Sports and hobbies: faire de, jouer à, jouer de

French uses three patterns for activities. Which one you need depends on the activity.

*1. faire de + activity.* For most sports and activities, especially ones you do alone or
that aren't really "games": *faire* + *du*, *de la*, *de l'* or *des*. These are the same
little words as the partitive in lesson 9 (*du pain, de la viande*), and they follow the
gender of the noun.

- *Je fais du sport.* — I do sport.
- *Tu fais du vélo ?* — Do you cycle? / Do you ride a bike?
- *Elle fait de la natation.* — She swims (as a sport).
- *Nous faisons de la randonnée.* — We go hiking.
- *Il fait de la musique.* — He plays music / makes music.

*2. jouer à + game or sport.* For games and ball sports you *play* against someone:
*jouer* + *à*, which joins with *le* and *les* exactly as in lesson 12: *au, à la, à l', aux*.

- *Je joue au football.* — I play football (soccer). (Often just *au foot*.)
- *On joue au tennis ?* — Shall we play tennis?
- *Les enfants jouent aux cartes.* — The children are playing cards. (*la carte*, lesson 10)

*3. jouer de + instrument.* For a musical instrument: *jouer* + *de*, which joins with *le*
and *les* into *du* and *des*: *du, de la, de l', des*.

- *Je joue de la guitare.* — I play the guitar.
- *Mon frère joue du piano.* — My brother plays the piano.
- *Tu joues d'un instrument ?* — Do you play an instrument?

The picture shows six activities with the pattern each one takes. Say each aloud as a
sentence about yourself: *Je fais du vélo. Je joue de la guitare.*

![Six picture tiles with captions: a bicycle (faire du vélo), a swimmer in waves (faire de la natation), mountains with a dotted path (faire de la randonnée), a football (jouer au football), a tennis racket and ball (jouer au tennis) and a guitar (jouer de la guitare).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Some sports work with both *faire de* and *jouer à*: *faire du tennis* and *jouer au tennis*
are both correct. *Jouer à* puts the stress on a match or a game today; *faire du tennis* on
the activity in general (*Je fais du tennis le samedi*, I play tennis on Saturdays). If in
doubt, use *jouer à* for ball games and *faire de* for everything else.

This chart sums up the choice:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: faire de, jouer à or jouer de?
  accDescr: A decision chart for talking about activities. First ask whether it is a musical instrument. If yes, use jouer de, as in je joue du piano and je joue de la guitare. If not, ask whether it is a game or ball sport you play against someone. If yes, use jouer à, as in je joue au tennis and je joue aux cartes. If not, use faire de, as in je fais du vélo and je fais de la natation.
  A{"Is it a musical instrument?"} -- yes --> B["jouer de: je joue du piano, de la guitare"]
  A -- no --> C{"A game or ball sport you play against someone?"}
  C -- yes --> D["jouer à: je joue au tennis, aux cartes"]
  C -- no --> E["faire de: je fais du vélo, de la natation"]
```

### In the negative

*Faire du* follows the rule from lesson 10: after *pas*, *du / de la / des* become *de* (*d'*
before a vowel).

- *Je ne fais pas de sport.* — I don't do any sport.
- *Elle ne fait pas de vélo.* — She doesn't cycle.

*Jouer au* does *not* change, because *au* is *à* + *le* (a preposition), not a word for an
amount:

- *Je ne joue pas au tennis.* — I don't play tennis.

## aimer + infinitive

You learned in lesson 7 that *aimer, adorer* and *détester* can be followed by a verb in the
infinitive. That's how you say what you like *doing*:

- *J'aime nager.* — I like swimming.
- *Tu aimes lire ?* — Do you like reading?
- *J'adore faire de la randonnée.* — I love hiking.
- *Il déteste jouer au football.* — He hates playing football.
- *Je n'aime pas faire du sport.* — I don't like doing sport.

English uses "-ing" here; French uses the infinitive. Don't conjugate the second verb:
~~J'aime je nage~~ is wrong. With a thing, use the definite article (lesson 9): *J'aime le
sport. J'adore la musique. Je déteste le froid.*

## lire and nager

| | lire (to read) | nager (to swim) |
|---|---|---|
| je | lis | nage |
| tu | lis | nages |
| il / elle / on | lit | nage |
| nous | lisons | *nageons* |
| vous | lisez | nagez |
| ils / elles | lisent | nagent |

*Lire* is irregular: the singular has no *-e* (*je lis*, *il lit*), and the plural adds an
*s* sound (*lisons, lisez, lisent*, said with a "z").

*Nager* is a regular *-er* verb with one spelling change. In *nous nageons* the *e* stays
after the *g*. Without it, *g* + *o* would sound hard, like the *g* in "go". It's the same
change as *nous mangeons* in lesson 9, and every verb ending in *-ger* does it.

- *Je lis un livre en français.* — I'm reading a book in French.
- *Nous nageons à la piscine.* — We swim at the pool.

## The weather: il fait …

To ask about the weather: *Quel temps fait-il ?* — What's the weather like? Literally, "what
weather does it make?". *Le temps* means both "weather" and "time" (as in "I don't have
time": *Je n'ai pas le temps*).

Most weather expressions use *il fait* + an adjective:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *Il fait beau.* | It's nice weather. It's fine. |
| *Il fait mauvais.* | The weather is bad. |
| *Il fait chaud.* | It's hot. It's warm. |
| *Il fait froid.* | It's cold. |
| *Il fait 20 degrés.* | It's 20 degrees. (*le degré*; always Celsius in France) |

Two kinds of weather have their own verbs, used only with *il*:

- *Il pleut.* — It's raining. / It rains.
- *Il neige.* — It's snowing. / It snows.

And for the sun, French uses *il y a* (lesson 5) with the partitive: *Il y a du soleil.* —
It's sunny. (Literally "there is some sun".)

The *il* in all these is an **[[impersonal]]** subject. It doesn't stand for a person or a thing;
it's an empty subject like English "it" in "it's raining". So the verb is always the *il*
form, and you never say ~~elle pleut~~ or ~~c'est froid~~ about the weather.

To talk about tomorrow, use the near future from lesson 12: *Demain, il va pleuvoir* (it's
going to rain), *il va faire beau, il va neiger*. *Pleuvoir* is the infinitive behind *il
pleut*.

Here is a weather map of France. Read it like a forecast: *À Brest, il pleut. À Marseille, il
fait beau.*

![A simplified outline map of France with five weather symbols, each labelled. Above Brest in the far west, a cloud with rain: il pleut. Near Strasbourg in the north-east, a thermometer with a low blue level: il fait froid. East of Bordeaux in the south-west, a thermometer with a high red level: il fait chaud. In the Alps near the eastern border, a cloud with snowflakes: il neige. North of Marseille in the south, a sun: il fait beau.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Hot and cold: il fait, j'ai or c'est?

English "I'm hot" and "it's hot" use *to be*. French splits them three ways:

- the weather: *Il fait chaud.* — It's hot (today).
- a person: *J'ai chaud. Tu as froid ?* — I'm hot. Are you cold? (with *avoir*)
- a thing: *Le café est chaud. C'est froid !* — The coffee is hot. It's cold!

Don't say ~~je suis chaud~~ for "I'm hot": in casual French it means "I'm up for it", which
is not what you meant.

## The four seasons

| Season | "in …" |
|---|---|
| *le printemps* (spring) | *au printemps* |
| *l'été* (summer) | *en été* |
| *l'automne* (autumn, fall) | *en automne* |
| *l'hiver* (winter) | *en hiver* |

All four are masculine. *L'été, l'automne* and *l'hiver* start with a vowel sound, and they
take *en*: *en été, en automne, en hiver*. *Printemps* starts with a consonant, so it takes
*au* (*à* + *le*). A quick hook: only spring is "au".

![A wheel divided into four quarters, one for each season, with an icon and the phrase for "in" that season: au printemps with a flower, en été with a sun, en automne with a falling leaf and en hiver with a snowflake. Arrows run around the wheel in order.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *En hiver, il fait froid et il neige à la montagne.* — In winter it's cold and it snows in
  the mountains. (*la montagne*, lesson 22)
- *Au printemps, je fais du vélo.* — In spring I cycle.
- *Quelle est ta saison préférée ?* — What's your favourite season? (*préféré*, lesson 15)

## Dialogue: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?

Léa and Hugo work in the same office. It's Friday afternoon.

> Léa : *Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end, Hugo ?*
>
> Hugo : *Je vais faire de la randonnée avec des amis. Tu aimes marcher ?*
>
> Léa : *Oui, mais quel temps fait-il demain ?*
>
> Hugo : *Il va faire beau, mais il va faire froid.*
>
> Léa : *Moi, je n'aime pas le froid. En hiver, je reste à la maison et je lis.*
>
> Hugo : *Et en été ?*
>
> Léa : *En été, je fais de la natation. Je nage beaucoup à la piscine.*
>
> Hugo : *Tu joues d'un instrument ?*
>
> Léa : *Oui, je joue de la guitare. Et toi ?*
>
> Hugo : *Je joue du piano, mais pas très bien ! On fait de la musique ensemble ?*
>
> Léa : *D'accord ! Et s'il pleut, on regarde un film.*

Translation:

> Léa: What are you doing this weekend, Hugo?
>
> Hugo: I'm going hiking with some friends. Do you like walking?
>
> Léa: Yes, but what's the weather like tomorrow?
>
> Hugo: It's going to be nice, but it's going to be cold.
>
> Léa: I don't like the cold. In winter I stay at home and read.
>
> Hugo: And in summer?
>
> Léa: In summer I swim. I swim a lot at the pool.
>
> Hugo: Do you play an instrument?
>
> Léa: Yes, I play the guitar. And you?
>
> Hugo: I play the piano, but not very well! Shall we make some music together?
>
> Léa: OK! And if it rains, we'll watch a film.

(*marcher* = to walk; *je reste* = I stay, from *rester*, lesson 22; *s'il* = *si il*, if it.
*Si* meaning "if" shortens to *s'* before *il* and *ils* only.)

## Pronunciation

- *il fait*: "eel feh". The *t* is silent, even before a vowel in most speech.
- *le temps*: "tahn", a nasal vowel; the *p* and *s* are silent. It sounds the same as *tant*
  (so much).
- *l'automne*: "lo-TON". The *m* is silent.
- *le printemps*: "pran-TAHN", two nasal vowels; the final *ps* is silent.
- *l'hiver*: the *h* is silent, so *l'hiver* and *en hiver* link: "ah-nee-VAIR".
- *la piscine*: "pee-SEEN"; *sc* before *i* is a single *s* sound.
- *le football*: French says "foot-BOL", stressed on the last syllable like every French word.
- *il pleut*: *eu* as in *deux*; *il neige*: "nezh".

## Common mistakes

- ~~Je joue le tennis~~ → *Je joue au tennis.* Games take *à*.
- ~~Je joue la guitare~~ → *Je joue de la guitare.* Instruments take *de*.
- ~~Je fais le vélo~~ → *Je fais du vélo.* *Faire* takes *du / de la / de l'*.
- ~~Il est beau~~ (about the weather) → *Il fait beau.* *Il est beau* means "he is
  handsome".
- ~~Je suis froid~~ → *J'ai froid.* People *have* hot and cold.
- ~~en printemps~~ → *au printemps*; but *en été, en automne, en hiver*.
- ~~vous faisez~~ → *vous faites*; ~~nous nagons~~ → *nous nageons*.

## Key points

- *faire*: *fais, fais, fait, faisons, faites, font*. It means "do" and "make".
- Activities: *faire du / de la / de l'* (*faire du vélo*), *jouer au / à la / aux* + game
  (*jouer au foot*), *jouer du / de la* + instrument (*jouer du piano*).
- After a negative: *Je ne fais pas de sport*, but *Je ne joue pas au tennis*.
- *aimer / adorer / détester* + infinitive: *J'aime lire.*
- *lire*: *lis, lis, lit, lisons, lisez, lisent*; *nager*: *nous nageons*.
- Weather: *Quel temps fait-il ? Il fait beau / mauvais / chaud / froid. Il pleut. Il neige.
  Il y a du soleil.*
- People: *J'ai chaud, j'ai froid* (never *je suis*).
- Seasons: *au printemps, en été, en automne, en hiver*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Getting around: prendre, venir and partir
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 12 you learned *aller* and how to say where you're going (*Je vais à la gare*). This
lesson is about *how* you get there and about travelling: buses, trains and planes, tickets,
stations, leaving and arriving, being on time or late.

You meet three irregular verbs that you will use constantly: *prendre* (to take), *venir* (to
come) and *partir* (to leave). Each one shows a pattern that other verbs share, so learning
these three well gives you several more for free.

## prendre and its family

| | prendre (to take) | comprendre (to understand) | apprendre (to learn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | prends | comprends | apprends |
| tu | prends | comprends | apprends |
| il / elle / on | prend | comprend | apprend |
| nous | prenons | comprenons | apprenons |
| vous | prenez | comprenez | apprenez |
| ils / elles | prennent | comprennent | apprennent |

The three verbs are one family: *comprendre* and *apprendre* are *prendre* with a prefix, so
they change in exactly the same places. Learn one table and you know three verbs.

The singular is easy: *prends, prends, prend*, all said "prahn" (a nasal vowel, no *d*
sound). The plural loses the *d*: *prenons, prenez*, said "pruh-NON, pruh-NAY". *Ils
prennent* has a double *n* and sounds different again: "PREN", like the start of "Prentice".

*Prendre* is used much more widely than English "take":

- *Je prends le bus.* — I take the bus. / I go by bus.
- *Nous prenons le train de 8 heures.* — We're taking the 8 o'clock train.
- *Tu prends un café ?* — Will you have a coffee? (food and drink, as in lesson 9)
- *Je prends le menu, s'il vous plaît.* — I'll have the set menu, please.

*Comprendre* and *apprendre*:

- *Vous comprenez ?* — Do you understand?
- *Je ne comprends pas le plan du métro.* — I don't understand the metro map.
- *J'apprends le français.* — I'm learning French.
- *Mes enfants apprennent à nager.* — My children are learning to swim. (*apprendre à* +
  infinitive = to learn to do something)

## venir and partir: two more patterns

| | venir (to come) | partir (to leave) |
|---|---|---|
| je | viens | pars |
| tu | viens | pars |
| il / elle / on | vient | part |
| nous | venons | partons |
| vous | venez | partez |
| ils / elles | viennent | partent |

*Venir* changes its vowel: *ie* in *je, tu, il* and *ils* (*viens, vient, viennent*), but
plain *e* in *nous* and *vous* (*venons, venez*). *Viens* and *vient* sound the same
("vyan", nasal); *viennent* has a clear *n*: "vyen". You'll see the same split between the
four "outside" forms and *nous, vous* again in lesson 15.

*Partir* drops the last consonant of its stem in the singular: *part-* becomes *par-*, then
takes *-s, -s, -t*. The plural keeps it: *partons, partez, partent*. *Sortir* (to go out,
lesson 22) and *dormir* (to sleep, lesson 16) follow the same pattern: *je sors, je dors*.
These are *not* like *finir* (lesson 16): there is no *-iss-* (~~nous partissons~~).

### venir de: where you come from

*Venir de* + a place says where you come from. It's the same *de* as in *Je suis de Lyon*
(lesson 3), with the same contractions: *du, de la, de l', des*.

- *Je viens de Lyon.* — I come from Lyon. / I'm from Lyon.
- *Tu viens d'où ?* or *D'où viens-tu ?* — Where are you from?
- *Ils viennent du Canada.* — They come from Canada. (*de* + *le Canada*)
- *Elle vient de la gare.* — She's coming from the station.

*Venir* also means "come along": *Tu viens au cinéma avec nous ?* — Are you coming to the
cinema with us?

(You will also hear *venir de* + infinitive: *Je viens de manger* means "I have just eaten".
For now, just recognize it.)

### partir: leaving

*Partir* means to leave or go away. It has no direct object: you leave *from* a place (*de*)
or *for* a place (*à, en, pour*).

- *Le train part de Paris.* — The train leaves from Paris.
- *Nous partons à Nice demain.* — We're leaving for Nice tomorrow.
- *Je pars en vacances.* — I'm going on holiday.
- *Tu pars quand ?* — When are you leaving?

To say "I leave the house", use *Je pars de la maison*, not ~~Je pars la maison~~.

## How do you travel? en or à

*Comment tu vas au travail ?* — How do you get to work? There are two ways to answer:

- *Je prends le bus.* — I take the bus. (*prendre* + *le / la / l'*)
- *Je vais au travail en bus.* — I go to work by bus. (*en* + vehicle, no article)

With a means of transport, use *en* for vehicles you sit *inside*, and *à* when you're on
top of it or on your own feet:

| *en* (inside) | *à* (on top, on foot) |
|---|---|
| *en bus* | *à pied* (on foot) |
| *en métro* | *à vélo* (by bike) |
| *en train* | *à moto* (by motorbike) |
| *en voiture* | *à cheval* (on horseback) |
| *en avion* | |
| *en taxi* | |

![Six transport pictures in two groups. The left group, headed en (inside), shows a bus, a train, a car and a plane, labelled en bus, en train, en voiture and en avion. The right group, headed à (on top, on foot), shows a bicycle labelled à vélo and a walking person labelled à pied.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In everyday speech you'll often hear *en vélo* too. Dictionaries accept both, and *à vélo* is
the form usage guides prefer, so learn *à vélo*. *À pied* never changes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: en or à with transport?
  accDescr: A decision chart for saying how you travel. If you go on foot, say à pied. Otherwise ask whether you sit inside the vehicle. If yes, use en with no article, as in en bus, en train, en voiture, en avion. If you sit on top of it, use à, as in à vélo or à moto. A note says that with prendre you use the article instead, as in je prends le bus.
  A{"On foot?"} -- yes --> B["à pied"]
  A -- no --> C{"Do you sit inside it?"}
  C -- yes --> D["en: en bus, en train, en voiture, en avion"]
  C -- "no, on top" --> E["à: à vélo, à moto"]
  D -.- F["With prendre use le, la, l': je prends le bus"]
```

## Places, tickets and times

*Where you catch it.* French has different words for different stops:

- *la gare* — the train station: *Le train part de la gare de Lyon.*
- *la station* — a metro station: *la station Bastille*.
- *l'arrêt* (masculine) — a bus or tram stop: *l'arrêt de bus*.
- *l'aéroport* (masculine) — the airport.

With *aller* or *être*, they all take *à* (lesson 12): *à la gare, à la station, à l'arrêt de
bus, à l'aéroport*.

*Tickets.* *Le billet* is the ticket for a train or a plane (it also means a banknote: *un
billet de 20 euros*). *Le ticket* is the small ticket for the metro, a bus or a tram, and you
see it on receipts and cinema stubs too. *Un aller-retour* is a return ticket (there and back),
from *aller* (to go) and *le retour* (the return).

- *Un aller-retour pour Lille, s'il vous plaît.* — A return to Lille, please.
- *Un ticket de métro coûte combien ?* — How much is a metro ticket?

*Travelling.* *Voyager* (to travel) is a *-ger* verb like *nager*: *nous voyageons*.
*Le voyage* is the trip or journey; *Bon voyage !* means "have a good trip". *Les vacances*
(holidays, vacation) is always plural in this meaning: *Les vacances sont finies*, *en
vacances* (on holiday). And you pack *une valise* (a suitcase).

*Departure, arrival and time.* On boards and tickets you'll see *le départ* (departure) and
*l'arrivée* (arrival, feminine). Two fixed phrases say whether things run on time:

- *Le train est à l'heure.* — The train is on time.
- *Je suis en retard !* — I'm late!
- *Le bus est en retard de dix minutes.* — The bus is ten minutes late. (*la minute*, lesson 18)

Don't use *tard* (late in the day, lesson 17) here: *en retard* means behind schedule.

## Dialogue: À la gare

Inès and Marc work for the same company. They meet on the platform in Paris.

> Marc : *Salut Inès ! Tu pars aussi à Lyon ?*
>
> Inès : *Oui, pour le travail. J'ai un aller-retour : je pars ce matin et je reviens demain.*
>
> Marc : *Moi aussi. Notre train part à neuf heures dix, non ?*
>
> Inès : *Oui, mais regarde : il est en retard !*
>
> Marc : *Oh non ! Bon, on prend un café ?*
>
> Inès : *Bonne idée. Au fait, tu viens d'où ? Tu es de Paris ?*
>
> Marc : *Non, je viens de Bordeaux. Et toi ?*
>
> Inès : *Je viens de Lille, mais j'habite à Paris. Je prends le métro pour aller au bureau.*
>
> Marc : *Moi, je vais au bureau à vélo. Je ne comprends pas le plan du métro !*
>
> Inès : *Tu apprends vite, tu vas voir. Oh, regarde, le train est là. On y va ?*

Translation:

> Marc: Hi Inès! Are you going to Lyon too?
>
> Inès: Yes, for work. I've got a return ticket: I'm leaving this morning and coming back
> tomorrow.
>
> Marc: Me too. Our train leaves at ten past nine, doesn't it?
>
> Inès: Yes, but look: it's late!
>
> Marc: Oh no! Well, shall we have a coffee?
>
> Inès: Good idea. By the way, where are you from? Are you from Paris?
>
> Marc: No, I'm from Bordeaux. And you?
>
> Inès: I'm from Lille, but I live in Paris. I take the metro to get to the office.
>
> Marc: I cycle to the office. I don't understand the metro map!
>
> Inès: You learn fast, you'll see. Oh, look, the train is here. Shall we go?

(*ce matin* = this morning; *je reviens* = I come back, from *revenir*, lesson 22; *au fait* =
by the way; *vite* = fast; *On y va ?* = shall we go?, a very common chunk.)

## Pronunciation

- *il prend* "prahn", *ils prennent* "pren"; *il vient* "vyan", *ils viennent* "vyen". In
  both verbs the *ils* form sounds different from the *il* form, so listen for it.
- *je pars, il part*: "par". The *s* and *t* are silent.
- *le train*: a nasal vowel, "tran". *En* links to a vowel: *en avion* is "ah-na-VYON".
- *l'aéroport*: "la-ay-ro-POR", four syllables; the final *t* is silent.
- *le billet*: "bee-YEH" (the *ll* sounds like *y*); *le ticket*: "tee-KEH".
- *l'arrêt*: "la-REH"; the *t* is silent.
- *en retard*: "ahn ruh-TAR", the *d* silent.
- *les vacances*: "lay va-KAHNSS".

## Common mistakes

- ~~Je vais en pied~~ → *Je vais à pied*. Also *à vélo*, but *en bus, en train, en voiture*.
- ~~Je prends bus~~ → *Je prends le bus*. *Prendre* needs the article; *en* doesn't
  (~~en le bus~~).
- ~~ils prendent~~ → *ils prennent*; ~~ils venent~~ → *ils viennent*.
- ~~nous partissons~~ → *nous partons*. *Partir* isn't a *finir* verb.
- ~~Je pars la gare~~ → *Je pars de la gare*.
- Mixing up *la gare* (trains) and *la station* (metro).
- ~~Je suis tard~~ → *Je suis en retard*.
- ~~la vacance~~ for a holiday → *les vacances*, always plural.

## Key points

- *prendre*: *prends, prends, prend, prenons, prenez, prennent*; *comprendre* and *apprendre*
  are the same.
- *venir*: *viens, viens, vient, venons, venez, viennent*. *Je viens de Lyon.*
- *partir*: *pars, pars, part, partons, partez, partent* (like *sortir, dormir*).
- *en* + vehicle you sit in (*en bus, en train, en voiture, en avion*); *à pied, à vélo*.
- *prendre le bus* = *aller en bus*.
- *la gare* (train), *la station* (metro), *l'arrêt* (bus); *le billet* (train, plane),
  *le ticket* (metro, bus); *un aller-retour*.
- *à l'heure* (on time), *en retard* (late).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Clothes and stem-changing -er verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 10 you went shopping for food and met *acheter*, with its odd *j'achète*. This lesson
takes you shopping for clothes, and on the way it explains that accent properly. *Acheter*
belongs to a group of **[[stem-changing verbs]]**: regular *-er* verbs whose endings are normal but
whose stem changes its spelling in some forms. Once you see the pattern (a "boot" shape), these
verbs stop being a surprise.

You also learn to point at things with *ce, cet, cette, ces* (this, that, these, those), the
difference between *porter* and *mettre*, and how to ask for your size.

## Clothes

*Le vêtement* is one item of clothing; *les vêtements* means clothes in general.

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *le pantalon* | trousers, pants |
| *le jean* | jeans |
| *la chemise* | shirt |
| *le tee-shirt* (or *t-shirt*) | T-shirt |
| *le pull* | jumper, sweater |
| *la veste* | jacket |
| *le manteau* (*les manteaux*) | coat |
| *la robe* | dress |
| *la jupe* | skirt |
| *le chapeau* (*les chapeaux*) | hat |
| *la chaussure* | shoe |

One trap: *un pantalon* and *un jean* are singular in French. English says "a pair of
trousers"; French just says *un pantalon*. *Des pantalons* means several pairs.

- *Je cherche un pantalon noir.* — I'm looking for some black trousers.
- *Ce jean est trop long.* — These jeans are too long.

*Long* (feminine *longue*) and *court* (short, feminine *courte*) describe length: *une jupe
longue, une robe courte*. For a short person, use *petit* (lesson 8), not *court*.

![A clothes rail with six items on hangers, each labelled: une chemise, un pull, une robe, une veste, une jupe and un pantalon. Under the rail stand a pair of shoes labelled des chaussures, and a hat labelled un chapeau sits on a shelf above.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## porter or mettre?

Both translate as "wear" in some sentences, but they're different:

- *porter* = to wear (what you have on) and also to carry. It's a regular *-er* verb.
- *mettre* = to put, and to put on (the action of dressing). It's irregular.

| | mettre (to put, to put on) |
|---|---|
| je | mets |
| tu | mets |
| il / elle / on | met |
| nous | mettons |
| vous | mettez |
| ils / elles | mettent |

- *Aujourd'hui, elle porte une robe rouge.* — Today she's wearing a red dress.
- *Il fait froid : je mets mon manteau.* — It's cold: I'm putting my coat on.
- *Je porte la valise.* — I'm carrying the suitcase.
- *Tu mets les clés sur la table ?* — Will you put the keys on the table?

*Mets* and *met* sound the same ("meh"), and the plural has a double *t*: *mettons, mettez,
mettent*.

## Stem-changing -er verbs: the boot

Look at *acheter* again:

| | acheter (to buy) |
|---|---|
| je | *achète* |
| tu | *achètes* |
| il / elle / on | *achète* |
| nous | achetons |
| vous | achetez |
| ils / elles | *achètent* |

The endings are the normal *-er* endings. Only the stem changes: *achet-* becomes *achèt-*. And
it changes in exactly four forms: *je, tu, il* and *ils*. Those are the four forms whose
ending is silent (*-e, -es, -e, -ent*). In *nous* and *vous* the ending is pronounced (*-ons,
-ez*), and the stem stays as in the infinitive.

Why? When the ending is silent, the last vowel of the stem carries the stress and sounds like
an open "eh", so French spells it *è* (or doubles the consonant after it, which does the same
job). When the ending is pronounced, that vowel is weak again.

If you draw a line around the four changed forms in a conjugation table, the shape looks like
a boot. Teachers call these **[[boot verbs]]**:

![A conjugation table of préférer in two columns: je préfère, tu préfères, il préfère on the left and nous préférons, vous préférez, ils préfèrent on the right. A thick boot-shaped outline goes round je, tu and il and turns along the bottom to include ils; those four forms have è, shaded. Nous and vous, outside the boot, keep é.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There are four boot patterns at A1, plus one spelling change that affects only *nous*.

### 1. e → è: acheter

*j'achète, nous achetons*. *Se lever* (to get up, lesson 17) and *se promener* follow it.

### 2. é → è: préférer, espérer

Only the *last* *é* before the ending changes; the first one stays.

- *préférer* (to prefer): *je préfère, tu préfères, il préfère, nous préférons, vous
  préférez, ils préfèrent*.
- *espérer* (to hope): *j'espère, nous espérons, ils espèrent*.

### 3. double the consonant: appeler

- *appeler* (to call): *j'appelle, tu appelles, il appelle, nous appelons, vous appelez, ils
  appellent*.

The double *l* does the same job as the *è*: it makes the *e* before it sound "eh". You'll meet
*s'appeler* (*je m'appelle*) in full in lesson 17; now you know why it has two *l*'s.

### 4. y → i: payer, essayer

- *payer* (to pay): *je paie, tu paies, il paie, nous payons, vous payez, ils paient*.
- *essayer* (to try, to try on): *j'essaie, nous essayons, ils essaient*.

For these two verbs both spellings are correct: *je paie* or *je paye*, *j'essaie* or
*j'essaye*. The *-ie* forms are more common in writing, and this course shows them; when you
type an answer, either spelling is accepted. (*Envoyer*,
lesson 23, always changes: *j'envoie*.)

### Not a boot: -cer and -ger (nous only)

*Commencer* (to start, to begin) and *manger, nager, voyager* change only in the *nous* form of
the present, and only to keep the sound of the *c* or *g* soft before *o*:

- *commencer*: *je commence … nous commençons*. Without the cedilla, *co* would sound "ko".
- *manger*: *nous mangeons* (lesson 9), like *nous nageons, nous voyageons*.

| | préférer | appeler | payer | commencer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| je | préfère | appelle | paie | commence |
| tu | préfères | appelles | paies | commences |
| il / elle / on | préfère | appelle | paie | commence |
| nous | préférons | appelons | payons | commençons |
| vous | préférez | appelez | payez | commencez |
| ils / elles | préfèrent | appellent | paient | commencent |

Examples:

- *Tu préfères la robe bleue ou la robe verte ?* — Do you prefer the blue dress or the green
  dress?
- *J'espère que c'est ma taille.* — I hope it's my size.
- *Nous payons par carte.* — We're paying by card.
- *Ils appellent un taxi.* — They're calling a taxi.
- *J'essaie la veste.* — I'm trying on the jacket.
- *Le film commence à huit heures.* — The film starts at eight.

## this, that, these: ce, cet, cette, ces

To point at something, French uses a **[[demonstrative]]** in place of the article. Like an
article, it agrees with the noun.

| | before a consonant | before a vowel or mute h |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *ce pull* | *cet anorak, cet homme* |
| feminine | *cette robe* | *cette écharpe* |
| plural | *ces chaussures* | *ces enfants* (liaison: "say-zahn-FAHN") |

- *Ce* before a masculine noun: *ce manteau, ce chapeau*.
- *Cet* before a masculine noun that starts with a vowel or mute *h*: *cet été, cet hiver,
  cet homme*. It sounds exactly like *cette*.
- *Cette* before every feminine noun: *cette jupe, cette veste*.
- *Ces* for all plurals: *ces vêtements, ces chemises*.

One word covers both "this" and "that". When you need to contrast them, add *-ci* (here) or
*-là* (there) to the noun: *ce pull-ci ou ce pull-là ?* — this jumper or that one?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: ce, cet, cette or ces?
  accDescr: A decision chart for the demonstrative. If the noun is plural, use ces, as in ces chaussures. If it is singular and feminine, use cette, as in cette robe. If it is singular and masculine, check the first sound. Before a vowel or mute h use cet, as in cet homme. Before a consonant use ce, as in ce pull.
  A{"Plural?"} -- yes --> B["ces: ces chaussures"]
  A -- no --> C{"Feminine?"}
  C -- yes --> D["cette: cette robe"]
  C -- no --> E{"Starts with a vowel or mute h?"}
  E -- yes --> F["cet: cet homme, cet été"]
  E -- no --> G["ce: ce pull"]
```

## In the shop: sizes

*La taille* is your size for clothes. The shop assistant asks *Quelle taille faites-vous ?*
(what size are you?), and you answer with *faire du* + the number:

- *Je fais du 38.* — I'm a 38. / I take a 38.
- *Vous avez ce pantalon en 42 ?* — Do you have these trousers in a 42?
- *Vous avez la taille au-dessus ?* — Do you have the next size up? (*au-dessus* = above)

French clothes sizes are numbers (34, 36, 38 …) or letters (*S, M, L, XL*), and they don't
match British or American numbers. Shoes have their own word, *la pointure*: the honors
lesson 16h3 covers sizes and sales in detail.

Useful sentences:

- *Je peux essayer cette veste ?* — Can I try on this jacket? (*je peux*, lesson 19)
- *C'est trop court.* — It's too short. *C'est trop grand.* — It's too big.
- *Je préfère ce manteau.* — I prefer this coat.
- *Je paie par carte.* — I'll pay by card.

## Dialogue: Dans un magasin de vêtements

Clara is shopping for a jacket. The shop assistant is *la vendeuse* (from *vendre*, to sell,
lesson 16).

> La vendeuse : *Bonjour, madame. Je peux vous aider ?*
>
> Clara : *Bonjour. Je cherche une veste pour l'hiver.*
>
> La vendeuse : *Quelle taille faites-vous ?*
>
> Clara : *Je fais du 40.*
>
> La vendeuse : *Voilà cette veste noire en 40. Et ce manteau gris, il est très chaud.*
>
> Clara : *Je préfère les vestes courtes. J'essaie la veste noire.*
>
> La vendeuse : *Alors ?*
>
> Clara : *Elle est un peu longue. Vous avez cette veste en 38 ?*
>
> La vendeuse : *Oui, voilà. Et avec ce pull rouge ? Les clients achètent souvent les deux.*
>
> Clara : *Non merci, j'ai beaucoup de pulls ! Je prends la veste. Je paie par carte.*

Translation:

> Shop assistant: Hello, madam. Can I help you?
>
> Clara: Hello. I'm looking for a jacket for the winter.
>
> Shop assistant: What size are you?
>
> Clara: I'm a 40.
>
> Shop assistant: Here's this black jacket in a 40. And this grey coat, it's very warm.
>
> Clara: I prefer short jackets. I'll try on the black jacket.
>
> Shop assistant: Well?
>
> Clara: It's a bit long. Do you have this jacket in a 38?
>
> Shop assistant: Yes, here you are. And with this red jumper? Customers often buy both.
>
> Clara: No thanks, I've got lots of jumpers! I'll take the jacket. I'll pay by card.

(*Je peux vous aider ?* = can I help you?; *le client* = the customer; *souvent* = often,
lesson 17; *les deux* = both. Notice *elle* for *la veste*: clothes are "he" or "she" by
gender, lesson 5.)

## Québec

In Québec, *magasiner* means to go shopping, and *le chandail* is the everyday word for a
sweater or another knitted top (even a T-shirt). In France you'd say *faire les magasins* and
*le pull*.

## Pronunciation

- *j'achète* "a-SHET", *nous achetons* "ash-TON": the *e* in the middle almost disappears
  when it isn't stressed.
- *je préfère* "pray-FAIR", *nous préférons* "pray-fay-RON": open *è* inside the boot, closed
  *é* outside.
- *j'appelle* "a-PEL", *nous appelons* "a-PLON".
- *je paie* "peh", *nous payons* "peh-YON".
- *le pull*: "pewl", with the French *u*; *le jean*: "djeen", as in English.
- *le tee-shirt*: "tee-sheurt", stress on the last syllable.
- *la chemise* "shuh-MEEZ"; *la chaussure* "sho-SEWR".
- *cet* and *cette* both sound "set"; *ces* sounds "say", like *les*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~je préfére~~, ~~nous préfèrons~~ → *je préfère, nous préférons*. Grave accent inside the
  boot, acute outside.
- ~~j'appele~~, ~~nous appellons~~ → *j'appelle, nous appelons*.
- ~~nous commencons~~ → *nous commençons*. Don't forget the cedilla.
- ~~ce homme~~, ~~ce été~~ → *cet homme, cet été*.
- ~~cet robe~~ → *cette robe*. *Cet* is only for masculine nouns.
- ~~des pantalons~~ for one pair → *un pantalon*.
- ~~Regarde, elle met une robe rouge~~ to describe what she has on → *Regarde, elle porte une
  robe rouge*. *Elle met* means she is putting it on right now.
- ~~Je suis 38~~ → *Je fais du 38*.

## Key points

- Clothes: *le pantalon, le jean* (both singular), *la chemise, le tee-shirt, le pull, la veste,
  le manteau, la robe, la jupe, le chapeau, la chaussure*.
- *porter* = wear, carry; *mettre* (*mets, mets, met, mettons, mettez, mettent*) = put, put on.
- Boot verbs change in *je, tu, il, ils* only: *achète, préfère, espère, appelle, paie
  (paye), essaie (essaye)*. *Nous* and *vous* keep the infinitive's stem.
- *-cer* and *-ger* verbs change in *nous* only (in the present): *commençons, mangeons*.
- *ce* (masculine), *cet* (masculine before a vowel), *cette* (feminine), *ces* (plural).
- *Quelle taille faites-vous ? — Je fais du 40.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Body and health: -ir and -re verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far, almost every regular verb you've conjugated ended in *-er*. French has two more
groups of regular verbs: **[[-ir verbs]]** like *finir* (to finish) and **[[-re verbs]]** like *vendre*
(to sell). Each group has its own set of endings, and once you know them you can conjugate
dozens of verbs.

The topic is the body and health: naming the parts of the body, saying where it hurts (*J'ai
mal à la tête*), saying you're ill or tired, and making an appointment with the doctor. Honors
lesson 16h2 goes further with the doctor and the pharmacy.

## The body

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *le corps* — the body | *la tête* — the head | *l'œil* — the eye (*les yeux*) |
| *l'oreille* (f.) — the ear | *le nez* — the nose | *la bouche* — the mouth |
| *la dent* — the tooth | *le bras* — the arm | *la main* — the hand |
| *le dos* — the back | *le ventre* — the stomach, belly | *la jambe* — the leg |
| *le pied* — the foot | | |

Two plural notes:

- *L'œil* has an irregular plural: *les yeux* (eyes). *Un œil, deux yeux.*
- *Le corps, le nez, le bras* and *le dos* already end in *-s* or *-z*, so the plural looks the
  same: *les bras, les nez*. Only the article tells you it's plural.

![A simple outline of a standing person seen from the front, with labels pointing to the parts: la tête, l'œil, l'oreille, le nez, la bouche, le bras, la main, le ventre, la jambe and le pied.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Where does it hurt? avoir mal à

To say that something hurts, French uses *avoir mal à* + the part of the body, with the
**[[definite article]]** (*le, la, les*), not "my":

- *J'ai mal à la tête.* — I have a headache. / My head hurts.
- *J'ai mal au ventre.* — I have a stomach ache.
- *Elle a mal aux dents.* — She has toothache.
- *Tu as mal à l'oreille ?* — Does your ear hurt? / Have you got earache?
- *J'ai mal au dos.* — My back hurts.
- *Où avez-vous mal ?* — Where does it hurt?

*À* joins with *le* and *les* exactly as in lesson 12: *à + le = au*, *à + les = aux*; *à la*
and *à l'* don't change. The chart walks you through it:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where does it hurt? avoir mal à + body part
  accDescr: A decision chart for avoir mal à. Look at the article of the body part. With le, use au, as in j'ai mal au dos. With la, use à la, as in j'ai mal à la tête. With l', use à l', as in j'ai mal à l'oreille. With les, use aux, as in j'ai mal aux dents.
  A["J'ai mal ..."] --> B{"Article of the body part?"}
  B -- le --> C["au: au dos, au ventre, au pied"]
  B -- la --> D["à la: à la tête, à la jambe"]
  B -- "l'" --> E["à l': à l'oreille, à l'œil"]
  B -- les --> F["aux: aux dents, aux pieds, aux yeux"]
```

Why no "my"? With *avoir mal*, it's already clear whose body it is: *j'ai* says it's mine. You'll
see the same habit later with reflexive verbs (*je me lave les mains*, I wash my hands).

### Feeling ill

- *Je suis malade.* — I'm ill. / I'm sick.
- *Il est fatigué. Elle est fatiguée.* — He's tired. She's tired.
- *J'ai de la fièvre.* — I have a temperature. (*la fièvre* with the partitive, lesson 9)
- *Je prends un médicament.* — I'm taking some medicine.
- *Je dors mal.* — I'm sleeping badly.

*Malade* ends in *-e*, so the feminine is the same. *Fatigué* adds *-e*: *fatiguée*.

## -ir verbs like finir

| | finir (to finish) | choisir (to choose) | réfléchir (to think, to think it over) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | finis | choisis | réfléchis |
| tu | finis | choisis | réfléchis |
| il / elle / on | finit | choisit | réfléchit |
| nous | fin*iss*ons | chois*iss*ons | réfléch*iss*ons |
| vous | fin*iss*ez | chois*iss*ez | réfléch*iss*ez |
| ils / elles | fin*iss*ent | chois*iss*ent | réfléch*iss*ent |

The stem is the infinitive minus *-ir* (*fin-*). The singular adds *-is, -is, -it* (all said
"ee"). The plural adds *-iss-* before the endings *-ons, -ez, -ent*. That *-iss-* is the mark
of this group; you'll hear it as a clear "eess" sound.

- *Le cours finit à midi.* — The class finishes at noon. (*midi*, lesson 18)
- *Nous finissons le travail.* — We're finishing the work.
- *Qu'est-ce que vous choisissez ?* — What are you choosing? / What will you have?
- *Je réfléchis.* — I'm thinking about it.
- *Ils réfléchissent à leurs vacances.* — They're thinking about their holidays. (*réfléchir
  à* = to think about)

## -re verbs like vendre

| | vendre (to sell) | attendre (to wait for) | répondre (to answer) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | vends | attends | réponds |
| tu | vends | attends | réponds |
| il / elle / on | vend | attend | répond |
| nous | vendons | attendons | répondons |
| vous | vendez | attendez | répondez |
| ils / elles | vendent | attendent | répondent |

The stem is the infinitive minus *-re* (*vend-*). The endings are *-s, -s, —, -ons, -ez,
-ent*: the *il* form has *no ending* at all, just the stem: *il vend, il attend*. In the
singular the *d* is silent ("vahn"); in the plural you hear it: *ils vendent* ("vahnd").

*Entendre* (to hear) and *perdre* (to lose) work the same way: *j'entends, il perd, nous
perdons*.

- *La pharmacie vend des médicaments.* — The pharmacy sells medicines.
- *J'attends le bus.* — I'm waiting for the bus.
- *Tu réponds à la question ?* — Are you answering the question? (*répondre à* + thing or
  person: *Je réponds à Marie*)
- *Je n'entends pas. Vous pouvez répéter ?* — I can't hear. Can you repeat that?
- *Il perd toujours ses clés.* — He's always losing his keys. (*toujours*, lesson 17)

Two traps from English: *attendre* already contains "for" (~~j'attends pour le bus~~), and
*répondre* needs *à* (~~je réponds la question~~).

The two sets of endings side by side:

![A chart comparing the endings of finir and vendre. For finir: je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent, with the -iss- of the plural highlighted. For vendre: je vends, tu vends, il vend, nous vendons, vous vendez, ils vendent, with the empty il ending marked "no ending".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## dormir: an -ir verb that isn't like finir

Not every verb ending in *-ir* belongs to the *finir* group. *Dormir* (to sleep) follows the
*partir* pattern from lesson 14: it drops the last consonant of the stem in the singular and
has no *-iss-*.

| | dormir (to sleep) | finir, for comparison |
|---|---|---|
| je | dors | finis |
| tu | dors | finis |
| il / elle / on | dort | finit |
| nous | dormons | finissons |
| vous | dormez | finissez |
| ils / elles | dorment | finissent |

- *Le bébé dort.* — The baby is sleeping.
- *Vous dormez bien ?* — Do you sleep well?

You can't tell from the infinitive which group an *-ir* verb is in, so the vocabulary list
marks each one. In this course the *finir* group is *finir, choisir, réfléchir*, and later
*remplir* (to fill in) and *réussir* (to succeed). *Partir, sortir* and *dormir* are the other
pattern.

## Making an appointment

*Le rendez-vous* is an appointment (with a doctor, a hairdresser, a bank) and also a meeting
or a date. The verb is *prendre*: *prendre rendez-vous* (no article) means to make an
appointment.

- *Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous avec le docteur Morel.* — I'd like to make an appointment
  with Dr Morel.
- *J'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin demain.* — I have a doctor's appointment tomorrow.
- *C'est pour quand ?* — For when?

When you speak to a doctor, call them *docteur* (*Bonjour, docteur*); *le médecin* is the
ordinary word for the job.

## Dialogue: Au téléphone, puis chez le médecin

Paul calls his doctor's surgery. The receptionist is *la secrétaire*.

> La secrétaire : *Cabinet du docteur Morel, bonjour.*
>
> Paul : *Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous, s'il vous plaît. Je suis malade.*
>
> La secrétaire : *Demain à dix heures, ça va ?*
>
> Paul : *Oui, très bien. Merci !*

The next day:

> Le docteur Morel : *Bonjour, monsieur. Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?*
>
> Paul : *J'ai mal à la tête et j'ai mal au ventre. Et je suis très fatigué.*
>
> Le docteur Morel : *Vous avez de la fièvre ?*
>
> Paul : *Oui, un peu. Et je dors mal.*
>
> Le docteur Morel : *Ce n'est pas grave. Vous prenez ce médicament, et vous dormez beaucoup.*
>
> Paul : *D'accord. Je finis le travail à quelle heure, alors ? Je travaille demain !*
>
> Le docteur Morel : *Ah non ! Demain, vous restez à la maison.*

Translation:

> Receptionist: Dr Morel's surgery, hello.
>
> Paul: Hello. I'd like to make an appointment, please. I'm ill.
>
> Receptionist: Tomorrow at ten, is that all right?
>
> Paul: Yes, very good. Thank you!
>
> Dr Morel: Hello. What's the matter?
>
> Paul: I've got a headache and a stomach ache. And I'm very tired.
>
> Dr Morel: Do you have a temperature?
>
> Paul: Yes, a bit. And I'm sleeping badly.
>
> Dr Morel: It's nothing serious. Take this medicine, and sleep a lot.
>
> Paul: OK. So what time do I finish work? I'm working tomorrow!
>
> Dr Morel: Oh no! Tomorrow you stay at home.

(*le cabinet* = the doctor's surgery or office; *Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?* = what's wrong?;
*Ce n'est pas grave* = it's not serious; *vous restez* = you stay, *rester*, lesson 22. Notice
how the doctor gives instructions with the plain present, *vous prenez, vous dormez*: very
common in French.)

## Pronunciation

- *l'œil*: "luh-y", one syllable, with a short "uh" and a *y* glide. *Les yeux*: "lay-ZYEU",
  with liaison.
- *le corps* "kor", *le dos* "doh", *le nez* "nay", *le bras* "bra", *le pied* "pyay": silent
  final consonants.
- *la main* "man" (nasal), *la dent* "dahn" (nasal), *la jambe* "zhahmb".
- *la bouche* "boosh", *l'oreille* "lo-RAY", *le ventre* "VAHN-truh".
- *ils finissent* "fee-NEESS"; *il vend* "vahn", *ils vendent* "vahnd".
- *le rendez-vous* "rahn-day-VOO": the *z* and *s* are silent.

## Common mistakes

- ~~J'ai mal à ma tête~~ → *J'ai mal à la tête*.
- ~~J'ai mal à le dos~~ → *J'ai mal au dos*; ~~à les dents~~ → *aux dents*.
- ~~les œils~~ → *les yeux*.
- ~~nous finons~~ → *nous finissons*; ~~nous dormissons~~ → *nous dormons*.
- ~~il vendt~~, ~~il vende~~ → *il vend*.
- ~~J'attends pour le bus~~ → *J'attends le bus*.
- ~~Je réponds la question~~ → *Je réponds à la question*.
- ~~Je suis fièvre~~ → *J'ai de la fièvre*.

## Key points

- *-ir* verbs (*finir, choisir, réfléchir*): *-is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent*.
- *-re* verbs (*vendre, attendre, répondre, entendre, perdre*): *-s, -s, (nothing), -ons, -ez,
  -ent*.
- *dormir* is not a *finir* verb: *dors, dors, dort, dormons, dormez, dorment*.
- *avoir mal à* + *la / l'* or *au / aux*: *J'ai mal à la tête, au dos, aux dents*.
- *l'œil, les yeux*. *Le bras, le dos, le nez, le corps* don't change in the plural.
- *Je suis malade, fatigué(e). J'ai de la fièvre. Je prends rendez-vous.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Les loisirs à la française
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 you learned to talk about your hobbies with *faire de* and *jouer à / de*, and
about the weather and the seasons. This honors lesson takes you into four pieces of French
leisure culture that every French person knows: a bike race, a game played in village squares,
a music festival around the longest day of the year and the comic book. Along the way you learn
one of the most useful small words in French, *depuis*, which says how long something has been
going on, and you go deeper into the choice between *jouer à*, *jouer de* and *faire de*.

The texts are original and written at A1 level or just above. New words are glossed.

## Le Tour de France

The *Tour de France* is the most famous cycle race in the world. It was first held in 1903,
organized by the sports newspaper *L'Auto* and its editor Henri Desgrange to sell more papers.
Today it usually takes three weeks in July. The race is divided into about twenty *étapes*
(stages), one per day, with a few rest days. The route changes every year, and sometimes the
start (*le Grand Départ*) is in another country.

The leader of the race wears *le maillot jaune*, the yellow jersey. It was introduced in 1919;
yellow was the colour of the pages of *L'Auto*. The race has traditionally finished in Paris on
the Champs-Élysées since 1975 (in 2024 it ended in Nice instead, because Paris was hosting the
Olympic Games).

For many French families, the Tour is a summer ritual: people watch the stages on television in
the afternoon, or wait for hours at the roadside to see the *coureurs* (riders) pass in a few
seconds.

> *Je m'appelle Lucas. J'habite dans un petit village dans les Alpes. En juillet, le Tour de
> France passe devant ma maison ! Le matin, nous attendons au bord de la route avec les voisins.
> Il fait chaud. Les coureurs arrivent vers trois heures. Ils passent très vite ! Le maillot
> jaune, c'est un coureur danois. Le soir, je regarde le résumé de l'étape à la télé.*

Translation: My name is Lucas. I live in a small village in the Alps. In July the Tour de France
goes past my house! In the morning we wait at the side of the road with the neighbours. It's
hot. The riders arrive around three o'clock. They go past very fast! The yellow jersey is a
Danish rider. In the evening I watch the highlights of the stage on TV.

(*passer* = to pass, go past; *au bord de la route* = at the side of the road; *les voisins* =
the neighbours; *danois* = Danish; *le résumé* = the summary, highlights. *Juillet*, July, is in
lesson 19.)

## La pétanque

*La pétanque* is a game of metal balls, *les boules*. Players throw their boules as close as
possible to a small wooden target ball, *le cochonnet* (literally "the piglet"). You play in
teams of one, two or three, on any flat ground of earth or gravel, and the first team to reach
13 points wins.

The game comes from Provence. Around 1907–1910, in La Ciotat near Marseille, a café owner
adapted an older game, in which players took a run before throwing, for a friend whose
rheumatism stopped him running. In the new game you throw standing still, with your feet
planted on the ground: in Provençal *pè tancat*, "foot fixed". The game was first called *pieds
tanqués*, and that became *pétanque*.

In the south of France especially, people play on summer evenings in the village square under
the plane trees, often with an *apéritif* nearby. That's a cliché, of course, but you'll see it
in real life too.

![A pétanque game seen from above: a small wooden jack in the centre, two red boules and two blue boules around it at different distances, and a throwing circle drawn on the ground at the bottom. The red boule closest to the jack is marked with an arrow.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The basic scoring idea: after all the boules are thrown, the team with the boule nearest the
cochonnet scores one point for each of its boules that is closer than the other team's best
boule. In the picture, red scores one point: its nearest boule beats both blue ones, but its
second boule is behind the best blue one.

## La Fête de la musique

Every year on 21 June, chosen because it is around the summer solstice (the longest day of the
year in the northern hemisphere, 20 or 21 June), France holds *la Fête de la musique*. It was launched in 1982 by the Ministry of Culture under Jack Lang.
The idea: music everywhere, by anyone, for free. Amateur and professional musicians play in the
streets, squares, bars and parks, from the afternoon until late at night. The idea spread, and
many cities around the world now hold their own version on the same day.

Here is a poster of the kind you might see in a French town:

> *Fête de la musique — Place du marché*
>
> 18 h : chorale de l'école (enfants)
>
> 19 h 30 : jazz avec le trio « Les Trois Pommes »
>
> 21 h : rock — groupe *Les Voisins*
>
> 23 h : DJ, on danse !
>
> Entrée libre. Venez avec vos amis !

Translation: Music festival, Market Square. 6 p.m.: school choir (children). 7:30 p.m.: jazz with
the trio "Les Trois Pommes". 9 p.m.: rock, the band *Les Voisins*. 11 p.m.: DJ, let's dance!
Free entry. Come with your friends!

(*la chorale* = the choir; *le groupe* = the band; *Entrée libre* = free entry, using *libre*
from lesson 11; *Venez* = come, the *vous* imperative of *venir*, lesson 20.)

## La bande dessinée

*La bande dessinée*, usually shortened to *la BD*, is the comic book or graphic novel. In France
and Belgium it's a serious art form for all ages, sometimes called *le neuvième art* (the ninth
art). Bookshops have whole BD sections, and adults read BD as much as children do.

Two series known by nearly everyone: *Tintin*, by the Belgian artist Hergé, first published in
1929, and *Astérix*, by René Goscinny and Albert Uderzo, first published in 1959. Since 1974 the
town of Angoulême, in the west of France, has held a large international comics festival in
late January. The 2026 edition was cancelled after a dispute over how the festival was run, and
a new festival has been announced for January 2027.

## depuis + present: how long so far

*Depuis* says how long something has been going on, or since when. The surprise for English
speakers: French uses the *present tense*, because the action is still going on.

- *J'apprends le français depuis deux mois.* — I've been learning French for two months.
- *Il joue de la guitare depuis trois ans.* — He has played the guitar for three years.
- *Nous habitons ici depuis 2020.* — We've lived here since 2020.
- *Je t'attends depuis une heure !* — I've been waiting for you for an hour!

*Depuis* covers both English "for" (a length of time: *depuis deux mois*) and "since" (a point
in time: *depuis 2020, depuis l'été*). To ask, use *Depuis quand … ?* (since when) or *Depuis
combien de temps … ?* (for how long):

- *Depuis combien de temps tu fais du vélo ?* — How long have you been cycling?
- *Depuis quand est-ce que vous habitez à Lyon ?* — Since when have you lived in Lyon?

Don't use *pour* for "for" here: ~~J'apprends le français pour deux mois~~ means you plan to
learn it for two months and then stop.

### Example 1: building a depuis sentence

You want to say: "My sister has been swimming at the pool for six years."

1. Is it still going on? Yes, she still swims. So the verb is in the *present*: not the
   English "has been swimming".
2. Choose the verb and pattern: *nager* (*elle nage*), or *faire de la natation* (*elle fait de
   la natation*).
3. Add the place: *à la piscine*.
4. Add *depuis* + the length of time: *depuis six ans*.

Result: *Ma sœur nage à la piscine depuis six ans.* or *Ma sœur fait de la natation depuis six
ans.*

## jouer à, jouer de, faire de: in depth

Here is the full picture behind lesson 13's chart.

*jouer à* + a game or sport played as a match or game: *jouer au tennis, au foot, à la
pétanque, aux cartes, aux échecs* (chess), *aux jeux vidéo* (video games, *le jeu, les jeux*).
*À* joins with *le* and *les*, so you get *au* and *aux*.

*jouer de* + a musical instrument: *jouer du piano, de la guitare, du violon, de l'accordéon*.
*De* joins with *le* and *les*, so you get *du* and *des*. Asking in general: *Tu joues d'un
instrument ?* (*l'instrument*, masculine).

*faire de* + an activity, sport or discipline: *faire du vélo, de la natation, de la
randonnée, du sport, de la musique*. Many people also say *faire du piano* or *faire de la
guitare* for an instrument they learn as a hobby (*Ma fille fait du piano* — my daughter does
piano lessons). And many ball sports take both: *jouer au tennis* (play a match) or *faire du
tennis* (do tennis as your sport).

*In the negative* the three behave differently, because the little word plays a different
role in each:

| Pattern | Positive | Negative | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| *faire de* | *Je fais du vélo.* | *Je ne fais pas de vélo.* | *du* is a partitive, so it becomes *de* (lesson 10) |
| *jouer à* | *Je joue au tennis.* | *Je ne joue pas au tennis.* | *au* is a preposition + article; it stays |
| *jouer de* | *Je joue du piano.* | *Je ne joue pas du piano.* | *du* is the preposition *de* + *le*; it stays |

The last row is the standard explanation, and it's what you should write. In speech you'll
also hear *Je ne joue pas de piano*; some native speakers prefer it, so don't be surprised.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Activities in the negative
  accDescr: A chart for making an activity negative. If the sentence uses faire du, de la or des, change it to pas de, as in je ne fais pas de vélo. If it uses jouer au or aux, keep it, as in je ne joue pas au tennis. If it uses jouer du or de la, keep it in standard French, as in je ne joue pas du piano, though pas de piano is also heard in speech.
  A{"Which pattern?"} -- "faire du, de la" --> B["pas de: je ne fais pas de vélo"]
  A -- "jouer au, aux" --> C["keep: je ne joue pas au tennis"]
  A -- "jouer du, de la" --> D["keep: je ne joue pas du piano"]
  D -.- E["also heard: pas de piano"]
```

### Example 2: choosing the pattern

Say that you play these: chess (*les échecs*, masculine plural), the violin (*le violon*),
volleyball (*le volley*), and that you go swimming (*la natation*).

1. Chess is a game you play against someone: *jouer à* + *les échecs* = *Je joue aux
   échecs.*
2. The violin is an instrument: *jouer de* + *le violon* = *Je joue du violon.*
3. Volleyball is a ball sport: *Je joue au volley.* (*Je fais du volley* is also correct.)
4. Swimming isn't a game: *faire de* + *la natation* = *Je fais de la natation.*

Now make the chess and violin sentences negative: *Je ne joue pas aux échecs. Je ne joue pas
du violon.* Swimming: *Je ne fais pas de natation.*

## A longer text: Mes loisirs

> *Salut ! Je m'appelle Nadia, j'ai 34 ans et j'habite à Marseille. J'adore la musique : je
> joue de la guitare depuis quinze ans, et je chante dans un groupe avec des amis. Le 21 juin,
> pour la Fête de la musique, nous jouons dans la rue, devant un café du quartier. En été, il
> fait très chaud à Marseille. Le soir, je joue à la pétanque avec mon père et ses amis. Ils
> jouent depuis cinquante ans, et ils gagnent toujours ! Je ne fais pas de sport, mais je
> nage beaucoup à la mer. Et j'adore les BD : j'ai toutes les aventures de Tintin.*

Translation: Hi! My name is Nadia, I'm 34 and I live in Marseille. I love music: I've played the
guitar for fifteen years, and I sing in a band with friends. On 21 June, for the Fête de la
musique, we play in the street, in front of a café in the neighbourhood. In summer it's very hot
in Marseille. In the evening I play pétanque with my father and his friends. They've been playing
for fifty years, and they always win! I don't do any sport, but I swim a lot in the sea. And I
love comics: I've got all the Tintin adventures.

(*gagner* = to win; *la mer* = the sea, lesson 22; *toutes les aventures* = all the adventures.)

## Common mistakes

- ~~J'apprends le français pour deux mois~~ (meaning "I've been learning") → *J'apprends le
  français depuis deux mois.*
- ~~J'ai appris le français depuis deux mois~~ → present tense: *J'apprends … depuis*.
- ~~Je joue la pétanque~~ → *Je joue à la pétanque.*
- ~~Je ne fais pas du vélo~~ → *Je ne fais pas de vélo.*
- ~~Je ne joue pas de tennis~~ → *Je ne joue pas au tennis.*
- ~~le BD~~ → *la BD* (from *la bande dessinée*).

## Key points

- *Le Tour de France*: since 1903, three weeks in July, *les étapes*, *le maillot jaune* (since
  1919) for the leader.
- *La pétanque*: from La Ciotat, Provence (around 1907–1910); *les boules*, *le cochonnet*; 13
  points to win.
- *La Fête de la musique*: 21 June, since 1982, free music everywhere.
- *La BD* (*la bande dessinée*): *Tintin* (1929), *Astérix* (1959); Angoulême festival since
  1974.
- *depuis* + *present* for something still going on: *J'apprends le français depuis deux
  mois.* *Depuis quand … ? Depuis combien de temps … ?*
- Negative: *pas de vélo* (faire de), but *pas au tennis* (jouer à) and *pas du piano* (jouer
  de).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Chez le médecin et à la pharmacie
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 gave you the body, *avoir mal à*, *malade* and *fatigué*, and a first call to make an
appointment. This honors lesson prepares you for the moment you actually need care in France:
booking with a doctor, describing common symptoms, understanding what the doctor or pharmacist
tells you to do (*il faut* + infinitive), finding a pharmacy at night, and knowing which number
to call in an emergency.

The language is simplified to A1, and so is the description of the French health system. This
lesson teaches French; it is not medical advice. In a real emergency, call even if your French
is limited: say where you are and what has happened, slowly, and don't hang up.

## Booking an appointment

Most people in France have a *médecin traitant*, a family doctor (GP) they've registered with.
You book by phone, or more and more often online through a booking website or app. For
a child, people often see a pediatrician, and for teeth *le dentiste*.

Useful sentences when you call:

- *Bonjour, je voudrais prendre rendez-vous avec le docteur Lambert.* — Hello, I'd like to make
  an appointment with Dr Lambert.
- *C'est urgent ?* — Is it urgent?
- *Oui, c'est un peu urgent. J'ai de la fièvre depuis trois jours.* — Yes, it's a bit urgent.
  I've had a temperature for three days.
- *Vous avez quelque chose aujourd'hui ?* — Do you have anything today? (*quelque chose*,
  lesson 21)
- *Je suis un nouveau patient.* — I'm a new patient.

At the surgery you give your name and, if you're insured in France, your *carte Vitale*, the
green health insurance card that lets your costs be reimbursed directly.

## Describing symptoms

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *Je tousse.* (*tousser*) | I'm coughing. I have a cough. |
| *J'ai mal à la gorge.* | I have a sore throat. |
| *J'ai un rhume.* | I have a cold. |
| *J'ai la grippe.* | I have the flu. |
| *J'ai de la fièvre.* | I have a temperature. |
| *J'ai le nez qui coule.* | I have a runny nose. |
| *J'ai mal au cœur.* | I feel sick (nauseous). |
| *J'ai une douleur ici.* | I have a pain here. |

*Tousser* is a regular *-er* verb: *je tousse, tu tousses, nous toussons*. Notice the article
with illnesses: *un rhume* (a cold) but *la grippe* (the flu), just like English.

### A false friend: avoir mal au cœur

*Le cœur* is the heart, but *J'ai mal au cœur* does *not* mean your heart hurts. It means you
feel sick, as if you're going to vomit: the same as *J'ai la nausée*. It's an old expression
(one common explanation is that the top of the stomach used to be called *le cœur* too). Children
say it in the car, and it's what you say on a rough boat trip.

If your chest hurts, a doctor needs to hear *J'ai mal à la poitrine* (*la poitrine* = the
chest) or *J'ai une douleur dans la poitrine*. That difference matters.

### Example 1: telling the doctor what's wrong

The doctor asks: *Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?* (What's wrong?) You have a sore throat, you're
coughing, and you've had a temperature for two days.

1. Sore throat: *avoir mal à* + *la gorge*: *J'ai mal à la gorge.*
2. Coughing: the verb *tousser* in the present: *Je tousse.*
3. A temperature: *avoir de la fièvre* (partitive). For how long: *depuis* + present (honors
   16h1): *J'ai de la fièvre depuis deux jours.*
4. Join them with *et*: *J'ai mal à la gorge et je tousse. J'ai de la fièvre depuis deux
   jours.*

The doctor might answer: *C'est un rhume ou c'est la grippe. Il faut dormir et boire beaucoup
d'eau.*

## il faut + infinitive

*Il faut* means "it is necessary", "you have to", "one must". Like *il pleut*, it's
impersonal: the *il* is empty, and the form never changes. The verb after it is an
infinitive.

- *Il faut dormir.* — You need to sleep.
- *Il faut prendre ce médicament trois fois par jour.* — You have to take this medicine three
  times a day.
- *Pour ce médicament, il faut une ordonnance.* — For this medicine you need a prescription.
  (*il faut* + noun = you need)

The negative needs care. *Il ne faut pas* means "you *must not*", not "you don't have to":

- *Il ne faut pas boire d'alcool avec ce médicament.* — You mustn't drink alcohol with this
  medicine.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: il faut and il ne faut pas
  accDescr: A chart showing the meaning of il faut. Il faut plus an infinitive means you have to, as in il faut dormir. Il faut plus a noun means you need, as in il faut une ordonnance. Il ne faut pas plus an infinitive means you must not, as in il ne faut pas boire d'alcool. A warning box says it does not mean you don't have to.
  A["il faut"] --> B["+ infinitive: you have to. Il faut dormir."]
  A --> C["+ noun: you need. Il faut une ordonnance."]
  A --> D["il ne faut pas + infinitive: you must NOT. Il ne faut pas boire d'alcool."]
  D -.- E["Not: you don't have to"]
```

## At the pharmacy

You find *la pharmacie* by its sign: a *green cross*, often lit up and flashing. In France,
medicines are sold almost only in pharmacies: you won't find painkillers on a supermarket
shelf. The pharmacist, *le pharmacien* or *la pharmacienne*, is a trained health professional
who gives advice about small problems (a cold, a sore throat, a sunburn) and tells you whether
you should see a doctor.

Some medicines you can buy without a prescription (*sans ordonnance*); others need
*l'ordonnance* (the prescription) that the doctor writes. Medicines often come as *des
comprimés* (tablets) or *du sirop* (syrup, for a cough).

*At night, on Sundays and on public holidays*, most pharmacies are closed, but one in the area
is open: *la pharmacie de garde* (the duty pharmacy). The nearest pharmacy puts the address of
the duty pharmacy on its door, and there's a national number, 32 37 (a paid call), and the website
3237.fr.

![A sign with a green cross on a white background above the word Pharmacie, next to a card titled Numéros d'urgence listing 15 SAMU (medical emergency), 17 Police, 18 Pompiers (fire brigade), 112 Europe (any emergency) and 114 by text message for deaf and hard-of-hearing people.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: reading the pharmacist's instructions

The pharmacist writes on the box:

> *1 comprimé 3 fois par jour, pendant 5 jours. Avec un verre d'eau, pendant le repas. Ne pas
> prendre avec de l'alcool.*

1. *Combien de comprimés par jour ?* "1 comprimé 3 fois par jour" = one tablet three times a
   day, so 3 tablets a day.
2. *Pendant combien de jours ?* *pendant 5 jours* = for 5 days (*pendant*, lesson 22).
3. *Combien de comprimés en tout ?* 3 a day × 5 days = 15 tablets.
4. *Avec quoi ?* With a glass of water (*un verre d'eau*), during the meal (*pendant le repas*).
5. *Ne pas prendre avec de l'alcool*: written instructions often use *ne pas* + infinitive for
   "don't". It means the same as *Il ne faut pas prendre ce médicament avec de l'alcool.*

## Emergency numbers

Calls to these numbers are free from any phone in France:

| Number | Service | When |
|---|---|---|
| 15 | *le SAMU* | a medical emergency |
| 17 | *la police* (or *la gendarmerie*) | a crime, danger, an attack |
| 18 | *les pompiers* (fire brigade) | fire, accidents, people in danger (they also handle many medical emergencies) |
| 112 | the European emergency number | any emergency, anywhere in the European Union, from any phone |
| 114 | by text message (SMS) or app | for deaf and hard-of-hearing people |

There is also *116 117* for an on-call doctor when your doctor's surgery is closed and it isn't
an emergency (available in many areas). For a serious problem at the hospital, you go to *les
urgences* (the emergency department, A&E, ER).

What to say on the phone, slowly and clearly:

- *Allô, c'est une urgence. Mon ami est tombé.* — Hello, it's an emergency. My friend has fallen.
  (*tomber*, lesson 22)
- *Je suis au 12, rue Victor-Hugo, à Lyon.* — I'm at 12 rue Victor-Hugo, in Lyon.
- *Je ne parle pas bien français. Vous parlez anglais ?* — I don't speak French well. Do you
  speak English?

### Example 3: which number?

Decide which number fits each situation (simplified):

1. *Il y a un feu dans la cuisine de votre voisin.* A fire (*le feu*): the fire brigade, 18
   (or 112).
2. *Votre amie a très mal à la poitrine.* A medical emergency: the SAMU, 15 (or 112).
3. *Vous êtes en vacances en Italie et il y a un accident.* Not in France: 112 works in every
   EU country.
4. *Vous avez un rhume et c'est dimanche.* Not an emergency: the duty pharmacy (*la pharmacie de
   garde*), found on the door of any pharmacy or via 32 37.

## Dialogue: À la pharmacie

> Le pharmacien : *Bonjour, madame. Je peux vous aider ?*
>
> Sarah : *Bonjour. J'ai mal à la gorge et je tousse depuis hier.*
>
> Le pharmacien : *Vous avez de la fièvre ?*
>
> Sarah : *Non, je ne pense pas. Mais je suis fatiguée.*
>
> Le pharmacien : *C'est sûrement un rhume. Voilà un sirop pour la toux et des pastilles pour la
> gorge.*
>
> Sarah : *Il faut une ordonnance ?*
>
> Le pharmacien : *Non, pas pour ça. Mais si vous avez de la fièvre, il faut aller chez le
> médecin.*
>
> Sarah : *D'accord. Merci beaucoup !*

Translation:

> Pharmacist: Hello. Can I help you?
>
> Sarah: Hello. I've got a sore throat and I've been coughing since yesterday.
>
> Pharmacist: Do you have a temperature?
>
> Sarah: No, I don't think so. But I'm tired.
>
> Pharmacist: It's probably a cold. Here's some cough syrup and some throat lozenges.
>
> Sarah: Do I need a prescription?
>
> Pharmacist: No, not for that. But if you get a temperature, you need to go to the doctor.
>
> Sarah: OK. Thank you very much!

(*hier* = yesterday, lesson 18; *je ne pense pas* = I don't think so; *sûrement* = probably,
surely; *la toux* = the cough; *les pastilles* = lozenges.)

## Common mistakes

- ~~J'ai mal au cœur~~ to say your heart or chest hurts → *J'ai mal à la poitrine.*
- ~~Il ne faut pas venir~~ for "you don't have to come" → it means "you mustn't come". For
  "you don't have to", say *Ce n'est pas nécessaire de venir*, or use *devoir* (lesson 19).
- ~~Il faut que dormir~~ → *Il faut dormir.* Just the infinitive.
- ~~Je suis toux~~ → *Je tousse* or *J'ai de la toux*.
- Asking for *la pharmacie de nuit*: that is a pharmacy open all night (big cities have a few).
  The one on duty in your area tonight is *la pharmacie de garde*.
- Looking for a pharmacy with a red cross: the French sign is *green*.

## Key points

- Book: *Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous. C'est urgent ?* Bring your *carte Vitale* if you have
  one.
- Symptoms: *je tousse, j'ai mal à la gorge, j'ai un rhume, j'ai la grippe, j'ai de la fièvre*.
- *J'ai mal au cœur* = I feel sick (nauseous), *not* heart pain.
- *il faut* + infinitive = you have to; *il faut* + noun = you need; *il ne faut pas* = you
  must not.
- Pharmacies: green cross, advice from the pharmacist, *l'ordonnance*, *la pharmacie de garde*
  (32 37).
- Emergencies: 15 (SAMU), 17 (police), 18 (pompiers), 112 (anywhere in the EU), 114 (text).
  Hospital emergency department: *les urgences*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Les soldes and sizes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 15 took you into a clothes shop: *Quelle taille faites-vous ?*, *ce pull, cette robe*,
*j'essaie, je préfère, je paie*. This honors lesson goes further. You learn when and how the
French sales work (they are set by law, which surprises many visitors), how French clothing and
shoe sizes work, how to give and understand opinions in a fitting room (*Ça te va bien !*), how
to ask "which one?" with *lequel*, and what to say if you want to exchange something.

## Les soldes: sales by law

In France, *les soldes* (the sales; masculine plural: *les soldes d'hiver*) aren't just any
discount. They are regulated by the commercial code. Shops can run promotions (*les promos*)
during the year, but they may only sell at a loss and use the word *soldes* during two official
periods:

- *winter sales* (*les soldes d'hiver*) start at 8 a.m. on the second Wednesday of January,
  or on the first Wednesday if the second one falls after the 12th;
- *summer sales* (*les soldes d'été*) start at 8 a.m. on the last Wednesday of June, or the
  Wednesday before if the last one falls after the 28th.

Each period lasts *four weeks* (six weeks until 2019). A few areas have their own dates, such
as the four départements of Lorraine (Moselle, Meurthe-et-Moselle, Meuse and Vosges) and the
overseas territories. The government can also change a period: in 2026 the summer sales were
extended by one week because of a heatwave.

Rules that protect shoppers: only items that were on sale in the shop for at least a month
before the sales may be reduced, and the label must show the real previous price next to the
sale price.

On the first morning of the sales, there are queues in front of some shops, and the windows
(*les vitrines*) are covered in signs: *SOLDES*, *-30 %*, *-50 %*, *Dernière démarque* (final
reductions). An item on sale is *en solde*: *Ce manteau est en solde.*

![A one-year timeline from January to December. A blue band covers about four weeks from early January into early February, labelled soldes d'hiver, starting on a Wednesday in January. An orange band covers about four weeks from late June into late July, labelled soldes d'été, starting on a Wednesday at the end of June. The rest of the year is marked promotions possible.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: when do the sales start?

When do the winter and summer sales start in 2027, by the general rule?

1. *Winter.* The Wednesdays in January 2027 are the 6th, 13th, 20th and 27th. The second
   Wednesday is the 13th, which is after the 12th. So the sales start on the *first*
   Wednesday: *Wednesday 6 January 2027* at 8 a.m., and run four weeks, to Tuesday 2
   February.
2. *Summer.* The Wednesdays in June 2027 are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th. The last one,
   the 30th, is after the 28th. So the sales start one week earlier: *Wednesday 23 June 2027*,
   for four weeks, to Tuesday 20 July.

In French: *En 2027, les soldes d'hiver commencent le mercredi 6 janvier et les soldes d'été
le mercredi 23 juin.* (Days and months are in lessons 18 and 19.) Always check the official
dates each year, because exceptions are possible.

### Example 2: reading the sale signs

A shop window says: *Pantalons : -30 %* and *Chemises : -50 % sur la deuxième* (50 % off the
second one).

1. A pair of trousers at 60 € with *-30 %*: 30 % of 60 is 18, so you pay 60 − 18 = 42 €
   (*quarante-deux euros*).
2. Two shirts at 40 € each, with *-50 % sur la deuxième*: the first costs 40 €, the second
   half price, 20 €, so 60 € for both. That's 25 % off the total of 80 €, not 50 %.
3. In French, at the till: *Ça fait combien ? — Soixante euros, madame.*

*La réduction* is the discount: *Il y a une réduction de 30 %*.

## Sizes: la taille and la pointure

For clothes, *la taille*; for shoes, *la pointure*:

- *Quelle taille faites-vous ? — Je fais du 38.* (or *du M*)
- *Quelle est votre pointure ? — Je fais du 39.* or *Je chausse du 39.* (*chausser* = to take
  a shoe size)

*Clothes.* Women's sizes in France are even numbers: 34, 36, 38, 40, 42, 44… Men's trousers
and jackets have their own numbers, and letters (*XS, S, M, L, XL*) are used everywhere. French
numbers don't match British or American ones, and they aren't even the same as German or
Italian numbers for the same garment, so check the brand's size chart. Treat any conversion as
approximate.

*Shoes.* Most of continental Europe uses the same shoe sizes, and France is no exception:
adults go from about 35 to 47. One size step is two-thirds of a centimetre (this unit is called
the *point de Paris*). As a rough guide, a European 42 is about a British 8; American sizes
differ for men and women. Shoe sizes also vary by brand, which is why you try shoes on.

## In the fitting room: opinions

*La cabine d'essayage* is the fitting room: *Les cabines d'essayage sont où ?* Here is how to say
what you think, and what a friend or the shop assistant might say:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *Ça te va bien !* / *Ça vous va bien !* | It suits you! It looks good on you! |
| *Ça ne te va pas.* | It doesn't suit you. |
| *C'est trop grand / trop petit.* | It's too big / too small. |
| *C'est trop serré.* | It's too tight. |
