| *C'est trop large.* | It's too loose / too wide. |
| *C'est trop long / trop court.* | It's too long / too short. |
| *J'aime bien la couleur.* | I like the colour. |
| *Ça me plaît.* | I like it. |
| *Je le prends. / Je la prends.* | I'll take it. |

Watch out for *large*: it's a false friend. For clothes, *large* means wide or loose, not big. A
large jumper is *un grand pull*. *Serré* (tight) is the opposite.

*Je le prends / Je la prends* uses an object pronoun (*le* for a masculine thing, *la* for a
feminine one) before the verb. Learn these two as chunks for now: *Le pull ? Je le prends. La
robe ? Je la prends.*

## lequel? which one?

You know *quel* (which, what) from lesson 11: *Quel pull ?* When you leave out the noun, *quel*
becomes *lequel*, "which one". Like *quel*, it agrees with the noun it stands for:

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *lequel ?* | *lesquels ?* |
| feminine | *laquelle ?* | *lesquelles ?* |

- *J'aime ce pull. — Lequel ?* — I like this jumper. — Which one?
- *Tu préfères quelle robe ? Laquelle ?* — Which dress do you prefer? Which one?
- *Je voudrais essayer ces chaussures. — Lesquelles ?* — I'd like to try these shoes. — Which
  ones?
- *Lequel tu préfères, le bleu ou le vert ?* — Which one do you prefer, the blue one or the
  green one?

The answer often uses *le / la / les* + colour or adjective: *le bleu* (the blue one), *la
noire* (the black one), *les grandes* (the big ones).

### Example 3: choosing the form of lequel

Your friend says each sentence. Ask "which one(s)?":

1. *Regarde cette veste !* *Veste* is feminine singular → *Laquelle ?*
2. *J'adore ces chapeaux.* *Chapeaux* is masculine plural → *Lesquels ?*
3. *Je prends le pantalon.* Masculine singular → *Lequel ?*
4. *Ces chaussures sont jolies.* *Chaussures* is feminine plural → *Lesquelles ?*

The trick is the same as for *ce / cette / ces*: find the noun, then its gender and number.

## Exchanges and refunds

You can ask: *Est-ce que je peux échanger ce pantalon ?* (Can I exchange these trousers?) or
*Vous pouvez me rembourser ?* (Can you refund me?). Keep *le ticket de caisse* (the till
receipt).

In a French shop, a seller doesn't have to take back or refund an item that isn't faulty, sale
item or not: an exchange is a favour, unless the shop promises one (*satisfait ou remboursé*,
"satisfied or your money back"). A faulty item is different: you're legally protected, sales
included. For online purchases there's a 14-day right to change your mind. (Simplified; the
rules have exceptions.)

*Échanger* is a *-ger* verb like *manger*: *nous échangeons*. *Rembourser* is regular: *je
rembourse, nous remboursons*.

## Dialogue: Premier jour des soldes

Emma and her friend Jade are shopping on the first day of the summer sales.

> Emma : *Regarde cette robe en vitrine : moins cinquante pour cent !*
>
> Jade : *Laquelle ? La rouge ?*
>
> Emma : *Non, la bleue. On entre ?*
>
> *(Dans le magasin.)*
>
> Emma : *Pardon, madame, vous avez cette robe en 38 ?*
>
> La vendeuse : *Oui, voilà. Les cabines d'essayage sont au fond.*
>
> *(Dans la cabine.)*
>
> Jade : *Alors ? Ah, elle te va très bien !*
>
> Emma : *Tu trouves ? Elle est un peu serrée, non ?*
>
> Jade : *Non, pas du tout. Et la couleur est super.*
>
> Emma : *D'accord, je la prends ! Et toi, tu essaies ces chaussures ?*
>
> Jade : *Lesquelles ? Ah, non, elles ne sont pas en solde. Je regarde seulement.*

Translation:

> Emma: Look at that dress in the window: fifty per cent off!
>
> Jade: Which one? The red one?
>
> Emma: No, the blue one. Shall we go in?
>
> (In the shop.)
>
> Emma: Excuse me, do you have this dress in a 38?
>
> Shop assistant: Yes, here you are. The fitting rooms are at the back.
>
> (In the fitting room.)
>
> Jade: Well? Oh, it really suits you!
>
> Emma: You think so? It's a bit tight, isn't it?
>
> Jade: No, not at all. And the colour is great.
>
> Emma: OK, I'll take it! And you, are you trying on those shoes?
>
> Jade: Which ones? Oh no, they're not on sale. I'm just looking.

(*au fond* = at the back; *Tu trouves ?* = you think so?; *pas du tout* = not at all; *Je regarde
seulement* = I'm just looking, a very useful sentence in any shop.)

## Common mistakes

- ~~la solde~~ for the sales → *les soldes*, masculine plural.
- ~~Quelle taille de chaussures ?~~ is understood, but the word is *la pointure*.
- ~~C'est trop large~~ to mean "it's too big" in general → *C'est trop grand.* *Large* = wide,
  loose.
- ~~Lequel ?~~ for a feminine noun → *Laquelle ?* (*la robe → laquelle*).
- ~~Ça te va bon~~ → *Ça te va bien.* *Bien* (well) is the adverb here.
- Expecting a refund for a change of mind in a shop: it's the shop's choice in France.

## Key points

- *Les soldes* (masculine plural): two legal periods of four weeks, from the second (or first)
  Wednesday of January and the last (or second-to-last) Wednesday of June, at 8 a.m.
- *en solde* = on sale; *la réduction* = the discount; *-30 %* = 30 % off.
- *la taille* (clothes), *la pointure* (shoes): *Je fais du 38. Je chausse du 39.*
- Opinions: *Ça te va bien. C'est trop serré / large / grand / petit. Je le prends.*
- *lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles* = which one(s), agreeing with the noun.
- Keep *le ticket de caisse*; exchanges of non-faulty items in shops are a favour, not a right.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: My day: reflexive verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 took you out of the house: sport, weather, transport, clothes and the doctor. Module 5
is about the shape of an ordinary day: when you get up, what time it is, what the date is, and
how to find your way. This first lesson gives you the words for a daily routine and the grammar
that comes with them, the **[[pronominal verb]]** (often called a **[[reflexive verb]]**).

You met one already in lesson 2: *Je m'appelle Sophie* — My name is Sophie. Literally that is
"I call myself Sophie". French uses this pattern for a whole family of everyday actions:

- *Je me lève.* — I get up. (literally "I raise myself")
- *Je me lave.* — I wash. ("I wash myself")
- *Je m'habille.* — I get dressed. ("I dress myself")

English often says these without "myself". French always needs the small extra word.

## The reflexive pronoun

A pronominal verb has two pronouns: the subject (*je, tu, il*…) and a **[[reflexive pronoun]]** that
points back to the same person. The reflexive pronoun goes right before the verb.

| subject | reflexive pronoun | se laver (to wash) |
|---|---|---|
| je | me | *je me lave* |
| tu | te | *tu te laves* |
| il / elle / on | se | *il se lave, elle se lave, on se lave* |
| nous | nous | *nous nous lavons* |
| vous | vous | *vous vous lavez* |
| ils / elles | se | *ils se lavent* |

Three things to notice:

1. The verb endings are the ordinary *-er* endings from lesson 7. Nothing new there.
2. *Nous* and *vous* appear twice: *nous nous lavons*. The first one is the subject, the second
   is the reflexive pronoun. It looks odd at first but it is correct.
3. *Se* covers *il, elle, on, ils* and *elles*. In the dictionary a pronominal verb is listed
   with *se*: *se laver, se coucher*.

### Elision: m', t', s'

Before a vowel or a mute *h*, *me, te, se* lose their *e* (the elision you know from lesson 1):

| s'habiller (to get dressed) | s'appeler (to be called) |
|---|---|
| *je m'habille* | *je m'appelle* |
| *tu t'habilles* | *tu t'appelles* |
| *il / elle s'habille* | *il / elle s'appelle* |
| *nous nous habillons* | *nous nous appelons* |
| *vous vous habillez* | *vous vous appelez* |
| *ils / elles s'habillent* | *ils / elles s'appellent* |

*Nous* and *vous* never elide. Instead you hear a liaison: *nous nous_habillons* sounds like
"noo noo-za-bee-yon".

Here is the reflexive pronoun as a picture: it always matches the subject, and it always sits
right in front of the verb.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the reflexive pronoun
  accDescr: Start from the subject. Je takes me, tu takes te, il, elle, on, ils and elles take se, nous takes nous and vous takes vous. Then check the verb. If it starts with a vowel or a mute h, me, te and se become m', t' and s', as in je m'habille. If not, keep the full form, as in je me lève. In both cases the pronoun goes directly before the verb.
  A["Subject"] --> B["je: me / tu: te"]
  A --> C["il, elle, on, ils, elles: se"]
  A --> D["nous: nous / vous: vous"]
  B --> E{"Does the verb start with a vowel or mute h?"}
  C --> E
  E -- "yes" --> F["m', t', s': je m'habille, il s'appelle"]
  E -- "no" --> G["me, te, se: je me lève, il se couche"]
  D --> H["Pronoun right before the verb: nous nous levons"]
  F --> H
  G --> H
```

## Two spelling changes: se lever, se promener, s'appeler

Most pronominal verbs in this lesson are regular *-er* verbs. Three change their spelling in the
four forms whose ending is silent (*je, tu, il, ils*), like *acheter* in lesson 10:

| | se lever (to get up) | se promener (to go for a walk) | s'appeler (to be called) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | *me lève* | *me promène* | *m'appelle* |
| tu | *te lèves* | *te promènes* | *t'appelles* |
| il / elle / on | *se lève* | *se promène* | *s'appelle* |
| nous | *nous levons* | *nous promenons* | *nous appelons* |
| vous | *vous levez* | *vous promenez* | *vous appelez* |
| ils / elles | *se lèvent* | *se promènent* | *s'appellent* |

Why? In *lever* the first *e* is a weak "uh" sound. When the ending is silent, that *e* would
end up in the last syllable you say (*lev*), and French doesn't allow a weak "uh" there. So it
opens to *è* (*lève*, "lev"), or the consonant doubles (*appelle*, "a-pel"). With *nous* and *vous* the ending
*-ons/-ez* is heard, so the stem stays as it is. Lesson 15 calls this the "boot" pattern.

## Negatives and questions

*Ne* goes before the reflexive pronoun and *pas* after the verb. The pronoun stays glued to the
verb:

- *Je ne me lève pas.* — I'm not getting up.
- *Il ne se rase pas.* — He doesn't shave. (*se raser*, to shave)
- *Nous ne nous couchons pas tard.* — We don't go to bed late.
- *Elle ne s'habille pas en noir.* — She doesn't wear black.

Questions work as in lesson 11. With intonation or *est-ce que* nothing moves:

- *Tu te lèves à quelle heure ?* — What time do you get up?
- *Est-ce que vous vous promenez le dimanche ?* — Do you go for a walk on Sundays?

## With an infinitive: Je vais me coucher

When a pronominal verb follows another verb, it stays in the infinitive, but its pronoun still
matches the subject. This is how you use the near future from lesson 12:

| | |
|---|---|
| *Je vais me coucher.* | I'm going to go to bed. |
| *Tu vas te reposer.* | You're going to rest. |
| *Il va se doucher.* | He's going to have a shower. |
| *Nous allons nous promener.* | We're going to go for a walk. |
| *Vous allez vous dépêcher.* | You're going to hurry. |

A very common mistake is *Je vais se coucher*. The *se* of the dictionary form must change to
*me* because the subject is *je*. In the negative, *ne … pas* goes around the first verb: *Je ne
vais pas me lever.* — I'm not going to get up.

## A day in order: d'abord, ensuite, puis, enfin

To tell your day as a sequence, use these four words at the start of a sentence:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *d'abord* | first (of all) |
| *ensuite* | next, afterwards |
| *puis* | then |
| *enfin* | finally |

*Ensuite* and *puis* are almost the same; using both avoids repeating yourself. Two prepositions
put things before or after something else:

- *avant le petit-déjeuner* — before breakfast
- *après le travail* — after work

*Après* can also stand alone: *Après, je me repose.* — Afterwards, I rest.

## Parts of the day: le matin, le soir

French uses the article where English uses "in the":

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *le matin* | in the morning, (every) morning |
| *l'après-midi* | in the afternoon |
| *le soir* | in the evening |
| *la nuit* | at night |

*Le matin, je bois du café.* — In the morning I drink coffee. With *le*, it usually means every
morning, as a habit. For a time of day there are two adverbs: *tôt* (early) and *tard* (late):
*Je me lève tôt, je me couche tard.*

*L'après-midi* is usually masculine (*un après-midi*); you'll also hear *une après-midi*. Both are
correct.

## How often? toujours, souvent, parfois

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *toujours* | always |
| *d'habitude* | usually |
| *souvent* | often |
| *parfois* | sometimes |
| *ne … jamais* | never (lesson 10) |

*Toujours, souvent* and *jamais* go after the verb: *Je me lève toujours à sept heures.*
*Il ne se repose jamais.* *D'habitude* and *parfois* often start the sentence: *D'habitude, je
prends le bus. Parfois, je vais au bureau à pied.* (*Parfois* can also follow the verb: *Je vais
parfois au bureau à pied.*)

## A morning in pictures

The pictures show one person's day. Times are written the French way (*7 h* = seven o'clock;
lesson 18 teaches the clock).

![A strip of six pictures with a time under each. 6 h 45: an alarm clock ringing, je me réveille (I wake up). 7 h: a person getting out of bed, je me lève (I get up). 7 h 10: a shower with water drops, je me douche (I shower). 7 h 30: a shirt on a hanger, je m'habille (I get dressed). 18 h: a path with a tree, je me promène (I go for a walk). 23 h: a bed with a moon above it, je me couche (I go to bed).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: la journée de Karim

> Je m'appelle Karim. Je suis infirmier à l'hôpital de Nantes. D'habitude, je me réveille à six
> heures. Je ne me lève pas tout de suite : je reste cinq minutes au lit. Ensuite, je me douche
> et je m'habille. Je me dépêche toujours le matin, parce que le bus part à sept heures ! Le
> soir, je me repose. Parfois, je me promène avec ma femme au bord de la Loire. Puis nous
> mangeons, et enfin, vers onze heures, nous nous couchons. Le week-end, je me lève tard.

*My name is Karim. I'm a nurse at the hospital in Nantes. I usually wake up at six. I don't get up
straight away (tout de suite): I stay in bed (au lit) for five minutes. Next I shower and get
dressed. I always hurry in the morning, because the bus leaves at seven! In the evening I rest.
Sometimes I go for a walk with my wife along the Loire (au bord de, on the bank of). Then we eat,
and finally, at around eleven, we go to bed. At the weekend I get up late.*

(*Je reste* is from *rester*, to stay, which you'll learn in lesson 22.)

## Dialogue: Tu te lèves à quelle heure ?

> Léa: Tu as l'air fatigué, Hugo !
>
> Hugo: Oui, je me lève très tôt cette semaine. À cinq heures et demie.
>
> Léa: À cinq heures et demie ? Pourquoi ?
>
> Hugo: Je commence le travail à six heures et demie. Et toi, tu te lèves à quelle heure ?
>
> Léa: D'habitude, à sept heures et demie. Je me douche, je m'habille et je pars.
>
> Hugo: Tu ne prends pas de petit-déjeuner ?
>
> Léa: Si, au bureau, avec un café. Ce soir, tu vas te reposer ?
>
> Hugo: Oui ! Je vais me coucher à neuf heures.

*Léa: You look tired (tu as l'air fatigué), Hugo! — Hugo: Yes, I'm getting up very early this
week. At half past five. — Léa: At half past five? Why? — Hugo: I start work at half past six. What
about you, what time do you get up? — Léa: Usually at half past seven. I shower, get dressed and
leave. — Hugo: You don't have breakfast? — Léa: Yes I do, at the office, with a coffee. Are you
going to rest tonight? — Hugo: Yes! I'm going to go to bed at nine.*

Notice Léa's *Si* (lesson 11): it answers "yes" to a negative question.

## Pronunciation

- *Je me lève*: three short syllables, and the *e* of *me* is often dropped in speech: "jem
  lev". *Je me couche* sounds like "jem koosh".
- *Nous nous levons* has no liaison, but *nous nous habillons* does: "noo noo-za-bee-yon". *Vous
  vous appelez*: "voo voo-za-play".
- *S'habiller*: the *h* is silent and the *ill* says "y": "sa-bee-yay". Compare *la fille* in
  lesson 6.
- *Ensuite* is "on-sweet"; *puis* is "pwee", one syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out the pronoun. *Je lève à sept heures* is wrong (it means "I lift at seven"). Say
  *Je me lève à sept heures.*
- Using the wrong pronoun. *Nous se levons* or *Je vais se coucher* are wrong: the pronoun must
  match the subject: *nous nous levons, je vais me coucher*.
- Splitting the pronoun from the verb. *Je me ne lève pas* is wrong. *Ne* comes before the
  pronoun: *Je ne me lève pas.*
- Forgetting the accent. *Je me leve* is a spelling mistake: *je me lève, tu te lèves*, but
  *nous nous levons*.
- Using *mes* with body parts. With a pronominal verb, French uses the article: *Je me lave les
  mains* (I wash my hands), not *mes mains*.
- Mixing up *tôt* and *en avance*. *Tôt* is early in the day; *en avance* (lesson 18) is early for
  an appointment.

## Key points

- A pronominal verb has a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject: *me, te, se, nous, vous,
  se*. It goes right before the verb; *me, te, se* become *m', t', s'* before a vowel or mute *h*.
- *Se lever* and *se promener* change *e* to *è* (*je me lève*); *s'appeler* doubles the *l* (*je
  m'appelle*), but never with *nous* and *vous*.
- Negative: *Je ne me lève pas.* With an infinitive, the pronoun still matches the subject: *Je
  vais me coucher.*
- Sequence: *d'abord, ensuite, puis, enfin*; *avant, après*.
- Parts of the day: *le matin, l'après-midi, le soir, la nuit*; *tôt, tard*.
- Frequency: *toujours, d'habitude, souvent, parfois*. *Toujours* and *souvent* follow the verb.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Telling the time and the days of the week
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 17 you told your day in order: *je me lève, je me douche, je m'habille*. Now you'll put
times on it: *Je me lève à sept heures et quart.* This lesson teaches how to ask and tell the time,
the everyday clock and the **[[24-hour clock]]** used for timetables, the days of the week, and the
small words that go with times: *à, vers, de … à, jusqu'à*. It uses the numbers from lesson 4, so
you might like to look back at 1–60 first.

## Quelle heure est-il ?

The question is *Quelle heure est-il ?* — What time is it? In conversation you'll also hear *Il est
quelle heure ?* The answer always starts with *Il est …* and always says *heure(s)*:

- *Il est une heure.* — It's one o'clock. (*une*, because *heure* is feminine)
- *Il est deux heures.* — It's two o'clock.
- *Il est dix heures.* — It's ten o'clock.

Never leave out *heures*: *Il est trois* is not French. In writing, *heure(s)* is shortened to *h*:
*3 h, 10 h*.

### Minutes after the hour

Put the minutes straight after *heures*: *trois heures cinq* (3:05), *trois heures dix* (3:10),
*trois heures vingt* (3:20). For a quarter and a half, French adds *et*:

| time | everyday French |
|---|---|
| 3:15 | *trois heures et quart* |
| 3:30 | *trois heures et demie* |

*Demie* ends in *-e* because *heure* is feminine. With *midi* and *minuit*, which are masculine, it
is *et demi*: *midi et demi* (12:30 p.m.), *minuit et demi* (12:30 a.m.).

### Minutes before the hour: moins

After half past, everyday French usually counts back from the next hour with *moins* (minus):

| time | everyday French | literally |
|---|---|---|
| 3:40 | *quatre heures moins vingt* | four hours minus twenty |
| 3:45 | *quatre heures moins le quart* | four hours minus the quarter |
| 3:50 | *quatre heures moins dix* | four hours minus ten |
| 3:55 | *quatre heures moins cinq* | four hours minus five |

Note the article in *moins le quart*, but not in *et quart*. It's just how the expression is
fixed; learn the two as a pair.

![Six clock faces with the time written under each. 3:00, il est trois heures. 3:15, il est trois heures et quart. 3:30, il est trois heures et demie. 3:45, il est quatre heures moins le quart. 3:50, il est quatre heures moins dix. 12:30, il est midi et demi.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Noon and midnight

*Midi* is 12 noon and *minuit* is midnight. Both are used without an article and without
*heures*: *Il est midi. Je mange à midi. Il est minuit et quart.* For the other hours, add *du
matin* (in the morning), *de l'après-midi* or *du soir* when you need to be clear: *Il est huit
heures du soir.* — It's eight p.m.

## The 24-hour clock

Timetables, opening hours, tickets, TV listings and appointments use the 24-hour clock. In
speech it is simpler than the everyday clock: say the hour, then *heures*, then the minutes as a
plain number. No *et quart*, *et demie* or *moins*:

| written | 24-hour, spoken | everyday |
|---|---|---|
| 8 h 15 | *huit heures quinze* | *huit heures et quart* |
| 12 h 30 | *douze heures trente* | *midi et demi* |
| 14 h 30 | *quatorze heures trente* | *deux heures et demie (de l'après-midi)* |
| 18 h 45 | *dix-huit heures quarante-cinq* | *sept heures moins le quart (du soir)* |
| 21 h 10 | *vingt et une heures dix* | *neuf heures dix (du soir)* |
| 0 h 20 | *zéro heure vingt* | *minuit vingt* |

The written form is *14 h 30* (or *14h30*); a colon (14:30) is common on screens but not in
careful writing. Note *vingt et une heures*: *une*, because *heure* is feminine.

![A bar of the day from midnight to midnight. Upper row: the 24-hour numbers 0 to 24. Lower row: the everyday time for the same hours, 12 midnight (minuit), 6 du matin, 12 noon (midi), 3 de l'après-midi, 6 du soir, 9 du soir, 12 midnight (minuit). Coloured bands under the bar show la nuit, le matin, l'après-midi, le soir and la nuit again. Two examples are marked: 14 h 30 = deux heures et demie de l'après-midi, and 20 h = huit heures du soir.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## At what time? à, vers, de … à, jusqu'à

| French | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| *À quelle heure ?* | at what time? | *À quelle heure commence le film ?* |
| *à* + time | at | *Le film commence à vingt heures.* |
| *vers* + time | at about, around | *J'arrive vers dix heures.* |
| *de … à …* | from … to … | *Je travaille de neuf heures à dix-sept heures.* |
| *jusqu'à* + time | until | *La boulangerie est ouverte jusqu'à dix-neuf heures.* |

*Jusqu'à* contracts with *le* and *les* like *à* in lesson 12: *jusqu'au soir* (until the
evening), *jusqu'au matin* (until the morning). With a single day there is no article, so no
contraction: *jusqu'à vendredi* (until Friday).

To say how long something lasts, use the plain number: *Le cours dure une heure et demie.* — The
class lasts an hour and a half. (*durer*, to last.)

## On time, early, late

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *à l'heure* | on time (lesson 14) |
| *en avance* | early (ahead of time) |
| *en retard* | late (lesson 14) |

*Le train est à l'heure. Je suis en avance de dix minutes.* — The train is on time. I'm ten minutes
early. Remember that *tôt* and *tard* (lesson 17) are about the time of day: *Je me lève tôt.*

## The days of the week

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *lundi* | Monday |
| *mardi* | Tuesday |
| *mercredi* | Wednesday |
| *jeudi* | Thursday |
| *vendredi* | Friday |
| *samedi* | Saturday |
| *dimanche* | Sunday |

Days are masculine and written with a small letter. In France the week starts on Monday, so
calendars begin with *lundi*.

### lundi or le lundi?

This is the one rule to learn about days:

- No article for one particular day, usually this coming one: *Lundi, je vais à la banque.* —
  On Monday (this Monday) I'm going to the bank.
- *le* + day for every week, a habit: *Le lundi, je vais à la piscine.* — On Mondays I go to
  the swimming pool.

So *Je travaille samedi* means this Saturday; *Je travaille le samedi* means every Saturday. To
be very clear, say *tous les samedis* (every Saturday) or *tous les jours* (every day).

### This week, next week, last week

*Prochain* (next) and *dernier* (last) come after the time word:

- *la semaine prochaine* — next week; *lundi prochain* — next Monday
- *la semaine dernière* — last week; *samedi dernier* — last Saturday

The feminine forms are *prochaine* and *dernière* because *semaine* is feminine. *Hier* is
yesterday: *Aujourd'hui, c'est mercredi. Hier, c'était mardi.* (*c'était* = it was; lesson 21.)

Here is a week planner with the time words from this lesson:

| | matin | après-midi | soir |
|---|---|---|---|
| lundi | travail 9 h–12 h | travail 14 h–17 h 30 | piscine 19 h |
| mardi | travail | travail | cours de français 18 h 30–20 h |
| mercredi | travail | libre | dîner chez Paul vers 20 h |
| samedi | marché | — | cinéma 21 h |
| dimanche | se reposer ! | promenade | — |

*Le lundi, je vais à la piscine à dix-neuf heures. Le mardi, j'ai un cours de français de
dix-huit heures trente à vingt heures. Mercredi soir, je dîne chez Paul vers vingt heures.*

## Opening hours: ouvert, fermé

Shop doors in France show their *horaires d'ouverture* (opening hours) like this sign:

> BOULANGERIE DUVAL
>
> Ouvert du mardi au samedi : 7 h – 19 h 30
>
> Dimanche : 7 h – 13 h
>
> Fermé le lundi

*Du mardi au samedi* means "from Tuesday to Saturday"; *de* and *à* contract with *le* (*du*,
*au*). *Fermé le lundi* means closed every Monday. Many small shops in France close at lunchtime or
on Monday; always check the sign. *Ouvert* and *fermé* agree like any adjective: *La pharmacie est
ouverte. Les magasins sont fermés.*

## Dialogue: À quelle heure ?

> Marc: Pardon, madame, quelle heure est-il ?
>
> Femme: Il est six heures moins dix.
>
> Marc: Merci. La poste est encore ouverte ?
>
> Femme: Non, elle est ouverte jusqu'à dix-huit heures, mais aujourd'hui c'est samedi. Le samedi,
> elle ferme à midi.
>
> Marc: Ah, zut ! Et lundi ?
>
> Femme: Lundi, elle ouvre à neuf heures. Mais attention, le lundi, il y a toujours la queue !
>
> Marc: D'accord. Merci beaucoup, madame.

*Marc: Excuse me, madam, what time is it? — Woman: It's ten to six. — Marc: Thanks. Is the post
office still (encore) open? — Woman: No, it's open until 6 p.m., but today is Saturday. On
Saturdays it closes (fermer, to close) at noon. — Marc: Oh, bother (zut)! And on Monday? — Woman:
On Monday it opens (ouvrir, to open) at nine. But careful, on Mondays there's always a queue (la
queue)! — Marc: OK. Thank you very much, madam.*

## Pronunciation

- *heure* sounds like "eur", with liaison before it: *deux_heures* "deu-zeur", *trois_heures*
  "trwa-zeur", *six_heures* "see-zeur", *dix_heures* "dee-zeur", *neuf heures* "neu-veur" (the f
  becomes v).
- *une heure* "u-neur", *onze heures* "on-zeur".
- *quart* rhymes with "car"; the *t* is silent.
- *minuit* is "mee-nwee"; *midi* is "mee-dee".
- *lundi* has a nasal *un*; *jeudi* "zheu-dee"; *vendredi* "von-dreu-dee".

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out *heures*. Say *Il est cinq heures*, not *Il est cinq*.
- Using *et* with *moins*. It's *quatre heures moins le quart*, not *et moins le quart*, and
  never *trois heures et quarante-cinq*.
- Mixing up *et demie* and *et demi*. *Trois heures et demie* (*heure* is feminine), but *midi et
  demi*.
- Using an article with a single day. *Le samedi, je vais au cinéma* means every Saturday. For
  this Saturday say *Samedi, je vais au cinéma.*
- Capital letters. Days are lower case: *mardi*, not *Mardi* (except at the start of a sentence).
- *Prochain* before the noun. It's *la semaine prochaine*, not *la prochaine semaine*, when you
  mean next week.

## Key points

- *Quelle heure est-il ? — Il est trois heures.* Always say *heure(s)*; *une heure* is feminine.
- Everyday clock: *et quart, et demie, moins le quart, moins dix*; *midi, minuit, midi et demi*.
- 24-hour clock: hour + *heures* + minutes as a number: *quatorze heures trente*; written *14 h
  30*.
- *à* (at), *vers* (around), *de … à* (from … to), *jusqu'à* (until); *à l'heure, en avance, en
  retard*.
- Days are masculine, lower case. *lundi* = this Monday; *le lundi* = on Mondays.
- *la semaine prochaine, lundi dernier*; *ouvert, fermé*; *tous les jours*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Dates, birthdays and invitations: vouloir, pouvoir, devoir
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 18 gave you the clock and the days of the week. This lesson adds the calendar: the months,
dates and years, birthdays and parties. Then it gives you three verbs you need for any plan or
invitation, *vouloir* (to want), *pouvoir* (can) and *devoir* (must), so that you can invite
someone, accept with pleasure, or say no politely: *Tu veux venir samedi ? — Désolé, je ne peux
pas, je dois travailler.*

## The months

| French | English | French | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *janvier* | January | *juillet* | July |
| *février* | February | *août* | August |
| *mars* | March | *septembre* | September |
| *avril* | April | *octobre* | October |
| *mai* | May | *novembre* | November |
| *juin* | June | *décembre* | December |

Like the days, the months are masculine and written with a small letter. They are used without an
article. "In May" is *en mai* (or *au mois de mai*):

- *En juillet, il fait chaud.* — In July it's hot.
- *Mon anniversaire est en octobre.* — My birthday is in October.

*Août* is said "oo" or "oot"; both are heard. The new spelling *aout*, without the circumflex, is
also correct (the 1990 spelling reform). In *mars* the *s* is pronounced: "marss".

## Dates: le premier, le deux, le trois

A date in French is *le* + number + month. Only the first day of the month uses an
**[[ordinal number]]** (first, second, third…): *le premier*. Every other day uses the ordinary
**[[cardinal number]]** (one, two, three…):

| written | said | English |
|---|---|---|
| *le 1er mai* | *le premier mai* | the first of May, May 1st |
| *le 2 mai* | *le deux mai* | the second of May |
| *le 8 mai* | *le huit mai* | the eighth of May |
| *le 14 juillet* | *le quatorze juillet* | the fourteenth of July |
| *le 21 juin* | *le vingt et un juin* | the twenty-first of June |
| *le 31 décembre* | *le trente et un décembre* | the thirty-first of December |

*1er* is the short written form of *premier* (feminine *1re*, *première*). Note *le vingt et un
juin* and *le trente et un décembre*: not *premier*, because only the first of the month is an
ordinal. *Le huit* and *le onze* keep *le* in full, with no elision: *le onze novembre*.

To give the weekday too, put it between *le* and the number: *le lundi 4 mai* — Monday 4 May.

![A calendar page for May 2026, with the week starting on Monday: lun., mar., mer., jeu., ven., sam., dim. Friday the 1st is circled and labelled le premier mai. Saturday the 2nd: le deux mai. Friday the 8th: le huit mai. Thursday the 14th: le quatorze mai. Thursday the 21st: le vingt et un mai. Sunday the 31st: le trente et un mai.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Asking the date

There are three common questions:

- *Quelle est la date aujourd'hui ?* — What's the date today?
- *On est le combien ?* — What's the date? (informal; literally "we are the how many?")
- *On est quel jour ?* — What day is it? (formal: *Quel jour sommes-nous ?*)

The answers use *on est* or *nous sommes* (more formal), or *c'est*:

- *On est le 10 novembre.* — It's the 10th of November.
- *Nous sommes le mardi 10 novembre.* — It's Tuesday the 10th of November.
- *C'est le premier avril !* — It's the first of April!

In writing, the day comes before the month: *10/11/2026* is 10 November 2026, not 11 October.
English speakers from the US should take special care with this.

### Years

French reads years as ordinary numbers (lesson 10 for *mille*):

- *2026* — *deux mille vingt-six*
- *2000* — *deux mille*
- *1995* — *mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze*, or in speech *dix-neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze*

"In 2026" is *en 2026*: *En 2026, je vais en France.* A full date: *le 3 mars 2026* (*le trois mars
deux mille vingt-six*).

## Birthdays and parties

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *l'anniversaire* (m.) | birthday |
| *Joyeux anniversaire !* / *Bon anniversaire !* | Happy birthday! |
| *la fête* | party, celebration, holiday |
| *la soirée* | (evening) party; the whole evening |
| *le cadeau* (pl. *les cadeaux*) | present |
| *Noël* | Christmas: *Joyeux Noël !* |

To give your birthday: *Mon anniversaire, c'est le 4 avril.* To ask: *C'est quand, ton
anniversaire ?* — When's your birthday? *Quand est ton anniversaire ?* is more formal.

*Le soir* (lesson 17) is a point in the day, "in the evening"; *la soirée* is the whole evening
or a party in it: *Bonne soirée !* (lesson 2) — Have a nice evening! *Une soirée chez Paul* — a
party at Paul's.

## Vouloir, pouvoir, devoir

These three irregular verbs are the most useful in French for plans. They are often called
**[[modal verbs]]**, as in English (want to, can, must). Each is followed by an infinitive.

| | vouloir (to want) | pouvoir (can, to be able to) | devoir (must, to have to) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | *veux* | *peux* | *dois* |
| tu | *veux* | *peux* | *dois* |
| il / elle / on | *veut* | *peut* | *doit* |
| nous | *voulons* | *pouvons* | *devons* |
| vous | *voulez* | *pouvez* | *devez* |
| ils / elles | *veulent* | *peuvent* | *doivent* |

A pattern helps: the *je, tu, il* forms all sound the same, and end in *-x, -x, -t* (*veux, veux,
veut*) or *-s, -s, -t* (*dois, dois, doit*). *Nous* and *vous* keep the infinitive's stem
(*voul-, pouv-, dev-*). The *ils* form has a new stem again: *veulent, peuvent, doivent*.

### + infinitive

- *Je veux apprendre le français.* — I want to learn French.
- *Tu peux venir samedi ?* — Can you come on Saturday?
- *Nous devons partir à huit heures.* — We have to leave at eight.
- *Vous voulez boire quelque chose ?* — Would you like something to drink? (*quelque chose* =
  something; lesson 21)

In the negative, *ne … pas* goes around the first verb: *Je ne peux pas venir.* — I can't come.
*Il ne veut pas danser.* — He doesn't want to dance. *Tu ne dois pas* means "you mustn't".

With a pronominal verb (lesson 17), the pronoun still matches the subject: *Je dois me lever tôt.*
— I have to get up early.

### Being polite

*Je veux* is direct, like "I want". To ask for something in a shop or café, use *je voudrais*
(lesson 9): *Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.* A question with *pouvoir* is the polite way to
ask someone to do something: *Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?* — Could you repeat that,
please?

*Devoir* also means "to owe": *Je vous dois combien ?* — How much do I owe you?

## Inviting, accepting, declining

*Inviter* is a regular *-er* verb: *Je t'invite à ma fête.* — I'm inviting you to my party. (*t'* =
you; object pronouns come before the verb.) Here is how an invitation usually goes:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Inviting someone, then accepting or declining
  accDescr: Someone invites: Tu veux venir à ma soirée samedi? The other person can accept or decline. To accept, say Oui, avec plaisir! or Oui, je veux bien! and then ask À quelle heure? To decline, say Désolé or Désolée, je ne peux pas, give a reason with devoir such as je dois travailler, and offer another time: Une autre fois? Both paths end with a friendly close such as Merci, à samedi! or Merci quand même!
  A["Invitation: Tu veux venir à ma soirée samedi ?"] --> B{"Can you go?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Oui, avec plaisir ! / Oui, je veux bien !"]
  C --> D["Ask the details: À quelle heure ? C'est où ?"]
  D --> E["Close: Super, merci ! À samedi !"]
  B -- "no" --> F["Désolé(e), je ne peux pas."]
  F --> G["Give a reason: Je dois travailler."]
  G --> H["Offer another time: Une autre fois ?"]
  H --> I["Close: Merci quand même !"]
```

*Je veux bien* (gladly, I'd like that) is softer than *je veux*. *Quand même* means "anyway, all the
same"; *Merci quand même !* — Thanks anyway! *Une autre fois* — another time.

## A message: une invitation

> Salut Emma ! Samedi, c'est mon anniversaire : j'ai trente ans ! Je fais une petite fête chez moi,
> le 16 mai à partir de 20 h. Tu veux venir ? Tu peux venir avec ton copain, bien sûr. Pas de
> cadeau, s'il te plaît ! Réponds-moi avant jeudi. Bises, Inès

*Hi Emma! On Saturday it's my birthday: I'm thirty! I'm having a little party at my place on 16 May
from 8 p.m. (à partir de, from). Do you want to come? You can come with your boyfriend (ton
copain), of course (bien sûr). No presents, please! Answer me before Thursday. Love, Inès*

> Salut Inès ! Merci pour l'invitation. Je veux bien venir, avec plaisir ! Mais Thomas ne peut pas :
> il doit travailler samedi soir. Je vais arriver vers 21 h. Joyeux anniversaire en avance !
> Emma

*Hi Inès! Thanks for the invitation. I'd love to come! But Thomas can't: he has to work on Saturday
evening. I'll arrive at around 9 p.m. Happy birthday in advance! Emma*

(*Réponds-moi* is an imperative, lesson 20; *bises* is how friends sign off, lesson 23.)

## Pronunciation

- *veux, peux* have the rounded "eu" sound; *veulent, peuvent* have the more open one, and the
  *-ent* is silent: "veul", "peuv".
- *doit* and *dois* sound the same: "dwa". *Doivent* is "dwav".
- *premier* "preu-myay"; *première* "preu-myair".
- *anniversaire* "a-nee-vair-sair"; *Noël* has two syllables: "no-el".
- *juin* and *juillet* start with a quick "zhw" sound: "zhwan", "zhwee-yay".

## Common mistakes

- *Le un mai*. Only the first is an ordinal: *le premier mai*. But *le vingt et un mai*, not *le
  vingt et unième*.
- *Le deuxième mai*. From the 2nd on, use plain numbers: *le deux mai*.
- *Mai 4*. The day comes first: *le 4 mai*.
- Capital letters on months. *janvier*, not *Janvier*.
- *Je peux de venir* or *Je dois à travailler*. No preposition after these verbs: *je peux venir,
  je dois travailler*.
- *Je veux* in a shop. It sounds demanding; say *je voudrais*.
- Writing *peut* for *peux*. *Je peux, tu peux* end in *-x*; only *il peut* ends in *-t*.

## Key points

- Months are masculine, lower case, without an article: *en mai, en août*.
- Dates: *le* + number + month: *le 2 mai, le 14 juillet*; only the first is *le premier (1er)*.
- Asking: *Quelle est la date ? On est le combien ?* Answer: *On est le 10 novembre.*
- Years: *deux mille vingt-six*; *en 2026*.
- *vouloir, pouvoir, devoir* + infinitive: *Tu veux venir ? Je ne peux pas, je dois travailler.*
- Accept: *Avec plaisir ! Je veux bien.* Decline: *Désolé(e), je ne peux pas.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Finding the way: the imperative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 12 you went into town: *Je vais à la banque, au musée, à la poste.* But how do you get
there? This lesson gives you the words for asking and giving directions, and the verb form you
need to give them: the **[[imperative]]**, the form for telling or asking someone to do something.
*Tournez à gauche !* — Turn left! *Prends la deuxième rue !* — Take the second street!

The good news: you already know almost every imperative form. It's the present tense from lessons
7, 14 and 16, without the subject pronoun.

## Asking the way

Start with *Pardon* or *Excusez-moi* (lesson 1), then use one of these:

- *Où est la gare ?* — Where is the station?
- *Où se trouve la poste ?* — Where is the post office? (*se trouver*, to be located)
- *Je cherche le musée.* — I'm looking for the museum.
- *Pour aller à la mairie, s'il vous plaît ?* — How do I get to the town hall, please?
- *C'est loin ? C'est près d'ici ?* — Is it far? Is it near here?
- *Il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?* — Is there a pharmacy near here?

*Se trouver* is a pronominal verb (lesson 17): *La gare se trouve au centre-ville. Les toilettes
se trouvent au premier étage* (*l'étage*, floor). It just means "is" or "are" for a place, a little more formal than
*être*.

## Directions

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *à droite* | on the right, to the right |
| *à gauche* | on the left, to the left |
| *tout droit* | straight ahead, straight on |
| *tourner* | to turn |
| *continuer* | to carry on, to continue |
| *traverser* | to cross |
| *le carrefour* | crossroads, junction |
| *le feu* (pl. *les feux*) | traffic light |
| *le pont* | bridge |
| *le coin* | corner |
| *le chemin* | way, path |
| *le plan* | (town) map |
| *le panneau* (pl. *les panneaux*) | sign |

Watch *droite* and *droit*: *à droite* (on the right) ends in *-e* and says the *t*; *tout droit*
(straight on) has no *-e* and a silent *t*. Mixing them up sends people the wrong way!

Useful chunks:

- *au carrefour* — at the crossroads; *au feu* — at the lights; *au coin de la rue* — on the
  corner of the street
- *après le pont* — after the bridge; *jusqu'au feu* — as far as the lights (lesson 18)
- *Suivez les panneaux.* — Follow the signs. (*suivre*, to follow)

### First, second, third: ordinal numbers

To say which street, use an ordinal number: *la première rue* (the first street), *la
deuxième rue*, *la troisième rue*. You met *premier/première* in lesson 19. All the others add
*-ième* to the number, dropping a final *-e*:

| number | ordinal | written |
|---|---|---|
| *un* | *premier / première* | 1er / 1re |
| *deux* | *deuxième* | 2e |
| *trois* | *troisième* | 3e |
| *quatre* | *quatrième* | 4e |
| *cinq* | *cinquième* (add *u*) | 5e |
| *neuf* | *neuvième* (*f* → *v*) | 9e |

*Prenez la deuxième rue à droite.* — Take the second street on the right. Ordinals go before the
noun, like in English. (Only the first one is used in dates: *le premier mai*, but *le deux mai*.)

## Where is it? à côté de, en face de, entre

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *à côté de* | next to |
| *en face de* | opposite |
| *entre … et …* | between … and … |
| *près de* | near |
| *loin de* | far from |

These all end in *de*, and *de* contracts with *le* and *les*, just as *à* does (lesson 12):

| | de + … | example |
|---|---|---|
| *de + le* | *du* | *à côté du parc* — next to the park |
| *de + la* | *de la* | *en face de la gare* — opposite the station |
| *de + l'* | *de l'* | *près de l'hôpital* — near the hospital |
| *de + les* | *des* | *en face des toilettes* — opposite the toilets |

Before a vowel or mute *h*, *de* becomes *d'*: *près d'ici, loin d'Annecy* (but *loin de Paris*). *Entre* takes no *de*: *entre la
banque et la poste*.

## The imperative

French has three imperative forms: one for *tu*, one for *vous* (one person formally, or several
people), and one for *nous* ("let's …"). Take the present-tense form and drop the subject:

| | tu | vous | nous |
|---|---|---|---|
| present | *tu prends* | *vous prenez* | *nous prenons* |
| imperative | *Prends !* | *Prenez !* | *Prenons !* |
| meaning | Take! | Take! | Let's take! |

### -er verbs drop the -s

There is one change. With *-er* verbs (and *aller*), the *tu* form loses its *-s*:

| infinitive | tu present | tu imperative | vous | nous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *tourner* | *tu tournes* | *Tourne !* | *Tournez !* | *Tournons !* |
| *continuer* | *tu continues* | *Continue !* | *Continuez !* | *Continuons !* |
| *traverser* | *tu traverses* | *Traverse !* | *Traversez !* | *Traversons !* |
| *aller* | *tu vas* | *Va !* | *Allez !* | *Allons !* |

Other verbs keep it: *Prends le bus !* (*prendre*), *Attends !* (*attendre*), *Finis !*
(*finir*), *Viens !* (*venir*), *Fais attention !* (*faire*; *fais attention* = be careful).

The rule comes in one chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to build the French imperative
  accDescr: Choose the person: tu, vous or nous. Take the present-tense form of the verb for that person and drop the subject pronoun: vous tournez becomes Tournez, nous prenons becomes Prenons. For tu, check the verb. If it is an -er verb or aller, drop the final s: tu tournes becomes Tourne, tu vas becomes Va. Other verbs keep the s: tu prends becomes Prends. A pronominal verb adds its pronoun after a hyphen: Lève-toi, Levez-vous, Levons-nous. A few verbs are irregular: être gives Sois, Soyez, Soyons, and avoir gives Aie, Ayez, Ayons.
  A["Choose: tu, vous or nous"] --> B["Take the present form, drop the pronoun: Tournez ! Prenons !"]
  B --> C{"tu form of an -er verb or aller?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["Drop the -s: Tourne ! Va !"]
  C -- "no" --> E["Keep it: Prends ! Finis !"]
  D --> F{"Pronominal verb?"}
  E --> F
  F -- "yes" --> G["Add the pronoun after a hyphen: Lève-toi ! Levez-vous !"]
  F -- "no" --> H["Done. Irregular: Sois, Soyez / Aie, Ayez"]
```

### Être and avoir

Two verbs have special forms. You don't need them for directions, but you will see them:

| | tu | vous | nous |
|---|---|---|---|
| *être* | *Sois !* | *Soyez !* | *Soyons !* |
| *avoir* | *Aie !* | *Ayez !* | *Ayons !* |

*Sois sage !* — Be good! (to a child). *Soyez à l'heure.* — Be on time. *N'ayez pas peur.* — Don't
be afraid. *Vouloir* has a very polite form, *veuillez*, which you'll see on signs and in letters:
*Veuillez patienter.* — Please wait.

### The negative imperative

*Ne … pas* goes around the verb, as usual:

- *Ne traverse pas !* — Don't cross!
- *Ne tournez pas à droite !* — Don't turn right!
- *N'allons pas au cinéma ce soir.* — Let's not go to the cinema tonight.

### Pronominal verbs: Lève-toi !

In the positive imperative of a pronominal verb, the pronoun moves after the verb with a
hyphen, and *te* becomes *toi*:

| | tu | vous | nous |
|---|---|---|---|
| *se lever* | *Lève-toi !* | *Levez-vous !* | *Levons-nous !* |
| *se dépêcher* | *Dépêche-toi !* | *Dépêchez-vous !* | *Dépêchons-nous !* |

In the negative, the pronoun goes back in front of the verb: *Ne te lève pas !* — Don't get up!
*Ne vous dépêchez pas.* — Don't rush.

### Making it polite

A bare imperative can sound blunt to strangers. Add *s'il vous plaît* (or *s'il te plaît* with
*tu*), or use a question with *pouvoir* (lesson 19): *Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?*
When you give directions to a stranger, the *vous* imperative is normal and polite: *Continuez
tout droit, puis tournez à gauche.* You can also use the present tense: *Vous prenez la deuxième
rue à droite.*

## A route on the map

Here is a small town. Follow the route from the star (*Vous êtes ici*, you are here) to the
station:

![A town map. A star near the bottom marks Vous êtes ici. The route goes straight up a street (tout droit) to a crossroads with a traffic light (le carrefour, le feu), turns right (à droite), crosses a bridge over a river (le pont), and turns left (à gauche) at a corner with a sign pointing up the street (le coin, le panneau) to reach la gare at the top right. Next to the start is le parc; next to the station is l'hôtel.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Allez tout droit jusqu'au carrefour. Au feu, tournez à droite. Traversez le pont. Au coin, au
panneau, tournez à gauche. La gare est là, à côté de l'hôtel.*

## North, south, east, west

| French | English | |
|---|---|---|
| *le nord* | north | *Lille est dans le nord de la France.* |
| *le sud* | south | *Marseille est dans le sud.* |
| *l'est* (m.) | east | *Strasbourg est dans l'est.* |
| *l'ouest* (m.) | west | *Brest est dans l'ouest.* |

*Dans le nord de la France* means in the north of France (inside it); *au nord de Paris* means
north of Paris (outside it). On French maps west is *O* for *ouest*, not *W*. Say the final
consonants: *le sud* "sood", *l'est* "lest", *l'ouest* "lwest".

![A compass rose with four arms: le nord at the top, le sud at the bottom, l'est on the right and l'ouest on the left, marked N, S, E and O. Around it, four French cities roughly in their directions from Paris in the centre: Lille to the north, Marseille to the south, Strasbourg to the east and Brest to the west.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Signs you will see

| sign | meaning |
|---|---|
| *Sortie* | Exit |
| *Toilettes* (often *WC*) | Toilets |
| *Attention !* | Watch out! Careful! |
| *Centre-ville* | Town centre |
| *Toutes directions* | All directions (road signs) |

*Les toilettes* is always plural for the room: *Où sont les toilettes, s'il vous plaît ?*

## Dialogue: Pour aller à la gare ?

> Touriste: Excusez-moi, monsieur. Pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
>
> Homme: La gare ? Ce n'est pas loin. Vous êtes à pied ?
>
> Touriste: Oui.
>
> Homme: Alors, allez tout droit jusqu'au carrefour. Au feu, tournez à droite.
>
> Touriste: Au feu, à droite. D'accord.
>
> Homme: Ensuite, traversez le pont et prenez la deuxième rue à gauche. La gare est au bout de la
> rue, en face d'un grand hôtel.
>
> Touriste: C'est à combien de minutes ?
>
> Homme: Dix minutes, à peu près. Attention, il y a beaucoup de voitures : traversez au feu !
>
> Touriste: Merci beaucoup, monsieur.
>
> Homme: De rien. Bonne journée !

*Tourist: Excuse me, sir. How do I get to the station, please? — Man: The station? It's not far.
Are you on foot? — Tourist: Yes. — Man: Then go straight on as far as the crossroads. At the lights,
turn right. — Tourist: At the lights, right. OK. — Man: Next, cross the bridge and take the second
street on the left. The station is at the end of the street (au bout de), opposite a big hotel. —
Tourist: How many minutes is it? — Man: About (à peu près) ten minutes. Careful, there are lots of
cars: cross at the lights! — Tourist: Thank you very much, sir. —
Man: You're welcome. Have a nice day!*

## Pronunciation

- *à droite* "a drwat" (t heard); *tout droit* "too drwa" (t silent).
- *carrefour* "kar-foor": the middle *e* is usually silent.
- *Tournez* "toor-nay"; *Tourne* "toorn".
- In the imperative, your voice falls at the end, like an order; a question rises.
- *Lève-toi* "lev-twa"; *Dépêche-toi* "day-pesh-twa".

## Common mistakes

- *Tournes à gauche !* With *-er* verbs the *tu* imperative has no *-s*: *Tourne à gauche !*
- *Vas tout droit !* Same rule for *aller*: *Va tout droit !*
- Keeping the pronoun. *Tu tourne à droite !* is a broken statement. The imperative has no
  subject: *Tourne à droite !*
- *Te lève !* In the positive, the pronoun goes after: *Lève-toi !* In the negative, before: *Ne te
  lève pas !*
- *À côté de le parc.* *De + le* becomes *du*: *à côté du parc.*
- *Tout droite*, *à droit*. Straight on is *tout droit*; on the right is *à droite*.
- *La deux rue.* Use the ordinal: *la deuxième rue*.

## Key points

- Asking: *Où est … ? Où se trouve … ? Pour aller à … ?* *C'est loin ?*
- *à droite, à gauche, tout droit*; *tourner, continuer, traverser*; *le carrefour, le feu, le pont,
  le coin*.
- Ordinals: *premier, deuxième, troisième*: add *-ième*.
- *à côté de, en face de, près de, loin de*; *de + le = du, de + les = des*; *entre … et …*.
- Imperative: the present without the pronoun, for *tu, vous, nous*. *-er* verbs and *aller* drop
  the *tu* *-s*: *Tourne ! Va !*. Negative: *Ne traverse pas !*
- Pronominal: *Lève-toi ! Levez-vous !*, but *Ne te lève pas !*
- *le nord, le sud, l'est, l'ouest*; *dans le nord de la France*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Departure boards and timetables
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 14 you took the train: *le billet, la gare, le départ, l'arrivée, l'aller-retour, en
retard*. In lesson 18 you learned the 24-hour clock, and in lesson 20 you learned to find your way.
A real French station puts all of that together, fast: a board that changes every minute, a voice
from a loudspeaker, a ticket office with a queue behind you.

This honors lesson trains you for that. You'll read a departure board, hear the 24-hour clock at
speed, learn three small words that change the meaning of a time (*dans, en, il y a*), buy a
one-way ticket, and decode station announcements. The texts and boards are invented, but they
follow the patterns you'll meet in France.

## Kinds of train

French trains have short names you'll see on every board:

| on the board | full name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| *TGV* | *train à grande vitesse* | high-speed train between big cities |
| *Intercités* | | long-distance train, not high-speed |
| *TER* | *transport express régional* (also *train express régional*) | regional train, run with the region |
| *RER* | *réseau express régional* | suburban train in and around Paris |

*Le TGV, le TER, le RER* are masculine (*le train*). Say the letters in French: "tay-zhay-vay",
"tay-eu-air", "air-eu-air".

## Reading a departure board

In the station, the board for trains leaving is *les départs*; for trains coming in, *les
arrivées* (both from lesson 14). Here is an invented departure board at two o'clock in the
afternoon:

![An invented departure board headed Départs, with the time 14:00 in the corner. Columns: Heure, Train, Destination, Voie, Informations. Row 1: 14 h 04, TGV 6603, Lyon Part-Dieu, voie 9, à l'heure. Row 2: 14 h 12, TER 17721, Dijon Ville, voie 3, retard 15 min. Row 3: 14 h 20, TGV 6115, Marseille Saint-Charles, no platform yet, à l'heure. Row 4: 14 h 31, TER 17725, Montereau, voie 5, supprimé. Row 5: 14 h 46, Intercités 5953, Nevers, no platform yet, à l'heure.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The columns:

- *Heure* — the planned time of departure, on the 24-hour clock.
- *Train* — the kind of train and its number. The number is printed on your ticket: check it.
- *Destination* — where the train is going: its last stop.
- *Voie* — the track the train leaves from. In everyday English you'd say "platform 9". *La voie*
  is the track (a number or letter on the board); *le quai* is the platform you stand on.
- *Informations* — the column to watch.

The four notes you'll see most:

| note | meaning |
|---|---|
| *à l'heure* | on time |
| *retard 15 min* | about 15 minutes late (*le retard*, the delay) |
| *retardé* | delayed (no time given yet) |
| *supprimé* | cancelled |

In big stations the *voie* often appears only about 20 minutes before departure, when the train
is ready. Until then the column is empty, so you wait in the hall and watch the board. The practice
varies from station to station. At Paris-Gare-de-Lyon, for example, some platforms have letters
instead of numbers (*voie B*).

### Example 1: Which train, which platform?

It's *14 h 00* and you have a ticket for the TER 17721 to Dijon.

1. Find the train number, not just the town: TER 17721, row 2.
2. *Heure: 14 h 12*. *Informations: retard 15 min*. So the train will leave at about 14 h 27.
3. *Voie 3*. You can go to platform 3 now, but you have time for a coffee.

Now your friend has a ticket for the TER to Montereau at 14 h 31. Row 4 says *supprimé*: there is
no train. She must go to the ticket office or ask staff about the next one: *Le train de 14 h 31
est supprimé. Quel est le prochain train pour Montereau ?*

## The 24-hour clock at speed

On boards, in announcements and on tickets, times are always on the 24-hour clock (lesson 18). In
announcements they come fast, and the word *heures* runs into the minutes. Practise saying these
out loud, with liaison where the hour ends in a consonant:

| written | said |
|---|---|
| *6 h 05* | *six heures cinq* ("see-zeur sank") |
| *9 h 50* | *neuf heures cinquante* ("neu-veur") |
| *13 h 15* | *treize heures quinze* |
| *17 h 52* | *dix-sept heures cinquante-deux* |
| *20 h 00* | *vingt heures* ("van-teur") |
| *21 h 34* | *vingt et une heures trente-quatre* |
| *23 h 08* | *vingt-trois heures huit* |
| *0 h 45* | *zéro heure quarante-cinq* |

Two traps: *vingt et une heures* (21 h) uses *une*, because *heure* is feminine; and *zéro heure*
has no *s*. Minutes under ten are said as a plain number: *8 h 05* is *huit heures cinq*, not
"huit heures zéro cinq".

## dans, en, il y a: three ways to put a number on time

These three small words all go in front of a length of time, and they mean very different things:

| word | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *dans* + time | in … (from now) | *Le train part dans dix minutes.* — The train leaves in ten minutes. |
| *en* + time | in … (how long it takes) | *Paris–Lyon en deux heures.* — Paris to Lyon in two hours. |
| *il y a* + time | … ago | *Il y a dix minutes, le train était à l'heure.* — Ten minutes ago, the train was on time. |

*Dans* looks forward to a moment: when will it happen? *En* measures a length: how long does it
take? *Il y a* looks back: how long ago? (*était* is a past form of *être*, "was"; past tenses
start in lesson 21.)

### Example 2: dans, en or il y a?

It's *13 h 50*. The TGV to Lyon leaves at *14 h 04* and arrives at *16 h 04*.

1. When does it leave, from now? 14 h 04 − 13 h 50 = 14 minutes ahead: *Le train part dans
   quatorze minutes.*
2. How long is the trip? 16 h 04 − 14 h 04 = 2 hours: *On va à Lyon en deux heures.* (Or with a
   verb from lesson 18: *Le voyage dure deux heures.*)
3. You got to the station at 13 h 30, which is 13 h 50 − 13 h 30 = 20 minutes ago: *il y a vingt
   minutes*. A full sentence needs a past tense (*Je suis arrivée il y a vingt minutes*, lesson 22),
   but you can already use the chunk: *Le café ? Il y a vingt minutes, il était fermé.* — The café?
   Twenty minutes ago it was closed.

A quick test: if you can put "from now" after the English, use *dans*. If you can say "it takes",
use *en*. If English says "ago", use *il y a*.

## Buying a ticket

You can buy a ticket online, at a machine or at *le guichet* (the ticket office). At the counter,
the order of information is the same as in English: kind of ticket, destination, day and time,
class.

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *un aller simple* | a one-way ticket, a single |
| *un aller-retour* | a return ticket (lesson 14) |
| *pour Lyon* | to Lyon |
| *en première (classe)* | in first class (written *1re*) |
| *en seconde (classe)* | in second class (written *2de* or *2nde*) |
| *direct* | direct, with no change |
| *une correspondance* | a connection, a change of train |

*Seconde* is said "seu-gond": the *c* sounds like *g*. You will also hear *en deuxième classe*.

> Voyageuse: Bonjour, monsieur. Je voudrais un aller simple pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
>
> Agent: Pour quel jour ?
>
> Voyageuse: Pour demain matin, vers neuf heures.
>
> Agent: Il y a un TGV direct à 9 h 04, et un TER à 9 h 12 avec une correspondance à Dijon.
>
> Voyageuse: Le direct, s'il vous plaît. En seconde classe.
>
> Agent: Alors, un aller simple Paris–Lyon, demain, 9 h 04, en seconde. Ça fait soixante-deux euros.
>
> Voyageuse: Je peux payer par carte ?
>
> Agent: Bien sûr. Voilà votre billet. Le train arrive à Lyon à 11 h 01.
>
> Voyageuse: Et c'est quelle voie ?
>
> Agent: On ne sait pas encore. Regardez le tableau des départs : la voie est affichée vingt
> minutes avant le départ.
>
> Voyageuse: Merci beaucoup. Bonne journée !

*Traveller: Hello. I'd like a one-way ticket to Lyon, please. — Agent: For which day? — Traveller:
For tomorrow morning, at around nine. — Agent: There's a direct TGV at 9:04, and a regional train
at 9:12 with a change in Dijon. — Traveller: The direct one, please. Second class. — Agent: So, a
single Paris–Lyon, tomorrow, 9:04, second class. That's sixty-two euros. — Traveller: Can I pay by
card (par carte)? — Agent: Of course. Here's your ticket. The train arrives in Lyon at 11:01. —
Traveller: And which platform is it? — Agent: We don't know yet. Look at the departures board: the
platform is shown (affichée) twenty minutes before departure. — Traveller: Thank you very much. Have
a nice day!*

The price is invented; real fares change with the day and how early you book.

## Station announcements

Announcements follow a small number of patterns. Once you know the frame, you only need to catch
the details: the train, the place, the time, the platform, the problem.

| frame | meaning |
|---|---|
| *Le TGV numéro … à destination de …* | The TGV number … to … |
| *Le train en provenance de …* | The train from … (arriving) |
| *… partira voie 9* | … will leave from platform 9 |
| *… est annoncé avec un retard de 15 minutes environ* | … is expected about 15 minutes late |
| *… est supprimé* | … is cancelled |
| *en raison de …* | because of … |
| *Attention, un train va entrer en gare voie 4.* | Careful, a train is coming into platform 4. |
| *Éloignez-vous de la bordure du quai.* | Stand back from the edge of the platform. |

*Partira* and *arrivera* are in the **[[simple future]]** ("will leave", "will arrive"), a tense for
A2. At A1, just recognise the ending *-ra* as "will". *Environ* means "about", like *vers* for
times.

### Example 3: Decoding an announcement

> « Votre attention, s'il vous plaît. Le TER numéro 17721, à destination de Dijon Ville, départ
> prévu à 14 h 12, est annoncé avec un retard de 15 minutes environ. Ce retard est dû à un problème
> technique. Le train partira voie 3. »

Take it piece by piece:

1. *Votre attention, s'il vous plaît* — the opening: listen now.
2. *Le TER numéro 17721, à destination de Dijon Ville* — which train: TER 17721, to Dijon.
3. *départ prévu à 14 h 12* — its planned departure (*prévu*, planned): 14:12.
4. *annoncé avec un retard de 15 minutes environ* — the news: about 15 minutes late.
5. *Ce retard est dû à un problème technique* — the reason (*dû à*, due to; *dû* is the participle
   of *devoir*): a technical problem.
6. *Le train partira voie 3* — the platform: 3.

The answer to "What should I do?": the train still leaves, from platform 3, at about 14:27. Compare
this with the board in Example 1: same train, same news.

Here is a second one, for an arrival:

> « Le TGV numéro 6604, en provenance de Lyon Part-Dieu, arrive voie 11. Attention, un train va
> entrer en gare voie 11. Éloignez-vous de la bordure du quai. »

*The TGV number 6604 from Lyon Part-Dieu is arriving at platform 11. Careful, a train is coming into
platform 11. Stand back from the edge of the platform.* If you are meeting someone off this train,
go to *voie 11*, but not too close to the edge.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing *dans* and *en*. *Le train part en dix minutes* is wrong when you mean "ten minutes
  from now": say *dans dix minutes*. *En* is for how long something takes.
- Mixing up *supprimé* and *retardé*. A *supprimé* train will not run at all.
- Looking for a platform number too early. An empty *Voie* column is normal; wait for it.
- *Vingt et un heures*. With *heure*, it's *vingt et une heures*.
- Saying *un simple* for a ticket. It's *un aller simple*; *un aller-retour* for a return.
- Reading *à destination de* as the place you are. It's where the train is going; *en provenance
  de* is where it comes from.

## Key points

- Boards: *Départs / Arrivées*; *Heure, Train, Destination, Voie, Informations*.
- Notes: *à l'heure, retard 15 min, retardé, supprimé*. *La voie* (track number), *le quai*
  (platform).
- 24-hour times in full: *vingt et une heures trente-quatre*; *zéro heure*; minutes as plain
  numbers.
- *dans* (from now), *en* (how long it takes), *il y a* (ago).
- Tickets: *un aller simple / un aller-retour pour Lyon, en seconde, direct* or *avec une
  correspondance*, at *le guichet*.
- Announcements: *à destination de, en provenance de, annoncé avec un retard de, supprimé, en
  raison de*; the simple future *partira* = will leave.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The French year: holidays and traditions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 gave you the months and the dates (*le premier mai, le 14 juillet*), birthdays and
Christmas. This honors lesson walks through the French year: the public holidays and what people
do on them, a few traditions every French person knows (the *galette des rois*, the *poisson
d'avril*, the *muguet*), the habit of *faire le pont*, New Year wishes, and how to write a date at
the top of a letter.

You'll use the date grammar from lesson 19 all the way through, so this is also extra practice
with *le* + number + month. Where the lesson describes what "French people" do, it is a
generalisation: families and regions differ.

## Les jours fériés: public holidays

*Un jour férié* is a public holiday. France has eleven, set by law (the *Code du travail*):

| date | name in French | what it marks |
|---|---|---|
| *le 1er janvier* | *le jour de l'an* | New Year's Day |
| a Monday in March or April | *le lundi de Pâques* | Easter Monday |
| *le 1er mai* | *la fête du Travail* | Labour Day |
| *le 8 mai* | *la Victoire 1945* | the end of the Second World War in Europe |
| a Thursday in May or early June | *l'Ascension* | Ascension Day (39 days after Easter) |
| a Monday in May or June | *le lundi de Pentecôte* | Whit Monday |
| *le 14 juillet* | *la fête nationale* | the national holiday |
| *le 15 août* | *l'Assomption* | Assumption Day |
| *le 1er novembre* | *la Toussaint* | All Saints' Day |
| *le 11 novembre* | *l'Armistice* | the end of the First World War (1918) |
| *le 25 décembre* | *Noël* | Christmas Day |

A few details, simplified:

- Many holidays come from the Christian calendar, so *Pâques* (Easter), and with it Easter Monday,
  Ascension and Whit Monday, move every year.
- Only *le 1er mai* is a day off for almost every employee by law. For the others, whether you
  work depends on your job and your contract, but offices, banks and many shops close.
- *Le lundi de Pentecôte* is also the *journée de solidarité* (since 2004): many employees work
  that day without extra pay, to fund care for older and disabled people. Employers can now choose
  another day instead.
- Alsace and Moselle, in the east, have two extra holidays: Good Friday (*le Vendredi saint*) and
  26 December.
- A holiday that falls on a Saturday or Sunday is usually not moved to a weekday. Bad luck!

To say a date is a holiday: *Le 11 novembre, c'est férié.* — The 11th of November is a holiday.
*Lundi, c'est férié ?* — Is Monday a holiday?

*Pâques* is masculine singular and used without an article: *à Pâques* (at Easter), *Pâques tombe
tôt cette année* (Easter falls early this year; *tomber*, to fall). With an adjective it becomes
feminine plural: *Joyeuses Pâques !*

## Faire le pont

*Le pont* is a bridge (lesson 20). When a holiday falls on a Thursday, many people take the Friday
off too, which "bridges" the holiday and the weekend: that's *faire le pont*. With a Tuesday
holiday, they take the Monday.

![A week in May 2026, Monday the 11th to Sunday the 17th. Monday to Wednesday are work days (travail). Thursday the 14th is marked jour férié, l'Ascension. Friday the 15th is marked le pont. Saturday the 16th and Sunday the 17th are le week-end. A bracket over Thursday to Sunday reads quatre jours de repos (four days off).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: Can we make a long weekend?

Look at the 2026 calendar. Which holidays give a *pont*?

1. *L'Ascension* is *le jeudi 14 mai 2026*. Thursday holiday, so take Friday 15 May off: Thursday to
   Sunday is four days. *On fait le pont de l'Ascension.*
2. *Le 14 juillet 2026* is a *mardi*. Take Monday 13 July off: Saturday to Tuesday, four days.
3. *Le 1er mai 2026* is a *vendredi*. No *pont* needed: Friday to Sunday is already a long weekend.
4. *Le 15 août 2026* is a *samedi*, and *la Toussaint* is a *dimanche*. No extra day off at all.

A colleague might say: *Le 14 juillet, c'est un mardi. Tu fais le pont ?* — *Oui, je ne travaille
pas lundi.* In French offices, May is famous for its *ponts*: in some years, with *le 1er mai, le
8 mai* and *l'Ascension*, there are several.

## The year in traditions

### January: Bonne année ! and the galette des rois

From *le jour de l'an*, people wish each other *Bonne année !* (Happy New Year!), often with *et
bonne santé !* (and good health; *la santé*, health). By custom you can keep saying it to people you
meet for the first time in the year until the end of January. In writing, you send *mes meilleurs
vœux* (my best wishes; *le vœu*, wish).

Early in January comes *l'Épiphanie* (Epiphany, 6 January). In France it is often celebrated on the
Sunday between 2 and 8 January, because 6 January is not a holiday. People eat *la
galette des rois*, a flat round pastry, usually filled with almond cream (*la frangipane*), with a
small hidden charm inside: *la fève*. Once a real bean (*fève* means broad bean), it is now usually
a little porcelain figure. Whoever finds *la fève* in their slice becomes *le roi* or *la reine*
(the king or the queen) and wears the paper crown (*la couronne*). In the south of France many
families have a brioche ring with candied fruit instead (*le gâteau des rois* or *la brioche des rois*),
also with a *fève* inside.

A family custom: the youngest child goes under the table and says who gets each slice, so nobody
can cheat. *Qui a la fève ? — Moi ! Je suis le roi !*

### April: le poisson d'avril

On *le 1er avril*, people play jokes on each other: *faire un poisson d'avril*. Children try to
stick a paper fish on someone's back without being seen, then shout *Poisson d'avril !* (April
fool!). Newspapers and radio sometimes publish invented stories that day.

### May: le muguet

On *le 1er mai*, people give each other a small bunch of *muguet* (lily of the valley) for good
luck (*porte-bonheur*). You'll see sellers on the pavements. The plant is poisonous to eat, so it
is for looking at only.

### July: le 14 juillet

*La fête nationale* remembers the storming of the Bastille, a royal prison in Paris, on 14 July
1789, and the *Fête de la Fédération* of 14 July 1790. It became the national holiday by a law of
1880. In English it is often called Bastille Day; in French, just *le 14 juillet* or *la fête
nationale*. On the morning of the 14th there is a military parade (*le défilé*) in Paris, usually
on the Champs-Élysées, shown on television; in the evening, towns have a *feu d'artifice*
(firework display), and often a dance (*le bal*).

### November: la Toussaint and le 11 novembre

*La Toussaint* (1 November) is when many families visit the graves of their relatives and bring
flowers, usually chrysanthemums (*les chrysanthèmes*). For this reason, chrysanthemums are not a
good gift for a dinner party in France. Schools have about two weeks of holiday around this time:
*les vacances de la Toussaint*. Ten days later, *le 11 novembre* remembers the armistice that ended
the First World War in 1918, with ceremonies at war memorials.

### December: Noël and the end of the year

*Noël* (lesson 19) is mostly a family celebration; the big meal is often on the evening of 24
December (*le réveillon de Noël*). On 31 December, the *réveillon de la Saint-Sylvestre* is the New
Year's Eve party, and at midnight people say *Bonne année !*

## Writing the date in a letter

At the top of a letter, an e-mail to an office or a card, French puts the place and the date
together, usually on the right:

> Lyon, le 3 mars 2026

The pattern is *place*, comma, *le* + day + month + year. Some people add the weekday (*Lyon, le
mardi 3 mars 2026*) or write *À Lyon, le 3 mars 2026*. The month is lower case and is written in
full; only the first of the month is an ordinal: *Paris, le 1er juin 2026*.

### Example 2: Write it the French way

You are writing from Bordeaux on 1 May 2026, then from Nice on 21 May 2026.

1. Place first, then a comma: *Bordeaux,*
2. *le*, then the day. The 1st is an ordinal: *le 1er*.
3. The month in lower case, the year in figures: *Bordeaux, le 1er mai 2026*.
4. For the 21st, write the plain number: *Nice, le 21 mai 2026*. Said aloud, it's *le vingt et un
   mai deux mille vingt-six* (not *vingt et unième*).

Compare the English "May 1, 2026" (US) or "1st May 2026" (UK): French has no comma before the year,
no "st" after numbers other than 1, and the month never comes first.

### Example 3: Which holiday is it?

A friend sends you this message on a Friday morning:

> Salut ! Aujourd'hui c'est férié, alors pas de travail. Ce matin, j'achète du muguet pour ma mère,
> et cet après-midi, on se promène au parc. Bises !

Which date is it? The clues: *férié* (a public holiday), *muguet* (lily of the valley). It is *le
1er mai*, *la fête du Travail*. In 2026 that is indeed a Friday (*le vendredi 1er mai 2026*).

## Dialogue: Tu fais quoi pour le 14 juillet ?

> Camille: Tu fais quoi pour le 14 juillet ?
>
> Sam: Je ne sais pas. C'est un mardi cette année, non ?
>
> Camille: Oui ! Moi, je fais le pont. Lundi, je ne travaille pas.
>
> Sam: Tu as de la chance ! Moi, je dois travailler lundi.
>
> Camille: Mardi matin, tu veux regarder le défilé à la télévision chez moi ?
>
> Sam: Avec plaisir ! Et le soir ?
>
> Camille: Le soir, on va voir le feu d'artifice sur la place. Ça commence à vingt-trois heures.
>
> Sam: Super. Après, il y a un bal ?
>
> Camille: Oui, jusqu'à deux heures du matin !

*Camille: What are you doing for the 14th of July? — Sam: I don't know. It's a Tuesday this year,
isn't it? — Camille: Yes! I'm taking the Monday off. I'm not working on Monday. — Sam: You're lucky
(tu as de la chance)! I have to work on Monday. — Camille: On Tuesday morning, do you want to watch
the parade on TV at my place? — Sam: I'd love to! And in the evening? — Camille: In the evening
we're going to see the fireworks on the square. They start at eleven p.m. — Sam: Great. Is there a
dance afterwards? — Camille: Yes, until two in the morning!*

## Common mistakes

- *Le 14 juillet* is not "French Independence Day". It remembers 1789–1790, not an independence.
- Capitals. Months are lower case (*juillet*), but holiday names have a capital where they are
  names: *la Toussaint, Noël, Pâques, l'Ascension*. *La fête nationale* and *la fête du Travail*
  are usually written like this.
- *La Pâques* or *les Pâques*. Easter has no article: *à Pâques*; with an adjective, *Joyeuses
  Pâques !*
- *Faire un pont* for a short holiday. The fixed phrase is *faire le pont*.
- Writing *Lyon, 3 mars 2026* without *le*, or *mars 3*. The date needs *le* + day + month: *Lyon,
  le 3 mars 2026*.
- Giving chrysanthemums as a dinner present. In France they are the flowers of *la Toussaint* and
  cemeteries.

## Key points

- *Un jour férié* = a public holiday; France has eleven. Only *le 1er mai* is off by law for
  almost everyone.
- *Faire le pont*: a Thursday or Tuesday holiday plus one day off = four days.
- January: *Bonne année !*, *la galette des rois* and *la fève*. April: *le poisson d'avril*. May:
  *le muguet* on 1 May. July: *la fête nationale*, *le défilé*, *le feu d'artifice*. November: *la
  Toussaint*, *l'Armistice*.
- *Pâques* is masculine singular without an article, but *Joyeuses Pâques !*
- In a letter: *Lyon, le 3 mars 2026*; *le 1er* only for the first of the month.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: What did you do? The passé composé with avoir
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far every sentence in this course has been about now or later: what you do every day
(the present) and what you are going to do (the near future with *aller*, lesson 12). In this
last module you learn to talk about the past: what you did last night, where you went at the
weekend, what happened on holiday.

Spoken French has one main past tense for finished actions: the **[[passé composé]]** ("compound
past"). It is called compound because it has two parts, a helper verb and a participle. This
lesson builds it with *avoir*, the helper for almost every verb. Lesson 22 adds the small group
of verbs that use *être* instead.

The good news: you already know the hard part. The helper is just the present of *avoir*
from lesson 6: *j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont*.

## How the passé composé is built

Passé composé = present of *avoir* + **[[past participle]]** of the verb.

The form of *avoir* is the **[[auxiliary verb]]** (the helper). It changes with the person, like
any verb in the present. The past participle is a fixed form of the main verb: for *manger*
it is *mangé*, and it stays *mangé* whoever is speaking.

| | avoir | participle | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | j'ai | mangé | I ate, I have eaten |
| tu | tu as | mangé | you ate |
| il / elle / on | il a | mangé | he ate |
| nous | nous avons | mangé | we ate |
| vous | vous avez | mangé | you ate |
| ils / elles | ils ont | mangé | they ate |

![Two building blocks joined by a plus sign: a blue block "avoir in the present: ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont" and a green block "past participle: mangé, fini, vendu, fait". Below, three sentences built from the blocks, with the avoir part in blue and the participle in green: "J'ai mangé une pizza.", "Nous avons fini.", "Elle a vendu sa voiture." At the bottom, the negative "Je n'ai pas mangé" split into five boxes labelled subject, ne, avoir (auxiliary), pas and past participle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One French tense covers three English ones. *J'ai mangé* can mean "I ate", "I have eaten"
or "I did eat", depending on the situation:

- *Hier, j'ai mangé une pizza.* — Yesterday I ate a pizza.
- *Tu as mangé ?* — Have you eaten? / Did you eat?
- *Nous avons téléphoné à Marie.* — We phoned Marie.
- *Elle a raconté une histoire aux enfants.* — She told the children a story.

So don't try to match the English tense. If the action is finished and in the past, use the
passé composé.

## Regular past participles

Most verbs build their participle by rule, from the infinitive:

| verb group | rule | examples |
|---|---|---|
| -er verbs (lesson 7) | -er → -é | parler → parlé, travailler → travaillé, acheter → acheté |
| finir-type -ir verbs (lesson 16) | -ir → -i | finir → fini, choisir → choisi, réfléchir → réfléchi |
| -re verbs (lesson 16) | -re → -u | vendre → vendu, attendre → attendu, perdre → perdu |

Every -er verb follows the rule, even the ones with spelling changes in the present: *j'achète*
but *j'ai acheté*; *je paie* but *j'ai payé*; *nous mangeons* but *j'ai mangé*.
*Dormir* also ends in -i: *j'ai dormi*.

- *Vous avez fermé la porte ?* — Did you close the door?
- *Ils ont choisi un restaurant italien.* — They chose an Italian restaurant.
- *J'ai attendu le bus.* — I waited for the bus.

### -é or -er? A spelling trap

*Parlé* and *parler* sound exactly the same, so in writing it is easy to mix them up. Use
the participle (-é) after *avoir*, and the infinitive (-er) after another verb or a
preposition: *J'ai parlé* but *Je vais parler*, *Je veux parler*, *pour parler*.

If you are not sure, swap in an -re verb such as *vendre*: you would say *j'ai vendu* (so
write *j'ai parlé*), but *je vais vendre* (so write *je vais parler*).

## Irregular past participles

Some common verbs have participles you can't work out from the infinitive. Learn
them with the verb. They fall into a few sound groups, which makes them easier to remember:

| ends in | verb → participle |
|---|---|
| -u | avoir → eu, boire → bu, lire → lu, voir → vu, vouloir → voulu, pouvoir → pu, devoir → dû, savoir → su, connaître → connu |
| -is | prendre → pris (comprendre → compris, apprendre → appris), mettre → mis |
| -it | faire → fait, dire → dit, écrire → écrit |
| others | être → été, ouvrir → ouvert |

- *Nous avons fait une randonnée.* — We went on a hike.
- *Tu as vu le film ?* — Did you see the film?
- *Il a pris le train de 8 heures.* — He took the 8 o'clock train.
- *Qu'est-ce que tu as dit ?* — What did you say?
- *J'ai ouvert la fenêtre.* — I opened the window.
- *J'ai été malade.* — I was ill.

*Dû* has a circumflex so that it doesn't look like *du* ("some"). *Savoir* and *connaître*
are lesson 24 words; you will see *su* and *connu* again there.

### Which participle? A checklist

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to find the past participle
  accDescr: First ask whether the verb is on the irregular list, such as faire, prendre, voir or ouvrir. If yes, learn its participle by heart, for example fait, pris, vu, ouvert. If no, look at the ending. An -er verb takes -é, as in parlé. A finir-type -ir verb takes -i, as in fini. An -re verb takes -u, as in vendu.
  A["Is the verb on the irregular list?"] -- yes --> B["Learn it: fait, pris, vu, ouvert, dit..."]
  A -- no --> C["Look at the ending"]
```
