```mermaid
  C -- "-er" --> D["-é: parlé, acheté"]
  C -- "-ir (finir type)" --> E["-i: fini, choisi"]
  C -- "-re" --> F["-u: vendu, attendu"]
```

## Two new irregular verbs: dire and ouvrir

*Dire* (to say, to tell) is irregular in the present. Watch *vous dites*: like *vous êtes* and
*vous faites*, it ends in *-tes*, not *-ez*.

| dire | ouvrir |
|---|---|
| je dis | j'ouvre |
| tu dis | tu ouvres |
| il dit | il ouvre |
| nous disons | nous ouvrons |
| vous dites | vous ouvrez |
| ils disent | ils ouvrent |
| participle: dit | participle: ouvert |

*Ouvrir* (to open) ends in -ir but takes -er endings in the present. Its participle is
*ouvert*, and *ouvert* is also the adjective "open" you met with opening hours in lesson 18:
*La pharmacie est ouverte.* Its opposite is *fermer* (to close), a regular -er verb: *J'ai
fermé la porte.*

## Saying "not": ne … pas around avoir

In the negative, *ne … pas* goes around the auxiliary *avoir*. The participle stays outside,
after *pas*:

- *Je n'ai pas mangé.* — I haven't eaten. / I didn't eat.
- *Il n'a pas téléphoné.* — He didn't phone.
- *Nous n'avons pas fini.* — We haven't finished.

The same goes for *ne … jamais* (lesson 10) and for *ne … rien* (nothing):

- *Je n'ai jamais vu la mer.* — I have never seen the sea.
- *Elle n'a rien dit.* — She didn't say anything.
- *Tu as acheté quelque chose ? — Non, je n'ai rien acheté.* — Did you buy anything? — No,
  I didn't buy anything.

*Rien* is "nothing" and *quelque chose* is "something" (also "anything" in a question). On its
own, as a one-word answer, *rien* needs no *ne*: *Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ? — Rien !*

As always, *un, une, des, du, de la* become *de* after the negative: *J'ai pris des photos* →
*Je n'ai pas pris de photos.*

## Asking questions

The three ways to ask from lesson 11 all work. With inversion, *avoir* and the pronoun swap
places, and the participle follows:

| style | question |
|---|---|
| intonation | *Tu as fini ?* |
| est-ce que | *Est-ce que tu as fini ?* |
| inversion | *As-tu fini ?* |

With *il, elle* and *on*, inversion adds *-t-* because *a* ends in a vowel: *A-t-il
téléphoné ? A-t-elle trouvé son sac ?* With a question word: *Qu'est-ce que vous avez fait
hier soir ? Où est-ce que tu as trouvé ça ? Qu'avez-vous mangé ?*

### déjà and pas encore

*Déjà* means "already" or, in a question, "yet" or "ever". *Pas encore* means "not yet". These short
words go between *avoir* and the participle:

- *Tu as déjà mangé ? — Oui, j'ai déjà mangé.* — Have you eaten yet? — Yes, I've already
  eaten.
- *Non, je n'ai pas encore mangé.* — No, I haven't eaten yet.
- *Vous avez déjà vu un spectacle à Paris ?* — Have you ever seen a show in Paris?
- *Le film ? Non, pas encore.* — The film? No, not yet.

In a full sentence, *pas encore* comes with *ne*: *Je n'ai pas encore fini.* As a short answer
it stands alone: *Pas encore !*

## Time words for the past

These words and phrases tell you a sentence is about the past. Many of them you know already;
*hier soir* is new.

| French | English |
|---|---|
| hier | yesterday |
| hier soir | last night, yesterday evening |
| ce matin | this morning |
| samedi, samedi dernier | on Saturday, last Saturday |
| la semaine dernière | last week |
| le week-end dernier | last weekend |
| il y a deux jours | two days ago |
| il y a un moment | a moment ago, a while ago |

*Il y a* + a length of time means "ago" and comes before the time, not after it: *il y a trois
ans* (three years ago). *Dernier* goes after the noun and agrees with it (lesson 18): *la
semaine dernière*.

![A strip of thirteen days in French: last week from Monday to Sunday, bracketed as "la semaine dernière", then this week from Monday to Saturday. Today is Friday (vendredi), shaded. Wednesday is labelled "il y a deux jours", Thursday "hier", a moon on Thursday evening "hier soir", Friday "aujourd'hui" and Saturday "demain". An arrow underneath runs from the past to the future.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Hier soir, j'ai regardé un film.* — Last night I watched a film.
- *Il y a deux jours, nous avons rencontré nos voisins.* — Two days ago we met our neighbours.
- *Le week-end dernier, ils ont fait un pique-nique.* — Last weekend they had a picnic.

(*Le voisin, la voisine* is a neighbour.) A time word can go at the start or at the end of
the sentence: *J'ai regardé un film hier soir* is just as good.

## C'était: "it was"

To say how something was, use *c'était* + an adjective. Learn it as a chunk for now; its
tense comes later.

- *C'était comment ? — C'était super !* — How was it? — It was great!
- *Le concert ? C'était génial.* — The concert? It was brilliant.
- *Le repas, c'était très bon.* — The meal was very good.
- *C'était un moment difficile.* — It was a difficult moment.

*Super* never changes (*des vacances super*). *Génial* agrees like other adjectives:
*une idée géniale, des films géniaux*. Both are a little informal, but you'll hear them all the
time.

## Dialogue: Monday morning

Camille and Hugo work in the same office.

> Camille : Salut Hugo ! Tu as passé un bon week-end ?
>
> Hugo : Oui, très bon ! Samedi soir, j'ai vu un concert de jazz avec des amis.
>
> Camille : Super ! C'était comment ?
>
> Hugo : Génial. Après le spectacle, on a mangé dans un petit restaurant. Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu as fait ?
>
> Camille : Dimanche, j'ai fait un pique-nique au parc avec ma famille. Mon grand-père a raconté des histoires de sa jeunesse.
>
> Hugo : Vous avez pris des photos ?
>
> Camille : Oui, beaucoup ! Mais j'ai oublié mon téléphone au parc…
>
> Hugo : Oh non ! Tu l'as trouvé ?
>
> Camille : Oui, une dame a trouvé le téléphone et elle a appelé ma mère. Je n'ai rien perdu !

Translation:

> Camille: Hi Hugo! Did you have a good weekend?
>
> Hugo: Yes, very good! On Saturday evening I saw a jazz concert with some friends.
>
> Camille: Great! How was it?
>
> Hugo: Brilliant. After the show we ate in a little restaurant. And you, what did you do?
>
> Camille: On Sunday I had a picnic in the park with my family. My grandfather told stories
> from when he was young.
>
> Hugo: Did you take any photos?
>
> Camille: Yes, lots! But I left my phone in the park…
>
> Hugo: Oh no! Did you find it?
>
> Camille: Yes, a lady found the phone and called my mother. I didn't lose anything!

Notes: *passer un bon week-end* is "to have a good weekend": *passer* means "to spend" with
time. *La jeunesse* is "youth"; *des histoires de sa jeunesse* are stories from his youth.
*Tu l'as trouvé ?* puts the pronoun *l'* ("it") before *avoir*; you only need to recognise it
here. *Oublier* means "to forget" and also "to leave something behind".

## More words from this lesson

- *J'ai rencontré Paul à l'université.* — I met Paul at university. (*Rencontrer*: to meet,
  often for the first time.)
- *Nous avons passé deux semaines en Italie.* — We spent two weeks in Italy.
- *C'est un bon souvenir.* — It's a good memory. *Le souvenir* is also a souvenir you buy.
- *L'histoire* is both a story and history: *J'aime l'histoire de France.*

## Pronunciation

- *J'ai* sounds like "zhay" [ʒe]. *Ai* and *é* sound almost the same, so *j'ai mangé* is
  [ʒe mɑ̃ʒe].
- *Ils ont* has a liaison with a z sound: [il‿zɔ̃]. Don't confuse it with *ils sont*
  (they are), with an s sound: [il sɔ̃]. *Ils ont fini* (they have finished) and *ils sont
  partis* (they left, lesson 22) differ only in that sound.
- The final consonants of *fait, dit, écrit, mis, pris* and *ouvert* are silent: [fɛ], [di],
  [ekʁi], [mi], [pʁi], [uvɛʁ].
- *Eu* (the participle of *avoir*) is just the vowel [y], like *tu* without the *t*.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out *avoir*. *Je mangé* is wrong: the passé composé always needs the auxiliary.
  *J'ai mangé.*
- Writing the infinitive after *avoir*: not *j'ai parler* but *j'ai parlé*.
- Putting *pas* after the participle. Not *Je n'ai mangé pas* but *Je n'ai pas mangé*:
  *ne … pas* wraps *avoir* only.
- Making regular participles from irregular verbs: not *j'ai prendu, j'ai faisé, j'ai ouvri*
  but *j'ai pris, j'ai fait, j'ai ouvert*.
- Adding "did" in questions. French has no helper for questions: "Did you see it?" is just
  *Tu as vu ?* or *Est-ce que tu as vu ?*
- Putting *il y a* after the time, like English "ago": not *deux jours il y a* but *il y a
  deux jours*.

## Key points

- Passé composé = present of *avoir* + past participle: *j'ai mangé, nous avons fini, ils
  ont vendu*. It means "I ate", "I have eaten" and "I did eat".
- Regular participles: -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u.
- Learn the irregular ones: *été, eu, fait, pris, mis, bu, lu, vu, dit, écrit, ouvert,
  voulu, pu, dû, su, connu*.
- *Ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … rien* go around *avoir*: *Je n'ai rien vu.*
- *Déjà* and *pas encore* go between *avoir* and the participle.
- Past time words: *hier, hier soir, la semaine dernière, il y a deux jours*. *C'était
  super !* says how it was.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The passé composé reference sheet lists every participle you need at A1.
From now on the conjugation drills include the passé composé.

lessons.title: Where did you go? The passé composé with être
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you built the passé composé with *avoir*: *j'ai mangé, nous avons fini*. That
works for almost every verb. But a small, very common group of verbs uses *être* as the
auxiliary instead: *je suis allé* (I went), *elle est partie* (she left), *nous sommes
rentrés* (we came home). They are the verbs you need to talk about trips and holidays, so this
lesson also gives you the words for holiday places: the sea, the mountains, the countryside.

There is one extra rule with *être*: the participle agrees with the subject, like an
adjective. *Il est parti, elle est partie.*

## The verbs that take être

About fifteen verbs use *être*. Most of them describe movement from one place to another, or
a change of state (being born, dying). They come in handy pairs of opposites:

| verb | participle | | verb | participle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aller (to go) | allé | | venir (to come) | venu |
| arriver (to arrive) | arrivé | | partir (to leave) | parti |
| entrer (to go in) | entré | | sortir (to go out) | sorti |
| monter (to go up) | monté | | descendre (to go down) | descendu |
| naître (to be born) | né | | mourir (to die) | mort |
| rester (to stay) | resté | | tomber (to fall) | tombé |
| retourner (to go back) | retourné | | revenir (to come back) | revenu |
| rentrer (to go home) | rentré | | | |

The picture puts them in a house: you arrive, go in, go up the stairs, stay, come down, go out
and leave. Learn the house and you know the list.

![A two-storey house with the être verbs. Outside on the left, a person walks towards the house: arriver. Outside on the right, a person walks away: partir. At the front door, one arrow goes in (entrer) and one comes out (sortir). Inside, an arrow goes up the stairs (monter) and a dashed arrow comes down (descendre). Upstairs, a person sits in an armchair (rester) and there is a baby's cradle (naître). A flowerpot falls from the balcony (tomber).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Some English-speaking learners use the memory aid "Dr and Mrs Vandertramp": each letter starts
one of the verbs (devenir, revenir, monter, rentrer, sortir, venir, aller, naître, descendre,
entrer, retourner, tomber, rester, arriver, mourir, partir). The house is easier for most
people, but use whatever works for you.

All pronominal verbs (lesson 17) take *être* as well: *je me suis levé, elle s'est
couchée*. More on those below.

Beyond A1, just to recognise: when *monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer* or *retourner* has a
direct object (something you carry, take out or turn), it takes *avoir*: *J'ai monté les
valises.* — I took the suitcases up. Without an object, as in this lesson, they take *être*.

- *Je suis allé au cinéma.* — I went to the cinema.
- *Le train est arrivé à 10 heures.* — The train arrived at 10 o'clock.
- *Nous sommes restés à la maison.* — We stayed at home.
- *Tu es tombé ?* — Did you fall?
- *Mon grand-père est né en 1950.* — My grandfather was born in 1950.

Notice that English says "was born" but French uses the passé composé of *naître*: *je suis
né* (said by a man) or *je suis née* (said by a woman). For the year, use *en*: *Je suis née en
1995.*

### Rentrer, retourner or revenir?

All three are about going back, and all three take *être*:

- *rentrer*: to go home, to come back home (or back to where you live). *Je suis rentré à
  minuit.* — I got home at midnight.
- *retourner*: to go back to a place you have been before. *Nous sommes retournés à Rome.* —
  We went back to Rome.
- *revenir*: to come back (to where the speaker is). It is conjugated like *venir*: *je
  reviens, nous revenons, ils reviennent*. *Reviens vite !* — Come back soon!

### monter and descendre with transport

*Monter dans* is "to get on (or into)" a bus, train or car; *descendre de* is "to get off".
*Descendre* is a regular -re verb (*je descends, nous descendons*), so its participle is
*descendu*.

- *Elle est montée dans le bus.* — She got on the bus.
- *Je suis descendu du train à Lyon.* — I got off the train in Lyon.

## Agreement: the participle acts like an adjective

With *être*, the past participle agrees with the subject, exactly like an adjective after
*être* (lesson 8): add *-e* for a feminine subject, *-s* for a plural one, *-es* for a
feminine plural. This is called **[[participle agreement]]**.

![A two-by-two chart for the participle of aller. Masculine singular: il est allé. Feminine singular: elle est allée, with the added e highlighted. Masculine plural: ils sont allés, with s highlighted. Feminine plural: elles sont allées, with es highlighted. A note says the four forms sound the same.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *il est allé* | *ils sont allés* |
| feminine | *elle est allée* | *elles sont allées* |

A mixed group counts as masculine: *Paul et Julie sont partis.*

*Je, tu, nous* and *vous* agree with the real person or people behind them:

- Thomas: *Je suis arrivé hier.* Léa: *Je suis arrivée hier.*
- To a woman: *Tu es sortie hier soir ?*
- Léa and Emma: *Nous sommes rentrées tard.*
- To one man (formal): *Vous êtes venu en train, Monsieur ?* To a group: *Vous êtes venus en
  train ?*

When *on* means "we", most people make the participle plural: *On est partis à 8 heures.*
(*On est parti*, with no agreement, is also correct.)

Most of the time you can't hear the agreement: *allé, allée, allés, allées* all sound the
same. *Mort/morte* is the exception you can hear (the *t* is pronounced in *morte*). So
agreement is mostly a matter of writing, and it matters in the DELF writing part.

With *avoir* there is no agreement with the subject: *Elle a mangé. Elles ont fini.*

## avoir or être? A quick decision

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Avoir or être in the passé composé
  accDescr: First ask whether the verb is pronominal, with se, like se lever. If yes, use être, as in je me suis levé. If no, ask whether it is one of the verbs in the house of être, such as aller, venir, partir, arriver, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, retourner, rentrer or revenir. If yes, use être and make the participle agree, as in elle est partie. If no, use avoir, with no agreement with the subject, as in elle a mangé.
  A["Is it a pronominal verb (se lever)?"] -- yes --> B["être: je me suis levé(e)"]
  A -- no --> C["Is it in the house of être?"]
  C -- yes --> D["être + agreement: elle est partie"]
  C -- no --> E["avoir, no agreement: elle a mangé"]
```

## Negatives and questions with être

Everything works as with *avoir*. *Ne … pas* goes around *être*; the participle stays
outside:

- *Elle n'est pas venue.* — She didn't come.
- *Je ne suis jamais allé en Espagne.* — I have never been to Spain.
- *Tu es rentré quand ?* — When did you get home?
- *Est-ce que vous êtes sortis samedi ?* — Did you go out on Saturday?
- *Est-elle partie ?* — Has she left?

Notice the second one: *Je suis allé en Espagne* is the normal way to say "I have been to Spain".
English uses "been", but French uses *aller*.

## Pronominal verbs in the passé composé

Reflexive verbs from lesson 17 (*se lever, se coucher, se promener…*) always take *être*. The
reflexive pronoun stays in front of the auxiliary:

| se lever | |
|---|---|
| je me suis levé(e) | nous nous sommes levé(e)s |
| tu t'es levé(e) | vous vous êtes levé(e)(s) |
| il s'est levé / elle s'est levée | ils se sont levés / elles se sont levées |

- *Ce matin, je me suis levée à 6 heures.* — This morning I got up at 6 o'clock (said by a
  woman).
- *Les enfants se sont couchés tard.* — The children went to bed late.
- *Nous nous sommes promenés au bord du lac.* — We went for a walk by the lake.

In the negative, *ne … pas* wraps the pronoun and *être* together: *Je ne me suis pas réveillé.*
— I didn't wake up. The honors lesson 24h1 looks at agreement with these verbs in more detail.

## Saying how long and how long ago

*Pendant* + a length of time means "for" (how long something lasted):

- *Nous sommes restés à la plage pendant deux heures.* — We stayed at the beach for two hours.
- *J'ai habité au Canada pendant trois ans.* — I lived in Canada for three years.

*Il y a* + a length of time means "ago" (lesson 21):

- *Ils sont partis il y a dix minutes.* — They left ten minutes ago.

Don't translate "for" with *pour* here: *pour* is for a purpose or a planned length (*pour
une semaine*, for a week, when booking). For how long something lasted, use *pendant*.

*Longtemps* means "(for) a long time": *Tu es resté longtemps ? — Non, pas longtemps.* — Did
you stay long? — No, not long.

## Holiday places

![A labelled landscape: snowy mountains (la montagne) with a pine forest (la forêt) at their foot, a lake (le lac), a village with a church (le village), fields (la campagne), a strip of sand (la plage), the sea (la mer) with a sailing boat (le bateau), and a small island with a palm tree (l'île).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| French | English | where you are |
|---|---|---|
| la mer | the sea | *à la mer, au bord de la mer* (at the seaside) |
| la plage | the beach | *à la plage, sur la plage* |
| la montagne | the mountains | *à la montagne* (in the mountains) |
| la campagne | the countryside | *à la campagne* (in the country) |
| le lac | the lake | *au bord du lac* (by the lake) |
| la forêt | the forest | *dans la forêt, en forêt* |
| le village | the village | *dans un petit village* |
| l'île | the island | *sur une île* |
| la nature | nature | *dans la nature* (out in nature) |
| le bateau | the boat | *en bateau* (by boat) |
| le camping | the campsite, camping | *au camping* (at the campsite) |
| l'étranger | abroad | *à l'étranger* (abroad) |

French says *la montagne* (singular) where English says "the mountains": *Nous sommes allés à la
montagne.* *L'étranger* also means "foreigner", but in *à l'étranger* it means "abroad": *Elle
est partie à l'étranger.* *L'île* is feminine; the circumflex on the *î* is part of the
spelling.

## Text: a postcard from the Alps

Inès writes to her friend Zoé.

> Chère Zoé,
>
> Je suis arrivée à Annecy il y a cinq jours avec ma sœur. Nous sommes venues en train. Notre camping est au bord du lac, au pied de la montagne. Lundi, nous sommes montées en haut d'une montagne : c'était magnifique ! Mardi, nous sommes restées à la plage du lac et nous sommes allées sur le lac en bateau. Hier, ma sœur est tombée de son vélo, mais ce n'est pas grave. Je suis seule aujourd'hui : elle est rentrée à Paris ce matin. Moi, je rentre dimanche.
>
> Bises,
>
> Inès

Translation:

> Dear Zoé,
>
> I arrived in Annecy five days ago with my sister. We came by train. Our campsite is by the
> lake, at the foot of the mountains. On Monday we went up to the top of a mountain: it was
> magnificent! On Tuesday we stayed on the lake beach and went out on the lake by boat.
> Yesterday my sister fell off her bike, but it's not serious. I'm on my own today: she went
> back home to Paris this morning. I'm going home on Sunday.
>
> Love,
>
> Inès

Notes: every participle with *être* has a feminine ending (*arrivée, venues, montées*) because
Inès and her sister are women. *Au pied de* is "at the foot of"; *en haut de* is "at the top
of". *Ce n'est pas grave* means "it's not serious, no problem". *Seule* is the feminine of
*seul* (alone, on my own). *Je rentre dimanche* is a present tense used for a fixed plan.

## Pronunciation

- *Ils sont* [il sɔ̃] (they are, with être) and *ils ont* [il‿zɔ̃] (they have, with avoir):
  *ils sont partis* vs *ils ont fini*. Listen for the s or z.
- *Mort* is [mɔʁ] with a silent *t*; *morte* is [mɔʁt].
- *Né* and *née* sound the same: [ne].
- *Naître* has a long *ai* sound [nɛtʁ]; the *î* doesn't change the sound much.
- *L'île* sounds like "eel" [il]. *La forêt* is [fɔʁɛ], with a silent *t*.

## Common mistakes

- Using *avoir* with these verbs. Not *j'ai allé, il a arrivé, elle a né* but *je suis allé,
  il est arrivé, elle est née*.
- Forgetting the agreement in writing: a woman writes *je suis partie*, two women *nous sommes
  parties*.
- Adding agreement with *avoir*: not *elle a mangée* but *elle a mangé*.
- Saying *je suis été* for "I have been": the passé composé of *être* takes *avoir*: *j'ai
  été*. And for "I've been to Rome", French uses *aller*: *Je suis allé à Rome.*
- Using *pour* for how long something lasted. Not *Je suis resté pour trois jours* but *Je
  suis resté pendant trois jours* (or just *trois jours*).
- Forgetting the pronoun with pronominal verbs: not *je suis levé* but *je me suis levé*.

## Key points

- About fifteen verbs take *être*: *aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, monter,
  descendre, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, retourner, rentrer, revenir*, and every pronominal
  verb.
- With *être*, the participle agrees with the subject: *allé, allée, allés, allées*.
- *Je suis né(e) en 1995. Elle est morte en 2010.*
- *Pendant* + time = for (how long); *il y a* + time = ago; *longtemps* = a long time.
- *À la mer, à la plage, à la montagne, à la campagne, à l'étranger.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The conjugation drills now give *être* verbs with every agreement they
accept.

lessons.title: Linking ideas and writing short messages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say what you do, what you are going to do and what you did. This lesson puts
those sentences together into real texts: a postcard, a text message, a short e-mail, and a
form with your personal details. These are exactly the kinds of writing you do at A1, in daily
life and in the writing part of the DELF A1 (lesson 24).

You learn the small words that link ideas (**[[connectors]]** such as *ou, alors, donc, quand*),
how to open and close a message to a friend or to someone you don't know, and three new verbs:
*écrire* (to write), *envoyer* (to send) and *recevoir* (to receive).

## Linking words

Short sentences are fine at A1, but a few linking words make your writing flow. You already
know *et* (and), *mais* (but) and *parce que* (because). Here are four more:

| connector | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| ou | or | *Tu préfères le thé ou le café ?* |
| alors | so, then (in that case) | *Il pleut, alors je reste à la maison.* |
| donc | so, therefore | *J'ai raté le bus, donc je suis arrivé en retard.* |
| quand | when | *Quand il fait beau, je vais à la plage.* |

- *Ou* (or) has no accent. *Où* (where) has one. *Tu viens ou tu restes ? Où est-ce que tu vas ?*
- *Alors* is very common in speech, to start a new idea ("so", "well then"): *Alors, qu'est-ce
  que tu as fait hier ?* It also gives a consequence: "so, in that case".
- *Donc* gives a logical result, "so, therefore", and is a little more careful in style:
  *Je suis malade, donc je ne vais pas travailler.*
- *Quand* (when) also asks questions (lesson 11), but here it links two parts: *Quand je suis
  arrivé, il est parti.* — When I arrived, he left.

(*Rater* = to miss a bus or train.) With *parce que* you give the reason, with *alors* or *donc*
the result. They are two views of the same link:

- *Je reste à la maison parce qu'il pleut.* — I'm staying at home because it's raining.
- *Il pleut, donc je reste à la maison.* — It's raining, so I'm staying at home.

## Three new verbs: écrire, envoyer, recevoir

| | écrire (to write) | envoyer (to send) | recevoir (to receive) |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | j'écris | j'envoie | je reçois |
| tu | tu écris | tu envoies | tu reçois |
| il / elle / on | il écrit | il envoie | il reçoit |
| nous | nous écrivons | nous envoyons | nous recevons |
| vous | vous écrivez | vous envoyez | vous recevez |
| ils / elles | ils écrivent | ils envoient | ils reçoivent |
| passé composé | j'ai écrit | j'ai envoyé | j'ai reçu |

- *Écrire* adds a *v* in the plural: *nous écrivons*. Its participle *écrit* ends in *-t*
  (lesson 21).
- *Envoyer* is an -er verb with the y → i change from lesson 15 (like *payer*), but unlike
  *payer* only the *i* spelling is correct: *j'envoie*, never *j'envoye*. The participle is
  regular: *envoyé*.
- *Recevoir* has a *ç* before *o* and *u* so that the *c* still sounds like s: *je reçois, j'ai
  reçu*. The vowel changes in the boot forms: *je reçois* but *nous recevons*.

Examples:

- *Je t'écris de Marseille.* — I'm writing to you from Marseille.
- *Tu as reçu mon message ?* — Did you get my message?
- *Nous avons envoyé une carte postale à notre grand-mère.* — We sent our grandmother a postcard.

*Je t'écris* has *te* (to you) before the verb, like *Je t'aime*. Just learn it as a phrase.

Two more verbs for forms: *remplir* (to fill in), a regular finir-type verb (*je remplis, j'ai
rempli*), and *signer* (to sign), a regular -er verb.

## Opening and closing a message

How you start and end depends on who you are writing to. Use *tu*-style openings for
friends and family, and *vous*-style openings for people you don't know or who are formal
contacts.

| | opening | closing |
|---|---|---|
| a friend, family | *Salut Léa !* / *Coucou !* / *Cher Paul,* / *Chère Léa,* | *Bises,* / *Grosses bises,* / *À bientôt !* / *À plus !* |
| someone you know a little (vous) | *Bonjour Madame Martin,* / *Chère Madame,* / *Cher Monsieur,* | *À bientôt,* / *Bonne journée,* / *Cordialement,* |
| a person or office you don't know | *Madame, Monsieur,* | *Cordialement,* |

- *Cher* (dear, lesson 10) agrees: *Cher Paul* for a man, *Chère Léa* for a woman, *Chers amis*
  for a group.
- *Bises* means "kisses", and at the end of a message it is like "love" or "hugs". It goes with
  *tu*. *Grosses bises* is "big kisses".
- *Cordialement* (regards) is the everyday closing for e-mails to people you call *vous*.
- *Madame, Monsieur,* is how you write to someone whose name you don't know.
- *Coucou* is a very casual "hi" for close friends and family.

Never mix the two styles. If you open with *Salut* and *tu*, close with *Bises* or *À bientôt*;
if you open with *Madame, Monsieur,* and *vous*, close with *Cordialement*. A full formal letter
has more parts; the honors lesson 24h2 shows them.

Two phrases for the middle of a message: *J'ai une bonne nouvelle !* (I have some good news!)
and *Bonnes vacances !* (Have a good holiday!). *La nouvelle* is one piece of news; *les
nouvelles* is "the news": *Donne-moi de tes nouvelles !* (Let me know how you are.)

## A message has a shape

Every short message, from a postcard to an e-mail, follows the same plan:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The shape of a short message
  accDescr: A short message has five steps in order. First the opening, such as Salut Léa or Madame, Monsieur. Second, why you are writing or a short greeting such as j'espère que tu vas bien. Third, the news or information, with linking words like et, mais, alors, donc. Fourth, a question or a request for the reader. Fifth, the closing and your name, such as Bises, Tom or Cordialement, Tom Petit.
  A["1. Opening: Salut Léa ! / Madame, Monsieur,"] --> B["2. Why you write: J'espère que tu vas bien."]
  B --> C["3. The news, with et, mais, alors, donc"]
  C --> D["4. A question: Et toi ? Tu viens ?"]
  D --> E["5. Closing and name: Bises, Tom / Cordialement, Tom Petit"]
```

*J'espère que tu vas bien* (I hope you're well) and *J'espère que vous allez bien* use
*espérer* from lesson 15. They are good second lines in almost any message.

## A postcard

A French postcard (*une carte postale*) has the message on the left and the address on the
right. The place and the date often go at the top of the message.

![A postcard with small yellow tags naming its parts. On the left half: the place and date "Biarritz, le 12 août" at the top right of the message; the opening "Chère Mamie,"; the message "Je suis à Biarritz avec Paul. Il fait très beau ! Hier, nous sommes allés à la plage et j'ai nagé dans la mer. Ce soir, on va manger du poisson au port. Je t'envoie de gros bisous. Tu me manques !"; the closing "Bises," and the name "Lucie". On the right half: the stamp in the top corner and the address on three lines, "Madame Jeanne Petit, 8 rue des Fleurs, 37000 TOURS".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Translation of the message: "Biarritz, 12 August. Dear Granny, I'm in Biarritz with Paul. The
weather is lovely! Yesterday we went to the beach and I swam in the sea. Tonight we're going to
eat fish at the harbour. I'm sending you big kisses. I miss you! Love, Lucie."

*Mamie* is "granny". *Tu me manques* (literally "you are missing to me") means "I miss you";
learn it as a chunk. *Des bisous* is another warm word for kisses.

Notice the mix of tenses: present for now (*je suis*), passé composé for what happened
(*nous sommes allés, j'ai nagé*), and the near future for what is planned (*on va manger*).
Using all three shows the reader you can.

## A text message

Text messages (*un SMS* or *un texto*) are short and casual:

> Salut Hugo ! Je suis à la gare mais mon train est en retard, donc je vais arriver vers 20 h. Tu peux venir me chercher ? Merci ! Léa

Translation: "Hi Hugo! I'm at the station but my train is late, so I'm going to arrive around 8
pm. Can you come and pick me up? Thanks! Léa"

*Venir chercher quelqu'un* is "to come and pick someone up". French texters also use many
abbreviations; the honors lesson 24h2 lists the common ones.

## A short e-mail of about 40 words

In the DELF A1, the second writing task asks for a short message such as an e-mail or a
postcard of about 40 to 50 words (the task always states the length: check it), that covers
several points given in the task. Here is a model of the same
kind (it is not an exam task). Imagine a friend, Marc, has invited you to his birthday party on
Saturday, and you can't go.

> Salut Marc,
>
> Merci beaucoup pour ton invitation ! Malheureusement, je ne peux pas venir samedi parce que je pars à Lyon pour le travail. Je rentre dimanche soir. Tu es libre la semaine prochaine ? On peut aller au restaurant ensemble pour ton anniversaire. J'ai un petit cadeau pour toi !
>
> Bon anniversaire et bises,
>
> Sophie

Translation: "Hi Marc, Thanks a lot for your invitation! Unfortunately I can't come on Saturday
because I'm going to Lyon for work. I'm coming back on Sunday evening. Are you free next week?
We can go to a restaurant together for your birthday. I've got a little present for you! Happy birthday and love, Sophie."

That is 46 words (without the opening and closing). It thanks Marc, says no with a reason
(*parce que*), suggests another day, and asks a question. *Malheureusement* means
"unfortunately". Count your words when you practise: a message that is too short loses points,
and so does one that leaves out a point you were asked to cover.

## Filling in a form

Forms (*un formulaire*) are everywhere: at a hotel, a language school, a library. You fill in
(*remplir*) the fields and sign (*signer*) at the bottom.

![A filled-in enrolment form for a language school, "École de langues du Parc: inscription". Rows: Nom: GARCIA. Prénom: Ana. Date de naissance: 14/03/1998. Lieu de naissance: Séville (Espagne). Nationalité: espagnole. Profession: infirmière. Adresse: 5 rue Victor Hugo. Code postal: 31000. Ville: Toulouse. Signature: a handwritten signature.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| on the form | meaning | notes |
|---|---|---|
| Nom | surname | often written in CAPITALS: GARCIA |
| Prénom | first name | |
| Date de naissance | date of birth | day/month/year: 14/03/1998 |
| Lieu de naissance | place of birth | town, and country if abroad |
| Nationalité | nationality | the adjective, no capital: *espagnole* |
| Profession | occupation | the job, no article: *infirmière* |
| Adresse | address | number first: *5 rue Victor Hugo* |
| Code postal | postcode | five figures in France: *31000* |
| Signature | signature | sign by hand |

Dates in French forms always go day, month, year: *14/03/1998* is 14 March 1998, never 3
December. Nationalities and jobs agree with the person: Ana writes *espagnole* and *infirmière*.

Forms also have questions (*la question*) and spaces for answers (*la réponse*): *Répondez aux
questions.* — Answer the questions.

## Pronunciation

- *Écrire* [ekʁiʁ], *j'écris* [ʒekʁi] with a silent *s*, *nous écrivons* [nuz‿ekʁivɔ̃] with
  a liaison.
- *Envoyer* [ɑ̃vwaje]; *j'envoie* [ʒɑ̃vwa], and the plural *ils envoient* sounds the same:
  [il‿zɑ̃vwa].
- *Recevoir* [ʁəsəvwaʁ], *je reçois* [ʁəswa], *ils reçoivent* [ʁəswav].
- *Cordialement* [kɔʁdjalmɑ̃]: three syllables in speech, cor-dial-ment; the *e* is written but
  silent.
- *Bises* [biz]: the *s* between vowels sounds like z.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing *tu* and *vous* in one message. Choose one at the opening and keep it all the way to
  the closing.
- *Ou* and *où*: *ou* (no accent) is "or"; *où* is "where".
- *Cher* with a woman: *Chère Léa*, not *Cher Léa*.
- Writing dates the English way: 03/14/1998 is not a French date. Write 14/03/1998.
- Putting an article before a job on a form or after *être*: *Profession : infirmière*, *Je
  suis infirmière*.
- Writing *j'envoye* or *je recois*: the correct forms are *j'envoie* and *je reçois*.

## Key points

- Connectors: *et, mais, ou, alors, donc, parce que, quand*. *Parce que* gives the reason;
  *alors* and *donc* the result.
- *Écrire* (*nous écrivons, j'ai écrit*), *envoyer* (*j'envoie, j'ai envoyé*), *recevoir* (*je
  reçois, j'ai reçu*).
- Friends: *Salut / Cher, Chère* … *Bises, À bientôt*. Formal: *Madame, Monsieur,* …
  *Cordialement*.
- A message: opening, why you write, news, a question, closing.
- Forms: *nom* in capitals, *date de naissance* as day/month/year, nationality and job with no
  capital and no article.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The DELF A1 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson explains what "A1" means, describes the best-known A1 exam, the **[[DELF]]**
A1, with strategies for each part, and reviews the grammar of the whole course with pointers to
the lessons. On the way you learn the words of exam instructions. You don't have to take an
exam, but the free official sample papers are a good way to check that you have reached A1.

## What A1 means

The levels A1 to C2 come from the **[[CEFR]]** (Common European Framework of Reference for
Languages) of the Council of Europe, used in Europe and far beyond. A1 is the first level. In
plain words, someone at A1 can:

- understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very simple sentences about concrete
  needs: food, shopping, times, directions;
- introduce themselves and others, and ask and answer simple questions about where someone
  lives, the people they know and the things they have;
- take part in a simple conversation, as long as the other person speaks slowly and clearly
  and is ready to help.

At A1 nobody expects you to follow two French people chatting at full speed; asking for help
is part of the level, and this lesson gives you the words for it.

![The six CEFR levels drawn as a staircase rising from left to right: A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2. A1 and A2 are bracketed as "basic user", B1 and B2 as "independent user", C1 and C2 as "proficient user". An arrow labelled "vous êtes ici" (you are here) points to A1.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The DELF A1

*DELF* stands for *Diplôme d'études en langue française*, an official diploma of the French
Ministry of Education run by France Éducation international and taken at exam centres in many
countries. Each level (A1, A2, B1, B2) is a separate diploma. The adult version is *DELF tout
public*; there are also versions for school pupils.

The exam has four parts, each marked out of 25 points:

| part | time | what it involves |
|---|---|---|
| *Compréhension de l'oral* (listening) | about 20 minutes | several very short recordings about everyday life (announcements, messages, short conversations), each heard twice, with questions |
| *Compréhension des écrits* (reading) | 30 minutes | several short everyday documents (notices, ads, messages, timetables), with questions |
| *Production écrite* (writing) | 30 minutes | two tasks: filling in a form, and writing simple sentences such as a short message or postcard |
| *Production orale* (speaking) | 5–7 minutes, after about 10 minutes of preparation | three tasks with an examiner: a guided interview about yourself, an exchange of information, and a short role-play |

![An overview chart of the DELF A1. A box for the written exam, 1 hour 20 minutes in total, holds three parts side by side: listening, about 20 minutes, 25 points; reading, 30 minutes, 25 points; writing, 30 minutes, 25 points. A separate box for the speaking exam: 5 to 7 minutes after 10 minutes of preparation, 25 points. Below: total 100 points; pass with 50, and at least 5 out of 25 in every part.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three written parts are taken together in one sitting of 1 hour 20 minutes. The speaking
test is separate, often later the same day or on another day.

To pass, you need 50 points out of 100, and at least 5 out of 25 in each part. A
very low mark in any one part (below 5) means you fail, even if your total is 50 or more. So
don't skip a part because it is your weakest: a few points there can make the difference.

The comprehension parts have been updated in recent years. In the newer version they have more
(and shorter) documents and only closed questions (mostly multiple choice, some matching or
yes/no), with no answers to write out in your own words; the writing and speaking parts stay much
the same. Older practice books may still show the earlier format, so look at the official sample
papers to see the current one before you register.

France Éducation international publishes the official description and free sample papers with
audio and answers:

- [DELF A1 tout public: description of the exam](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-a1)
- [DELF A1 sample papers (exemples de sujets)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-a1/exemples-sujets)
- [Advice for preparing the DELF A1 (entraînement)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-a1/entrainement)
- [The official regulation of the DELF and DALF (Bulletin officiel, 2009, PDF)](https://cache.media.education.gouv.fr/file/31/55/2/DELF-DALF_reglement-epreuve_101552.pdf)

Dates, fees and practical details are set by each exam centre, so always check with the centre
where you register.

## Words for instructions and the classroom

Exam papers and textbooks give instructions (*la consigne*) in French. These words come up
again and again:

| French | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| l'exercice | exercise | *Exercice 2* |
| la partie | part | *la première partie de l'examen* |
| le texte | text | *Lisez le texte.* (Read the text.) |
| la phrase | sentence | *Écrivez des phrases simples.* |
| l'exemple | example | *Regardez l'exemple.* |
| cocher | to tick | *Cochez la bonne réponse.* (Tick the right answer.) |
| compléter | to complete, to fill in | *Complétez le formulaire.* |
| vrai / faux | true / false | *Vrai ou faux ?* |

*Cochez, complétez, lisez, écrivez, répondez* are *vous* imperatives (lesson 20). *Compléter*
changes é → è in the boot forms like *préférer* (lesson 15): *je complète*, but *nous
complétons*. *Faux* has an irregular feminine: *une réponse fausse*.

*Réussir* is a regular finir-type verb (*je réussis, j'ai réussi*). It means "to succeed" and,
with an exam, "to pass": *J'ai réussi mon examen !* — I passed my exam! Watch out: *passer un examen* means to *take* an
exam, not to pass it.

### Asking for help in French

These sentences work in an exam, a class or real life:

- *Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?* — Could you repeat that, please? (lesson 1)
- *Vous pouvez expliquer ?* — Can you explain?
- *Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?* — What does that mean? (lesson 1)
- *Comment dit-on "holiday" en français ?* — How do you say "holiday" in French?

*Répéter* also changes é → è: *je répète, nous répétons*. *Expliquer* is a regular -er verb.

## savoir or connaître?

Both mean "to know", but French splits the meaning in two.

| savoir | connaître |
|---|---|
| je sais | je connais |
| tu sais | tu connais |
| il sait | il connaît |
| nous savons | nous connaissons |
| vous savez | vous connaissez |
| ils savent | ils connaissent |
| j'ai su | j'ai connu |

- *savoir*: to know a fact or information, and to know how to do something (+ infinitive).
  It is often followed by *que, où, quand, si* or a question word.
  - *Je sais que le DELF a quatre parties.* — I know that the DELF has four parts.
  - *Tu sais où est la gare ?* — Do you know where the station is?
  - *Elle sait nager.* — She can (knows how to) swim.
- *connaître*: to know (be familiar with) a person, a place or a thing, followed by a noun.
  - *Tu connais Marc ?* — Do you know Marc?
  - *Je connais bien Lyon.* — I know Lyon well.

A quick test: if a noun follows (a person, a city, a book), use *connaître*. If a verb, a
clause or a question word follows, use *savoir*. (A few nouns for facts you have learned go with
*savoir*: *Je sais la réponse.* The test still works for people and places.) The circumflex in *il connaît* (and in
*connaître*) is optional in the 1990 spelling: *il connait, connaitre*.

## A few small words: quelqu'un, tout, autre

- *Quelqu'un* (someone, anyone in a question) pairs with *quelque chose* and *rien* from lesson
  21: *Il y a quelqu'un ? — Oui, il y a quelqu'un à la porte.* — Is anybody there? — Yes, there's
  someone at the door.
- *Tout* (all, everything) agrees when it goes with a noun: *tout le texte, toute la journée, tous
  les jours, toutes les questions*. On its own it means "everything": *Tout va bien.* —
  Everything's fine. *J'ai tout compris !* — I understood everything!
- *Autre* (other): *un autre exemple* (another example), *l'autre partie* (the other part), *les
  autres* (the others).

*Tous* is said [tu] before a noun (*tous les jours*) but [tus] when it stands alone as a pronoun
(*Ils sont tous là*: they are all here).

## Strategies for each part

### Listening

- Read the questions before the recording starts. They tell you what to listen for: a time, a
  price, a place, a day.
- You don't need every word. Listen for the key facts, especially numbers (lessons 4 and 10),
  times (lesson 18) and dates (lesson 19).
- You hear each recording twice: answer what you can the first time, check the second time.
- Watch out for corrections: *Le rendez-vous est à 15 heures… non, pardon, à 16 heures.* The
  second piece of information is the one that counts.

### Reading

- Look at the type of document first (a sign, an ad, an e-mail, a timetable), then read the
  question, then look for the part of the text that answers it.
- Notices use words you know: *ouvert, fermé, sortie, toilettes* (lessons 18 and 20).
- Don't panic about unknown words: many look like English (*la réservation, le programme*).

### Writing

- In the form, copy information exactly: the surname in capitals, the date as day/month/year
  (lesson 23).
- In the message, cover every point the task asks for. A missing point costs more than a small
  grammar mistake. Write at least the number of words asked for.
- Use a matching opening and closing and keep *tu* or *vous* all the way through (lesson 23).
- Check at the end: agreement of adjectives (lesson 8) and of participles with *être* (lesson
  22), accents, *ne … pas* around the verb.

### Speaking

- Prepare your self-introduction until it is automatic: name, age, nationality, where you live,
  family, job or studies, hobbies (lessons 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 13). Add one sentence in the past:
  *L'année dernière, je suis allé en France.*
- In the exchange of information you ask the examiner questions from a word card. A short
  correct question beats a long one you can't finish: *Qu'est-ce que vous faites le week-end ?*
- The role-play is an everyday situation, such as buying something. Use polite chunks: *Je
  voudrais…, C'est combien ?, Vous avez… ?, Merci, au revoir.*
- If you don't understand, ask: *Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?* It is much better than
  silence. Use *vous* with the examiner unless told otherwise.

## Review of the course

Use this table to go back to the lesson you need.

| topic | the core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| sounds and spelling | accents, silent letters, elision (*j'ai, l'école*), liaison | 1 |
| tu and vous, être | *Comment vous appelez-vous ? Je suis canadienne.* | 2, 3 |
| numbers | *soixante-dix, quatre-vingts*; prices *3,50 €* | 4, 10 |
| gender and articles | *le/la/les, un/une/des*: learn every noun with its article | 5 |
| avoir, possessives | *J'ai deux frères. Sa mère* (his or her mother) | 6 |
| present tense | -er: *-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent*; -ir, -re verbs; irregular verbs | 7, 13, 14, 16 |
| adjectives | agreement; most go after the noun; *beau, petit, grand* before | 8 |
| partitive | *du pain, de la viande*; *de* after a negative | 9, 10 |
| negation | *ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … rien* around the verb | 10, 21 |
| questions | intonation, *est-ce que*, inversion | 11 |
| aller, au/aux, near future | *Je vais au cinéma. Je vais partir.* | 12 |
| stem-changing verbs | *j'achète, je préfère, j'appelle, je paie* | 15 |
| reflexive verbs | *je me lève, je me suis levé(e)* | 17, 22 |
| time and dates | *Il est trois heures et demie. Le 14 juillet.* | 18, 19 |
| modal verbs | *vouloir, pouvoir, devoir* + infinitive | 19 |
| imperative | *Tournez à gauche ! Prends le bus !* | 20 |
| passé composé | *j'ai mangé*; *je suis allé(e)* | 21, 22 |
| writing | connectors, openings and closings, forms | 23 |

If you had to remember only three things from this course, make them these: every noun has a
gender, so learn it with *le* or *la*; adjectives and past participles with *être* agree with the
noun they describe; and *ne … pas* goes around the conjugated verb.

## Dialogue: practising for the speaking test

Ana and Tom are practising together for the DELF.

> Tom : Bon, on commence. Présentez-vous, s'il vous plaît.
>
> Ana : Je m'appelle Ana Garcia. Je suis espagnole, j'ai 28 ans et j'habite à Toulouse. Je suis infirmière. J'apprends le français depuis un an.
>
> Tom : Très bien ! Vous connaissez bien Toulouse ?
>
> Ana : Oui, je connais bien le centre-ville. Mais je ne sais pas encore parler très vite !
>
> Tom : Pas de problème. Maintenant, posez-moi une question avec ce mot : "week-end".
>
> Ana : Qu'est-ce que vous avez fait le week-end dernier ?
>
> Tom : Je suis allé à la montagne avec quelqu'un… mais c'est un secret !
>
> Ana : Pardon, je n'ai pas compris le mot "secret". Vous pouvez expliquer ?
>
> Tom : Un secret, c'est quelque chose que je ne dis à personne.
>
> Ana : Ah, d'accord ! En espagnol, on dit "secreto".
>
> Tom : Parfait. Tu vois ? Tu vas réussir ton examen.

Translation:

> Tom: Right, let's start. Introduce yourself, please.
>
> Ana: My name is Ana Garcia. I'm Spanish, I'm 28 and I live in Toulouse. I'm a nurse. I've been
> learning French for a year.
>
> Tom: Very good! Do you know Toulouse well?
>
> Ana: Yes, I know the town centre well. But I can't speak very fast yet!
>
> Tom: No problem. Now ask me a question with this word: "weekend".
>
> Ana: What did you do last weekend?
>
> Tom: I went to the mountains with someone… but it's a secret!
>
> Ana: Sorry, I didn't understand the word "secret". Can you explain?
>
> Tom: A secret is something I don't tell anybody.
>
> Ana: Ah, OK! In Spanish we say "secreto".
>
> Tom: Perfect. You see? You're going to pass your exam.

Notes: Tom uses *vous* while he plays the examiner and switches back to *tu* at the end.
*J'apprends le français depuis un an* uses the present with *depuis* for something that started in
the past and is still going on ("I've been learning for a year"). *Poser une question* is "to ask a
question". *Je ne dis à personne* means "I don't tell anybody"; *ne … personne* (nobody) works
like *ne … rien*.

## Pronunciation

- *L'examen* [lɛɡzamɛ̃]: the *x* sounds like "gz", and the final *-en* is [ɛ̃], like *-in*.
- *Quelqu'un* [kɛlkœ̃] has two syllables. *Faux* [fo], *fausse* [fos].

## Common mistakes

- *Savoir* with a person: not *Je sais Marc* but *Je connais Marc*.
- *Connaître* with a clause: not *Je connais où il habite* but *Je sais où il habite*.
- *Passer* and *réussir*: *J'ai passé l'examen* means you took it; *J'ai réussi l'examen* means
  you passed.
- Leaving a part of the exam blank. With 5/25 needed in every part, every point counts.
- Answering a different question in the speaking test. Listen for the question word: *où, quand,
  comment, pourquoi, combien, qu'est-ce que*.

## What comes next

At A2 you will learn the *imparfait* to describe the past (*il faisait beau*, *j'étais
content*), object pronouns (*je le vois, je lui parle*), comparisons (*plus grand que*), the
future tense, and more connectors to explain and give opinions. Keep your vocabulary reviews
going, and use the reading list, slow French podcasts and the official sample papers to keep
growing on your own.

## Key points

- A1 means you can manage simple, everyday situations if people speak slowly and help.
- The DELF A1 has four parts of 25 points: listening (about 20 min), reading (30 min), writing
  (30 min), speaking (5–7 min after 10 min of preparation). Pass: 50/100, with at least 5/25 in
  each part.
- Practise with the free sample papers from France Éducation international.
- *Savoir* for facts and skills, *connaître* for people and places.
- Ask for help in French: *Vous pouvez répéter ? Comment dit-on … en français ?*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Félicitations : you have finished the core of French A1!

lessons.title: Honors: telling a story in the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 21 and 22 gave you the passé composé: *j'ai mangé* with *avoir*, *je suis allé(e)* with
*être*. With those you can say what happened, one sentence at a time. A real story needs more:
the events in a clear order, little words such as *bien* or *jamais* in the right place, a
setting ("it was raining, there were lots of people"), and the feelings of the people in it.

This honors lesson shows you how to put those pieces together. You learn to link a sequence of
events, where short adverbs go in the passé composé, how agreement works with pronominal verbs
such as *elle s'est levée*, and two chunks for description, *c'était* and *il y avait*, as a
first look at a second past tense, the **[[imparfait]]**. At the end you read a diary entry that uses
all of it. A few points here go slightly beyond A1; they are labelled.

## Step 1: put the events in order

A story is a chain of finished events, so each step is in the passé composé. The sequence words
from lesson 17 (*d'abord, ensuite, puis, enfin*) work exactly as they did in the present: they
go at the start of the sentence, and the passé composé follows.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Linking the events of a story
  accDescr: A chain of five steps in order. Start with the time: samedi matin. Then d'abord, the first event: d'abord, j'ai pris le petit-déjeuner. Then ensuite, the next event: ensuite, je suis allé au marché. Then puis, or après, another event: puis j'ai rencontré Paul. Then enfin, the last event: enfin, nous sommes rentrés à midi.
  T["Time: Samedi matin, ..."] --> A["D'abord, j'ai pris le petit-déjeuner."]
  A --> B["Ensuite, je suis allé au marché."]
  B --> C["Puis (après), j'ai rencontré Paul."]
  C --> D["Enfin, nous sommes rentrés à midi."]
```

Two more words help a story come alive:

- *Tout à coup* means "suddenly". It marks the moment when something unexpected happens: *Tout
  à coup, il a commencé à pleuvoir.* — Suddenly it started to rain.
- *Après* + a noun means "after": *après le repas, après le concert*. Used alone at the start
  it means "afterwards": *Après, on est allés au café.*

And two to show how you feel about an event:

- *Heureusement* — fortunately, luckily: *Heureusement, j'avais mon parapluie.*
- *Malheureusement* — unfortunately: *Malheureusement, le musée était fermé.*

Don't use *d'abord, ensuite, puis* in every sentence: two or three in a short story are
enough. Time words (*à 8 heures, le soir, le lendemain*) do the same job. *Le lendemain* means "the
next day".

### Example 1: from a list to a story

Here is a list of what Malik did on Sunday:

- get up at 9; have breakfast; walk in the park; rain; go into a café; meet a friend; go home at
  6.

Step by step:

1. Choose the auxiliary for each verb. *Se lever* is pronominal and *entrer, rentrer* are in the
   house of *être*, so they take *être*. *Prendre, marcher, rencontrer* take *avoir*.
2. Write the participles: *levé, pris, marché, entré, rencontré, rentré*. Malik is a man, so the
   *être* participles have no extra ending.
3. Add sequence words, but not on every line.
4. Add one feeling word and one *c'était* to finish.

Result:

> Dimanche, je me suis levé à 9 heures. D'abord, j'ai pris le petit-déjeuner, puis j'ai marché dans le parc. Tout à coup, il a commencé à pleuvoir ! Heureusement, je suis entré dans un café, et là, j'ai rencontré un ami. Nous avons parlé pendant deux heures. Enfin, je suis rentré à 18 heures. C'était un dimanche super.

Translation: "On Sunday I got up at 9 o'clock. First I had breakfast, then I walked in the park.
Suddenly it started to rain! Luckily, I went into a café, and there I met a friend. We talked for
two hours. Finally, I got home at 6 pm. It was a great Sunday."

*Marcher* is "to walk" (and, for machines, "to work": *Mon téléphone ne marche pas*). *Il a
commencé à pleuvoir* uses *commencer à* + infinitive (to start to); *pleuvoir* is the verb behind
*il pleut*.

## Step 2: where the small words go

In the passé composé, short common adverbs go between the auxiliary and the participle, as
*déjà* and *pas encore* did in lesson 21:

![Three sentences split into boxes. First: "J'", "ai", an empty dashed slot, "dormi"; under the slot, the short adverbs that fit in it: bien, mal, beaucoup, trop, déjà, souvent, toujours, vite. Second: "Je n'ai jamais vu la mer", with ne before the auxiliary and jamais in the same slot. Third: "Je suis arrivé hier", where the time word hier comes after the participle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| adverb | example | English |
|---|---|---|
| bien | *J'ai bien dormi.* | I slept well. |
| mal | *Il a mal dormi.* | He slept badly. |
| beaucoup | *Nous avons beaucoup marché.* | We walked a lot. |
| trop | *Tu as trop mangé !* | You ate too much! |
| déjà | *J'ai déjà vu ce film.* | I've already seen this film. |
| souvent | *Elle est souvent venue chez nous.* | She often came to our place. |
| toujours | *J'ai toujours aimé Paris.* | I've always loved Paris. |
| vite | *Ils ont vite compris.* | They understood quickly. |

The negative words take the same slot: *pas, jamais, rien* go between the auxiliary and the
participle, with *ne* in front of the auxiliary:

- *Je n'ai jamais vu la mer.* — I've never seen the sea.
- *Elle n'a rien mangé.* — She didn't eat anything.
- *Il n'a pas bien dormi.* — He didn't sleep well. (*pas* first, then *bien*)

Time and place words don't go in the slot. They go at the start or the end of the sentence:
*hier, aujourd'hui, tôt, tard, ici, là-bas, ce matin*.

- *Je suis arrivé hier.* or *Hier, je suis arrivé.* (not *je suis hier arrivé*)
- *Nous nous sommes levés tôt.* — We got up early.

*Longtemps* can go in either place: *J'ai longtemps habité à Lyon* and *J'ai habité longtemps à
Lyon* are both correct. Long adverbs ending in *-ment* often go at the start or the end, and
words that comment on the whole sentence usually stand first: *Heureusement, il est venu.*

## Step 3: agreement with pronominal verbs

In lesson 22 you saw that pronominal verbs take *être*: *je me suis levé(e)*. As with the other
*être* verbs, the participle normally agrees with the subject:

| subject | se réveiller | se promener |
|---|---|---|
| il | il s'est réveillé | il s'est promené |
| elle | elle s'est réveillée | elle s'est promenée |
| ils | ils se sont réveillés | ils se sont promenés |
| elles | elles se sont réveillées | elles se sont promenées |
| nous (two women) | nous nous sommes réveillées | nous nous sommes promenées |

- *Ce matin, Julie s'est réveillée tard, alors elle s'est dépêchée.* — This morning Julie woke up
  late, so she hurried.
- *Les enfants se sont habillés tout seuls.* — The children got dressed all by themselves.
- *Nous nous sommes bien reposés.* — We had a good rest. (*bien* in the adverb slot)

In the negative, *ne … pas* goes around the reflexive pronoun and *être*:

- *Elle ne s'est pas couchée tôt.* — She didn't go to bed early.

Preview, beyond A1: when a body part or another object follows the verb, the participle does
*not* agree: *Elle s'est lavée* (she washed), but *Elle s'est lavé les mains* (she washed her
hands). The reason is grammatical (in the second sentence *se* means "for herself", not
"herself"). You don't need this at A1; just don't be surprised when you see it.

### Example 2: changing the speaker

Paul wrote: *Hier, je me suis levé à 7 heures, je me suis douché et je suis parti au travail.* Now
tell the same story about his sister Léa, and then about Paul and Léa together.

1. Find the *être* verbs: *se lever, se doucher* (pronominal) and *partir* (house of *être*). All
   three participles must agree.
2. Léa is one woman: add *-e*. The pronoun *je me* becomes *elle se*, and *me suis* becomes *s'est*.
3. Paul and Léa are a mixed group: masculine plural, add *-s*. *Ils se sont*.

Results:

- *Hier, Léa s'est levée à 7 heures, elle s'est douchée et elle est partie au travail.*
- *Hier, Paul et Léa se sont levés à 7 heures, ils se sont douchés et ils sont partis au travail.*

Read them aloud: *levé, levée, levés* sound the same. The agreement only shows in writing.

## Step 4: describe the scene with c'était and il y avait

Events are only half a story. The other half is the background: what it was like, what there
was, the weather, how people felt. For this, French uses a different past tense, the
imparfait. You will learn it fully at A2. For now, two chunks will take you a long way:

- *C'était* — it was (lesson 21): *C'était magnifique. C'était un petit hôtel.*
- *Il y avait* — there was, there were: the past of *il y a*. *Il y avait beaucoup de monde.* —
  There were lots of people. *Il y avait une belle vue.* — There was a beautiful view.

Like *il y a*, *il y avait* is the same for one thing or many: *il y avait un problème, il y avait
des problèmes*.

Preview, beyond A1: you will often meet three more imparfait forms in stories. Understand
them; you don't need to make them yet:

| imparfait | from | example |
|---|---|---|
| il faisait (beau, froid…) | faire | *Il faisait très chaud.* — It was very hot. |
| j'étais | être | *J'étais fatigué.* — I was tired. |
| j'avais | avoir | *J'avais peur.* — I was scared. |

The rule of thumb: the passé composé says what happened (an event, a step in the story); the
imparfait describes the situation around it. *Il pleuvait* (it was raining: background) and
*il a commencé à pleuvoir* (it started to rain: an event) are both correct, but they say
different things.

*Avoir peur* (to be afraid) works like *avoir faim* (lesson 11): *J'ai peur des chiens.* — I'm
afraid of dogs. *J'ai eu peur !* — I got a fright!

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Event or background
  accDescr: For something that happened, a step in the story, use the passé composé, as in je suis arrivé or il a commencé à pleuvoir. For the background, what it was like or what there was, use c'était, il y avait or another imparfait chunk, as in c'était beau or il y avait du monde.
  Q["What are you saying?"] -- "what happened" --> E["Passé composé: je suis arrivé"]
  Q -- "what it was like" --> B["C'était beau. Il y avait du monde."]
```

### Example 3: adding background to events

Events only: *Samedi, nous sommes allés à la plage. Nous avons nagé. Nous sommes rentrés à 19
heures.* Add a setting and a feeling:

1. After the first event, describe the place with *il y avait*: *Il y avait beaucoup de monde.*
2. Add the weather with the chunk *il faisait*: *Il faisait très beau.*
3. Add a feeling about the day with *c'était*: *C'était une journée parfaite.*

Result: *Samedi, nous sommes allés à la plage. Il faisait très beau et il y avait beaucoup de
monde. Nous avons nagé. Nous sommes rentrés à 19 heures. C'était une journée parfaite !*

## Text: Mon journal

Emma, a student in Bordeaux, keeps a diary (*un journal*).

> Samedi 14 juin
>
> Quelle journée ! Ce matin, je me suis réveillée tôt et je me suis dépêchée, parce que j'avais rendez-vous avec Chloé à 9 heures à la gare. D'abord, nous avons pris le train pour Arcachon. Il y avait beaucoup de monde dans le train, mais c'était sympa.
>
> À Arcachon, il faisait beau. Nous avons beaucoup marché sur la plage et nous avons mangé des huîtres au port. Après le repas, nous sommes montées en haut de la dune du Pilat. C'était magnifique : il y avait la mer d'un côté et la forêt de l'autre.
>
> Tout à coup, le ciel est devenu noir et la pluie est arrivée. Malheureusement, je n'avais pas de parapluie ! Nous sommes vite descendues et nous sommes entrées dans un café. Heureusement, le serveur a été très gentil : il nous a donné des serviettes.
>
> Enfin, nous sommes rentrées à Bordeaux à 20 heures. Je suis fatiguée, mais j'ai passé une très bonne journée. Je n'ai jamais vu une dune aussi grande !

Translation:

> Saturday 14 June
>
> What a day! This morning I woke up early and hurried, because I was meeting Chloé at the station
> at 9. First we took the train to Arcachon. There were lots of people on the train, but it was
> nice.
>
> In Arcachon the weather was lovely. We walked a lot on the beach and we ate oysters at the
> harbour. After the meal we climbed to the top of the Dune du Pilat. It was magnificent: there
> was the sea on one side and the forest on the other.
>
> Suddenly the sky went black and the rain came. Unfortunately I didn't have an umbrella! We
> quickly went down and went into a café. Luckily the waiter was very kind: he gave us towels.
>
> Finally we got back to Bordeaux at 8 pm. I'm tired, but I had a really good day. I've never
> seen such a big dune!

Notes: Emma and Chloé are women, so every *être* participle is feminine plural (*montées,
descendues, entrées, rentrées*), and Emma's own *je me suis réveillée* is feminine singular.
*Les huîtres* are oysters, a speciality of the Arcachon bay. *La dune du Pilat*, near Arcachon,
is the highest sand dune in Europe. *Le ciel est devenu noir* uses *devenir* (to become), another
*être* verb. *Il nous a donné* means "he gave us". *Aussi grande* is "so big".

## Common mistakes

- Putting a time word in the adverb slot: not *je suis hier arrivé* but *je suis arrivé hier*.
- Putting *bien* or *jamais* after the participle: not *j'ai dormi bien* but *j'ai bien dormi*;
  not *je n'ai vu jamais* but *je n'ai jamais vu*.
- Forgetting agreement with pronominal verbs: a woman writes *je me suis levée*.
- Using the passé composé for every description: *il y a eu beaucoup de monde* is possible but
  unusual; for a scene, *il y avait beaucoup de monde* is what people say.
- Starting every sentence with *ensuite*. Vary your links, or use time words.

## Key points

- Events in order: passé composé + *d'abord, ensuite, puis, après, enfin*; *tout à coup* for a
  surprise; *heureusement, malheureusement* for how it turned out.
- Short adverbs and negative words go between the auxiliary and the participle: *j'ai bien
  dormi, je n'ai jamais vu*. Time words go at the start or end: *je suis arrivé hier*.
- Pronominal verbs agree with the subject: *elle s'est levée, ils se sont promenés*.
- For the background: *c'était, il y avait*, and as a preview *il faisait, j'étais, j'avais*
  (the imparfait, taught at A2).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: letters, e-mails and texts the French way
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 23 taught you to write short, friendly messages: a postcard, a text, an e-mail of about 40
words, with *Salut* and *Bises* or *Madame, Monsieur* and *Cordialement*. This honors lesson
looks at the conventions around those messages, the things French people do without thinking
and learners often get wrong:

- how a formal letter is laid out, from the sender's address to the signature;
- the polite closing sentences of French letters, which are much longer than in English;
- how to write an address on an envelope so that it arrives;
- the abbreviations people use in text messages;
- how to decide between *tu* and *vous* when you write.

You won't need the long formal formulas to pass A1, but you will see them on every official
letter you receive in France, and knowing them helps you read those letters with confidence.

## The layout of a formal letter

A formal letter (*une lettre formelle*: to a landlord, a school, a company, a town hall) has a
fixed layout. The picture shows the usual one.

![A formal French letter with yellow tags naming its parts. Top left, l'expéditeur: "Thomas Bernard, 4 rue du Port, 44000 Nantes". On the right, le destinataire: "École de langues Atlantique, 10 place Royale, 44000 Nantes", and below it le lieu et la date: "Nantes, le 2 octobre 2026". On the left, l'objet: "Objet : demande d'informations", then la formule d'appel: "Madame, Monsieur,". The body is shown as grey lines. Then la formule de politesse: "Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées." At the bottom right, la signature and the name Thomas Bernard.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

From top to bottom:

1. The sender (*l'expéditeur*): your name and address, top left.
2. The recipient (*le destinataire*): the name and address of the person or organization, on
   the right. In France the recipient's address goes on the right, where it shows through the
   window of a window envelope.
3. Place and date, on the right: *Nantes, le 2 octobre 2026*. (The honors lesson 20h2 shows
   how to write dates in letters.)
4. *Objet :* the subject line, a few words saying what the letter is about: *Objet :
   inscription au cours de français*, *Objet : demande d'informations*. In an e-mail, *l'objet* is
   the subject field.
5. The opening: *Madame, Monsieur,* if you don't know who will read it; *Madame,* or
   *Monsieur,* if you know whether it is a woman or a man.
6. The body: short paragraphs, *vous* throughout.
7. The **[[closing formula]]** (*la formule de politesse*): a full sentence, explained below.
8. The signature and your name.

A note on the colon: French puts a space before *:* (and before *; ! ?*), as in *Objet :*. In
careful typing it is a non-breaking space (a narrow one before *; ! ?*), so the mark never
starts a new line. Many people ignore this in e-mails, but you will
see it in every printed text.

### Openings: what not to write

- Don't add the surname after *Madame* or *Monsieur* in the opening. English writes "Dear Mr
  Bernard", but in French *Monsieur,* alone is the polite form. *Cher Monsieur,* is used when you
  already know the person.
- Don't write *Cher Monsieur Bernard* to someone you've never met: it sounds over-familiar.
- For a job title, add it after *Madame* or *Monsieur*: *Madame la Directrice, Monsieur le Maire*.

## Closing formulas: a ladder of politeness

French formal closings are long and fixed. You don't need to make them up; choose one and copy it
exactly. From most formal to least formal:

| closing | use | rough English equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| *Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.* | official letters (administration, a complaint, a job application) | Yours faithfully |
| *Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.* | formal letters, a little shorter | Yours faithfully |
| *Je vous remercie par avance de votre réponse. Bien cordialement,* | formal e-mails | Thank you in advance. Kind regards, |
| *Cordialement,* / *Bien cordialement,* | everyday e-mails with *vous* | Regards, Kind regards, |
| *Bien à vous,* | e-mails with *vous*, warmer | Best wishes, |
| *Bonne journée,* / *À bientôt,* | people you know a little | Have a nice day, See you soon |
| *Bises,* / *Bisous,* | friends and family, with *tu* | Love, |

Two rules:

- Repeat the opening in the closing. If you opened with *Madame,*, the formula says *Je vous
  prie d'agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.*
- Don't mix levels. A letter that starts *Madame, Monsieur,* doesn't end *Bises*. An e-mail
  to a friend doesn't end with *salutations distinguées*.

*Merci d'avance* (thanks in advance) is common in e-mails of every kind; in a formal letter, *Je
vous remercie par avance* is more careful.

### Example 1: a short formal e-mail

Thomas wants to know the dates and the price of a French course. He writes to a language school.

> Objet : cours de français pour débutants
>
> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> Je voudrais suivre un cours de français pour débutants dans votre école. Pouvez-vous m'envoyer les dates des cours et les prix, s'il vous plaît ? Je suis libre le soir et le samedi.
>
> Je vous remercie par avance de votre réponse.
>
> Bien cordialement,
>
> Thomas Bernard

Translation: "Subject: French course for beginners. Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to take a
French course for beginners at your school. Could you send me the dates of the courses and the
prices, please? I am free in the evenings and on Saturdays. Thank you in advance for your reply.
Kind regards, Thomas Bernard."

How it was built:

1. *Objet* first, a few words, no full sentence.
2. *Madame, Monsieur,* because Thomas doesn't know who will read it.
3. One sentence for why he writes (*je voudrais* …), one polite question with inversion
   (*Pouvez-vous* … ?, lesson 11), one useful detail.
4. A thank-you sentence and a closing from the e-mail level of the ladder.

*Suivre un cours* means "to take (attend) a course". *M'envoyer* is "to send me".

## Writing an address

La Poste, the French postal service, asks for the address in a fixed order, from the person
down to the town, on up to six lines (seven for abroad), with no punctuation:

![An envelope. Top left, small: the sender, "Exp. : Lucie Petit, 3 avenue Jean Jaurès, 64200 BIARRITZ". Top right: a stamp. Lower right, the address on three lines, "Madame Claire MARTIN", "12 RUE DES LILAS", "69003 LYON", with arrows from notes on the left: title and name; number, then street; postcode + TOWN.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. Title and name: *Madame Claire MARTIN* (the surname is often in capitals).
2. If needed: flat, floor or building (*Appartement 12, Bâtiment B*).
3. Number and street, with no comma after the number: *12 rue des Lilas*.
4. Postcode and town on the last line, the town in capitals: *69003 LYON*.
5. For a letter abroad, the country on a final line: *FRANCE*.

La Poste recommends capital letters for the lower lines too (*12 RUE DES LILAS*). French postcodes
(*le code postal*) have five figures. For most of mainland France the first two figures are the
number of the *département*: 69 is the Rhône (Lyon), 75 is Paris, 13 the Bouches-du-Rhône
(Marseille). Big cities add the district at the end: *75011* is Paris's 11th *arrondissement*.

You stick the stamp (*le timbre*) on the top right of the envelope (*l'enveloppe*). Letters and
parcels are *le courrier* (the mail): *J'ai reçu du courrier.*

### Example 2: correcting an address

A learner wrote this on an envelope:

> Mr. Paul Durand, / Rue Victor Hugo, 8 / Bordeaux 33000

What's wrong, line by line?

1. *Mr.* is English. Write *Monsieur*, or the abbreviation *M.* (with a full stop). The commas at
   the ends of lines should go too.
2. The number goes before the street, with no comma: *8 rue Victor Hugo*.
3. The postcode goes before the town, and the town in capitals: *33000 BORDEAUX*.

Corrected:

> Monsieur Paul DURAND
>
> 8 RUE VICTOR HUGO
>
> 33000 BORDEAUX

## Text messages: the common abbreviations

French text messages (*les SMS, les textos*) and chat messages use many abbreviations. They are
informal: use them with friends, never in a formal e-mail, a form or a DELF answer. These are
the ones you will see most:

| abbreviation | full form | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| slt | salut | hi |
| bjr | bonjour | hello |
| cc | coucou | hi (very casual) |
| stp / svp | s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît | please |
| mdr | mort de rire | LOL (literally "dead of laughter") |
| dsl | désolé(e) | sorry |
| bcp | beaucoup | a lot |
| pk | pourquoi | why |
| rdv | rendez-vous | appointment, meeting |
| tkt | t'inquiète (pas) | don't worry |
| jsp | je (ne) sais pas | I don't know |
| a+ / @+ | à plus (tard) | see you later |

A typical exchange:

> Léa : slt ! tu es où ?
>
> Hugo : dsl, bus en retard rdv au café à 19 h ?
>
> Léa : ok tkt, a+

Translation: "Léa: hi! where are you? Hugo: sorry, bus late. Meet at the café at 7 pm? Léa: OK,
don't worry, see you."

Notice that texters often drop *ne* and articles (*bus en retard*), as people do when they speak.
That is fine in a text; in your own writing at A1, write full sentences.

## tu or vous in writing?

The rules are the same as in speech (lesson 2), but in writing the choice is visible from the
first word, so it's worth thinking about before you start.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Tu or vous in a written message
  accDescr: Ask whether the reader is a friend, a family member, a child, or someone who already says tu to you. If yes, write with tu, open with Salut or Cher, Chère, and close with Bises or À bientôt. If no, write with vous, open with Madame, Monsieur or Bonjour Madame, and close with Cordialement or a formal closing formula. If you are not sure, choose vous: it is never rude.
  A["Friend, family, child, or someone who says tu to you?"] -- yes --> B["tu: Salut / Cher, Chère ... Bises"]
  A -- no --> C["vous: Madame, Monsieur / Bonjour Madame ... Cordialement"]
  A -- "not sure" --> C
```

- When in doubt, use *vous*. It is never rude. If the other person writes back with *tu*, you
  can switch.
- Colleagues often use *tu* with each other in many French workplaces, especially among
  younger people, but not everywhere. Follow what the others do. (This is a generalization; habits
  vary by company and region.)
- Keep one form. The most common learner mistake in writing is a message that starts with
  *vous* and slips into *tu* (*Vous pouvez m'envoyer les prix ? Merci, à bientôt, bises !*). Read
  your message once just to check the *tu/vous* forms: verbs, possessives (*ton/votre*), and the
  closing.
- No capital for vous. Unlike German *Sie*, French *vous* normally has no capital letter in
  letters. (A capital *Vous* to show special respect exists in very formal letters, but you
  don't need it.)

### Example 3: from vous to tu

Thomas's new classmate, Inès, wrote to him with *tu*. He answers. Here is his first draft and the
fixes:

> Draft: *Bonjour Inès, merci pour votre message ! Oui, je suis libre samedi. Vous voulez aller au cinéma ? Cordialement, Thomas*

1. Inès used *tu*, and she is a classmate, so Thomas should use *tu* too.
2. *votre message* → *ton message*; *Vous voulez* → *Tu veux*.
3. *Bonjour Inès* is fine, but *Salut Inès* matches *tu* better.
4. *Cordialement* is for *vous*: use *À samedi !* or *Bises*.

> Final: *Salut Inès, merci pour ton message ! Oui, je suis libre samedi. Tu veux aller au cinéma ? À samedi ! Thomas*

## Common mistakes

- Adding the surname in a formal opening: not *Cher Monsieur Bernard,* to a stranger, but
  *Monsieur,*.
- Forgetting *Objet :* in a formal letter or e-mail. The reader should know what it is about
  before reading.
- Mixing levels: *Madame, Monsieur, … Bises* or *Salut … salutations distinguées*.
- Writing an address the English way, with a comma after the number or the town before the
  postcode.
- Using text abbreviations in a formal e-mail or in an exam answer.
- Switching between *tu* and *vous* in the same message.

## Key points

- Formal letter: sender top left, recipient right, place and date, *Objet :*, *Madame,
  Monsieur,*, body, closing formula, signature.
- Closings, from formal to friendly: *Je vous prie d'agréer … salutations distinguées*;
  *Cordialement* or *Bien cordialement*; *Bien à vous*; *Bises*. Repeat the opening in a formal formula.
- Address: name; number and street; postcode and TOWN. No punctuation.
- Text abbreviations (*slt, stp, mdr, dsl, tkt*) are informal only.
- When in doubt, write with *vous*, and keep the same form all the way through.
