lessons.title: Chercher un logement: flat ads, visits and the lease
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 5 you named the rooms of a flat (*la chambre, la cuisine, la salle de bains*), in lessons
4 and 10 you learned numbers and prices, and in lesson 11 you learned to ask questions. This
honors lesson puts all of that to work on a real task: finding a flat to rent in France. You'll
read flat ads full of abbreviations, phone a landlord, visit the flat, and learn the two words
that come up when you sign: *le bail* (the lease) and *la caution* (the deposit).

The rules here are for France only, and they are simplified: they describe the usual case for
a private landlord. Belgium, Switzerland and Québec have their own rules. Before you sign a real
lease, check the official site service-public.fr or ask an ADIL (a free local housing advice
office).

## Reading a flat ad

*Une annonce* is an ad. Flat ads are short, and they save space with abbreviations. Here is one,
written for this course:

![A French flat ad for a T2 in Lyon: 45 m², third floor with a lift, a living room and one bedroom, a fitted kitchen, a bathroom and a balcony, unfurnished, free on 1 March, rent 690 euros including 60 euros of charges, deposit 630 euros. Labels point to the number of rooms, the floor area, the floor, the rent, the charges and the deposit.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The most important line is the first: *T2*. The *T* (for *type*) is followed by the number of
*pièces principales*, the main rooms you live in: the living room and the bedrooms. The kitchen,
the bathroom, the toilet and the hall don't count. So a T2 is a living room plus one bedroom, a T3
is a living room plus two bedrooms, and so on. You'll also see *F2, F3*: in practice F and T mean
the same thing.

| In the ad | Say | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *studio* | *un studio* | one room with a kitchen corner |
| *T1, T2, T3* (or *F1, F2, F3*) | *un T2* (té-deux) | 1, 2, 3 main rooms |
| *45 m²* | *quarante-cinq mètres carrés* | the floor area |
| *3e ét.* | *au troisième étage* | on the third floor |
| *asc.* | *avec ascenseur* | with a lift |
| *RDC* | *au rez-de-chaussée* | on the ground floor |
| *ch.* | *une chambre* | a bedroom |
| *cuis. éq.* | *une cuisine équipée* | a fitted kitchen (with cooker, fridge…) |
| *sdb* | *une salle de bains* | a bathroom |
| *CC* | *charges comprises* | charges included |
| *HC* | *hors charges* | not including charges |
| *meublé / non meublé* | | furnished / unfurnished |
| *libre le 1er mars* | | available on 1 March |

Two words in the table need a closer look.

*La pièce* is any room you count in a home. *La chambre* is only a bedroom (lesson 5). So *un
T3 de trois pièces* has two *chambres*. If you ask *Il y a combien de chambres ?* you'll get a
smaller number than the number of *pièces*.

*L'étage* is a floor (storey). The floor at street level is *le rez-de-chaussée*, and *le
premier étage* is the floor above it. That is the British system; in American English, *le
premier étage* is the second floor. *Au troisième étage sans ascenseur* means three flights of
stairs.

Ads also show an energy rating from A (very good) to G (very poor), the *DPE* (*diagnostic de
performance énergétique*). A flat rated G costs a lot to heat.

### Example 1: Decoding the ad

Read the ad above line by line, and say what each part means.

1. *À louer — Lyon 7e*: for rent, in the 7th *arrondissement* (district) of Lyon. *Louer* means
   to rent; *à louer* on a sign means "for rent".
2. *T2, 45 m²*: two main rooms, 45 square metres in total. The next line confirms it: *séjour + 1
   chambre*, a living room (*le séjour*) and one bedroom.
3. *3e étage avec ascenseur*: third floor (fourth floor for Americans), with a lift.
4. *Cuisine équipée, salle de bains, balcon*: the kitchen and bathroom aren't counted in the T2,
   but they're there.
5. *Non meublé. Calme et lumineux.*: unfurnished; quiet (*calme*) and bright (*lumineux*, full of
   light).
6. *Libre le 1er mars*: you can move in on 1 March (*le premier mars*, lesson 19).
7. *Loyer : 690 € CC (dont 60 € de charges)*: the rent is 690 euros a month, charges included, of
   which (*dont*) 60 euros are charges. So the rent alone is 630 euros.
8. *Dépôt de garantie : 630 €*: the deposit is 630 euros, one month of rent without the charges.

## Le loyer et les charges

*Le loyer* is the rent, paid every month. *Les charges* (always plural here) are the building's
shared costs that the tenant pays on top: cleaning the stairs, the lift, often cold water and
rubbish collection. They are paid with the rent, as a fixed amount each month, and adjusted once
a year to the real costs.

So when you compare two ads, compare the same thing:

- *650 € CC*: you pay 650 euros a month in total.
- *620 € HC + 50 € de charges*: you pay 670 euros a month in total.

The second looks cheaper but costs 20 euros more. Electricity, gas, internet and home insurance
usually come on top of both.

### Example 2: What does the first month cost?

You want this flat: *Studio meublé, 25 m², 520 € HC, charges 40 €.* How much is the monthly
total, and what's the most the landlord can ask as a deposit?

1. Monthly total: 520 + 40 = 560 euros. In an ad that would be *560 € CC*.
2. Deposit: for a furnished flat, the law allows at most two months of rent without charges:
   2 × 520 = 1 040 euros. (For an unfurnished flat the maximum is one month: here it would be 520
   euros.)
3. On the day you sign, you'll usually pay the first month and the deposit: 560 + 1 040 = 1 600
   euros. Notice the French way of writing it: *1 600 €*, with a space between the thousands.

## Calling the landlord

*Le propriétaire* (or *la propriétaire*) is the owner, here the landlord. You are *le locataire*
or *la locataire*, the tenant. Many flats are also let through an agency (*une agence
immobilière*).

Clara calls about the ad:

> Clara : Bonjour, monsieur. Je vous appelle pour l'annonce du T2, rue de Marseille. Il est toujours libre ?
>
> M. Moreau : Bonjour, madame. Oui, il est libre le premier mars.
>
> Clara : Très bien. Le loyer est de 690 euros, charges comprises ?
>
> M. Moreau : C'est ça. Dans les charges, il y a l'eau froide, l'ascenseur et le ménage de l'escalier.
>
> Clara : D'accord. Et l'appartement est à quel étage ?
>
> M. Moreau : Au troisième, avec ascenseur. Il y a un petit balcon sur la cour, c'est très calme.
>
> Clara : Est-ce que je peux le visiter ?
>
> M. Moreau : Bien sûr. Vous êtes libre samedi matin, à dix heures ?
>
> Clara : Oui, parfait. Je vais apporter mon dossier.
>
> M. Moreau : Très bien. À samedi, madame !

*Clara: Hello. I'm calling about the ad for the T2 on rue de Marseille. Is it still available? —
Mr Moreau: Hello. Yes, it's free from 1 March. — Clara: Very good. The rent is 690 euros, charges
included? — Mr Moreau: That's right. The charges cover cold water, the lift and cleaning the
stairs. — Clara: OK. And what floor is the flat on? — Mr Moreau: The third, with a lift. There's a
small balcony over the courtyard; it's very quiet. — Clara: Can I visit it? — Mr Moreau: Of
course. Are you free on Saturday morning at ten? — Clara: Yes, perfect. I'll bring my file. — Mr
Moreau: Very good. See you on Saturday!*

New in passing: *le ménage* (cleaning), *l'escalier* (the stairs), *la cour* (the courtyard),
*le dossier* (the file of papers you give a landlord). *Je peux le visiter ?*: *le* = it (the
flat); object pronouns go before the verb (A2 teaches them).

*Le dossier* matters: in big French cities, finding *un logement* (a place to live) isn't easy, and many people apply for the same flat, and the landlord
picks a tenant from their files. A typical file holds a copy of your ID, your last three payslips
or proof of your grant, and often the papers of *un garant*, a person (often a parent) who
promises to pay the rent if you don't.

## Le bail et la caution (simplified)

When the landlord says yes, you sign *le bail*, the lease (plural *les baux*). In France the
usual length is:

- three years for an unfurnished flat let by a private person;
- one year for a furnished flat, or nine months for a student.

The tenant can leave before the end by giving notice (*le préavis*): three months for an
unfurnished flat (but only one month in many large towns where housing is scarce), and one month
for a furnished one.

On the day you move in, you and the landlord walk through the flat together and write down the
state of every room: *l'état des lieux*. You do it again when you leave. Keep your copy: it
decides whether you get your deposit back.

*La caution* is where English speakers get confused, because the word has two meanings:

1. In everyday speech, *la caution* is the deposit: *J'ai payé une caution de 630 euros.* The
   official name is *le dépôt de garantie*, which you'll read in the ad and the lease. For an
   unfurnished flat it's at most one month of rent without charges, for a furnished flat at most
   two. The landlord must give it back within one month after you leave if the second *état des
   lieux* matches the first, or within two months if there is damage to pay for.
2. In legal language, *la caution* is the guarantee given by a *garant*, the person who will pay
   if you don't, and also that person. On a form, *Avez-vous une caution ?* means "Do you have a guarantor?"

The whole path, from ad to keys:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Renting a flat in France, step by step
  accDescr: First you read the ads (les annonces). You call or write to the landlord (le propriétaire). You visit the flat (la visite) and give your file (le dossier) with your papers and your guarantor's. If the landlord chooses you, you sign the lease (le bail) and pay the first month's rent and the deposit (le dépôt de garantie). On moving-in day you and the landlord do the état des lieux, a written check of every room, and you get the keys. When you leave, you give notice (le préavis), do a second état des lieux, and the landlord returns the deposit within one or two months.
  A["Lire les annonces"] --> B["Appeler le propriétaire"]
  B --> C["La visite + le dossier"]
  C --> D["Signer le bail, payer le loyer et le dépôt de garantie"]
  D --> E["L'état des lieux d'entrée, les clés"]
  E --> F["Plus tard : le préavis, l'état des lieux de sortie"]
  F --> G["Le propriétaire rend le dépôt de garantie"]
```

## A short text: Clara déménage

> Clara a trouvé un appartement ! Samedi, elle a visité le T2 de la rue de Marseille avec M. Moreau. L'appartement est petit, mais il est lumineux et les voisins sont sympas : sa voisine du troisième, Mme Petit, a un chat très gentil. Lundi, elle a signé le bail et elle a payé le premier loyer et la caution. Le premier mars, elle va déménager. Ses amis vont l'aider : il n'y a pas beaucoup de meubles, parce que l'appartement n'est pas meublé ! Elle va acheter un lit et une table.

*Clara has found a flat! On Saturday she visited the T2 on rue de Marseille with Mr Moreau. The
flat is small, but it's bright and the neighbours are nice: her neighbour on the third floor, Mrs Petit, has a very sweet cat. On Monday she signed the lease and paid
the first rent and the deposit. On 1 March she's going to move. Her friends are going to help her
(l' = her): there isn't much furniture (les meubles), because the flat isn't furnished! She's going
to buy a bed and a table.*

*Déménager* (to move house) is a regular *-er* verb, but like *manger* it keeps an *e* in *nous
déménageons*. Its partner is *emménager*, to move in.

## Pronunciation

- *le bail*: like English "bye"; the plural *les baux* rhymes with *beau*.
- *le loyer*: "lwa-YAY". *Louer* is usually one syllable, "lway" (in careful speech "loo-AY").
- *le rez-de-chaussée*: "ray-d-sho-SAY"; the *z* is silent.
- *l'ascenseur*: "ah-sahn-SUR"; liaison in *un_ascenseur* ("uh-n-ah…").
- *meublé*: the *eu* of *heure*, with rounded lips: "meu-BLAY".
- *T2* is said *té-deux*, *F3* *èf-trois*, *m²* *mètres carrés*.

## Common mistakes

- Counting the bedrooms for *T*: a T3 has three main rooms, usually two of them bedrooms.
- Reading *premier étage* as the ground floor. The ground floor is the *rez-de-chaussée*.
- Comparing a *CC* price with an *HC* price. Add the charges first.
- Thinking *la location* means "the location". It means renting, or a rental: *une location
  meublée* is a furnished rental. A place is *un lieu* or *un endroit*.
- Using *louer* for the landlord only. *Louer* works both ways: *M. Moreau loue son appartement*
  (he lets it) and *Clara loue un appartement* (she rents it).
- Taking *la caution* to mean "caution". Here it's a deposit or a guarantee; "be careful" is *faire
  attention*.

## Key points

- *T2 / F2* = two main rooms (living room + one bedroom); kitchen and bathroom don't count.
- *Le rez-de-chaussée* is the ground floor; *le premier étage* is one floor up.
- *CC* = charges included; *HC* = without charges. Total = *loyer* + *charges*.
- *Le propriétaire* lets the flat; *le locataire* rents it; both *louent*.
- *Le bail* (lease): usually three years unfurnished, one year furnished (simplified).
- *La caution* = the deposit in everyday speech (officially *le dépôt de garantie*: one month
  unfurnished, two months furnished at most), or a guarantor's guarantee in legal language.
- *L'état des lieux* at the start and the end decides whether you get the deposit back.

lessons.title: La France en régions: a tour of France and overseas France
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 3 you met *la France* and its neighbours, in lesson 20 the compass points (*le nord, le
sud, l'est, l'ouest*), and in lessons 21 and 22 the passé composé. This honors lesson takes you on
a tour of France itself: its regions, a few things each one is famous for, and the parts of France
that lie far away across the oceans, *l'outre-mer*. At the end you'll read a travel blog written
in the passé composé.

## L'Hexagone and its regions

The French often call mainland France *l'Hexagone*, because its outline has roughly six sides:
three coasts (*les côtes*) and three land borders (*les frontières*). With Corsica, the mainland is *la France métropolitaine* (or
*la métropole*).

France has about 68 million inhabitants (*habitants*). Since 1 January 2016, metropolitan France has had 13 regions (*les régions*); before that it
had 22, and several were merged into bigger ones. Each region has a capital (*la capitale
régionale*), and each is divided into *départements*: 101 in all, five of them overseas. Every
*département* has a number that you see in postcodes: 75 is Paris, 13 is the Bouches-du-Rhône
(Marseille), 69 the Rhône (Lyon). A Parisian postcode starts with 75: *75007 Paris*.

![A simplified map of metropolitan France with its 13 regions and their names: Hauts-de-France in the north, Normandie and Bretagne in the north-west, Île-de-France around Paris, Grand Est in the north-east, Pays de la Loire and Centre-Val de Loire in the west and centre, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté in the east, Nouvelle-Aquitaine in the south-west, Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes in the south-east, Occitanie in the south, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur in the south-east and the island of Corse. Dots mark nine big cities. A compass rose shows N, S, E and O. A box below shows the five overseas regions, not to scale: Guadeloupe and Martinique in the Caribbean, Guyane in South America, La Réunion and Mayotte in the Indian Ocean.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Use the compass words from lesson 20 to place a region. Two patterns:

- inside France: *dans le nord de la France*, *dans l'ouest*, *dans le sud-est* (in the north of
  France, in the west, in the south-east);
- next to something: *La Normandie est au nord de la Bretagne ? Non ! Elle est à l'est de la
  Bretagne.* (*au nord de* = to the north of.)

Notice the compass rose: in French, west is *O* (*ouest*), not W.

## A few regions and what they're known for

You can't learn France in one lesson, so here are some of the things a French person would
mention first. "Known for" is a generalization: every region has much more.

| Region | Capital | Famous for (places) | A speciality |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bretagne (north-west) | Rennes | the rocky coast, lighthouses | *les crêpes*, *les galettes* (buckwheat pancakes) |
| Normandie (north-west) | Rouen | *le Mont-Saint-Michel*, the D-Day beaches | *le camembert*, *le cidre* |
| Hauts-de-France (north) | Lille | belfries (town bell towers) | *les frites*, *le maroilles* (a strong cheese) |
| Île-de-France (centre-north) | Paris | Paris, Versailles | *le brie* |
| Grand Est (north-east) | Strasbourg | Strasbourg's cathedral, the European Parliament | *la choucroute*, *le champagne* |
| Centre-Val de Loire (centre) | Orléans | the Loire châteaux (Chambord) | goat's cheeses |
| Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (east) | Dijon | vineyards | *la moutarde de Dijon*, *le comté* |
| Nouvelle-Aquitaine (south-west) | Bordeaux | the Dune du Pilat, Europe's highest sand dune | Bordeaux wine |
| Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (south-east) | Lyon | *le mont Blanc*, the volcanoes (*les volcans*) of Auvergne | Lyon's cooking, *la raclette* |
| Occitanie (south) | Toulouse | the walled city of Carcassonne, the Pont du Gard | *le cassoulet* |
| Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur (south-east) | Marseille | lavender fields, the Riviera | *la bouillabaisse* (fish soup) |
| Corse (island) | Ajaccio | mountains that drop into the sea | *la charcuterie* |

Two traps. *Le Mont-Saint-Michel*, *célèbre* (famous) all over the world, is in Normandie, not Bretagne, though it's right on the border.
And the region names are written with a capital, but the adjectives aren't: *la Bretagne*, *la
cuisine bretonne*, but *les Bretons* (the people) with a capital again, as with nationalities in
lesson 3.

France's four great rivers that flow into the sea are its *fleuves*: *la Loire* (the longest, about
1,000 km, all of it in France), *la Seine* (Paris), *le Rhône* (Lyon) and *la Garonne* (Toulouse,
Bordeaux). A river that flows into another river is *une rivière*.

## En, à or dans? Saying "in" a region

You know *en France, au Canada* from lesson 3. Regions work the same way:

- feminine regions take *en*: *en Bretagne, en Normandie, en Provence, en Occitanie, en
  Île-de-France, en Nouvelle-Aquitaine, en Corse*. Most regions are feminine.
- masculine and plural names vary in use: *dans le Grand Est* or *en Grand Est*, *dans les
  Hauts-de-France*. Both forms appear; *dans le / dans les* is the safe choice.
- islands vary, so learn each one: *à La Réunion, à Mayotte* (and *à Tahiti*), but *en Corse, en
  Martinique, en Guadeloupe* (*à la Martinique* is also heard). Size isn't the rule: La Réunion is
  bigger than Martinique. *La Guyane* isn't an island: *en Guyane*.

### Example 1: Where is it?

Say where these places are, with the region and a compass word.

1. Lille, Hauts-de-France, north: *Lille est dans le nord de la France, dans les Hauts-de-France.*
2. Rennes, Bretagne, west: *Rennes est dans l'ouest de la France, en Bretagne.* Bretagne is
   feminine, so *en*.
3. Saint-Denis, La Réunion, Indian Ocean: *Saint-Denis est à La Réunion, dans l'océan Indien.*
   La Réunion takes *à* (learn it as a set phrase), and its *La* keeps its capital.

## L'outre-mer: France beyond Europe

Not all of France is in Europe. Five overseas regions (*les régions d'outre-mer*) are also
departments, with much the same status as a region of the mainland (simplified: in Martinique
and Guyane a single assembly now does both jobs); their departments are numbered 971 to 976
(there is no 975):

| | Where | A few facts |
|---|---|---|
| la Guadeloupe | the Caribbean (*les Antilles*) | islands; bananas, sugar cane, rum |
| la Martinique | the Caribbean (*les Antilles*) | an island with a volcano, the Montagne Pelée |
| la Guyane | South America | mostly Amazon rainforest; Europe's space centre at Kourou, where Ariane rockets are launched |
| La Réunion | the Indian Ocean | a volcanic island; the Piton de la Fournaise is one of the world's most active volcanoes |
| Mayotte | the Indian Ocean | two main islands in a lagoon; a department since 2011 |

The people there are French citizens, they vote in French elections, they pay in euros, and these
five regions are part of the European Union. Other territories, such as French Polynesia and New
Caledonia in the Pacific, have their own status and their own currency, the CFP franc. Together
all of these are called *l'outre-mer* or *les Outre-mer*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How France's territory is organized
  accDescr: France is made of metropolitan France and overseas France. Metropolitan France, also called l'Hexagone, has 12 mainland regions plus Corsica, 13 regions in all. Overseas France has five overseas regions that are also departments, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane, La Réunion and Mayotte, and other territories with their own status, such as French Polynesia and New Caledonia.
  A["La France"] --> B["La France métropolitaine (l'Hexagone + la Corse)"]
  A --> C["L'outre-mer"]
  B --> D["13 régions"]
  C --> E["5 régions et départements d'outre-mer : Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane, La Réunion, Mayotte"]
  C --> F["Autres territoires : Polynésie française, Nouvelle-Calédonie…"]
```

## A travel blog: Mon tour de France

Sofia, a Canadian student, wrote this blog after two weeks in France. New words: *la tour* (tower;
*le tour* is a tour), *la vue* (view), *le phare* (lighthouse), *sauvage* (wild), *les huîtres* (oysters),
*monter* (to climb, lesson 22), *énorme* (huge).

> **Mon tour de France en deux semaines**
>
> Je suis arrivée à Paris le 2 juillet. J'ai visité le Louvre et je suis montée à la tour Eiffel : quelle vue ! Après trois jours, j'ai pris le train pour la Normandie. Le Mont-Saint-Michel est magnifique, mais il y a beaucoup de touristes.
>
> Ensuite, je suis allée en Bretagne. J'ai découvert une côte sauvage, avec des phares et des petits ports. J'ai mangé des crêpes et des galettes tous les jours. C'est la spécialité de la région !
>
> Puis j'ai pris le train pour Bordeaux. La dune du Pilat est énorme : je suis montée sur la dune et j'ai vu l'océan Atlantique. J'ai goûté des huîtres… je n'ai pas aimé !
>
> Après, je suis descendue vers le sud. À Carcassonne, j'ai visité la vieille ville et son château. Enfin, je suis restée quatre jours à Marseille. Il a fait très chaud, alors j'ai nagé dans la mer tous les jours.
>
> Je suis rentrée à Montréal hier. Le paysage change beaucoup d'une région à l'autre. L'année prochaine, je veux découvrir l'est : l'Alsace et les Alpes !

*My tour of France in two weeks. I arrived in Paris on 2 July. I visited the Louvre and went up the
Eiffel Tower: what a view! After three days I took the train to Normandy. The Mont-Saint-Michel is
magnificent, but there are lots of tourists. Next I went to Brittany. I discovered a wild coast,
with lighthouses and little harbours. I ate crêpes and galettes every day. It's the region's
speciality! Then I took the train to Bordeaux. The Dune du Pilat is huge: I climbed the dune and
saw the Atlantic Ocean. I tasted oysters… I didn't like them! After that I went down towards the
south. In Carcassonne I visited the old town and its castle. Finally I stayed four days in
Marseille. It was very hot, so I swam in the sea every day. I came back home to Montreal yesterday.
The landscape changes a lot from one region to the next. Next year I want to discover the east:
Alsace and the Alps!*

*L'Alsace* isn't a region of its own any more; it's part of the Grand Est. But people still use the old names
of the provinces (*l'Alsace, la Provence, la Bourgogne*), as Sofia does.

### Example 2: Following the verbs in the blog

Sort Sofia's verbs by their auxiliary, and check the agreement.

1. With *être*: *je suis arrivée, je suis montée, je suis allée, je suis descendue, je suis
   restée, je suis rentrée*. These are all verbs of the "house of être" (lesson 22). Sofia is a
   woman, so each participle takes *-e*.
2. With *avoir*: *j'ai visité, j'ai pris, j'ai découvert, j'ai mangé, j'ai vu, j'ai goûté, j'ai
   nagé*, and the negative *je n'ai pas aimé*. No agreement with the subject.
3. Two irregular participles: *pris* (*prendre*) and *découvert* (*découvrir*, which works like
   *ouvrir → ouvert*, lesson 21).
4. *Il a fait très chaud*: weather in the past uses *faire* in the passé composé.

So *je suis montée à la tour Eiffel* (I went up), but *Il a fait chaud* (it was hot): *monter* is an
*être* verb, *faire* is not.

## Pronunciation

- *Bretagne*: "bruh-TAN-yuh"; *gn* as in *champagne*.
- *Lyon*: one syllable, "lyohn", with a nasal *on*; never "lee-on".
- *Strasbourg*: the *s* sounds like *z*, and the final *g* is silent: "straz-BOOR".
- *Marseille*: "mar-SAY", with a final *y* sound.
- *Guyane*: "gwee-YAN"; *La Réunion*: "ray-ü-NYOHN", with the French *u* of *tu* (not *ou*).
- *le fleuve*: the *eu* of *heure*, with open rounded lips.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the Mont-Saint-Michel in Bretagne. It's in Normandie.
- *À la Bretagne* or *dans la Bretagne*: say *en Bretagne*.
- *En La Réunion*: say *à La Réunion* (and *à Mayotte*).
- Capital letters on adjectives: *la cuisine bretonne*, not *Bretonne*.
- Thinking *la Guyane* is Guyana, the English-speaking country next door. *La Guyane* is French
  Guiana, a part of France.
- Using *rivière* for the Loire or the Seine: rivers that reach the sea are *fleuves*.

## Key points

- Metropolitan France (*l'Hexagone* + Corse) has 13 regions since 2016; France has 101
  numbered departments in all, 96 of them in the metropole (75 = Paris).
- Place regions with compass words: *dans le nord de la France*, *à l'est de la Bretagne*.
- *En* + feminine region (*en Bretagne*); *dans le Grand Est*, *dans les Hauts-de-France*; islands
  vary: *à La Réunion, à Mayotte*, but *en Corse, en Martinique*.
- Five overseas regions and departments: Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane, La Réunion, Mayotte;
  they use the euro and are in the EU. Other territories (Polynésie, Nouvelle-Calédonie) have
  their own status.
- A travel story uses the passé composé: *être* for movement (*je suis allée*), *avoir* for the
  rest (*j'ai goûté*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Lire une fable: La Cigale et la Fourmi
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 21 and 22 you learned the passé composé, the past tense of conversation. This honors
lesson is your first real piece of French literature: *La Cigale et la Fourmi* (The Cicada and the
Ant), a fable by Jean de La Fontaine, published in 1668. It's 22 short lines (*vers*) long, and almost
everyone who went to school in France has learned it.

The text is more than 350 years old, so it has a few old words and one tense you haven't met. You
won't need to use them: the goal is to read the poem with a line-by-line gloss, recognise the
**[[passé simple]]** (the past tense of written stories), and then read a retelling in A1 French.

## Jean de La Fontaine and his fables

Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) was born in Château-Thierry, in Champagne, and became one of the
great French poets of the age of Louis XIV. In 1668 he published his first collection, *Fables
choisies mises en vers* (selected fables put into verse): six books, dedicated to the king's
six-year-old son. More collections followed, until there were about 240 fables in twelve books.

A **[[fable]]** is a short story, often with talking animals, that teaches a lesson about life: its
*morale*. La Fontaine took most of his stories from the ancient fables of Aesop (Greek) and
Phaedrus (Latin), and retold them in lively, witty verse.

*La Cigale et la Fourmi* is the very first fable of the first book. That's one reason it's so
famous: for generations, French children have learned it by heart (*par cœur*) in primary school
and recited it in class. Phrases from it, like *crier famine* (to plead poverty) and *Eh bien,
dansez maintenant*, are part of everyday French, and people speak of *une cigale* for someone who
spends without thinking about tomorrow, and *une fourmi* for someone who saves.

*Une cigale* is a cicada, the insect (*l'insecte*) that sings in the trees of southern France in summer.
English versions usually make it a grasshopper (*une sauterelle*).

## The text

Here is the fable. The spelling and punctuation follow the 1874 Paris edition by Bernardin-Béchet
(editions differ a little in punctuation and capitals; in 1668 it was printed with the spellings
of the time, such as *Esté* for *été*). The version you'll most often meet differs in two ways:
many editions, the first one of 1668 among them, print line 21 as a question, *Vous chantiez ?
j'en suis fort aise.*, and many school editions put the speeches in quotation marks (*« Je vous
paierai … principal. »*) and end with *Eh bien ! dansez maintenant.* The words are the same.

> **La Cigale et la Fourmi**
>
> La cigale, ayant chanté\
> Tout l'été,\
> Se trouva fort dépourvue\
> Quand la bise fut venue :\
> Pas un seul petit morceau\
> De mouche ou de vermisseau.\
> Elle alla crier famine\
> Chez la fourmi, sa voisine,\
> La priant de lui prêter\
> Quelque grain pour subsister\
> Jusqu'à la saison nouvelle.\
> Je vous paierai, lui dit-elle,\
> Avant l'oût, foi d'animal,\
> Intérêt et principal.\
> La fourmi n'est pas prêteuse :\
> C'est là son moindre défaut.\
> — Que faisiez-vous au temps chaud ?\
> Dit-elle à cette emprunteuse.\
> — Nuit et jour à tout venant\
> Je chantais, ne vous déplaise.\
> — Vous chantiez, j'en suis fort aise !\
> Eh bien, dansez maintenant.
>
> Jean de La Fontaine, *Fables*, livre I, fable 1 (1668)

![Winter in the fable: snow is falling, and a thin, shivering cicada with a little guitar stands in the snow. Beside a warm earth mound with a window and a door, an ant stands in the doorway next to two full sacks of grain. Labels: la cigale, la fourmi, le grain, la fenêtre.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Line by line

| | La Fontaine | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | *La cigale, ayant chanté / Tout l'été,* | The cicada, having sung all summer long, |
| 3 | *Se trouva fort dépourvue* | found herself completely without food (*fort* = very, a literary use today; *dépourvue* = with nothing) |
| 4 | *Quand la bise fut venue :* | when the north wind had come. (*La bise* is a cold, dry north wind: winter.) |
| 5–6 | *Pas un seul petit morceau / De mouche ou de vermisseau.* | Not one little piece of fly or little worm (*le vermisseau*). |
| 7 | *Elle alla crier famine* | She went to cry hunger (to say she was starving) |
| 8 | *Chez la fourmi, sa voisine,* | at the home of the ant, her neighbour, |
| 9–11 | *La priant de lui prêter / Quelque grain pour subsister / Jusqu'à la saison nouvelle.* | begging her to lend her some grain to live on until the new season (spring). |
| 12 | *Je vous paierai, lui dit-elle,* | "I'll pay you back," she told her, |
| 13 | *Avant l'oût, foi d'animal,* | "before the harvest, on my word as an animal, |
| 14 | *Intérêt et principal.* | the interest and the loan itself." |
| 15–16 | *La fourmi n'est pas prêteuse : / C'est là son moindre défaut.* | The ant is no lender: that's the least of her faults. |
| 17–18 | *— Que faisiez-vous au temps chaud ? / Dit-elle à cette emprunteuse.* | "What were you doing in the warm weather?" she said to this borrower. |
| 19–20 | *— Nuit et jour à tout venant / Je chantais, ne vous déplaise.* | "Night and day, for everyone who came by, I sang, if you don't mind." (*ne vous déplaise* = may it not displease you) |
| 21–22 | *— Vous chantiez, j'en suis fort aise ! / Eh bien, dansez maintenant.* | "You were singing! I'm delighted. Well then, dance now." (With the question mark of other editions: "You were singing? …") |

A few notes:

- *L'oût* is an old form of *août* (August), here meaning the harvest season; the 1874 edition's
  footnote says simply that it means *moisson* (harvest). Like *août*, it's said "oo" (or "oot").
- *Lui* means "to her" and *la* means "her": *la priant* (begging her), *lui prêter* (to lend to
  her), *lui dit-elle* (she said to her). Object pronouns come before the verb; you'll learn them
  at A2.
- *Paierai* is the future of *payer*: I will pay.
- The two insects say *vous* to each other. In the 17th century, *vous* was normal between
  neighbours, and it keeps the ant cold and formal.
- Every line but the second has seven syllables. The lines rhyme in pairs (*chanté / été*,
  *dépourvue / venue*) or in fours, one pair wrapped around another (*prêteuse … emprunteuse*
  around *défaut / chaud*).

## Reading the passé simple

Look at lines 3, 7 and 12: *se trouva, alla, dit*. These are the **[[passé simple]]**, a past tense
that French uses in written stories, novels, history books and fables. It means the same as the
passé composé: *elle alla* = *elle est allée* (she went). In conversation and in your own writing,
keep using the passé composé. You only need to *recognise* the passé simple, and in stories it's
almost always in the *il/elle* or *ils/elles* form.

| Verb type | il / elle | ils / elles | Passé composé |
|---|---|---|---|
| -er verbs: *chanter, trouver, aller* | *chanta, trouva, alla* | *chantèrent, allèrent* | *il a chanté, il est allé* |
| -ir and -re verbs: *finir, vendre, dire, faire* | *finit, vendit, dit, fit* | *finirent, dirent, firent* | *il a fini, il a dit, il a fait* |
| u-type verbs: *être, avoir, vouloir, pouvoir* | *fut, eut, voulut, put* | *furent, eurent* | *il a été, il a eu* |
| *venir* | *vint* | *vinrent* | *il est venu* |

Careful: *il dit* and *il finit* look exactly like the present. In a story told in the past,
they are passé simple.

Line 4 has a close cousin: *fut venue* is the passé simple of *être* + a participle (a tense
called the passé antérieur), and it means "had come" (*quand la bise était venue*). Lines 17–21 use the imparfait (*faisiez, chantais,
chantiez*): "were doing", "was singing" (a preview: A2 teaches it).

Line 1 shows one more form: *ayant chanté* (having sung) uses the **[[present participle]]** of
*avoir*, *ayant* (an irregular one). The present participle ends in *-ant* and is usually built on
the *nous* form of the present: *nous chantons → chantant* (singing), *nous prions → priant* (begging, line 9).

### Example 1: From the fable to everyday French

Rewrite three lines of the fable in the passé composé, as you would tell the story to a friend.

1. *Elle alla crier famine chez la fourmi.* *Alla* is the passé simple of *aller*, an *être* verb
   (lesson 22), and the cicada is feminine: *Elle est allée chez la fourmi.*
2. *Je vous paierai, lui dit-elle.* *Dit* is the passé simple of *dire*, an *avoir* verb with the
   participle *dit* (lesson 21): *Elle lui a dit : « Je vais vous payer. »* (The futur proche of
   lesson 12 replaces the future *paierai*.)
3. *La cigale se trouva fort dépourvue.* *Se trouver* is pronominal, so it takes *être*, and the
   participle agrees: *La cigale s'est trouvée sans rien* (with nothing).

## What does it mean?

The ending is a cruel joke. The cicada sang all summer; the ant answers *Dansez maintenant*: you
sang, so now dance, out in the cold, with nothing to eat. And *j'en suis fort aise* (I'm delighted)
is **[[irony]]**: the ant is anything but delighted for her.

La Fontaine doesn't state a moral here, and readers have long argued about whose side he is on.
One lesson is clear: plan ahead. But look again at lines 15–16: *La fourmi n'est pas prêteuse : C'est là son moindre défaut.* It can be read as
"that's the least of her faults" (she has worse ones) or as "lending is the fault she has least"
(she would never lend). Either way, the narrator doesn't sound like an admirer of the ant. This is
interpretation, not fact; French pupils are often asked which character they side with.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The story of La Cigale et la Fourmi
  accDescr: In summer the cicada sings all day and night. Winter comes with the cold north wind, and the cicada has nothing to eat. She goes to her neighbour the ant and asks her to lend some grain, promising to pay it back with interest before August. The ant asks what she was doing in the warm weather. The cicada says she was singing. The ant answers: you sang? Then dance now. And she gives nothing.
  A["L'été : la cigale chante"] --> B["L'hiver : la bise, rien à manger"]
  B --> C["La cigale va chez la fourmi : « Prêtez-moi du grain ! »"]
  C --> D["La fourmi : « Que faisiez-vous l'été ? »"]
  D --> E["La cigale : « Je chantais. »"]
  E --> F["La fourmi : « Dansez maintenant ! » Rien pour la cigale."]
```

### Example 2: Reading the last two lines

*— Vous chantiez, j'en suis fort aise ! Eh bien, dansez maintenant.* Take it apart:

1. *Vous chantiez*: "you were singing". The ant throws the cicada's own word back at her.
2. *J'en suis fort aise*: *fort* = very (literary use), *aise* = glad, *en* = about it. Glad that her
   neighbour sang all summer? That's the irony.
3. *Eh bien*: "well then".
4. *Dansez maintenant*: the *vous* imperative of *danser* (lesson 20). Singing goes with dancing,
   so the ant finishes the cicada's idea for her, and refuses.

## A retelling in A1 French

Here is the same story, retold in simple French for this course, in the present and the passé
composé. New words: *Il était une fois* (once upon a time, the opening of fairy tales), *le vent*
(wind), *promis* (promised).

> Il était une fois une cigale et une fourmi. C'est l'été. Il fait chaud et beau. La cigale chante tout le temps : le matin, l'après-midi et le soir. La fourmi, elle, travaille. Elle cherche des grains et elle les rentre dans sa maison.
>
> « Tu ne chantes pas avec moi ? » demande la cigale.
>
> « Non, je travaille. L'hiver va arriver ! » répond la fourmi.
>
> Puis l'été finit. Le vent du nord arrive, il fait froid et il neige. La pauvre cigale n'a rien à manger : pas une mouche, pas un petit ver. Elle a très faim. Alors elle va chez sa voisine, la fourmi.
>
> « Bonjour, voisine ! Est-ce que tu peux me prêter un peu de grain ? Je vais te payer avant le mois d'août, c'est promis ! »
>
> La fourmi n'aime pas prêter. Elle demande : « Et cet été, qu'est-ce que tu as fait ? »
>
> « J'ai chanté, jour et nuit ! » répond la cigale.
>
> « Tu as chanté ? Très bien. Alors maintenant, danse ! »
>
> Et la fourmi ferme sa porte.

*Once upon a time there was a cicada and an ant. It's summer. It's hot and sunny. The cicada sings all the time: in the morning, the afternoon
and the evening. The ant, for her part, works. She looks for grains and brings them into her
house. "Aren't you singing with me?" asks the cicada. "No, I'm working. Winter's coming!" answers
the ant. Then summer ends. The north wind arrives, it's cold and it snows. The poor cicada has
nothing to eat: not one fly, not one little worm. She's very hungry. So she goes to her neighbour,
the ant. "Hello, neighbour! Can you lend me a little grain? I'll pay you back before August, I
promise!" The ant doesn't like lending. She asks: "And this summer, what did you do?" "I sang, day
and night!" answers the cicada. "You sang? Very good. So now, dance!" And the ant shuts her door.*

*Les rentre* = brings them in (*les* = them). Notice that the old *vous* has become *tu*, as two
neighbours would say today.

## Pronunciation

- *la fourmi*: "foor-MEE"; *la cigale*: "see-GAL".
- *le vers* (line of poetry), *le ver* (worm), *vert* (green) and *le verre* (glass) all sound the
  same: "vair".
- In poetry, a final *-e* before a consonant is pronounced to make the count: *Quand la bi-se fut
  ve-nue*. In ordinary speech it's silent.

## Common mistakes

- Using the passé simple in conversation or in a DELF message. Recognise it; write the passé
  composé.
- Reading *il dit* or *il finit* in a story as the present. In a past narrative, they're passé
  simple.
- Mixing up *prêter* (to lend: give for a time) and *emprunter* (to borrow: take for a time). The
  cicada wants to *emprunter*; she asks the ant to *prêter*.
- Translating *fort* as "strong" here: in *fort aise* it means "very".
- Calling the *cigale* a grasshopper: it's a cicada.

## Key points

- La Fontaine (1621–1695) published his first *Fables* in 1668; *La Cigale et la Fourmi* is fable 1
  of book 1, and French children learn it by heart.
- The story: the cicada sings all summer, has nothing in winter, asks the ant to lend her grain;
  the ant asks what she did in summer and says *Dansez maintenant*.
- The passé simple is the written story tense: *il chanta, elle alla, il dit, il fit, il fut, il
  eut, il vint*. Recognise it; use the passé composé yourself.
- *-ant* is the present participle (*chantant, priant*); *ayant chanté* = having sung.
- *Prêter* = to lend; *emprunter* = to borrow.

lessons.title: Savoir-vivre: bonjour, tu or vous, la bise and dinner with friends
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 2 you learned *bonjour*, *tu* and *vous*; in lesson 19 you learned to accept an
invitation. This last honors lesson is about what the French call *le savoir-vivre*: knowing how
to behave. When to say *bonjour*, when to switch from *vous* to *tu*, how many kisses to give, and
what to do when friends invite you to dinner. It ends with a dialogue that uses grammar from the
whole course.

Everything here is a generalization. Habits change with the region, the generation and the
family, and the French themselves disagree about them. Use it as a starting point, and watch what
the people around you do.

## Bonjour first, always

In France *bonjour* isn't just a greeting: it opens every exchange. You say it when you walk into
a shop, a bakery, a doctor's waiting room or a lift with a neighbour, when you get on a bus, and
before you ask anyone a question. Going straight to your question (*Une baguette, s'il vous
plaît*) without *bonjour* sounds rude (*pas poli*), even if you add *s'il vous plaît*. For the
French, *la politesse* (politeness) starts with this one word.

The full polite form adds *monsieur* or *madame* (lesson 2), without the name:

- *Bonjour, madame.* — *Bonjour, monsieur. Une baguette, s'il vous plaît.*
- To a stranger in the street: *Bonjour, excusez-moi, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?*
- When you leave: *Merci, au revoir ! Bonne journée !* (or *Bonne soirée !* in the evening).

Shop staff will often greet you first with *Bonjour !* from behind the counter. Answer it. That
small exchange is the start of being treated as a polite customer, not a rude tourist.

## Tu or vous in practice

To use *tu* with someone is **[[tutoyer]]**; to use *vous* is **[[vouvoyer]]**. Both are regular *-er*
verbs with the *y → i* change of *payer* (lesson 15): *je tutoie, nous tutoyons*. Unlike *payer*,
*-oyer* verbs have only the *i* spelling: never *je tutoye*. With *se* they
mean "to each other": *On se tutoie ?* (Shall we say *tu*?), *Nous nous vouvoyons* (we say *vous*
to each other). The nouns are *le tutoiement* and *le vouvoiement*.

| Usually *tu* | Usually *vous* | It depends |
|---|---|---|
| family, friends, children | shop and office staff, waiters | colleagues (each workplace has its habit) |
| people your age at a party, students among themselves | people you don't know, older people | your boss (often *vous*, sometimes *tu* in young companies) |
| online gaming, sport clubs | doctors, officials, teachers (for adults) | your partner's parents (wait for them to offer *tu*) |

The switch from *vous* to *tu* is usually offered by the older person or the one with more
status: *On peut se tutoyer, si vous voulez.* — *Avec plaisir !* Once you've switched, don't go
back to *vous*: it would sound cold. And remember that *vous* is also the plural (lesson 2): two
friends together are *vous*, however well you know them.

### Example 1: Tu or vous?

Choose, and say why.

1. You ask the pharmacist for aspirin. *Vous*: a stranger at work. *Bonjour, madame, vous avez de
   l'aspirine ?*
2. At a friend's party you meet another guest about your age. Usually *tu* among young people at
   a party: *Salut, moi c'est Ben. Et toi ?* If in doubt, start with *vous* and let the other
   person switch.
3. Your new boss, about 50, says *Vous pouvez m'appeler Hélène* (you can call me Hélène). First
   name, but still *vous*: in France the two go together easily. Wait until she says *On se
   tutoie*.
4. Your friend's two children. *Tu* to one child; *vous* to the two together, because it's plural:
   *Vous voulez du gâteau, les enfants ?*

## La bise

*Faire la bise* is greeting someone by touching cheeks, one side then the other, with a small
kiss sound in the air. Usually the lips don't touch the cheek. It's for friends, family, friends of friends
at a party, and in some workplaces colleagues; between two men it's usual mainly in families and
among close friends. Strangers, shop staff and business contacts get a
handshake (*une poignée de main*).

How many? Two in most of France. A large online survey by the linguist Mathieu Avanzi (18,600
answers, reported in *Slate* in 2019) found one *bise* in the north of Finistère (Brittany), three in
parts of the south (Languedoc and the south of the former Rhône-Alpes region, around the Drôme),
and four in parts of the north and west (around the Loire and eastern Brittany), mostly among
older people. Even which cheek comes first varies. These are tendencies, not rules.

The safest method: let the other person lead. Turn your head slowly, follow their rhythm, and
stop when they stop. If you prefer not to kiss, offer your hand first with a smile; nobody will be
offended.

At the end of a message, *Bises !* or *Grosses bises !* (lesson 23) means "love": friendly, but not
romantic.

## Invited to dinner

French friends invite you *à dîner* or *à l'apéro*. As *un invité* or *une invitée* (a guest), a
few habits help:

**Arrive a little late.** For dinner at someone's home, arriving 10 to 15 minutes after the time
given is polite: the hosts may still be getting ready. People call it *le quart d'heure de
politesse*. Never arrive early. (For a restaurant, a train or a doctor, be on time.)

**Bring something.** A bottle of wine, flowers or a dessert from the *pâtisserie*. Ask first:
*Est-ce que je peux apporter quelque chose ?* Avoid chrysanthemums: in France they're the flowers
people put on graves for *la Toussaint* (1 November). The hosts usually serve (*servir*: *ils servent*) the
dessert you brought, but not necessarily the wine, which they may keep for another day.

**L'apéro.** Before the meal comes *l'apéritif*, almost always called *l'apéro*: drinks (a kir,
a glass of wine, beer, juice) with small things to eat (olives, crisps, *saucisson*, cherry
tomatoes). It can last an hour, and it's a good time to talk. *Un apéro dînatoire* has so much
food that it replaces dinner. Everyone waits until all the glasses are full, then raises them:
*Santé !* (or *À la vôtre ! / À la tienne !*). Look the other person in the eye as your glasses
touch.

**À table !** The host calls everyone to the table. The meal usually runs *entrée, plat, fromage,
dessert* (the module 3 honors lesson explains it), then coffee. Wait for the host to say *Bon
appétit !* before you start.

![A French place setting seen from above: a plate in the middle, the fork on the left, the napkin to the left of the fork, the knife on the right with its blade towards the plate, the spoon to the right of the knife, a glass at the top right and a piece of bread at the top left, straight on the tablecloth. Labels: l'assiette, la fourchette, la serviette, le couteau, la cuillère, le verre, le pain.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To set the table is *mettre la table*: the fork (*la fourchette*) on the left of the plate (*l'assiette*), the knife (*le couteau*) on the right with the blade towards the plate, the spoon (*la cuillère*) to the right of the knife, the napkin (*la serviette*) on the left or on the plate. In a formal French setting the forks lie with the points down. The bread usually goes straight on the tablecloth, next to your plate; there's often no bread plate. Keep both hands on the table (wrists on the edge), not in your lap.

**Leaving.** Dinners last; leaving right after dessert can seem abrupt. When you go: *Merci pour
cette excellente soirée !* A short message the next day is a nice touch: *Merci encore pour hier
soir, c'était délicieux ! Bises.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A dinner invitation in France, from arrival to the next day
  accDescr: You arrive about a quarter of an hour late with a gift such as wine, flowers or a dessert. You greet everyone, with la bise for friends. Then comes the apéro, drinks and small things to eat, with a toast, Santé. The host says À table and the meal follows: starter, main course, cheese, dessert, then coffee. You stay and talk, then leave with thanks: Merci pour cette excellente soirée. The next day you send a short thank-you message.
  A["Arriver un quart d'heure après l'heure, avec un cadeau"] --> B["Bonsoir ! La bise ou la main"]
  B --> C["L'apéro : Santé !"]
  C --> D["À table ! Entrée, plat, fromage, dessert, café"]
  D --> E["Partir : Merci pour cette excellente soirée !"]
  E --> F["Le lendemain : un petit message pour dire merci"]
```

## Dialogue: Un dîner chez Camille et Julien

Ben, from London, works with Camille in Lyon. Tonight she has invited him to dinner. Julien is
Camille's partner; Ben hasn't met him yet.

> Camille : Bonsoir, Ben ! Entre, entre. Je te présente Julien.
>
> Ben : Bonsoir ! Enchanté. Vous allez bien ?
>
> Julien : Très bien, merci. Mais on se tutoie, non ? Ici, tout le monde se dit tu !
>
> Ben : D'accord, avec plaisir ! Tenez, je vous ai apporté des fleurs et une bouteille de vin.
>
> Camille : Oh, elles sont magnifiques ! C'est très gentil, merci.
>
> Julien : Qu'est-ce que tu bois pour l'apéro ? Il y a du jus de pomme, de la bière ou du kir.
>
> Ben : Un kir, s'il te plaît. Qu'est-ce que c'est, exactement ?
>
> Julien : Du vin blanc avec un peu de crème de cassis. Tiens. Santé !
>
> Ben : Santé ! Mmm, c'est très bon.
>
> Camille : Alors, Ben, tu es à Lyon depuis combien de temps ?
>
> Ben : Depuis trois mois. Je suis arrivé en août. Au début, c'était difficile, mais maintenant j'adore la ville. Le mois prochain, je vais visiter la Bretagne.
>
> Camille : Tu vas adorer ! Bon, à table ! Assieds-toi ici, à côté de Julien.
>
> Ben (plus tard) : Ce gâteau est délicieux ! C'est toi qui l'as fait ?
>
> Camille : Oui, c'est la recette de ma grand-mère. Tu en veux encore un peu ?
>
> Ben : Oui, volontiers ! … Oh, il est déjà minuit ! Je dois rentrer. Merci pour cette excellente soirée.
>
> Julien : Merci d'être venu ! Rentre bien !

*Camille: Good evening, Ben! Come in, come in. This is Julien. — Ben: Good evening! Pleased to
meet you. How are you? — Julien: Very well, thanks. But let's say tu, shall we? Everybody says tu
here! — Ben: OK, with pleasure! Here, I've brought you some flowers and a bottle of wine. —
Camille: Oh, they're beautiful! That's very kind, thank you. — Julien: What are you drinking for
the apéro? There's apple juice, beer or kir. — Ben: A kir, please. What is it, exactly? — Julien:
White wine with a little blackcurrant liqueur. Here you are. Cheers! — Ben: Cheers! Mmm, it's very
good. — Camille: So, Ben, how long have you been in Lyon? — Ben: Three months. I arrived in August.
At first it was hard, but now I love the city. Next month I'm going to visit Brittany. — Camille:
You'll love it! Right, let's eat! Sit here, next to Julien. — Ben (later): This cake is delicious!
Did you make it? — Camille: Yes, it's my grandmother's recipe. Would you like a little more? — Ben:
Yes, I'd love some! … Oh, it's already midnight! I have to go home. Thank you for a lovely evening.
— Julien: Thanks for coming! Get home safely!*

New in passing: *Tenez / Tiens* (here you are: *vous* and *tu* forms), *depuis* (for, since),
*Assieds-toi* (sit down), *volontiers* (gladly), *en* (some of it), *la recette* (the recipe).

### Example 2: The whole course in one dialogue

Find the grammar of the course in Ben's evening.

1. *Tu or vous* (lessons 2 and 3): Ben starts with *Vous allez bien ?* to Julien, a stranger, until
   Julien offers *on se tutoie*. Then *Tenez … je vous ai apporté* is plural *vous*, for the two
   hosts.
2. The partitive (lesson 9): *du jus de pomme, de la bière, du kir, du vin blanc*, and *un peu de
   crème* after a quantity (lesson 10).
3. Questions (lesson 11): *Qu'est-ce que tu bois ?* and *Qu'est-ce que c'est ?*
4. The futur proche (lesson 12): *je vais visiter*, *Tu vas adorer*.
5. The imperative (lesson 20): *Entre, Tiens, Assieds-toi, Rentre bien*: all *tu* forms, because
   they're friends now.
6. The passé composé (lessons 21 and 22): *je vous ai apporté* (avoir), *je suis arrivé* (être;
   no *-e* because Ben is a man), *C'est toi qui l'as fait ?*
7. A modal verb (lesson 19): *Je dois rentrer*.

## Pronunciation

- *la bise*: "beez", with a *z* sound; *les bises*: "lay beez".
- *tutoyer*: "tu-twa-YAY"; *je tutoie*: "tu-TWA". *Vouvoyer*: "voo-vwa-YAY".
- *l'apéro*: "la-pay-RO".
- *Santé !*: "sahn-TAY", with a nasal *an*.
- *la cuillère*: "kwee-YAIR".

## Common mistakes

- Asking a question in a shop without *bonjour* first.
- Using *tu* with a shop assistant, a waiter or an older stranger.
- Going back to *vous* after you've agreed to say *tu*.
- Saying *tu* to two people: more than one person is always *vous*.
- Arriving early to a dinner at someone's home.
- Calling the switch to *tu* rude: *On se tutoie ?* is friendly, and saying yes is normal.
- Mixing up *apporter* (to bring a thing) and *amener* (to bring a person): *J'apporte du vin. J'amène
  mon ami.*

## Key points

- *Bonjour, madame / monsieur* before anything else; *Au revoir, bonne journée* when you leave.
- *Tutoyer* = say *tu*; *vouvoyer* = say *vous* (*je tutoie, nous tutoyons*). Strangers, shops and
  officials: *vous*; friends and family: *tu*. The older or senior person offers *On se tutoie ?*
- *La bise*: cheeks touch, usually a kiss in the air; two in most of France, one to four elsewhere (a
  generalization). Let the other person lead.
- Dinner: arrive about 15 minutes late, bring wine, flowers or dessert (no chrysanthemums), wait
  for *Santé !* and *Bon appétit !*, keep your hands on the table, thank your hosts.
- *Mettre la table*: fork on the left, knife and spoon on the right, glass above the knife.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: The past and the DELF A1
Honors: Art de vivre (the French way of life)

questions.stem: A flat ad says "T3". What does the flat have?
choices: Three main rooms, for example a living room and two bedrooms
Three bedrooms plus a living room
Three rooms in all, counting the kitchen and the bathroom
questions.explanation: The number after T counts the main rooms (pièces principales): the living room and the bedrooms. The kitchen and the bathroom don't count, so a T3 usually has a living room and two bedrooms. Counting the bedrooms only is the most common mistake.

questions.stem: Your French friend lives "au premier étage". Where is her flat?
questions.explanation: Street level is le rez-de-chaussée. Le premier étage is one floor up: the "first floor" in British English, the "second floor" in American English.

questions.stem: Ad A: "650 € CC". Ad B: "620 € HC + 50 € de charges". Which is cheaper per month, and by how much?
questions.explanation: CC means charges included, so A costs 650 euros in total. HC means without charges, so B costs 620 + 50 = 670 euros. A is 20 euros cheaper. Comparing 650 with 620 directly is the trap.

questions.stem: Which word means a bedroom only, not any room of a home?
questions.explanation: La chambre is a bedroom (lesson 5). La pièce is any main room counted in an ad; le salon and le séjour are the living room.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this flat ad.

image.alt: A French flat ad for a T2 in Lyon: T2, 45 m², 3e étage avec ascenseur, a short description, Loyer 690 € CC (dont 60 € de charges), Dépôt de garantie 630 €. Six items are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 T2 is the number of main rooms; 2 45 m² is the floor area (la surface); 3 3e étage is the floor; 4 690 € CC is the rent, charges included; 5 60 € are the charges; 6 630 € is the deposit (le dépôt de garantie), one month of rent without charges.

questions.stem: Complete with the French word for "the lease": Nous avons signé ___ lundi.
questions.explanation: Le bail is the lease (plural les baux). It rhymes with English "bye".

questions.stem: A friend says: "J'ai payé une caution de 700 euros." What did she pay?
questions.explanation: In everyday French, la caution is the deposit (officially le dépôt de garantie). It isn't "caution" in the English sense. In legal language it can also mean the guarantee given by a guarantor.

questions.stem: An unfurnished flat costs 630 € a month without charges, plus 60 € of charges. Under the simplified rules in the lesson, what is the most the landlord can ask as a deposit?
questions.explanation: For an unfurnished flat the deposit is at most one month of rent without charges: 630 €. 690 € wrongly includes the charges; 1 260 € is two months, the maximum for a furnished flat.

questions.stem: Put the steps of renting a flat in France in order.
choices: Visiter l'appartement et donner son dossier
Faire l'état des lieux d'entrée et recevoir les clés
questions.explanation: You read the ads, visit and give your file, sign the lease, do the entry inventory and get the keys. When you leave you give notice, do the exit inventory, and the landlord returns the deposit within one or two months.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: the written check of every room
questions.explanation: Le propriétaire owns and lets the flat; le locataire rents it and pays le loyer plus les charges. L'état des lieux is done when you move in and when you leave. The lease is le bail; the guarantor is le garant.

questions.stem: Which of these are true of renting in France, according to the lesson's simplified rules? Select all that apply.
choices: A furnished flat's lease is usually one year
The deposit for an unfurnished flat is at most one month of rent without charges
The landlord keeps the deposit after you leave
Une location means the place where the flat is
An unfurnished flat's lease with a private landlord is usually three years
questions.explanation: Leases are usually one year furnished (nine months for students) and three years unfurnished with a private landlord, and the unfurnished deposit is at most one month without charges. The landlord must return the deposit within one or two months. Une location is a rental, a false friend.

questions.stem: You phone about an ad. Which question is natural and correct?
choices: Est-ce que je peux le visiter ?
Est-ce que je peux le louer à vous ?
Est-ce que je visite le peux ?
questions.explanation: "Est-ce que je peux le visiter ?" – Can I visit it? The object pronoun le goes before the infinitive. "Je peux visite" forgets the infinitive after pouvoir, and the other two have the words in the wrong place.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses "louer" correctly for a tenant?
choices: Je loue un studio près de la gare.
questions.explanation: "Je loue un studio" – I rent a studio. Louer takes a direct object (the flat). "Je loue au propriétaire" has no flat to rent, "chez" is for people and homes, not a direct object, and "je suis loué" is the passive, "I am rented".

questions.stem: Read: "Studio meublé, 4e ét. sans asc., libre de suite." Which is true?
choices: It is on the ground floor.
You will climb four floors of stairs.
questions.explanation: 4e ét. sans asc. = fourth floor without a lift, so you walk up four flights. Meublé means furnished, and the ground floor would be RDC. (De suite = right away; ads use it, careful French says tout de suite.)

questions.stem: How many regions has metropolitan France (the mainland and Corsica) had since 2016?
questions.explanation: Since 1 January 2016 there are 13 metropolitan regions. 22 was the number before the mergers, 18 counts the five overseas regions too, and 101 is the number of departments.

questions.stem: In which region is the Mont-Saint-Michel?
questions.explanation: The Mont-Saint-Michel is in Normandie, right on the border with Bretagne, which is why people often put it in the wrong region.

questions.stem: Name the numbered regions on this map.

image.alt: A simplified map of France with dashed region borders, dots for big cities and a compass rose, but no names. Six regions are numbered: one at the western tip, one on the north-west coast, one in the north-east, one in the south-west, one in the south and one in the south-east.

questions.explanation: 1 Bretagne is the western tip; 2 Normandie is on the Channel coast east of it; 3 Grand Est is in the north-east, along Germany; 4 Nouvelle-Aquitaine is the big region of the south-west (Bordeaux); 5 Occitanie is in the south (Toulouse); 6 Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur is in the south-east (Marseille).

questions.stem: Match each region to a speciality it is known for.
questions.explanation: Crêpes and buckwheat galettes are Breton; choucroute comes from Alsace (Grand Est); cassoulet from Occitanie; bouillabaisse from Marseille; camembert from Normandie. Raclette belongs to the Alps (Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes) and Switzerland.

questions.stem: Choose the right preposition: "J'ai passé une semaine ___ Bretagne."
questions.explanation: Feminine regions take en, like feminine countries: en Bretagne, en Normandie, en Provence. Au is for masculine countries (au Canada).

questions.stem: Choose the right phrase: "Mon frère habite ___ ; il travaille à Saint-Denis."
questions.explanation: Islands vary and are best learned one by one: à La Réunion, à Mayotte, but en Corse, en Martinique. La Réunion keeps its article: à La Réunion.

questions.stem: Which of these are French overseas regions (régions d'outre-mer)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The five overseas regions are Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane, La Réunion and Mayotte. Corse is a metropolitan region. French Polynesia is overseas but is not a region: it has its own status and currency.

questions.stem: What is "la Guyane"?
choices: An island in the Indian Ocean
A part of France in South America
A region in the south of mainland France
questions.explanation: La Guyane is French Guiana, a French region and department in South America, home to Europe's space centre at Kourou. Guyana is its English-speaking neighbour.

questions.stem: A river that flows into the sea, like the Loire, is not "une rivière" but "un ___".
questions.explanation: Un fleuve reaches the sea (la Loire, la Seine, le Rhône, la Garonne); une rivière flows into another river.

questions.stem: Sofia writes in her blog. Which sentence is correct?
choices: Je suis allé en Bretagne et j'ai mangé des crêpes, dit Sofia.
Je suis montée sur la dune et j'ai vu l'océan.
questions.explanation: Monter is an être verb, and Sofia is a woman, so "je suis montée"; voir takes avoir: "j'ai vu". Aller takes être (je suis allée, with -e for Sofia, not allé); goûter takes avoir (j'ai goûté).

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Lille is in the north of France."
questions.explanation: "Lille est dans le nord de la France." Inside a country, use dans le nord (in the north) + de la France. Au nord de means "to the north of" something.

questions.stem: Which sentence is spelled correctly?
choices: Les Bretons adorent la cuisine bretonne.
questions.explanation: Region names and the people take a capital (la Bretagne, les Bretons); adjectives don't (la cuisine bretonne), as with nationalities.

questions.stem: Read: "Les départements ont un numéro : 75 pour Paris, 13 pour les Bouches-du-Rhône." Where do you often see this number?
choices: At the start of the postcode
questions.explanation: The department number begins the postcode: 75007 Paris, 13001 Marseille.

questions.stem: Which statement about the five overseas regions is true?
choices: Their people are not French citizens.
They use the euro and are part of the European Union.
They are all in the Pacific Ocean.
questions.explanation: The five overseas regions use the euro, are part of the EU, and their people are French citizens. Two are in the Caribbean, one in South America and two in the Indian Ocean. The CFP franc is used in territories such as French Polynesia, which are not regions.

questions.stem: When did La Fontaine publish the first collection of his Fables, which opens with La Cigale et la Fourmi?
questions.explanation: The first collection, Fables choisies mises en vers, appeared in 1668, in the reign of Louis XIV. La Fontaine lived from 1621 to 1695.

questions.stem: What is "une cigale"?
questions.explanation: Une cigale is a cicada, the insect that sings in the trees of southern France in summer. English versions often call it a grasshopper, which in French is une sauterelle.

questions.stem: Put the events of the fable in order.
choices: L'hiver arrive et elle n'a rien à manger.
Elle demande du grain à la fourmi.
La fourmi demande : « Que faisiez-vous au temps chaud ? »
questions.explanation: Summer singing, winter hunger, the request for a loan, the ant's question, the cicada's answer, and the ant's cruel reply.

questions.stem: Match each line from the fable to its meaning.
choices: found herself with nothing at all
when the cold north wind had come
she went to say she was starving
I will pay you before the harvest
questions.explanation: Fort = very (literary use), dépourvue = with nothing; la bise is a cold north wind; crier famine = to say you are starving; prêteuse = someone who lends. "I will pay you before the harvest" is "Je vous paierai … avant l'oût", not in the list.

questions.stem: In "Elle alla crier famine", what is "alla"?
choices: The passé simple of aller: she went
The present of aller: she goes
The imparfait of aller: she was going
The future of aller: she will go
questions.explanation: Alla is the passé simple, the past tense of written stories. In conversation you'd say "elle est allée". The present is va, the imparfait allait, the future ira.

questions.stem: Match each passé simple form to its passé composé.
questions.explanation: -er verbs end in -a (chanta). Fut and eut come from être and avoir, fit from faire, and vint from venir, which takes être in the passé composé.

questions.stem: Rewrite "La cigale se trouva fort dépourvue" as you would say it today, in the passé composé.
choices: La cigale a trouvé sans rien.
La cigale s'est trouvée sans rien.
La cigale s'est trouvé sans rien.
La cigale se trouve sans rien.
questions.explanation: Se trouver is pronominal, so it takes être, and the participle agrees with la cigale: s'est trouvée. Without the -e it doesn't agree; "a trouvé" uses the wrong auxiliary; "se trouve" is the present.

questions.stem: The ant says: "Vous chantiez, j'en suis fort aise !" What tone is this?
choices: Irony: she isn't glad at all
questions.explanation: "I'm delighted" is ironic: the ant is mocking the cicada and then tells her to dance in the cold. She says the opposite of what she means.

questions.stem: The cicada wants to borrow grain. She asks the ant to lend it. Type the French verb for "to lend": ___
questions.explanation: Prêter = to lend (give for a time). The cicada is the one who wants to emprunter (borrow).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this picture of the fable.

image.alt: A winter scene with no labels: a cicada with a little guitar stands in the snow on the right; an ant stands in the doorway of an earth mound with a window; two sacks of grain lie beside the door. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 the cicada (la cigale) in the snow, 2 the ant (la fourmi) in her doorway, 3 the sacks of grain (le grain) she saved in summer, 4 the window (la fenêtre) of her warm house.

questions.stem: Which of these are passé simple forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Trouva and chantèrent are -er verbs in the passé simple (-a, -èrent), and fut is the passé simple of être. "Il a trouvé" is the passé composé and "il chantait" the imparfait.

questions.stem: Why do almost all French people know this fable?
choices: It is the French national anthem.
It is the first fable of the first book, and children learn it by heart at school.
It was written in the 20th century for television.
It is printed on euro banknotes.
questions.explanation: La Cigale et la Fourmi opens book I of La Fontaine's Fables, and generations of French pupils have learned it by heart (par cœur) in primary school.

questions.stem: In a story told in the past you read: "Il dit : « Merci ! » et il partit." What is "dit"?
questions.explanation: Il dit looks like the present, but in a story in the past, next to partit (passé simple of partir), it is the passé simple: he said. In conversation: il a dit.

questions.stem: What does "ayant chanté" (line 1) mean?
questions.explanation: Ayant is the present participle of avoir; ayant + a past participle means "having done": having sung all summer. "While singing" would be en chantant.

questions.stem: You walk into a bakery in France. What do you say first?
questions.explanation: Bonjour (with madame or monsieur) comes first, always. Ordering straight away sounds rude even with s'il vous plaît, and salut is too familiar for a shop.

questions.stem: What does "On se tutoie ?" mean?
choices: Shall we say tu to each other?
Shall we kiss on the cheek?
questions.explanation: Tutoyer is to say tu; se tutoyer, to say tu to each other. It's a friendly offer, usually made by the older person or the one with more status.

questions.stem: Tu or vous? Match each person to the usual choice.
left: an older stranger in the street
questions.explanation: Strangers, staff and older people get vous; friends and children get tu. Two or more people are always vous, however well you know them.

questions.stem: Complete with the present of "vouvoyer": Je ___ ma voisine : elle a quatre-vingts ans.
questions.explanation: Vouvoyer changes y to i before a silent e: je vouvoie, tu vouvoies, il vouvoie, but nous vouvoyons, vous vouvoyez.

questions.stem: According to the survey in the lesson, how many bises do people give in most of France?
questions.explanation: Two is the most common. One is usual in the north of Finistère, three in parts of the south, four in parts of the north and west: tendencies, not rules. Let the other person lead.

questions.stem: Friends invite you to dinner at their home at 8 p.m. When is it polite to arrive?
questions.explanation: The quart d'heure de politesse: about 10 to 15 minutes after the time given, so the hosts can finish getting ready. Arriving early is the mistake to avoid; an hour and a half late is too late. (A generalization.)

questions.stem: Which of these are good gifts to bring to a French dinner, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Wine, a dessert or flowers are classic gifts. Chrysanthemums are the flowers put on graves for la Toussaint, and money would be strange between friends.

questions.stem: Everyone has a glass at the apéro. What do you say as you raise yours?
questions.explanation: Santé ! (or À la vôtre ! / À la tienne !) is the toast; look the other person in the eye. Bon appétit is for starting to eat, à bientôt for leaving, enchanté for meeting someone.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this French place setting.

image.alt: A place setting seen from above with no labels: a plate in the middle, a fork to its left, a napkin left of the fork, a knife and a spoon to the right, a glass at the top right and bread at the top left. Six items are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 the plate (l'assiette), 2 the fork (la fourchette) on the left, 3 the knife (le couteau) on the right with its blade towards the plate, 4 the spoon (la cuillère) right of the knife, 5 the glass (le verre) above the knife, 6 the napkin (la serviette).

questions.stem: Choose the right verb: "Ce soir, j'___ mon ami Paul et j'___ une bouteille de vin."
questions.explanation: Amener is for bringing a person (j'amène Paul), apporter for bringing a thing (j'apporte du vin).

questions.stem: Put the evening of a French dinner invitation in order.
choices: Manger le fromage, puis le dessert
Dire : Merci pour cette excellente soirée !
Le lendemain, envoyer un petit message
questions.explanation: Arrival with a gift, the apéro and its toast, the meal (cheese before dessert in France), thanks when you leave, and a short message the next day.

questions.stem: Julien has just said "On se tutoie, non ?" Ben gives him a bottle of wine. What does he say?
questions.explanation: Once they've agreed on tu, Ben uses the tu imperative tiens (here you are) and toi. Going back to vous would sound cold, and mixing tiens with vous is inconsistent. The imperative has no subject pronoun.

questions.stem: Which statement about la bise is true, according to the lesson?
choices: It is used with shop staff.
Cheeks touch and the kiss is in the air.
Everyone in France gives exactly two.
questions.explanation: Cheeks touch, with a small kiss sound in the air. Shop staff get bonjour, not a bise, and the number varies by region and generation.

questions.stem: In the dialogue Ben says: "Je suis arrivé en août." Why "arrivé" and not "arrivée"?
choices: Ben is a man, so the être participle takes no -e.
questions.explanation: Arriver takes être, and with être the participle agrees with the subject. Ben is a man, so arrivé; Camille would say je suis arrivée.

questions.stem: How is the "u" in "tu" (you) pronounced?
questions.explanation: French u has no English equivalent: keep your tongue forward where it is for "ee" and round your lips. The "oo" of "food" is French ou, as in tout (all) or vous, so tu and tout are different words.

questions.stem: You spell the name "Julie" in French. How do you say the first letter?
questions.explanation: French J is called "zhee" and G is "zhay", almost the English names swapped. "Jay" is the English name, and "ee" is the French name of I.

questions.stem: Which spelling of "to spell" is correct?
questions.explanation: épeler has an acute accent on the first e only. The accent is part of the spelling, so epeler is a mistake; è would give the wrong sound, and the second e is a weak e with no accent.

questions.stem: In which word is the final consonant pronounced?
questions.explanation: Final c, r, f and l are usually said (the CaReFuL rule), so the c of avec is heard: "a-VEK". Most other final consonants are silent: petit is "puh-TEE", vous is "voo", beaucoup is "boh-KOO".

questions.stem: How is "ils parlent" (they speak) pronounced?
choices: "eelz parl": the s links to parlent
questions.explanation: The -ent ending of a verb is completely silent, so ils parlent sounds exactly like il parle. -ent is only nasal in other kinds of words (lentement). There is no liaison because parlent starts with a consonant.

questions.stem: Which of these words has a nasal vowel?
questions.explanation: In bon, the o + n at the end of the word is a nasal vowel and the n is not said. In bonne and fine, a second n or a vowel follows, so the vowel is not nasal and you hear a real n. Une has no nasal: "ün".

questions.stem: What does the cedilla do in "ça"?
choices: It makes the c sound like k.
It makes the c sound like s.
questions.explanation: Before a, o and u, c is a k sound (café). The cedilla (ç) turns it into an s sound: ça, français. A lost s is marked by the circumflex (hôpital), not the cedilla.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly? (I live in Lyon.)
questions.explanation: Before a vowel or mute h, je drops its e and takes an apostrophe: j'habite. This elision is compulsory in writing as well as in speech, so "je habite" is a mistake.

questions.stem: Where is the strongest stress in "merci beaucoup"?
questions.explanation: French stresses the last syllable of a whole rhythm group, not each word. Alone, merci is "mer-CI", but inside merci beaucoup the stress moves to the end: beau-COUP.

questions.stem: In which phrase do you hear a "z" sound between the two words?
questions.explanation: Liaison: the silent s of les is said as "z" because amis starts with a vowel: "lé-za-mi". Mots and parlez start with consonants, so there is no liaison. After et there is never a liaison.

questions.stem: Someone says to you: "Merci beaucoup !" What is the usual reply?
questions.explanation: De rien (literally "of nothing") means "you're welcome". Pardon ? asks someone to repeat; s'il vous plaît means please; Je ne comprends pas means I don't understand.

questions.stem: A receptionist says your room number too fast. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Vous pouvez répéter ? (Can you repeat that?) asks to hear it again; you can add lentement (slowly). Comment ça s'écrit ? asks for a spelling, de rien answers thanks, and voilà is said when handing something over.

questions.stem: Read the exchange: "Mme Roux : Votre nom ? — Sam : Okafor. — Mme Roux : Pardon ? Comment ça s'écrit ? — Sam : O, K, A, F, O, R." What does Mme Roux want?
choices: to know how Sam spells his surname
to know what his name means
questions.explanation: Comment ça s'écrit ? means "How do you spell that?", and Sam answers with the letters. Votre nom on a form is the surname. To ask what something means you'd say Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?

questions.stem: How is "s'il vous plaît" pronounced?
questions.explanation: The s of vous and the t of plaît are silent (plaît starts with a consonant, so no liaison), aî sounds like "eh", and the stress falls on the last syllable of the group.

questions.stem: Two French vowels: pick the right label for each numbered part.

image.alt: Two simplified side views of the mouth. Numbers 1 and 2 are above the left and the right mouth. In the left mouth, number 3 is on the tongue, which is raised high at the front. In the right mouth, number 4 is on the tongue, which is raised high at the back. In both mouths the lips are rounded.

choices: Tongue high at the front, as for ee
Tongue high at the back, as in food
Tongue flat and low, as in father
questions.explanation: For both u and ou the lips are rounded. The tongue makes the difference: for u (left, 1) it stays at the front, as for "ee" (3); for ou (right, 2) it is pulled back (4), as in English "food". Neither sound has a flat tongue or spread lips.

questions.stem: Join "de" and "accord" the French way (it means OK): ___
questions.explanation: Before a vowel, de drops its e and takes an apostrophe (elision): d'accord. The d is silent: "dah-KOR".

questions.stem: Fill in the missing letter (it sounds like s): fran___ais (French)
questions.explanation: Before a, a plain c would sound like k ("frankay"). The cedilla makes it an s sound: français. The same goes for ça and garçon.

questions.stem: Match each spelling to its usual sound.
questions.explanation: ou = "oo", oi = "wah", eau (and au) = "oh", gn = "ny", ch = "sh". French ch is never the "ch" of church.

questions.stem: In which of these words is the last consonant pronounced? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Final c, r and f follow the CaReFuL rule and are said: avec, bonjour, neuf. The t of petit, the s of vous and the p of beaucoup are silent.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask "What does that mean?"
questions.explanation: Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ? Literally "What is it that that wants to say?". Learn it as one block; it's one of the most useful questions for a learner.

questions.stem: It's 8 p.m. You arrive at a friend's parents' house for dinner. What do you say?
