questions.explanation: Bonsoir is the evening greeting. Bonne nuit is only for someone going to bed, and bonne soirée (have a good evening) and au revoir are said when you leave.

questions.stem: You pay at a bakery at 10 a.m. and leave. What does the baker most likely say?
questions.explanation: Bonne journée (have a good day) is said when someone leaves during the day, often after au revoir. Salut and à plus are too casual for a customer, bonne nuit is for bedtime, and enchanté is for meeting someone for the first time.

questions.stem: You meet two friends together and ask them how they are. Which question fits?
questions.explanation: Vous is the only plural "you": with two or more people it's vous, however well you know them. Comment vas-tu ? and et toi ? speak to one person, and Comment tu t'appelles ? asks a name. (Ça va ? also works with a group.)

questions.stem: You walk into a small shop and the owner, a woman you don't know, looks up. What do you say first?
questions.explanation: In France you always greet before anything else, and adding madame or monsieur is polite. Salut and ça va, toi ? are for friends; bonne journée is said when you leave.

questions.stem: Hugo asks "Ça va ?" and Inès answers "Ça va, et toi ?" What does Inès mean?
questions.explanation: Ça va ? with a rising voice asks how someone is; ça va with a falling voice answers "I'm fine". Et toi ? (and you?) sends the question back.

questions.stem: Complete the informal reply: "Ça va ? — Pas mal, et ___ ?"
questions.explanation: After et, a pronoun stands alone, so you need the stressed pronoun toi. Tu can never stand alone ("et tu" is wrong), and moi would mean "and me?".

questions.stem: A receptionist asks you: "Comment vous appelez-vous ?" What is a good answer?
questions.explanation: Comment vous appelez-vous ? means "What's your name?" (formal), so answer with Je m'appelle … Très bien, merci answers "How are you?"; à demain and bonne soirée are goodbyes.

questions.stem: Awa (a woman) writes "Pleased to meet you!" in a message to a new colleague. Which spelling is correct for her?
questions.explanation: Enchanté is an adjective, so it agrees with the person speaking: a woman writes enchantée. Both sound the same. Enchantés is masculine plural, and enchanter is a verb (to delight).

questions.stem: In France today, what is the safe polite word for addressing any adult woman you don't know?
questions.explanation: Madame works for any adult woman, whatever her age or marital status. Mademoiselle was removed from official forms in 2012 and can sound old-fashioned or condescending. Monsieur is for a man, and salut is an informal greeting, not a title.

questions.stem: When do you say "Bonne nuit !"?
choices: when you arrive at a party at 9 p.m.
when you leave work at 6 p.m.
when you meet someone for the first time
when someone is going to bed
questions.explanation: Bonne nuit is only said to someone going to bed. Arriving in the evening you say bonsoir; leaving work in the evening, au revoir or bonne soirée; meeting someone, enchanté.

questions.stem: Read: "M. Mercier : Bonjour, madame. — Mme Diallo : Bonjour, monsieur. Comment allez-vous ? — M. Mercier : Très bien, merci. Et vous ?" Which statement is true?
choices: They speak to each other formally, with vous.
It is late in the evening.
Mme Diallo is going to bed.
questions.explanation: Comment allez-vous ? and Et vous ? are formal; old friends would use tu (Ça va ? Et toi ?). Bonjour shows it isn't evening, and nobody says bonne nuit.

questions.stem: Which of these questions is informal?
questions.explanation: Comment tu t'appelles ? uses tu, for a friend, a child or someone your age in a relaxed setting. The other three use vous, the polite (or plural) form.

questions.stem: Which greeting or goodbye fits each part of the day? Pick one for each number.

image.alt: A timeline of the day from 6:00 to 24:00. The top row, saying hello, has two parts: number 1 from 6:00 to about 18:00 and number 2 from about 18:00 to 24:00. The row below, when you leave, has the same two parts: number 3 during the day and number 4 in the evening. Number 5 is on a bed with a moon.

questions.explanation: Bonjour (1) until the evening and bonsoir (2) from about 6 p.m. When you leave: bonne journée (3) during the day, bonne soirée (4) in the evening. Bonne nuit (5) is only for going to bed. Enchanté is for meeting someone, and à demain means see you tomorrow at any time.

questions.stem: Complete the introduction: "Je ___ Léa." (My name is Léa.)
questions.explanation: Je m'appelle Léa: literally "I call myself Léa". Learn it as a block for now; the verb s'appeler comes in Lesson 17. Note the elision m' and the double l.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask a stranger "What's your name?"
questions.explanation: Comment vous appelez-vous ? The question word comes first, then vous (the reflexive part), then the verb joined to vous by a hyphen. The informal version is Comment tu t'appelles ?

questions.stem: Whom would you normally address with tu? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Tu is for family, children and friends. A waiter you don't know and a new boss get vous, at least until they suggest tu.

questions.stem: Match each French phrase to its meaning.
questions.explanation: à bientôt = see you soon, à demain = see you tomorrow, à plus tard = see you later (à plus among friends), bonne soirée = have a good evening. Good night (at bedtime) is bonne nuit.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ canadiens."
questions.explanation: être with nous is sommes: nous sommes. Sont goes with ils/elles, êtes with vous, and est with il/elle/on.

questions.stem: Complete: "Vous ___ de Paris ?"
questions.explanation: vous êtes, said with a liaison: "voo-ZET". Es goes with tu, sont with ils/elles, suis with je.

questions.stem: Léa is from Montréal. Which sentence describes her using a nationality adjective?
questions.explanation: The adjective is feminine singular and lowercase: canadienne. Elle est Canadienne is also possible when Canadienne is a noun naming a person, but this question asks for the adjective.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Marc. ___ canadien."
questions.explanation: Use c'est before a name (C'est Marc) and il est before an adjective on its own (Il est canadien).

questions.stem: Complete: "J'habite ___ Canada."
questions.explanation: Le Canada is masculine, and masculine countries take au: au Canada. En is for feminine countries (en France), à for cities (à Montréal) and aux for plural countries (aux États-Unis).

questions.stem: Complete: "Sofia et Luca habitent ___ Italie."
questions.explanation: L'Italie is feminine (most countries ending in -e are), so it takes en with no article: en Italie.

questions.stem: Complete: "Julia habite ___ Montréal."
questions.explanation: Cities take à: à Montréal, à Paris. En and au are for countries.

questions.stem: A friend says: "On est à Paris !" What does she mean?
questions.explanation: In everyday speech on usually means "we". It takes the il form of the verb (on est), which is why it can look like "he is".

questions.stem: You talk about Awa, Inès and Hugo together. Which pronoun replaces them?
questions.explanation: Ils covers any group with at least one man or masculine noun in it. Il is for one man, and on means "we" or "people". Elles is only for groups that are all female or all feminine nouns.

questions.stem: Which of these countries is masculine?
questions.explanation: Le Maroc is masculine (au Maroc). La Belgique, l'Espagne and l'Italie are feminine, like most country names ending in -e.

questions.stem: Which spelling means "where"?
questions.explanation: Où (where) has a grave accent; ou without it means "or". The accent changes no sound: it only tells the two words apart. Où is the only French word with ù.

questions.stem: Read: "Je m'appelle Nadia. Je suis marocaine, de Rabat, mais j'habite en Belgique, à Bruxelles. Mes amis Tom et Lucy sont anglais. Ils habitent à Londres." (marocaine = Moroccan, mais = but, mes amis = my friends) Which statement is true?
choices: Tom and Lucy live in Brussels.
questions.explanation: J'habite en Belgique, à Bruxelles: she lives in Brussels. She is Moroccan and from Rabat (de Rabat). Tom and Lucy live in London (à Londres).

questions.stem: Which two forms of être sound exactly the same?
questions.explanation: Es and est are both said "eh": the s and the t are silent. Suis ("swee") and sont ("sohn") sound different, and so do sommes ("som") and êtes ("et").

questions.stem: Name the numbered countries around France.

image.alt: A sketch of France and the countries around it, without names. Number 1 is across the Channel to the north. Number 2 is a small country to the north-east of France. Number 3 is a large country to the east. Number 4 is a small country to the south-east. Number 5 is a long country further south-east. Number 6 is to the south-west, across the Pyrenees. France itself and a country across the Mediterranean have no number.

questions.explanation: England (1) is across the Channel; Belgium (2) is to the north-east; Germany (3) to the east; Switzerland (4) and Italy (5) to the south-east; Spain (6) to the south-west. Canada and the United States are across the Atlantic. The country across the Mediterranean is le Maroc.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of être: "Je ___ de Montréal."
questions.explanation: je suis (I am): "zhuh SWEE". The full verb: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont.

questions.stem: Write the feminine: "Marc est canadien. Julie est ___."
questions.explanation: Canadien doubles its n before the feminine -e: canadienne. You can hear the difference: the nasal "-dyan" becomes "-dyen" with a real n.

questions.stem: Which word means "in" before each place? (A word can be used more than once.)
questions.explanation: au Canada (masculine country), en France and en Italie (feminine countries, no article), aux États-Unis (plural country), à Paris (city). Dans isn't used with country or city names like these.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The words « française » and « suisses » are adjectives. Elle est Belge is also correct: Belge can be a noun naming a person after être. C’est un ami uses a noun. In Il est un canadien, the noun naming a Canadian person would need a capital C.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "They live in the United States."
questions.explanation: Ils habitent aux États-Unis. Subject, verb, then aux + the plural country. Say it with liaisons: "eel-za-BEET o-zay-ta-zü-NEE".

questions.stem: How is 70 said in France?
questions.explanation: 70 = 60 + 10: soixante-dix. Septante is Belgian and Swiss; it's understood in France but not used there. "Sept-dix" and "soixante et dix" don't exist.

questions.stem: What number is "quatre-vingt-dix-sept"?
questions.explanation: quatre-vingt (4 × 20 = 80) + dix (10) + sept (7) = 97. 87 would be quatre-vingt-sept and 77 soixante-dix-sept.

questions.stem: Which spelling of 83 is correct?
questions.explanation: Quatre-vingts keeps its s only when nothing follows; before trois it drops it: quatre-vingt-trois. The parts are joined with hyphens, and quatre never takes an s.

questions.stem: How do you say 71?
questions.explanation: 71 = 60 + 11, and like 21, 31 … 61 it takes et: soixante et onze (1990 spelling: soixante-et-onze).

questions.stem: How do you say 81?
questions.explanation: 81 and 91 have no et: quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze. The s of quatre-vingts goes because a number follows. The t of vingt is not said: "katr-van-UN".

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm 25"?
questions.explanation: French uses avoir (to have) for age and always says ans (years): J'ai vingt-cinq ans. "Je suis vingt-cinq" is the English pattern and means nothing in French.

questions.stem: How is "six" pronounced in "six ans" (six years)?
questions.explanation: Before a vowel the x of six links with a z sound: "see-ZAHN". Alone, six is "sees"; before a consonant, "see" (six mots).

questions.stem: You hear: "zéro six, quarante-quatre, quatre-vingt-dix-neuf, dix-sept, soixante". Which number is it?
questions.explanation: Phone numbers are read in pairs: zéro six (06), quarante-quatre (44), quatre-vingt-dix-neuf (4 × 20 + 19 = 99), dix-sept (17), soixante (60).

questions.stem: Complete: "Votre ___ de téléphone, s'il vous plaît ?"
questions.explanation: Le numéro is a number that labels something: a phone, a house, a room. L'adresse is an address, le nom a name, and ans are years.

questions.stem: You give your e-mail address. How do you say "@"?
questions.explanation: @ is arobase. Point is the dot (.), tiret the hyphen (-), and accent a written accent.

questions.stem: Read Tom's form: "Nom : WRIGHT — Prénom : Tom — Âge : 34 ans — Téléphone : 07 15 92 36 80". How does Tom say the third pair of his phone number?
questions.explanation: The third pair is 92 = 4 × 20 + 12: quatre-vingt-douze. Pairs are read as one number, not digit by digit. Quatre-vingt-deux is 82 and soixante-douze is 72.

questions.stem: What number is "seize"?
questions.explanation: seize = 16. Six is 6, soixante 60 and sept 7. Remember the -ze family: onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize (11–16).

questions.stem: Read this phone number the French way: pick the words for each numbered pair.

image.alt: A French mobile number in five boxes: 06, 12, 45, 78 and 97, with a number under each box: 1 under 06, 2 under 12, 3 under 45, 4 under 78 and 5 under 97.

questions.explanation: 06 = zéro six, 12 = douze, 45 = quarante-cinq, 78 = 60 + 18 = soixante-dix-huit, 97 = 80 + 17 = quatre-vingt-dix-sept. Soixante-huit is 68 and quatre-vingt-sept is 87.

questions.stem: Write 80 in letters.
questions.explanation: 80 = 4 × 20 = quatre-vingts, with an s because nothing follows (quatre-vingt-un loses it).

questions.stem: You hear "soixante-dix-huit". Write the number in digits. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: soixante (60) + dix-huit (18) = 78. Think "sixty-something", then add 10 to 19.

questions.stem: Put these numbers in order, from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: seize (16), soixante (60), soixante-dix-sept (77), quatre-vingts (80), quatre-vingt-onze (91).

questions.stem: Which of these are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 21 and 71 take et (vingt et un, soixante et onze); 80 is quatre-vingts. 81 has no et (quatre-vingt-un), and 90 is quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10).

questions.stem: Match each number to its French name.
questions.explanation: 17 = dix-sept (10 + 7), 60 = soixante, 70 = soixante-dix (60 + 10), 90 = quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10). Soixante-sept is 67.

questions.stem: In which phrase is the liaison compulsory?
questions.explanation: A pronoun and its verb always link: vous êtes is "voo-ZET". A liaison is forbidden after et, after a singular noun (étudiant | anglais) and before an aspirated h (les | héros).

questions.stem: Why is there no liaison in "les héros"?
choices: héros starts with an aspirated h
the liaison is only optional and people skip it
questions.explanation: The h of héros is aspirated: silent, but it blocks elision and liaison. With a liaison, les héros would sound like les zéros (the zeros). After les, a liaison is normally compulsory (les amis).

questions.stem: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Haricot has an aspirated h, so le doesn't elide: le haricot, and in the plural les | haricots with no liaison. It is masculine.

questions.stem: What is the difference between liaison and enchaînement?
choices: Liaison happens before consonants; enchaînement before vowels.
They are two names for the same thing.
Liaison brings back a silent consonant; enchaînement links a consonant that is always said.
Liaison is spoken; enchaînement is only written.
questions.explanation: In les amis, the s is silent on its own and only appears in the liaison. In il est, the l of il is always pronounced and simply slides into the next syllable: "ee-LEH". That's enchaînement.

questions.stem: How is "petit" often said in everyday speech?
questions.explanation: The mute e of petit is often dropped in everyday speech: "ptee". It is always kept in writing. The final t is silent, and the stress is on the last syllable.

questions.stem: Why does "vendredi" (Friday) keep its mute e in speech, while "samedi" often loses it?
choices: Dropping it in vendredi would put three consonants together.
The e in vendredi has an accent.
Days of the week never lose an e.
questions.explanation: The mute e usually drops when only one consonant comes before it (sam-di), and stays when dropping it would crush three consonants together ("vahndrdi" is unsayable), so vendredi stays "vahn-druh-DEE".

questions.stem: How does the voice usually move at the end of "Tu es français ?" asked as a question?
choices: It rises on tu and falls at the end.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question asked with the voice alone rises at the end; the rise is what turns the statement Tu es français. into a question.

questions.stem: Which pair of words differs only in an open or closed vowel?
questions.explanation: Et has a closed "ay" (é), est an open "eh" (è). Tu / tout differ in u and ou, bon / bonne in a nasal vowel, and vin / vent in two different nasal vowels.

questions.stem: In "neuf heures" (nine o'clock), how is the f pronounced?
questions.explanation: Neuf becomes "neuv" before ans and heures: "neuh-VEUR". In liaison, d becomes t and s/x become z, but f becomes v only in these fixed cases.

questions.stem: In which phrases is the liaison forbidden? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: No liaison after et, before onze, or after a singular noun. Nous avons (pronoun + verb) and les hôtels (determiner + noun, mute h) are compulsory liaisons.

questions.stem: Sort each liaison into its group.
questions.explanation: Determiner + noun (mon_ami) and pronoun + verb (ils_ont) are compulsory. After et and before an aspirated h (les | héros), liaison is forbidden. After a verb (c'est_un ami) it is optional.

questions.stem: Write "the hero" in French (aspirated h): ___
questions.explanation: Le héros: the aspirated h blocks elision, so le keeps its e. Compare the feminine l'héroïne, which has a mute h.

questions.stem: Match each word to the pronunciation term it shows best.
questions.explanation: Les amis brings back the silent s (liaison); il est slides a pronounced l into est (enchaînement); sam'di drops the mute e; le haricot keeps le because of the aspirated h.

questions.stem: Daniel writes: "Les liaisons, ça va : « les amis », « vous êtes »… Mais « un étudiant anglais », c'est une liaison interdite." Is he right about "un étudiant anglais"?
choices: Partly: un_étudiant is compulsory, but étudiant | anglais is forbidden.
Yes: there is no liaison anywhere in it.
No: every liaison in it is compulsory.
No: every liaison in it is optional.
questions.explanation: un + étudiant is determiner + noun, so the liaison is compulsory ("uh-nay-tü-DYAHN"). Between étudiant and anglais, after a singular noun, it is forbidden.

questions.stem: Complete: "Awa habite ___ Sénégal."
questions.explanation: Le Sénégal is masculine (it doesn't end in -e), so: au Sénégal. En is for feminine countries such as la Côte d'Ivoire.

questions.stem: Marc lives in Québec City, not just somewhere in the province. Which sentence says so?
questions.explanation: The city has no article and takes à: à Québec. The province is le Québec, so au Québec means "in the province of Québec".

questions.stem: Which is the usual way to say "in Haiti"?
questions.explanation: En Haïti has become the usual form; à Haïti (as for islands) is also correct. The h is mute: d'Haïti.

questions.stem: A Belgian friend says "septante-cinq". What number is it?
questions.explanation: Septante is 70 in Belgium and Switzerland, so septante-cinq = 75 (soixante-quinze in France).

questions.stem: Where would you hear "huitante" for 80?
questions.explanation: Huitante is used in the Swiss cantons of Vaud, Valais and Fribourg. Belgium, Québec and France say quatre-vingts.

questions.stem: A friend in Montréal invites you "pour dîner". When should you come?
choices: late at night, after a show
questions.explanation: In Québec (and in Belgium and Switzerland), le dîner is the midday meal; the evening meal is le souper. In France, dîner is the evening meal.

questions.stem: What does "Bonne fin de semaine !" mean in Québec?
choices: Have a good end of the week at work!
questions.explanation: La fin de semaine is Québec's word for the weekend; France says Bon week-end ! Have a good evening is Bonne soirée !

questions.stem: What is la Francophonie, with a capital F?
choices: an international organization of states and governments that share French
the French spoken in France only
the official language office of Québec
questions.explanation: With a capital F it is the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF). With a small f, la francophonie is all the people and places that speak French. Québec's language office is the OQLF.

questions.stem: In which of these countries is French an official language? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: French is an official language in Belgium (with Dutch and German), Senegal and Luxembourg (with Luxembourgish and German). Spain and Germany are neighbours of France but don't have French as an official language.

questions.stem: Match each Belgian or Swiss number to the way it is said in France.
questions.explanation: septante = 70 = soixante-dix; nonante = 90 = quatre-vingt-dix; huitante = 80 = quatre-vingts; septante-deux = 72 = soixante-douze. Soixante-deux is 62.

questions.stem: Which meal is it in France? Match each Québec word.
questions.explanation: Québec (like Belgium and Switzerland): déjeuner = breakfast, dîner = lunch, souper = dinner. In France: petit-déjeuner, déjeuner, dîner. (Le goûter is a children's afternoon snack in France.)

questions.stem: A Swiss friend says "nonante-huit". Write the number in digits. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Nonante (90) + huit = 98. In France: quatre-vingt-dix-huit.

questions.stem: Complete with the right little word: "Kofi habite ___ Côte d'Ivoire."
questions.explanation: La Côte d'Ivoire is feminine, so en Côte d'Ivoire, with no article.

questions.stem: Read: "Je suis belge et j'habite à Bruxelles. Ma mère est suisse, de Lausanne. Chez nous, on dit « septante » et « nonante », mais ma mère dit aussi « huitante »." (ma mère = my mother, chez nous = at home, on dit = we say) Which statement is true?
choices: Élise's mother uses a word for 80 that Belgians don't use.
questions.explanation: Huitante (80) is used in parts of Switzerland, including Lausanne, but not in Belgium. Élise is Belgian, lives in Brussels, and says septante at home.

questions.stem: How do you say 3 × 4 = 12 in French?
choices: Trois divisé par quatre égale douze.
questions.explanation: Fois means times (×). Plus is +, moins is −, and divisé par is ÷.

questions.stem: What does "Cent moins neuf, ça fait quatre-vingt-onze" mean?
questions.explanation: Moins is minus and ça fait means "that makes". Quatre-vingt-onze = 80 + 11 = 91.

questions.stem: Where does the name of the Paris hospital "les Quinze-Vingts" come from?
choices: It was founded for 300 blind people: 15 × 20.
It had fifteen doctors and twenty nurses.
It is at number 15, rue de Vingt.
questions.explanation: Founded by Louis IX around 1260 as a home for 300 blind people, it was named in the old way of counting in twenties: quinze-vingts, fifteen twenties.

questions.stem: A French student says: "J'ai quatorze sur vingt." How did she do?
choices: Perfectly: it is the top mark.
questions.explanation: Marks are out of 20 and the pass mark (la moyenne) is 10, so 14 is good (at the bac it would earn the distinction bien). 20/20 is rare.

questions.stem: Why do French people cross their 7?
choices: to mark it as a phone digit
so it is not mistaken for their 1, which has a long upstroke
to show it is a lucky number
questions.explanation: The French handwritten 1 has a long sloping upstroke, so an uncrossed 7 could be read as a 1. The bar keeps them apart.

questions.stem: Complete: "Un numéro de téléphone français a dix ___."
questions.explanation: Un chiffre is a single digit, 0 to 9. Un nombre is a number as a quantity, un numéro labels something (a phone, a room), and une note is a school mark.

questions.stem: You hear "zéro sept, soixante-quatorze…" and write "07 6". What went wrong?
choices: You wrote too early: soixante-quatorze is 74.
questions.explanation: Soixante could start anything from 60 to 79. Wait for the end of the pair: soixante-quatorze = 60 + 14 = 74.

questions.stem: Write the answer in French words: "Quatre fois vingt égale ___."
questions.explanation: 4 × 20 = 80 = quatre-vingts, with an s because nothing follows. The French name of 80 is this very sum.

questions.stem: You hear "quatre-vingt-seize". Write the number in digits. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: quatre-vingt (80) + seize (16) = 96. Don't write 8 and 6 after the first word: wait for the whole pair.

questions.stem: Which digit is it, and in which style? Pick a label for each numbered digit.

image.alt: Four handwritten digits in two boxes. In the left box, digit 1 has a long sloping upstroke and a short base, and digit 2 is a 7 with a bar across the middle. In the right box, digit 3 is a single straight line and digit 4 is a 7 with no bar.

questions.explanation: The French 1 (1) has a long upstroke, and the French 7 (2) is crossed so it can't be taken for that 1. The typical American 1 (3) is a plain line, and the American 7 (4) has no bar.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the history of French counting in order, oldest first.
choices: Counting in twenties is common (deux vins = 40).
The Quinze-Vingts hospital is founded for 300 blind people.
Grammarians fix soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix as standard.
questions.explanation: In the Middle Ages twenties were common; the Quinze-Vingts dates from around 1260; the standard forms were settled in the 17th century.

questions.stem: Which of these marks out of 20 are below the pass mark? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: La moyenne (the pass mark) is 10 out of 20, so 8, 9.5 and 6 are below it; 10 and 12 pass. (French writes 9.5 as 9,5.)

questions.stem: Match each sign to its French word.
questions.explanation: + plus ("plüss"), − moins, × fois, ÷ divisé par. Un chiffre is a digit.

questions.stem: Read: "Le père : Et ta note en maths, c'est combien ? — Chloé : Dix-huit sur vingt ! — Le père : C'est génial !" Why is her father so pleased?
choices: 18/20 is an excellent mark in France.
Chloé has just passed, with exactly the pass mark.
questions.explanation: Dix-huit sur vingt is 18 out of 20, an excellent mark (16 or more is excellent; 20/20 is rare). The pass mark is 10, and Chloé is nine.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "livre" (book)?
questions.explanation: Livre is masculine: le livre. It ends in -e, which tempts many learners to choose la, but -e is only a weak hint. Learn every noun with its article.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ordinateur est sur la table."
questions.explanation: Before a vowel or mute h, le and la both shorten to l': l'ordinateur. "Le ordinateur" is never written. Les would need a plural verb (sont) and noun (ordinateurs).

questions.stem: What is the plural of "le bureau" (office)?
questions.explanation: Nouns in -eau add -x, not -s: les bureaux. The article changes too: le becomes les. The -x is silent, so you hear the plural only in the article.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "There are two chairs in the kitchen"?
choices: Il est deux chaises dans la cuisine.
Là sont deux chaises dans la cuisine.
Il y a deux chaises dans la cuisine.
Ils sont deux chaise dans la cuisine.
questions.explanation: "There is" and "there are" are both il y a, which never changes. A word-for-word "il est" or "là sont" doesn't work, and chaise needs its plural -s after deux.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il y a ___ livres sur la table."
questions.explanation: Livres is plural, and "a" has a plural in French: des. English says just "There are books", but French can't leave the article out. Un and une are singular.

questions.stem: Look at the picture. Where is the bag?

image.alt: A table with a book on it, a cat under it, a chair behind it, and a bag standing on the floor in front of it with a phone in the bag.

questions.explanation: The bag stands on the floor in front of the table, partly hiding a table leg: devant la table. The cat is under the table (sous), the book on it (sur) and the chair behind it (derrière). Il stands for le sac, which is masculine.

questions.stem: Complete the answer: "Où est la clé ? — ___ est dans le sac."
questions.explanation: For a thing already named, "it" is il for a masculine noun and elle for a feminine one. La clé is feminine, so: Elle est dans le sac. C'est is for saying what something is, not where.

questions.stem: Which noun is feminine?
questions.explanation: It is la fenêtre. The others are le téléphone, le lit and le stylo. Téléphone ends in -e like fenêtre, so the ending alone can't tell you: learn the article.

questions.stem: Read the note: "Salut Nora ! La clé est sous le livre, sur la table de la cuisine. Les sacs sont dans la chambre. Thomas" Where is the key?
questions.explanation: "La clé est sous le livre": the key is under the book, and the book is on the kitchen table. The bags (les sacs) are in the bedroom.

questions.stem: You hear "lay livres" in a shop. How do you know it means several books?
choices: You hear the -s at the end of livres.
The article sounds different: les (lay), not le (luh).
The verb is always plural after a noun.
You can't: it only shows in writing.
questions.explanation: The plural -s is silent, so livre and livres sound the same. The article carries the number you hear: le (one) sounds like "luh", les (several) like "lay".

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Before a vowel the article shortens: l'appartement (masculine, un appartement). The other three are correct: une chaise, un ordinateur (un never shortens), ce sont + a plural.

questions.stem: How do you say "The key is there"?
questions.explanation: The article la (the) has no accent; the adverb là (there) has a grave accent. So: La clé est là.

questions.stem: What does "La chaise est derrière la porte" mean?
choices: The chair is behind the door.
The chair is in front of the door.
The chair is next to the door.
The chair is under the door.
questions.explanation: Derrière means behind (think "der-" = rear). In front of is devant, under is sous.

questions.stem: Write the article: ___ chaise (the), ___ lit (a), ___ ordinateur (the).
questions.explanation: la chaise is feminine; le lit is masculine, so "a bed" is un lit; ordinateur starts with a vowel, so "the" is l' (l'ordinateur).

questions.stem: Name the numbered rooms and things in this flat, with their articles.

image.alt: The floor plan of a small flat with four rooms. Top left a kitchen with a table and two chairs; top right a bedroom with a bed; bottom left a living room with a sofa, a window and the front door; bottom right a bathroom with a bath. Six places are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the kitchen (la cuisine), 2 the bedroom (la chambre), 3 the living room (le salon), 4 the bathroom (la salle de bains), 5 the bed (le lit) and 6 the kitchen table (la table). La maison is the whole house, and there's no bag in the picture.

questions.stem: Where is each numbered thing? Choose the place for each one.

image.alt: A table with five numbered things: a book on the table, a chair behind it, a cat under it, a bag on the floor in front of it, and a phone sticking out of the bag.

questions.explanation: The book (1) is on the table: sur. The chair (2) is behind it: derrière. The cat (3) is under it: sous. The bag (4) is in front of it: devant. The phone (5) is in the bag: dans le sac.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Il y a des livres sur le lit.
questions.explanation: Il y a des livres, Ce sont des clés and L'appartement est ici are all correct. Ordinateur is masculine (un ordinateur), and after deux the noun needs its plural -s: deux chambres.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "There are books under the bed." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: Il y a stays together as one unit, then the noun with its article (des livres), then the place: sous le lit.

questions.stem: Match each noun to its plural.
questions.explanation: Most nouns add a silent -s (livres). Nouns in -eau add -x (bureaux), nouns in -al change to -aux (journaux), and nouns already ending in -s don't change (cours).

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ deux enfants."
questions.explanation: The nous form of avoir is avons: nous avons. Sommes is from être (we are), avez goes with vous and ont with ils/elles.

questions.stem: Complete: "Julie et ___ père habitent à Nice." (her father)
questions.explanation: The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not the owner. Père is masculine, so it's son père, even though Julie is a woman. Sa is for a feminine noun (sa mère).

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul et ___ mère sont à Lyon." (his mother)
questions.explanation: Mère is feminine, so it's sa mère, even though Paul is a man. French son/sa doesn't show whether the owner is male or female; the noun decides.

questions.stem: Complete: "C'est ___ amie Sophie." (my)
questions.explanation: Amie is feminine, but it starts with a vowel, so ma becomes mon: mon amie (mo-na-mee). Ma never shortens to m'.

questions.stem: Which one means "they have"?
questions.explanation: Ils ont (with a z sound: eel-ZON) means "they have". Ils sont (with an s sound) means "they are". Ils a and ils avons mix up the persons.

questions.stem: Complete: "Marc et Sophie ont un fils. ___ fils s'appelle Hugo." (their son)
questions.explanation: Two owners (Marc and Sophie) and one son: leur fils. Leurs is only for several things (leurs enfants). Fils ends in -s but is singular here: un fils.

questions.stem: In "Il y a une fille de dix ans dans le salon", what does "fille" mean?
questions.explanation: La fille means both "daughter" and "girl". With a possessive (ma fille) or a parent (la fille de Marc) it is "daughter"; here nobody's daughter is meant, just a ten-year-old girl in the living room.

questions.stem: Read: "Je m'appelle Karim. Ma femme s'appelle Nadia. Nous avons deux enfants : un fils, Adam, et une fille, Lina. Nous avons aussi un chat." Who is Lina?
questions.explanation: "Nous avons deux enfants : un fils, Adam, et une fille, Lina": Lina is one of the two children, so she is Karim's daughter. His wife is Nadia.

questions.stem: Your friend points at a photo: "Qui est-ce ?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: To say who someone is with a noun and a possessive, use c'est: C'est ma sœur. Il/elle est goes with adjectives, sœur is feminine (ma), and ce sont is for several people.

questions.stem: You're talking to a friend you call "tu". How do you say "your parents"?
questions.explanation: With tu the possessives are ton/ta/tes, and parents is plural: tes parents. Vos goes with vous (formal or several people).

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: French gives age with avoir: J'ai trente ans. "Je suis trente ans" is a word-for-word copy of English "I am thirty".

questions.stem: How is "le fils" (son) pronounced?
choices: like "feess": the l is silent, the s is spoken
questions.explanation: Fils is said "feess": a rare word where the final s is spoken and the l is silent. Fille (daughter) is "fee-y".

questions.stem: Which is correct for "their daughters"?
questions.explanation: Leur takes -s when there are several things: leurs filles. Ses means his or her, not their.

questions.stem: This is Léa's family tree. Name each numbered person from Léa's point of view ("moi").

image.alt: A family tree with first names only. Top row: Pierre and Monique. Middle row: their son Marc and his wife Sophie. Bottom row: their children Hugo, Léa (moi) and Chloé, and the dog Max. Six people are numbered.

questions.explanation: Pierre and Monique are the parents of Léa's father, so they are her grand-père and grand-mère. Marc and Sophie are her père and mère; Hugo and Chloé are her frère and sœur. From Marc's point of view Léa would be sa fille, but the question asks from Léa's.

questions.stem: Write the correct form of avoir: "Tu ___ un chien ?" "Ils ___ trois enfants."
questions.explanation: avoir: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. Ils ont has a z sound (eel-ZON); don't confuse it with ils sont (they are).

questions.stem: Match each pronoun to its possessive before a masculine noun (… père).
questions.explanation: mon père, ton père, son père, notre père, votre père, leur père. Sa is the feminine form (sa mère) and nos the plural of notre (nos parents).

questions.stem: Which words can mean "her" (as in "her brother", "her bag")? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Son, sa and ses all mean "his" or "her": son frère can be her brother, sa clé her key, ses parents her parents. Leur means their, and mon means my.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "My parents have a dog." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: Subject (mes parents), verb (ont, the ils form of avoir), object (un chien). Parents is plural, so mes and ont.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ français." (parler)
questions.explanation: The nous ending of -er verbs is -ons: nous parlons. -ez goes with vous, -ent with ils/elles, -e with je and il/elle.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mes parents ___ beaucoup." (travailler)
questions.explanation: Mes parents = ils, so the ending is -ent: ils travaillent. It sounds exactly like il travaille, because -ent is silent, but it must be written.

questions.stem: Which form sounds different from the other three?
questions.explanation: Parle, parles and parlent are all said "parl": -e, -es and -ent are silent. Vous parlez ends in a sound you can hear (par-LAY).

questions.stem: How do you say "She is a doctor"?
questions.explanation: After être, a job takes no article: Elle est médecin. With c'est you need one: C'est un médecin. "Elle est le médecin" means "she is the doctor" (a particular one).

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm studying French"?
questions.explanation: Je becomes j' before a vowel, the je ending is -e, and language names take a small letter: J'étudie le français. With étudier the language keeps its article.

questions.stem: Complete: "Tu parles ___ ?" (English)
questions.explanation: Language names are masculine and written with a small letter, and after parler the article is usually left out: Tu parles anglais ? Anglaise is the feminine adjective (une amie anglaise).

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm looking for my key"?
questions.explanation: Chercher already means "to look for", so no extra word: Je cherche ma clé. The je form ends in -e, not -es.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'aime ___." (to dance)
questions.explanation: After aimer, adorer and détester, a second verb stays in the infinitive: J'aime danser (I like dancing). Only the first verb is conjugated.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'adore ___ chocolat."
questions.explanation: For likes and dislikes, French uses le, la, les for things in general: J'adore le chocolat. English says "I love chocolate" with no article, but French needs one.

questions.stem: Read: "Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Inès. Je suis infirmière à Lille. Je parle français et arabe, et j'étudie l'anglais. Le soir, j'écoute de la musique et je chante. Je déteste regarder la télé." What does Inès hate?
questions.explanation: "Je déteste regarder la télé": she hates watching TV. She sings in the evening, studies English and says nothing bad about her job (infirmière, nurse).

questions.stem: In which phrase do you hear a z sound between the two words?
questions.explanation: The s of ils is silent before a consonant but links as a z before a vowel: ils_écoutent (eel-zé-KOOT). In the others, ils is just "eel".

questions.stem: What does "J'aime bien Paul" mean?
questions.explanation: With a person, aimer means to love; aimer bien softens it to "like". So J'aime bien Paul = I like Paul (as a friend).

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: After être a job takes no article: Elle est infirmière. With c'est the article is needed, so "C'est un ingénieur" is right.

questions.stem: Write the correct present-tense forms: "Vous ___ (parler) anglais ?" "Nous ___ (étudier) le français."
questions.explanation: Vous takes -ez: vous parlez. Nous takes -ons on the stem étudi-: nous étudions (the i of the stem stays).

questions.stem: Name the numbered people and thing.

image.alt: Five numbered pictures: a person in a white coat with a stethoscope, a person pointing at a board with letters, a person in a hard hat holding a plan, a person with a backpack and a pile of books, and an office desk with a computer.

questions.explanation: 1 is a doctor (stethoscope): le médecin. 2 is a teacher at a board: le professeur. 3 is an engineer with a hard hat and a plan: l'ingénieur. 4 is a student with books and a backpack: l'étudiant. 5 is a desk in an office: le bureau (the same word means desk and office).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first three are right. After être a job has no article (Elle est étudiante), and chercher already means "to look for", so no pour: Nous cherchons la clé.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "We speak a little Spanish." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: Un peu (a little) goes straight after the verb, and parler takes the language without an article: Nous parlons un peu espagnol.

questions.stem: Match each subject pronoun to the ending of a regular -er verb in the present.
questions.explanation: je parle, tu parles, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent (il/elle also takes -e). -ont is the ending of ils ont and ils sont, not of -er verbs.

questions.stem: Complete: "une maison ___" (white)
questions.explanation: Maison is feminine singular, and blanc has an irregular feminine: blanche. Blance doesn't exist, and blanches is plural.

questions.stem: Which is the usual way to say "a small house"?
questions.explanation: Petit is one of the BAGS adjectives (size), which go before the noun, and it agrees with maison (feminine): une petite maison.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'habite dans un ___ appartement." (new)
questions.explanation: Appartement is masculine and starts with a vowel, so nouveau becomes nouvel: un nouvel appartement. Likewise un bel appartement, un vieil appartement.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ma sœur est très ___." (happy)
questions.explanation: Adjectives in -eux make their feminine in -euse: heureux → heureuse. Heureuses would be feminine plural.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'ai trois sacs ___." (brown)
questions.explanation: Marron is invariable: it never takes -e or -s. Trois sacs marron. (It means "chestnut", and colours named after things usually don't change.)

questions.stem: Complete: "Les gens ici sont très ___." (kind)
questions.explanation: Les gens is always plural and takes masculine plural adjectives: gentils.

questions.stem: How do you say "a red door"?
questions.explanation: Colours always go after the noun: une porte rouge. Porte is feminine (une), and rouge already ends in -e, so it doesn't change in the feminine singular.

questions.stem: Your friend says about a hotel room: "La chambre est trop petite." What does she mean?
choices: The room is very small, and that's nice.
The room is too small: it's a problem.
questions.explanation: Trop means "too": it's a complaint. Very is très, quite is assez.

questions.stem: Read the ad: "Appartement à Nantes : grand salon, deux petites chambres, cuisine jaune, salle de bains blanche. Les voisins sont sympas !" What is small?
questions.explanation: "deux petites chambres": the two bedrooms are small. The living room is big (grand salon), the kitchen yellow and the bathroom white.

questions.stem: Which adjective normally goes before the noun?
questions.explanation: Jeune is a BAGS adjective (age), so it goes before: un jeune homme. Intéressant, rouge and facile go after: un livre intéressant, un sac rouge, une langue facile.

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul et Julie sont ___." (tall)
questions.explanation: A mixed group (a man and a woman) takes the masculine plural: grands. Grandes would be for two women.

questions.stem: Complete: "C'est un ___ homme." (handsome)
questions.explanation: Homme is masculine and starts with a mute h, so beau becomes bel: un bel homme. Bel sounds like belle, but belle is for feminine nouns.

questions.stem: Which phrase contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Porte is feminine, so it's une vieille porte. Vieil is right before a masculine vowel noun (un vieil homme), and vieux before a masculine consonant (un vieux lit).

questions.stem: What does "Le français est assez facile" mean?
questions.explanation: Assez before an adjective means "quite" or "fairly". Too is trop, very is très.

questions.stem: Name the colour of each numbered square.

image.alt: Nine colour squares in three rows. Top row: red, blue, green. Middle row: yellow, black, white. Bottom row: grey, brown, pink. Six of them are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 rouge (red), 2 vert (green), 3 jaune (yellow), 4 noir (black), 5 marron (brown), 6 rose (pink). The squares without numbers are bleu (blue), blanc (white) and gris (grey).

questions.stem: Write the feminine: un homme heureux → une femme ___; un sac blanc → une porte ___.
questions.explanation: -eux becomes -euse (heureuse), and blanc has the irregular feminine blanche.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its feminine form.
questions.explanation: bon doubles the n (bonne) and gentil the l (gentille); blanc becomes blanche; vieux and nouveau have special feminines, vieille and nouvelle.

questions.stem: Which adjectives normally go before the noun? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Petit (size), bon (good) and vieux (age) are BAGS adjectives, which go before the noun. Colours (rouge), long adjectives like intéressant and nationalities (français) go after.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "a small white house".
questions.explanation: Petite is a BAGS adjective and goes before the noun; blanche is a colour and goes after: une petite maison blanche.

questions.stem: All four nouns end in -age. Which one is masculine?
questions.explanation: Le fromage follows the rule: -age nouns are masculine. La page, la plage and l'image (une image) are the famous feminine exceptions.

questions.stem: Which ending is the most reliable sign of a feminine noun?
questions.explanation: Nouns in -tion are almost always feminine (la solution, la question). -ment, -age and -isme point to masculine.

questions.stem: You meet the word "gouvernement" (government) for the first time. What is its most likely gender?
questions.explanation: -ment is a strong masculine ending: le gouvernement, le bâtiment, le moment. A final -e on its own is only a weak hint.

questions.stem: Which noun is an exception to the rule for its ending?
questions.explanation: Most nouns in -ée are feminine (l'idée, l'année, l'entrée), but le musée and le lycée are masculine. The other three follow their rules.

questions.stem: Complete: "L'eau est ___." (cold: froid)
questions.explanation: L'eau is feminine, the big exception among -eau nouns, so the adjective takes -e: l'eau est froide.

questions.stem: What is the feminine of "l'acteur" (actor)?
questions.explanation: Nouns in -teur usually make their feminine in -trice: acteur → actrice, directeur → directrice.

questions.stem: What is the feminine of "le chanteur" (singer)?
questions.explanation: Chanteur comes from the verb chanter, and nouns in -eur made from a verb you can recognise take -euse: la chanteuse (like le serveur, la serveuse).

questions.stem: In France today, how do you most often write that a woman is a teacher (professeur)?
questions.explanation: Professeur has no everyday verb behind it, so its feminine adds -e: professeure, which is now standard in France. After être there is no article. Professeuse and professrice don't exist. (You'll also hear Elle est prof.)

questions.stem: Which statement about feminine job titles is accurate?
choices: The Académie française still forbids them.
Feminine titles such as la ministre are normal in France, and the Académie française accepted them in 2019.
They are only used in Québec.
Every masculine job title now has exactly one official feminine.
questions.explanation: Québec recommended feminine titles in 1979, France's government in 1986 and 1998, and the Académie française adopted a report accepting them on 28 February 2019. Some forms still compete, such as auteure and autrice.

questions.stem: A woman writes novels. Which word for "author" is correct?
questions.explanation: Both feminine forms are used today. Auteure was the more frequent when the Académie reported in 2019; autrice, which follows the -teur → -trice pattern, has been gaining ground. This is a point where usage varies.

questions.stem: Read: "La directrice de l'école s'appelle Madame Roux. Son mari est acteur et sa fille est chanteuse." Who sings?
questions.explanation: "sa fille est chanteuse": her daughter is a singer. Madame Roux is the head of the school (la directrice), and her husband is an actor.

questions.stem: Which nouns are feminine? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: la liberté (-té), la voiture (-ure) and l'idée (-ée) are feminine. Le problème is masculine despite its -e, and le bâtiment has the masculine ending -ment.

questions.stem: Match each masculine job title to its feminine.
questions.explanation: -teur → -trice (directrice), -eur from a verb → -euse (chanteuse), -ier → -ière (infirmière), -ien → -ienne (musicienne), and words in -e change only the article (la journaliste).

questions.stem: Write "the" for each noun: ___ plage (beach), ___ fromage (cheese), ___ tourisme (tourism).
questions.explanation: la plage is one of the feminine -age exceptions; le fromage follows the masculine -age rule; le tourisme has the masculine ending -isme.

questions.stem: Sort the endings: which gender does each one usually point to?
questions.explanation: -té and -ette point to feminine (la liberté, la baguette); -ment, -eau and -isme to masculine (le bâtiment, le bureau, le tourisme). Remember the exceptions l'été and l'eau.

questions.stem: Write the feminine job titles: l'acteur → l'___; le directeur → la ___.
questions.explanation: Both end in -teur, so both take -trice: l'actrice, la directrice.

questions.stem: How do you say "She has blue eyes"?
questions.explanation: French uses avoir + les + noun + adjective: Elle a les yeux bleus. Colours go after the noun and agree with yeux (masculine plural).

questions.stem: How do you say "He has red hair"?
questions.explanation: Red hair is roux, never rouge, and hair is plural: les cheveux. Roux already ends in -x, so the masculine plural doesn't change.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ma sœur est très ___." (sporty)
questions.explanation: Adjectives in -if make their feminine in -ive: sportif → sportive, actif → active.

questions.stem: What is the feminine of "roux" (red-haired)?
questions.explanation: Roux becomes rousse with a double s: Elle est rousse.

questions.stem: What does "mon ancien professeur" mean?
questions.explanation: Before the noun, ancien means "former": the teacher you used to have. After the noun it means old or antique: une maison ancienne.

questions.stem: What does "un homme grand" mean?
questions.explanation: After the noun, grand has its literal meaning: tall. Before the noun, un grand homme is a great man.

questions.stem: What does "un restaurant cher" mean?
questions.explanation: After the noun, cher means expensive. Before the noun it means dear: mon cher ami.

questions.stem: Complete: "C'est une couleur ___." (natural: naturel)
questions.explanation: Adjectives in -el double the l before -e: naturel → naturelle, like culturel → culturelle.

questions.stem: Read: "À gauche, c'est mon grand-père. Il a les cheveux gris, une barbe et des lunettes. À côté de lui, c'est ma mère. Elle a les cheveux longs et frisés." Who has curly hair? (à gauche = on the left)
questions.explanation: "Elle a les cheveux longs et frisés" is about the mother. The grandfather has grey hair, a beard and glasses.

questions.stem: What does "Elle est brune" mean?
questions.explanation: Être + brun describes hair colour: dark brown or black hair. Brown eyes are les yeux marron.

questions.stem: Name the numbered features in this family photo.

image.alt: A family photo of five people: a grandfather with grey hair, a beard and glasses; a mother with long curly brown hair; a father with short dark hair; a girl with red hair in a ponytail; and a small boy with short blond hair. Six features are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the grandfather's beard (la barbe) and 2 his glasses (les lunettes). 3 is the mother's long curly hair, 4 the father's short dark hair, 5 the girl's red hair (roux, not rouge) and 6 the boy's blond hair.

questions.stem: Write the feminine: un bébé mignon → une fille ___; un ancien professeur → une ___ école.
questions.explanation: -on becomes -onne (mignonne) and -en becomes -enne (ancienne): the doubled n shows that the vowel is no longer nasal.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its feminine form.
questions.explanation: -if → -ive, -er → -ère, -on → -onne, -eux → -euse, and roux → rousse with a double s.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Cheveux is masculine plural, so it needs longs, not longue; marron never changes (les yeux marron). Paul et Léa takes the masculine plural (sportifs), and rousse is the feminine of roux.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "She's a very funny woman." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: C'est + a noun with its article; drôle (funny) goes after the noun, with très in front of it: C'est une femme très drôle.

questions.stem: Complete: "Le matin, je mange ___ pain." (le pain)
questions.explanation: You're eating an amount of bread, so you need the partitive, and pain is masculine: du pain. "de la" is for feminine nouns, "de l'" for nouns starting with a vowel, and "des" for plurals.

questions.stem: Complete: "Elle boit ___ eau." (l'eau)
questions.explanation: Eau starts with a vowel, so the partitive is de l': Elle boit de l'eau. Eau is feminine, but "de la eau" is never written: before a vowel, la and le both become l'. "du eau" is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'adore ___ chocolat." (I love chocolate.)
questions.explanation: After verbs of liking and disliking (aimer, adorer, détester) you talk about a food in general, so French uses the definite article: J'adore le chocolat. "du chocolat" is for an amount you eat or buy (Je mange du chocolat).

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ du poisson le vendredi." (manger)
questions.explanation: The nous form of manger keeps an e after the g: nous mangeons. Without it, "mangons" would be read with a hard g. "mangez" is the vous form and "mangent" the ils/elles form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les enfants ___ du lait." (boire)
questions.explanation: boire is irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent. "buvent" mixes the nous/vous stem buv- with the ils ending, and "boit" is the il/elle form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Vous ___ du thé ou du café ?" (boire)
questions.explanation: nous and vous use the stem buv-: nous buvons, vous buvez. "boivez" uses the ils stem (boivent), and "boit" is the il/elle form.

questions.stem: What does "Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît" mean?
questions.explanation: Je voudrais means "I would like": it's the polite way to order. Un café is one cup of coffee. "I like coffee" would be J'aime le café.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Bière is feminine, so "some beer" is de la bière. "J'aime du fromage" needs le after aimer (J'aime le fromage), "Je mange fromage" has no article (du fromage), and "du eau" should be de l'eau.

questions.stem: Read: "Le matin, Paul boit un café et mange du pain avec du beurre. À midi, il mange de la viande et des légumes. Le soir, il mange un fruit et du fromage." (à midi = at noon) What does Paul eat at lunchtime?
choices: a piece of fruit and some cheese
questions.explanation: À midi (at noon, lunchtime) Paul eats de la viande et des légumes: meat and vegetables. Bread and butter is his breakfast, and fruit and cheese are his evening meal. There is no fish or pasta in the text.

questions.stem: In France, which meal is "le déjeuner"?
questions.explanation: In France le déjeuner is lunch, le petit-déjeuner is breakfast and le dîner is the evening meal. (In Belgium, Switzerland and Québec le déjeuner is breakfast, but the course uses the French of France.)

questions.stem: In a café you want one cup of coffee. Complete: "Je voudrais ___, s'il vous plaît."
questions.explanation: One cup is counted, so you say un café. "du café" means an amount of coffee in general (Je bois du café le matin), and "le café" is coffee as a category (J'aime le café).

questions.stem: In which of these is the final f of "œuf" NOT pronounced?
questions.explanation: In the singular you hear the f (un œuf). In the plural the f and s are both silent and the vowel changes: des œufs sounds like "day-ZUH".

questions.stem: Name the numbered things on this breakfast table, as you would ask for them ("some …" or "an …").

image.alt: A breakfast table with six numbered things on it, from left to right: a glass carafe of water, a white jug of milk, a cup of coffee on a saucer, a baguette on a board, a block of butter on a dish and a boiled egg in an egg cup.

questions.explanation: 1 is a carafe of water (de l'eau, because eau starts with a vowel), 2 a jug of milk (du lait), 3 a cup of coffee (du café), 4 a baguette (du pain), 5 butter (du beurre) and 6 one egg, which you count: un œuf. There is no meat or tea on the table.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of boire: "Le matin, nous ___ du thé."
questions.explanation: nous and vous use the stem buv-: nous buvons, vous buvez. The other forms use boi-: je bois, il boit, ils boivent.

questions.stem: Complete with the partitive article: "Tu manges ___ viande ?" (la viande)
questions.explanation: Viande is feminine, so "some meat" is de la viande. du is only for masculine nouns, and de l' for nouns that start with a vowel.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to the article that fills the blank.
questions.explanation: Liking verbs take the definite article (J'adore le fromage). Eating an amount takes the partitive (du fromage). An egg is counted (un œuf). Eau starts with a vowel, so the partitive is de l'eau.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Je bois du lait", "J'aime le thé" and "Il boit de l'eau" are correct. "Nous mangons" needs the e: nous mangeons. "Tu manges pain ?" has no article: Tu manges du pain ?

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "I'd like some bread, please."
questions.explanation: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît. The partitive du goes straight before the noun, and s'il vous plaît comes at the end.

questions.stem: Make this sentence negative: "Je mange de la viande."
choices: Je ne mange pas de la viande.
Je ne mange pas de viande.
Je mange ne pas de viande.
Je ne pas mange de viande.
questions.explanation: ne and pas go around the verb (ne mange pas), and after a negative de la becomes de: Je ne mange pas de viande. Keeping "de la" is the most common mistake; "ne pas" can't sit together before or after the verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il ___ aime ___ le poisson." (He doesn't like fish.)
questions.explanation: aime starts with a vowel, so ne becomes n': Il n'aime pas le poisson. le stays le after a negative, because it is fish in general. "ne aime" is never written.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ce ne pas est un livre.
questions.explanation: After être nothing changes: C'est un livre → Ce n'est pas un livre. The rule that un becomes de only applies to verbs like avoir, manger, acheter (Je n'ai pas de livre).

questions.stem: How do you say the price 3,50 €?
questions.explanation: Say the euros, the word euros, then the cents: trois euros cinquante. Prices are not read with virgule (comma). At a till you'll also hear just "trois cinquante", but never with euros at the end.

questions.stem: How do you write 200 in words?
questions.explanation: cent takes an s when it is multiplied and no other number follows it: deux cents. With a number after it, the s goes: deux cent un. (With 1990 hyphens it is deux-cents, still with s.)

questions.stem: Which number is "deux mille cinq cents"?
questions.explanation: deux mille = 2 000, cinq cents = 500, so 2 500. French writes thousands with a space: 2 500. 2 005 would be deux mille cinq.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je voudrais un kilo ___ tomates."
questions.explanation: After an amount (un kilo, une bouteille, beaucoup) French uses plain de, whatever the noun: un kilo de tomates. "des" is the mistake English speakers make, thinking of "of the".

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ du pain à la boulangerie." (acheter)
questions.explanation: acheter takes è only when the ending is silent (j'achète, ils achètent). In the nous and vous forms you hear the ending, so there is no accent: nous achetons.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'___ une bouteille d'eau." (acheter)
questions.explanation: In the je form the ending is silent, so the e becomes è: j'achète. "achètes" is the tu form.

questions.stem: A sign at the market says: "Fromage de Savoie : 22 € le kilo". How much do 500 grams cost?
questions.explanation: "22 € le kilo" means 22 euros per kilo. 500 grams is half a kilo, so it costs 11 € (onze euros).

questions.stem: At the market the seller asks "Et avec ça ?". You don't want anything else. What do you say?
questions.explanation: "Et avec ça ?" means "anything else?". C'est tout, merci (that's all, thanks) ends your order. After that you can ask C'est combien ? to pay.

questions.stem: In a shop you hear "J'ai pas de monnaie." (la monnaie = change, coins) What does it mean, and how is it written carefully?
choices: I have some change. — J'ai de la monnaie.
I never have change. — Je n'ai jamais de monnaie.
I don't have any change. — Je n'ai pas de monnaie.
I don't have the change. — Je n'ai pas la monnaie.
questions.explanation: In casual speech ne is often dropped, but pas still makes it negative: "J'ai pas de monnaie" = Je n'ai pas de monnaie, I don't have any change. Write the ne yourself.

questions.stem: How do you say "He never drinks coffee"?
choices: Il ne boit pas jamais de café.
Il ne boit jamais du café.
Il ne boit jamais de café.
questions.explanation: jamais takes the place of pas: ne + verb + jamais. Like any negative, it turns du into de: Il ne boit jamais de café. "pas jamais" doubles the negative.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things for sale at this market stall.

image.alt: A market stall with five numbered crates, each with a price sign: 1 red tomatoes at 3,20 € le kilo, 2 green apples at 2,50 € le kilo, 3 brown potatoes at 1,80 € le kilo, 4 oranges at 2,90 € le kilo, 5 a box of eggs at 3,60 € la boîte de 6.

questions.explanation: 1 tomatoes (les tomates), 2 apples (les pommes), 3 potatoes (les pommes de terre, "apples of the earth"), 4 oranges (les oranges) and 5 eggs, sold by the box of six (les œufs). There is no cheese or meat on this stall.

questions.stem: Write the price 3,20 € the way you say it: "___ euros ___"
questions.explanation: Euros first, then the word euros, then the cents without the word centimes: trois euros vingt.

questions.stem: Make the sentence negative. "J'ai du lait." → "Je n'ai pas ___ lait."
questions.explanation: After a negative, du, de la and des become de: Je n'ai pas de lait. Keeping du is the most common mistake.

questions.stem: Match each number to the way it is written in words.
questions.explanation: mille never takes an s (deux mille), and cent only keeps its s when no other number follows (deux cents, but deux cent cinquante). The distractors break those two rules.

questions.stem: Which are correct ways to ask for an amount? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: After a quantity, use plain de (d' before a vowel): un kilo de pommes, un paquet de pâtes, une boîte de tomates. So it is une bouteille d'eau, not de l'eau, and beaucoup de sucre, not du sucre.

questions.stem: Put this conversation at the bakery in order.
choices: Cliente : Bonjour ! Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: Greeting, order, "anything else?", "that's all, how much?", the price, then paying and leaving. Each line answers the one before it.

questions.stem: Which is the inversion form of "Vous avez une table ?"
questions.explanation: Inversion puts the verb before the pronoun and joins them with a hyphen: Avez-vous une table ? Without the hyphen it is misspelled, and "Est-ce vous avez" is missing que.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ il a faim ?"
questions.explanation: est-ce que becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel: Est-ce qu'il a faim ? (Is he hungry?) "Qu'est-ce qu'il a" would ask "what does he have", which doesn't fit with faim.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: parle ends in a vowel, and il starts with one, so French adds a linking t between hyphens: Parle-t-il anglais ? Only the verb and pronoun are joined, not the object.

questions.stem: Your friend asks "Tu n'as pas faim ?" You ARE hungry. What do you answer?
questions.explanation: To say yes to a negative question, French uses si: Si, j'ai faim ! "Oui" sounds wrong after a negative question, and hunger takes avoir, never être.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ boisson voulez-vous ?" (la boisson)
questions.explanation: quel agrees with its noun, and boisson is feminine singular: Quelle boisson ? "Qu'est-ce que" is followed by a subject and verb, not by a noun.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ est-ce que tu cherches ? — Mon frère."
questions.explanation: The answer is a person (mon frère), so the question word is qui: Qui est-ce que tu cherches ? "Qu'est-ce que tu cherches ?" would ask what (a thing).

questions.stem: Complete the answer: "Pourquoi tu ne manges pas ? — ___ je n'ai pas faim."
questions.explanation: The answer to pourquoi (why) begins with parce que (because). "Pour" means for, and "quand" means when.

questions.stem: In a French restaurant, what is "le menu"?
choices: a set meal at a fixed price
the list of all the dishes
questions.explanation: le menu is a fixed-price set meal (for example starter + main course). The list of all the dishes is la carte, the main course is le plat and the bill is l'addition.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm thirsty"?
questions.explanation: French says "I have thirst", with avoir and no article: J'ai soif. In the same way, J'ai faim = I'm hungry.

questions.stem: Look at the menu. Léo takes the menu du jour with a starter and a main course, and a coffee. How much does he pay?

image.alt: The Café du Marché menu card. Entrées, Plats, Desserts and Boissons with prices; café 2,00 €. Menu du jour: entrée + plat ou plat + dessert 18,50 €, entrée + plat + dessert 23,00 €.

questions.explanation: The menu du jour with entrée + plat costs 18,50 €, and a coffee from the drinks list costs 2,00 €: 18,50 + 2,00 = 20,50 € (vingt euros cinquante). 23,00 € is the three-course menu.

questions.stem: Which question means the same as "Où est-ce que tu vas ?"
questions.explanation: With inversion, the verb and pronoun swap after the question word: Où vas-tu ? The tu form is vas, with an s, and there is no linking t with tu.

questions.stem: On a French menu, what is "l'entrée"?
questions.explanation: In France l'entrée is the starter, the dish that "enters" the meal. The main course is le plat. (L'entrée also means entrance, but not on a menu.)

questions.stem: How do you call the waiter politely?
questions.explanation: Say S'il vous plaît ! or Monsieur ! / Madame !. "Garçon !" is old-fashioned and rude today, and tu (toi, viens) is too familiar with staff.

questions.stem: The headings of this menu are hidden. Name each numbered section.

image.alt: A menu card, Café du Marché, La carte, with five numbered headings hidden. 1 above salad, soup and egg mayonnaise; 2 above chicken and chips, fish of the day and pasta with cheese; 3 above chocolate cake, apple tart and a cheese plate; 4 above coffee, tea, juice, water, beer and wine; 5 at the top of a box with two set-price meals.

questions.explanation: The sections follow the order of a meal: 1 starters (les entrées), 2 main courses (les plats), 3 desserts (les desserts), 4 drinks (les boissons). Box 5, a fixed-price meal, is le menu. The whole card is la carte, and the bill (l'addition) comes at the end.

questions.stem: Turn the statement into an inversion question. "Il mange de la viande." → "___ de la viande ?"
questions.explanation: Swap the verb and the pronoun and join them with hyphens. mange ends in a vowel, so add the linking t: Mange-t-il de la viande ?

questions.stem: Complete: "___ est le plat du jour ?" (What is the dish of the day? le plat)
questions.explanation: quel + être + noun asks "what is …?", and quel agrees with plat (masculine singular): Quel est le plat du jour ? For a feminine noun: Quelle est votre adresse ?

questions.stem: Match each question word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: où = where, quand = when, pourquoi = why, comment = how, qui = who. "Which" is quel, and "how much" is combien.

questions.stem: Put these lines from a restaurant visit in order.
choices: Bonjour, vous avez une table pour deux ?
Oui, voilà. Et voici la carte.
Oui. Pour moi, le menu du jour.
questions.explanation: You ask for a table, the waiter gives you the menu card, asks if you've chosen, you order, and at the end you ask for the bill. (voici = here is)

questions.stem: Which are correct ways to ask "Do you speak English?"? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The three styles are all correct: intonation (Vous parlez anglais ?), est-ce que, and inversion (Parlez-vous anglais ?). "Est-ce vous" is missing que, and the hyphen in inversion joins the verb and pronoun, not the pronoun and object.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je vais ___ cinéma." (le cinéma)
questions.explanation: à + le always contracts to au: Je vais au cinéma. "à le" is never written, "à la" is for feminine nouns and "aux" for plurals.

questions.stem: Complete: "Elle va ___ banque." (la banque)
questions.explanation: banque is feminine, and à la never contracts: Elle va à la banque. "au" is the mistake you make if you forget the gender.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous allons ___ hôpital." (l'hôpital)
questions.explanation: hôpital starts with a mute h, so the article is l', and à l' doesn't contract: à l'hôpital. au is only for le + a consonant (au musée).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ils ___ au musée." (aller)
questions.explanation: aller is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. "allent" follows the -er pattern, which aller doesn't.

questions.stem: Complete: "Vous ___ à la poste ?" (aller)
questions.explanation: The vous form is allez (with a liaison: vous_allez). vont is ils/elles, allons is nous and vas is tu.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'm going to visit the museum"?
choices: Je vais à visiter le musée.
questions.explanation: The futur proche is aller + infinitive, with nothing in between: Je vais visiter le musée. "Je visite" is the present, "à visiter" adds a word that isn't there, and "visite" is not the infinitive.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm not going to work"?
questions.explanation: ne … pas goes around the conjugated verb, which is vais; the infinitive stays outside: Je ne vais pas travailler.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je vais au cinéma avec ___." (with him)
questions.explanation: After a preposition such as avec, use a stressed pronoun: avec lui (with him). il is only a subject, and eux means them.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ce soir, on mange chez ___." (at their place: three men)
questions.explanation: After chez you need a stressed pronoun, and for men or a mixed group it is eux: chez eux. elles is for a group of women only, and ils and leur are not used after a preposition.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: People take chez (chez le médecin, chez Paul); places take à (à la pharmacie). So "chez la pharmacie" and "à Paul" are wrong, and "à le" must contract anyway.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ l'église d'ici." (voir: We can see the church from here.)
questions.explanation: voir: je vois, tu vois, il voit, nous voyons, vous voyez, ils voient. The i becomes y in the nous and vous forms. voyez is vous, voient is ils.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm going to visit my grandmother"?
questions.explanation: visiter is for places (visiter un musée). For people French says aller voir: Je vais voir ma grand-mère. "Je vais à ma grand-mère" would need chez: Je vais chez ma grand-mère.

questions.stem: Read Sophie's message: "Salut ! Aujourd'hui, je vais à la bibliothèque. Ce soir, je vais au restaurant avec Marc. Demain, nous allons visiter le musée." What is Sophie going to do tomorrow?
questions.explanation: Demain (tomorrow), nous allons visiter le musée: they're going to visit the museum. The library is today (aujourd'hui) and the restaurant is this evening (ce soir).

questions.stem: What is "la bibliothèque"?
questions.explanation: la bibliothèque is a library, where you borrow books. A bookshop is la librairie, a false friend. The town hall is la mairie.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this town map.

image.alt: A town centre map with twelve unlabelled buildings along two streets. Six are numbered: 1 a church with a steeple and a cross, 2 a building with a film strip, 3 a building with a euro sign, 4 a square with a fountain, 5 a building with a large H, 6 a green area with trees.

questions.explanation: 1 the church (l'église), 2 the cinema (le cinéma), 3 the bank (la banque, with the euro sign), 4 the square with its fountain (la place), 5 the hospital (l'hôpital, with an H) and 6 the park (le parc). The other buildings are the town hall, museum, pharmacy, post office, library and hotel.

questions.stem: Complete with à + the article: "Les enfants vont ___ toilettes." (les toilettes = the toilets)
questions.explanation: à + les always contracts to aux: aux toilettes. In the same way à + le = au; à la and à l' don't change.

questions.stem: Complete the futur proche: "Demain, nous ___ voir un film." (aller)
questions.explanation: The futur proche is the present of aller + infinitive. The nous form is allons: nous allons voir un film (we're going to see a film).

questions.stem: Match each place to "to the …" with à.
questions.explanation: à + le = au (au parc), à + les = aux (aux États-Unis); à la (à la mairie) and à l' (à l'hôtel) don't change. "à le" is never written, and mairie is feminine, so "au mairie" is wrong.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "Tomorrow, I'm not going to work."
questions.explanation: Demain, je ne vais pas travailler. ne and pas wrap the conjugated verb vais, and the infinitive travailler comes after them.

questions.stem: Which sentences use the pronoun correctly? Select all that apply.
choices: Je vais au parc avec toi.
Je vais au cinéma avec lui.
Ce soir, je reste chez il.
questions.explanation: After prepositions (avec, pour, chez) French uses the stressed pronouns: avec toi, chez eux, avec lui. "pour ils" should be pour eux, and "chez il" should be chez lui. (je reste = I'm staying)

questions.stem: In a French café, what do you get if you order "un café"?
choices: a large coffee with hot milk
questions.explanation: un café is a small, strong black espresso. For a large coffee with hot milk, ask for un crème (un café crème); for a longer black coffee, un café allongé.

questions.stem: Put the courses of a full French meal in order.
questions.explanation: Starter, main course, cheese, dessert, then a small black coffee. The cheese comes before the dessert, not after it.

questions.stem: Where do you go to buy a chicken?
questions.explanation: la boucherie (the butcher's) sells meat, including chicken. The boulangerie sells bread, the fromagerie cheese and the pâtisserie cakes.

questions.stem: The shop signs are blank. Name each numbered shop from its window.

image.alt: Five shop fronts with blank signs, numbered 1 to 5. 1 baguettes and a round loaf in the window; 2 a slice of layer cake and a strawberry tart; 3 a leg of meat and hanging sausages; 4 a wheel of cheese and a wedge; 5 jars, a tin, a bottle and some fruit.

questions.explanation: 1 bread: la boulangerie. 2 cakes and tarts: la pâtisserie. 3 meat: la boucherie. 4 cheese: la fromagerie. 5 tins, jars and drinks: l'épicerie, the grocer's. A pharmacy and a bookshop (la librairie) don't sell food.

questions.stem: What does "service compris" at the bottom of a French menu mean?
choices: Service is included in the prices.
questions.explanation: compris means included: the menu prices already include service, as they must in France. A tip (le pourboire) is optional and usually small.

questions.stem: When were the artisanal know-how and culture of baguette bread added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage?
questions.explanation: UNESCO added them on 30 November 2022. 1993 is the year of the French decree that defines "pain de tradition française", and 1987 the year from which menu prices had to include service.

questions.stem: Bread sold as "pain de tradition française" must NOT contain which of these?
questions.explanation: The 1993 decree allows only flour, water, salt and yeast or sourdough (plus tiny amounts of a few listed flours), with no additives, and the dough may not be frozen.

questions.stem: Order with the futur proche of prendre: "Je ___ ___ le plat du jour, s'il vous plaît." (I'll have the dish of the day.)
questions.explanation: The futur proche is aller + infinitive: je vais prendre. It's the neutral, natural way to say "I'll have" to a waiter.

questions.stem: Your friend wants a big coffee with hot milk. What should she order?
questions.explanation: un crème (un café crème) is a large coffee with hot milk. un café and un déca are small black espressos (the second decaffeinated), and une noisette is an espresso with only a dash of milk.

questions.stem: Match each shop to the person who runs it.
questions.explanation: Drop the shop ending to find the person: boulangerie → boulanger, boucherie → boucher, fromagerie → fromager, pâtisserie → pâtissier. The distractors are invented forms.

questions.stem: Which are polite ways to order a tea? Select all that apply.
choices: Je voudrais un thé, s'il vous plaît.
J'aimerais un thé, s'il vous plaît.
Je vais prendre un thé, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: je voudrais and j'aimerais (both conditional, "I would like") and je vais prendre (I'll have) are all polite with s'il vous plaît. "Je veux" sounds blunt, and "Donne-moi" is a command with tu.
