questions.stem: The board says: "Formule entrée + plat 15,50 € — Plat du jour seul 11,00 € — Café 2,00 €" (seul = on its own). You take the plat du jour and a coffee; your friend takes the formule. What is the total?
questions.explanation: You: 11,00 + 2,00 = 13,00 €. Your friend: 15,50 €. Total: 13,00 + 15,50 = 28,50 € (vingt-huit euros cinquante). 26,50 € forgets the coffee.

questions.stem: What is "le goûter"?
choices: an afternoon snack, especially for children
questions.explanation: le goûter is the afternoon snack, around 16:30, that children eat after school: bread and chocolate, a biscuit or fruit.

questions.stem: Read: "Au restaurant, Paul mange une entrée et un plat. Après, il prend le fromage, puis un dessert. Enfin, il boit un café." (puis = then, enfin = finally) What does Paul eat just before the dessert?
questions.explanation: Paul takes le fromage, puis (then) un dessert: the cheese comes just before the dessert, as in the traditional order of a French meal.

questions.stem: Write the French word for a tip (money you leave for the waiter), with its article.
questions.explanation: le pourboire, literally "for drinking". In France service is included in the price, so a tip is optional.

questions.stem: Which question is in the most formal register?
questions.explanation: Inversion (Où vas-tu ?) is the formal register. Où est-ce que tu vas ? is standard, and Tu vas où ? and Où tu vas ? are casual spoken forms.

questions.stem: Which is the correct formal way to ask "Does your son speak English?"
questions.explanation: Complex inversion: the noun stays in front and a matching pronoun follows the verb, with -t- between two vowels: Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ? fils needs il, not elle, and the verb can't simply come first in a yes/no question.

questions.stem: Complete the complex inversion: "Les enfants ont-___ faim ?"
questions.explanation: The pronoun repeats the noun: les enfants → ils. ont already ends in t, so no extra -t- is needed: Les enfants ont-ils faim ?

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: que must be followed by inversion: Que fais-tu ? At the end of a casual question you use quoi (Tu fais quoi ?), never que.

questions.stem: Which question is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Simple inversion with a noun works after où, quand, comment, combien and que, but not after pourquoi. Say Pourquoi Paul part-il ? (complex inversion) or Pourquoi est-ce que Paul part ?

questions.stem: Match each question to its register.
questions.explanation: quoi at the end and the tag hein are casual; qu'est-ce que is the standard, safe form; que + inversion is formal.

questions.stem: You're texting a good friend to ask if she's coming tonight. Which question fits best?
choices: Est-ce que vous venez ce soir ?
questions.explanation: With a friend in a text, use tu and plain intonation: Tu viens ce soir ? The others use vous and sound formal or distant.

questions.stem: You're writing an e-mail to a hotel. Which question fits best?
choices: Il y a un parking, hein ?
questions.explanation: A formal e-mail suits inversion: Y a-t-il un parking ? (Is there a car park?) hein, quoi and the question at the end belong to casual speech.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ est votre plat préféré ?" (What is your favourite dish? le plat)
questions.explanation: "What is …" + noun uses quel + être, and quel agrees with plat (masculine): Quel est votre plat préféré ? qu'est-ce que can't be used before est + noun.

questions.stem: Which questions are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Votre sœur mange-t-elle de la viande ?
questions.explanation: Où est-ce que vous habitez ? (standard), Votre sœur mange-t-elle … ? (complex inversion with -t-) and Tu fais quoi ce soir ? (casual) are correct. "Est-ce que tu vas où ?" mixes two styles, and "Qu'est-ce que est ton nom ?" should be Quel est ton nom ?

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask formally "When does the train arrive in Lyon?"
questions.explanation: Complex inversion after a question word: question word, noun subject, verb + pronoun, then the rest: Quand le train arrive-t-il à Lyon ? (Quand arrive le train à Lyon ? is also correct, but uses no pronoun.)

questions.stem: What does "n'est-ce pas ?" add to "Vous êtes français, n'est-ce pas ?"
choices: It asks where the person is from.
questions.explanation: n'est-ce pas ? is a tag that asks the listener to agree, like "aren't you?" or "right?". The sentence itself stays positive.

questions.stem: In the DELF A1 speaking test you ask the examiner, whom you don't know, about their job. Which question is the best choice?
choices: Qu'est-ce que vous faites comme travail ?
questions.explanation: With an examiner you don't know, use vous, and est-ce que is always correct and natural: Qu'est-ce que vous faites comme travail ? The others use tu or casual forms (quoi at the end, hein).

questions.stem: Which word for "what" goes at the end of a casual question, as in "Tu manges ___ ?"
questions.explanation: quoi is the casual "what" at the end of a question or on its own: Tu manges quoi ? que needs inversion (Que manges-tu ?), and quel goes with a noun.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ du vélo le week-end." (faire)
questions.explanation: The nous form of faire is "faisons" (said "fuh-ZON"). "Faites" is the vous form and "font" the ils form; "fesons" is an old spelling no longer used.

questions.stem: Complete: "Qu'est-ce que vous ___ ce soir ?" (faire)
questions.explanation: "Vous faites" is irregular: with "vous êtes" and "vous dites", it is one of only three vous forms ending in -tes. "Faisez" follows the regular pattern but doesn't exist.

questions.stem: How do you say "I play the guitar"?
questions.explanation: Instruments take "jouer de": de + la guitare = "de la guitare". "Jouer à" is for games and sports, and French doesn't use "jouer" with a bare article.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mon frère joue ___ tennis."
questions.explanation: Games and ball sports take "jouer à", and à + le always contracts to "au": "jouer au tennis". "Du" would be for an instrument (jouer du piano).

questions.stem: Complete: "Elle fait ___ natation."
questions.explanation: "Faire de" + activity, and "natation" is feminine: "faire de la natation". "Du" is for masculine nouns (faire du vélo).

questions.stem: How do you say "I don't do any sport"?
choices: Je ne fais pas du sport.
Je ne fais pas de sport.
Je ne fais pas le sport.
Je fais ne pas de sport.
questions.explanation: After a negative, du / de la / des become "de": "Je ne fais pas de sport" (lesson 10). "Ne" goes before the verb and "pas" after it.

questions.stem: How do you say "It's cold" about the weather?
questions.explanation: Weather uses "il fait" + adjective: "Il fait froid". "J'ai froid" means "I'm cold" (a person), and "c'est froid" describes a thing, like a cold coffee.

questions.stem: You come in from the sun and want to say "I'm hot". Which sentence is right?
questions.explanation: People "have" hot and cold in French: "J'ai chaud". "Il fait chaud" is about the weather. Avoid "je suis chaud": in casual French it means "I'm up for it".

questions.stem: Complete: "___ printemps, je fais du vélo."
questions.explanation: Spring is the only season with "au": "au printemps". The others start with a vowel sound and take "en": en été, en automne, en hiver.

questions.stem: Which phrase is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: "Printemps" starts with a consonant, so it takes "au": "au printemps". "En été, en hiver, en automne" are all correct.

questions.stem: Read: "Marc adore le sport. En été, il nage à la piscine et il joue au tennis. En hiver, il fait froid : il reste à la maison et il lit." What does Marc do in winter?
choices: He stays at home and reads.
questions.explanation: "En hiver ... il reste à la maison et il lit" = in winter he stays at home and reads. Swimming and tennis are what he does "en été" (in summer).

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "Quel temps fait-il ?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: "Quel temps fait-il ?" asks about the weather, so "Il pleut" (it's raining) fits. "Il est trois heures" answers a question about the time, a different meaning of English "time".

questions.stem: Complete: "Mes parents ___ le journal." (lire)
questions.explanation: Lire: je lis, tu lis, il lit, nous lisons, vous lisez, ils lisent. The plural forms add an s (said "z") to the stem: "lisent".

questions.stem: Type the right form of "nager": "Nous ___ à la piscine."
questions.explanation: Nager is a regular -er verb, but in the nous form the e stays after the g to keep it soft: "nous nageons", like "nous mangeons".

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I don't do any sport."
questions.explanation: "Ne" goes before the verb and "pas" after it, and du becomes "de" after the negative: Je ne fais pas de sport.

questions.stem: Match each activity to the words that go before it.
questions.explanation: Instruments take jouer de (jouer de la guitare), games take jouer à (jouer aux cartes), and other activities take faire de (faire de la natation, faire du vélo). "À le" always contracts to "au", and "faire au" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct French for the weather? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Weather uses "il fait" (il fait beau), the il-only verbs (il pleut, il neige) and "il y a du soleil". "Il est chaud" means "he is hot", and the weather subject is always the impersonal "il", never "elle".

questions.stem: What is the weather at each numbered symbol on the map?

image.alt: An outline map of France with five numbered weather symbols: a cloud with rain near Brest, a thermometer with a low blue level near Strasbourg, a thermometer with a high red level near Bordeaux, a cloud with snowflakes in the Alps and a sun north of Marseille.

questions.explanation: Rain is "il pleut", the low thermometer "il fait froid", the high one "il fait chaud", snow "il neige" and the sun "il fait beau". No symbol shows "il fait mauvais" (bad weather) in general.

questions.stem: Say what each numbered person does, with the right verb pattern.

image.alt: Six numbered picture tiles: a bicycle, a swimmer in waves, mountains with a dotted path, a football, a tennis racket and ball, and a guitar.

questions.explanation: Activities that aren't games take faire de (du vélo, de la natation, de la randonnée), ball games take jouer à (au football, au tennis) and instruments take jouer de (de la guitare), never jouer à. No tile shows a piano.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ils ___ le train de huit heures." (prendre)
questions.explanation: Prendre: ils prennent, with a double n and no d. "Prendent" keeps the d of the infinitive, which the plural loses; "prends" is the je/tu form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ le français." (apprendre)
questions.explanation: Apprendre goes like prendre: nous apprenons (one n, no d). Only the ils form has a double n: ils apprennent.

questions.stem: Complete: "Elle ___ de Lyon." (venir)
questions.explanation: Venir: je viens, tu viens, il/elle vient. The il form ends in -t. "Elle vient de Lyon" = she comes from Lyon.

questions.stem: Complete: "Vous ___ quand ?" (partir)
questions.explanation: Partir: nous partons, vous partez. It is not a finir-type verb, so there is no -iss- ("partissez" is wrong). "Pars" is the je/tu form, "partent" the ils form.

questions.stem: How do you say "I go to work by bus"?
choices: Je vais au travail à bus.
Je vais au travail en le bus.
Je vais au travail en bus.
Je vais au travail par le bus.
questions.explanation: With a vehicle you sit inside, use "en" with no article: en bus, en train, en voiture. (Or: Je prends le bus.)

questions.stem: How do you say "I walk to school" (I go on foot)?
choices: Je vais à l'école à pied.
Je vais à l'école en pied.
Je vais à l'école par pied.
Je vais à l'école au pied.
questions.explanation: "On foot" is always "à pied". "En" is only for vehicles you sit in.

questions.stem: Where do you catch the metro in Paris?
questions.explanation: A metro station is "la station" (la station Bastille). "La gare" is for trains, "l'arrêt" for buses and trams.

questions.stem: At the ticket office you ask for "un aller-retour pour Lille". What are you buying?
questions.explanation: "Un aller-retour" (from aller, to go, and le retour, the return) is a return ticket, there and back.

questions.stem: The board shows that your train is 20 minutes behind schedule. What do you say?
questions.explanation: "En retard" = late, behind schedule. "Tard" means late in the day and isn't used this way; "à l'heure" means on time and "en avance" early.

questions.stem: Read: "Sophie habite à Lille. Demain, elle part à Paris pour le travail. Elle prend le train à la gare de Lille. À Paris, elle va au bureau en métro." How does Sophie get to the office in Paris?
questions.explanation: "À Paris, elle va au bureau en métro" = in Paris she goes to the office by metro. The train is how she travels from Lille to Paris.

questions.stem: Someone asks you: "Tu viens d'où ?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: "Tu viens d'où ?" = where are you from? Answer with venir de + place: "Je viens de Montréal."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Je pars la maison à huit heures.
questions.explanation: Partir has no direct object: you leave from a place with "de": "Je pars de la maison". The other three are correct.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous partons ___ vacances demain."
questions.explanation: "Partir en vacances" = to go on holiday. "Les vacances" is always plural, and the fixed phrase is "en vacances".

questions.stem: Type the right form of "venir": "Mes parents ___ de Bordeaux."
questions.explanation: Mes parents = ils, and venir gives "ils viennent": ie in the stem and a double n, like "ils prennent".

questions.stem: Type the right form of "prendre": "Tu ___ le métro ou le bus ?"
questions.explanation: Prendre: je prends, tu prends, il prend. The tu form ends in -s; the d stays in the singular.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "They don't understand the metro map."
questions.explanation: Ne ... pas goes around the verb: Ils ne comprennent pas le plan du métro. Comprendre goes like prendre: ils comprennent.

questions.stem: Match each place to its English meaning.
questions.explanation: French uses different words for different stops: la gare (trains), la station (metro), l'arrêt (bus, tram), l'aéroport (planes).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Je vais à Paris en train.
Je vais au bureau à pied.
questions.explanation: "En train", "à pied" and "en avion" are right. "Prendre" needs the article (Je prends le bus), and "on foot" is always "à pied", never "en pied".

questions.stem: How does each numbered picture travel? Choose en or à.

image.alt: Six numbered pictures in two groups: a bus, a train, a car and a plane on the left; a bicycle and a walking person on the right.

questions.explanation: You sit inside a bus, a train, a car and a plane, so they take "en". You sit on top of a bike and you walk on your feet, so those take "à": à vélo, à pied.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je ___ le pull bleu." (préférer)
questions.explanation: In the je form the last é becomes è because the ending is silent: "je préfère". The first é never changes.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ le thé." (préférer)
questions.explanation: Nous and vous are outside the "boot": the ending is pronounced, so the stem keeps both é: "nous préférons". "Préfèrent" is the ils form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ils ___ un taxi." (appeler)
questions.explanation: Appeler doubles the l when the ending is silent: j'appelle, ils appellent. "Appelent" forgets the double l, and appeler never takes an accent.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ le cours à neuf heures." (commencer)
questions.explanation: Before o, c needs a cedilla to keep its s sound: "nous commençons". Without it, "co" would sound "ko".

questions.stem: Which is a correct je form of "payer"?
questions.explanation: "Je paie" (or "je paye": both spellings are correct). The y changes to i before a silent e. "Payons" is the nous form.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ homme porte un chapeau."
questions.explanation: "Homme" is masculine and starts with a mute h, so "ce" becomes "cet": cet homme. "Cette" is only for feminine nouns.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ chaussures sont trop petites."
questions.explanation: "Chaussures" is plural, and every plural takes "ces", masculine or feminine.

questions.stem: What does "Je mets mon manteau" mean?
questions.explanation: Mettre = to put, to put on (the action of dressing). "I'm wearing my coat" would be "Je porte mon manteau", and porter can also mean to carry.

questions.stem: You buy one pair of jeans. Which sentence is right?
questions.explanation: "Le jean" is masculine and singular for one pair: "un jean", like "un pantalon". "Des jeans" means several pairs, and "du jean" is denim, the fabric.

questions.stem: The shop assistant asks: "Quelle taille faites-vous ?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: Sizes use "faire du" + the number: "Je fais du 40". "J'ai 40 ans" gives your age, not your size.

questions.stem: Read: "Clara cherche une veste. Elle fait du 38. Elle essaie une veste noire en 38, mais elle est trop longue. Alors elle prend une veste grise, plus courte." Why doesn't Clara take the black jacket?
questions.explanation: "Elle est trop longue" = it's too long. It is her size (38), and the text says nothing about the price.

questions.stem: What does "Cette jupe est trop courte" mean?
questions.explanation: "Court, courte" = short (for length). Its opposite is "long, longue".

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake?
questions.explanation: Vous is outside the boot, so the l is not doubled: "vous appelez". The other three are correct: nous achetons (no accent), j'espère, ils paient.

questions.stem: Type the right form of "essayer": "Vous ___ la robe rouge ?"
questions.explanation: Vous is outside the boot, so the y stays: "vous essayez". The change to i happens only before a silent ending (j'essaie).

questions.stem: Type the je form of "espérer" (the j' is given): "J'___ que c'est ma taille."
questions.explanation: Inside the boot the last é becomes è: "j'espère". The first e has no accent and doesn't change.

questions.stem: Match each noun to the demonstrative that goes before it.
questions.explanation: Ce before a masculine noun (ce manteau), cet before a masculine noun with a vowel or mute h (cet été), cette before a feminine noun (cette veste) and ces for all plurals (ces vêtements). "Cettes" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Which forms are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The stem changes only in je, tu, il and ils: j'achète, ils préfèrent, tu paies. Nous and vous keep the infinitive's stem: nous achetons, vous appelez.

questions.stem: Name the numbered clothes on the rail.

image.alt: A clothes rail with six numbered items on hangers: a white shirt with buttons, a red jumper, a purple dress, a blue jacket with lapels, a short orange skirt and grey trousers. A hat is on a shelf and a pair of shoes stands under the rail.

questions.explanation: From left to right: une chemise (buttons and a collar), un pull (knitted, no buttons), une robe (a dress), une veste (a jacket with lapels), une jupe (a skirt) and un pantalon (trousers, singular in French).

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I prefer this black jacket."
questions.explanation: The demonstrative goes before the noun, like an article, and colours go after it: Je préfère cette veste noire.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ le travail à midi." (finir)
questions.explanation: Finir-type verbs add -iss- in the plural: nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent. "Finons" leaves it out.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ils ___ un dessert." (choisir)
questions.explanation: Choisir is a finir-type verb: ils choisissent. "Choisit" is the il form; "choisissant" is not a present-tense form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il ___ le bus." (attendre)
questions.explanation: -re verbs have no ending in the il form: just the stem, "il attend". "Attends" is the je/tu form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Vous ___ à la question ?" (répondre)
questions.explanation: Répondre is a -re verb: vous répondez. There is no -iss- in -re verbs; that belongs to finir.

questions.stem: Complete: "Le bébé ___." (dormir)
questions.explanation: Dormir drops the m in the singular: je dors, tu dors, il dort. It isn't a finir-type verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ bien à l'hôtel." (dormir)
questions.explanation: In the plural dormir keeps its m and has no -iss-: nous dormons. "Dormissons" treats it like finir, which it is not.

questions.stem: How do you say "My head hurts" / "I have a headache"?
choices: Je suis mal à la tête.
questions.explanation: Avoir mal à + the definite article: "J'ai mal à la tête". French doesn't use "my" here, and "tête" is feminine, so it's "à la", not "au".

questions.stem: Complete: "J'ai mal ___ dents."
questions.explanation: À + les always contracts to "aux": "J'ai mal aux dents" (I have toothache).

questions.stem: Complete: "Il a mal ___ dos."
questions.explanation: "Le dos" is masculine, and à + le contracts to "au": "Il a mal au dos".

questions.stem: What is the plural of "l'œil" (the eye)?
questions.explanation: L'œil has an irregular plural: les yeux (said "lay-ZYEU" with liaison). Un œil, deux yeux.

questions.stem: You call a doctor's surgery. The receptionist says: "Cabinet du docteur Morel, bonjour." What do you say?
questions.explanation: "Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous" = I'd like to make an appointment. "Prendre rendez-vous" uses prendre and no article.

questions.stem: Read: "Paul est malade. Il a de la fièvre et il a mal à la tête. Il ne dort pas bien. Demain, il a rendez-vous chez le médecin." Which is true?
choices: Paul has a temperature and a headache.
Paul is seeing the doctor today.
questions.explanation: "Il a de la fièvre et il a mal à la tête" = he has a temperature and a headache. He doesn't sleep well ("il ne dort pas bien"), and the appointment is tomorrow ("demain").

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: "Attendre" already means "to wait for", so there's no "pour": "J'attends le bus". The other three are correct.

questions.stem: Type the right form of "vendre": "Le magasin ___ des chaussures."
questions.explanation: Le magasin = il, and -re verbs have no ending in the il form: "il vend". The d is written but not pronounced.

questions.stem: Type the right form of "réfléchir": "Nous ___ à nos vacances."
questions.explanation: Réfléchir is a finir-type verb, so the nous form adds -iss-: "nous réfléchissons". Réfléchir à = to think about.

questions.stem: Complete "J'ai mal ___": match each body part to the right word.
questions.explanation: À + le = au (au ventre), à + les = aux (aux pieds); à la and à l' don't change (à la tête, à l'oreille). "À le" and "à les" never appear: they always contract.

questions.stem: Which verbs add -iss- in the plural (nous, vous, ils)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Finir, choisir and réfléchir are finir-type verbs: nous finissons, choisissons, réfléchissons. Dormir and partir end in -ir too but follow the other pattern: nous dormons, nous partons.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the body.

image.alt: An outline of a standing person seen from the front with six numbered markers: on the top of the head, on an ear, on an upper arm, on a hand, on a leg and on a foot.

questions.explanation: From top to bottom: la tête (head), l'oreille (ear), le bras (arm), la main (hand), la jambe (leg), le pied (foot). The back (le dos) can't be seen from the front.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I don't sleep well."
questions.explanation: Ne ... pas goes around the verb, and "bien" comes after pas: Je ne dors pas bien.

questions.stem: How do you say "I've been learning French for two months"?
choices: J'apprends le français pour deux mois.
J'apprends le français depuis deux mois.
J'apprends le français dans deux mois.
J'apprends le français il y a deux mois.
questions.explanation: For something still going on, French uses depuis + the present: "J'apprends le français depuis deux mois". "Pour deux mois" would mean you plan to learn for two months; "dans deux mois" means two months from now.

questions.stem: How do you say "We've lived in Lyon since 2020"?
choices: Nous avons habité à Lyon depuis 2020.
Nous sommes habités à Lyon depuis 2020.
questions.explanation: You still live there, so the verb is in the present: "Nous habitons à Lyon depuis 2020". The English present perfect ("have lived") is a trap.

questions.stem: In the Tour de France, who wears "le maillot jaune"?
choices: the overall leader of the race
questions.explanation: The yellow jersey, introduced in 1919, is worn by the leader of the race overall. Yellow was the colour of the pages of the newspaper L'Auto, which ran the race.

questions.stem: When is the Fête de la musique?
choices: on the first Sunday of summer
questions.explanation: The Fête de la musique is on 21 June, around the longest day of the year. It was launched in 1982.

questions.stem: In pétanque, what is "le cochonnet"?
choices: a metal ball each player throws
questions.explanation: Le cochonnet (literally "piglet") is the small wooden target ball. The metal balls are "les boules".

questions.stem: What is the standard negative of "Je joue du piano"?
choices: Je ne joue pas du piano.
Je ne joue pas au piano.
Je ne joue pas de le piano.
Je ne joue du piano pas.
questions.explanation: In "jouer du piano", du is the preposition de + le, not a partitive, so the standard negative keeps it: "Je ne joue pas du piano". (You'll also hear "pas de piano" in speech.)

questions.stem: Look at the pétanque game. If all the boules have been thrown, who scores, and how many points?

image.alt: A pétanque game seen from above: a small jack in the centre, a red boule very close to it, a blue boule a little farther, a second blue boule farther still and a second red boule farthest away.

questions.explanation: The nearest boule is red, so red scores. Red gets one point for each red boule closer than blue's best boule: only one red boule is, because the second red boule is farther away than the nearer blue one.

questions.stem: Read: "Je m'appelle Nadia, j'ai 34 ans. Je joue de la guitare depuis quinze ans. Le soir, je joue à la pétanque avec mon père. Il joue depuis cinquante ans." How long has Nadia played the guitar?
questions.explanation: "Je joue de la guitare depuis quinze ans" = I've played the guitar for fifteen years. Fifty years is how long her father has played pétanque.

questions.stem: Which statement about la bande dessinée is true?
choices: Tintin was created by the Belgian artist Hergé.
The Angoulême festival takes place in July.
In France, comics are only for children.
questions.explanation: Tintin is by Hergé, a Belgian artist, first published in 1929. Astérix dates from 1959, the Angoulême festival is held in late January, and adults read BD as much as children.

questions.stem: Complete with one word: "Le dimanche, mon grand-père joue ___ échecs." (chess: les échecs)
questions.explanation: Chess is a game, so it takes jouer à, and à + les contracts to "aux": jouer aux échecs.

questions.stem: Complete the question "How long have you been cycling?": "Depuis ___ de temps tu fais du vélo ?"
questions.explanation: "Depuis combien de temps ... ?" asks how long something has been going on. "Depuis quand ... ?" asks since when.

questions.stem: Match each pattern to a correct example.
questions.explanation: Jouer à + game (aux cartes), jouer de + instrument (du violon), faire de + activity (de la randonnée). "Je joue la guitare" and "Je fais au tennis" are both wrong.

questions.stem: Which negative sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Je ne fais pas de vélo.
Je ne joue pas de tennis.
Je ne joue pas au tennis.
Je ne fais pas du sport.
Elle ne joue pas du violon.
questions.explanation: Faire du becomes "pas de" (pas de vélo), but jouer au and jouer du keep their preposition: pas au tennis, pas du violon. "Pas du sport" and "pas de tennis" mix up the patterns.

questions.stem: Put the words in order, starting with "Ma sœur": "My sister has been playing the guitar for three years."
questions.explanation: Subject, verb in the present, the instrument with jouer de, then depuis + the length of time: Ma sœur joue de la guitare depuis trois ans.

questions.stem: What does "J'ai mal au cœur" mean?
questions.explanation: It's a false friend: "avoir mal au cœur" means to feel sick, as if you're going to vomit. For chest pain, say "J'ai mal à la poitrine".

questions.stem: What does "Il ne faut pas boire d'alcool avec ce médicament" mean?
choices: You don't have to drink alcohol with this medicine.
You mustn't drink alcohol with this medicine.
You need to drink alcohol with this medicine.
There's no alcohol in this medicine.
questions.explanation: "Il ne faut pas" + infinitive means "you must not". It never means "you don't have to".

questions.stem: There's a fire in your building in France. Which number is the fire brigade (les pompiers)?
questions.explanation: 18 is the fire brigade (les pompiers). 15 is the SAMU (medical emergencies), 17 the police, and 114 the number for deaf and hard-of-hearing people. 112 also works.

questions.stem: What is 112?
choices: the emergency number that works in every EU country
the number for the police only
the number for a duty pharmacy
the number for a doctor's appointment
questions.explanation: 112 is the European emergency number: free, from any phone, in every EU country. In France, 15, 17 and 18 work too.

questions.stem: It's Sunday and the pharmacies are closed. What is the open one in your area called?
questions.explanation: "La pharmacie de garde" is the duty pharmacy, open at night, on Sundays and on public holidays. Its address is on the door of the nearest pharmacy, or call 32 37.

questions.stem: What sign shows a pharmacy in France?
questions.explanation: French pharmacies have a green cross, often lit up. Medicines, even common painkillers, are sold almost only in pharmacies.

questions.stem: The box says: "1 comprimé 2 fois par jour, pendant 7 jours." How many tablets is that in total?
questions.explanation: One tablet twice a day (2 fois par jour) is 2 a day; for 7 days (pendant 7 jours) that's 2 × 7 = 14.

questions.stem: What does "Je tousse depuis hier" mean?
questions.explanation: Depuis + present = something that started in the past and is still going on: I've been coughing since yesterday.

questions.stem: You tell the pharmacist: "J'ai mal à la gorge." What is the problem?
questions.explanation: "La gorge" is the throat: avoir mal à la gorge = to have a sore throat.

questions.stem: Complete with one word: "Tu es fatigué ? Il ___ dormir !" (you need to)
questions.explanation: "Il faut" + infinitive = you have to, you need to. The form is always "il faut": it is impersonal, like "il pleut".

questions.stem: Type the right form of "tousser": "Mon fils ___ beaucoup la nuit."
questions.explanation: Tousser is a regular -er verb: il tousse. (Mon fils = il.)

questions.stem: Match each French emergency number to its service.
questions.explanation: 15 is the SAMU, 17 the police, 18 the fire brigade (les pompiers), and 114 takes text messages from deaf and hard-of-hearing people. The duty pharmacy is found through 32 37, not an emergency number.

questions.stem: Which sentences describe symptoms correctly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Illnesses and pains go with avoir: j'ai un rhume, j'ai la grippe, j'ai mal à la gorge. For a temperature say "j'ai de la fièvre", and for a cough "je tousse".

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "You mustn't take this medicine."
questions.explanation: Ne ... pas goes around "faut", and the infinitive comes after: Il ne faut pas prendre ce médicament.

questions.stem: By the general rule, when do the winter sales (les soldes d'hiver) start in France?
choices: on the last Wednesday of June
on any day the shop chooses
on the second Wednesday of January (or the first, if the second is after the 12th)
questions.explanation: Winter sales start at 8 a.m. on the second Wednesday of January, or the first Wednesday if the second falls after the 12th. Shops can't choose the dates; some areas have exceptions.

questions.stem: How long does each official sales period last today?
questions.explanation: Each period lasts four weeks. It was six weeks until 2019. The government can change a period, as it did in summer 2026.

questions.stem: A jumper costs 50 € and the sign says "-20 %". How much do you pay?
questions.explanation: 20 % of 50 € is 10 €, so you pay 50 − 10 = 40 €. 10 € is only the discount (la réduction).

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ce pantalon est trop large." What does she mean?
questions.explanation: "Large" is a false friend: it means wide or loose. Too tight is "trop serré", and "big" in general is "grand".

questions.stem: What is "la pointure"?
questions.explanation: La pointure is your shoe size: "Quelle est votre pointure ? — Je fais du 39." For clothes you say "la taille".

questions.stem: Your friend says: "J'adore cette jupe !" You ask "which one?". What do you say?
questions.explanation: "Jupe" is feminine singular, so "which one?" is "Laquelle ?". Lequel is masculine; lesquelles is feminine plural.

questions.stem: You bought a jumper in a shop in France. It isn't faulty, but you changed your mind. What is the shop's obligation?
choices: None: an exchange or refund is the shop's choice, unless it promised one.
It must refund you within 14 days.
It must exchange it, but only during the sales.
It must refund you if you paid by card.
questions.explanation: In a French shop there's no legal right to change your mind: exchanges are a favour, unless the shop promises one. The 14-day right applies to online purchases. A faulty item is different: you are protected.

questions.stem: Your friend comes out of the fitting room, and the dress looks great on her. What do you say?
questions.explanation: "Ça te va bien" = it suits you. "Bien" is the adverb (well), so not "bon". "Tu vas bien ?" asks whether someone is well.

questions.stem: The Wednesdays in June 2028 are the 7th, 14th, 21st and 28th. By the general rule, when do the summer sales start?
questions.explanation: Summer sales start on the last Wednesday of June unless it falls after the 28th. The 28th is not after the 28th, so the sales start on Wednesday 28 June 2028.

questions.stem: Type the right form of "échanger": "Nous ___ ce pantalon, s'il vous plaît."
questions.explanation: Échanger is a -ger verb, so the nous form keeps the e after the g: "nous échangeons", like "nous mangeons".

questions.stem: Complete with one word: "Quelle est votre ___ ? — Je fais du 39." (You are buying shoes.)
questions.explanation: For shoes the word is "la pointure". "La taille" is for clothes.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to "which one(s)?".
questions.explanation: Lequel agrees with the noun: masculine singular lequel (le pull), feminine singular laquelle (la robe), masculine plural lesquels (les chapeaux), feminine plural lesquelles (les chaussures).

questions.stem: Which statements about les soldes in France are true? Select all that apply.
choices: There are two official periods a year.
Each shop chooses its own sales dates.
By the general rule they start on a Wednesday.
questions.explanation: Two periods (winter and summer), four weeks each, starting on a Wednesday at 8 a.m. The dates are set by law, not by each shop, and they apply in shops and online.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I'd like to try this dress in a 38."
questions.explanation: Je voudrais + infinitive (essayer), then the thing (cette robe) and the size with en: Je voudrais essayer cette robe en 38.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je ___ lève à sept heures."
questions.explanation: The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: je goes with me, so "Je me lève." Se is the dictionary form (se lever) and goes with il, elle, on, ils, elles; te goes with tu; moi is a stressed pronoun, not a reflexive one.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nous ___ couchons tard le samedi."
questions.explanation: With nous, the reflexive pronoun is also nous, so it appears twice: "Nous nous couchons." "Nous se couchons" is a common mistake: se only goes with il, elle, on, ils and elles.

questions.stem: Which is the correct negative of "Je me lève tôt"?
choices: Je me ne lève pas tôt.
Je ne lève me pas tôt.
Je ne me lève pas tôt.
Je ne me pas lève tôt.
questions.explanation: Ne goes before the reflexive pronoun and pas after the verb; the pronoun stays glued to the verb: je ne me lève pas. Putting ne between me and lève, or pas before the verb, breaks the pattern.

questions.stem: Complete: "Tu vas ___ coucher à quelle heure ?"
questions.explanation: After aller, the pronominal verb stays in the infinitive, but its pronoun still matches the subject: tu vas te coucher. Keeping the dictionary form ("tu vas se coucher") is the classic mistake.

questions.stem: Which form of "se promener" is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Se promener changes e to è only in the forms with a silent ending: je me promène, tu te promènes, il se promène, ils se promènent. With nous and vous the ending is heard, so there is no accent: nous nous promenons, vous vous promenez. "je me promene" is missing the accent.

questions.stem: How do you say "She gets dressed"?
questions.explanation: Habiller starts with a mute h, so se elides to s': elle s'habille. "Elle se habille" forgets the elision; "Elle habille" has no reflexive pronoun (it would mean she dresses someone); t' goes with tu.

questions.stem: What does "D'habitude, je me couche tôt" mean?
choices: I usually go to bed early.
I always go to bed late.
Today I'm going to bed early.
questions.explanation: D'habitude means usually; se coucher is to go to bed (not to get up, which is se lever); tôt is early (tard is late).

questions.stem: Read: "Le matin, Paul se réveille à six heures, mais il ne se lève pas tout de suite. D'abord, il écoute la radio. Ensuite, il se douche. Puis il prend un café. Enfin, il part au travail." What does Paul do first after he wakes up?
questions.explanation: D'abord (first) introduces the radio. Ensuite (next) is the shower, puis (then) the coffee and enfin (finally) leaving for work. Tout de suite means straight away: he doesn't get up straight away.

questions.stem: Which sentence puts "souvent" in the right place?
choices: Je souvent me promène le dimanche.
Je me souvent promène le dimanche.
Je me promène souvent le dimanche.
Souvent je me le dimanche promène.
questions.explanation: Souvent, like toujours, goes after the verb: je me promène souvent. It never goes between the pronoun and the verb, which stay together.

questions.stem: Which word means "next, afterwards"?
questions.explanation: Ensuite means next or afterwards. Enfin means finally, avant means before, and parfois means sometimes.

questions.stem: "Tu te lèves à quelle heure le week-end ?" What is a good answer?
choices: Le matin, je bois du thé.
questions.explanation: The question asks what time (à quelle heure) you get up at the weekend, so an answer with a time fits: "Late, at about ten." "Oui" answers a yes/no question, not "what time?"

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: With an infinitive the pronoun still matches the subject: je vais me doucher, not se. The other three are correct: nous nous, vous vous, ils se.

questions.stem: Write the missing reflexive pronoun: "Ils ___ réveillent à six heures."
questions.explanation: Ils takes se: ils se réveillent. Réveiller starts with a consonant, so there is no elision.

questions.stem: Write the present tense of "se lever" with tu, pronoun included: "Tu ___ tôt ?"
questions.explanation: Tu takes te, and se lever changes e to è when the ending is silent: tu te lèves. The -s of the tu ending is silent but must be written.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I'm not going to get up."
questions.explanation: Ne … pas goes around the conjugated verb (vais), and the infinitive comes after with its pronoun matching je: Je ne vais pas me lever.

questions.stem: Match each French word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Le matin, le soir and la nuit use the article where English says in the / at. Tôt is early and tard is late. Always is toujours and sometimes is parfois.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Je m'habille (elision before a mute h), tu te lèves (te with tu, and the accent) and je vais me reposer (me matches je) are correct. Nous se levons needs nous nous levons; il se habille needs the elision: il s'habille.

questions.stem: Name the action in each numbered picture.

image.alt: Six pictures with a time under each: an alarm clock ringing at 6 h 45, a person standing up next to a bed at 7 h, a shower at 7 h 10, a shirt on a hanger at 7 h 30, a person walking past a tree at 18 h, and a person in bed under a moon at 23 h. Each picture is numbered.

questions.explanation: The alarm clock is se réveiller (to wake up); standing up beside the bed is se lever (to get up); the shower is se doucher; the shirt on a hanger is s'habiller (to get dressed); walking past a tree is se promener (to go for a walk); lying in bed at night is se coucher (to go to bed). Se dépêcher (to hurry) and s'appeler (to be called) aren't shown.

questions.stem: What time is it? "Il est trois heures et quart."
questions.explanation: Et quart is quarter past: 3:15. 3:45 would be quatre heures moins le quart, and 3:30 trois heures et demie.

questions.stem: How do you say 5:45 in everyday French?
choices: six heures et moins le quart
questions.explanation: After half past, everyday French counts back from the next hour: 5:45 is six heures moins le quart. "cinq heures moins le quart" is 4:45. There is no et with minutes like quarante-cinq or with moins.

questions.stem: Which is correct for 12:30 p.m.?
questions.explanation: Midi is masculine, so it is midi et demi, without -e. Et demie with -e goes with heure(s), which is feminine: une heure et demie.

questions.stem: A station announcement gives the departure "19 h 40". How is it said?
questions.explanation: Announcements use the 24-hour clock: hour + heures + minutes as a plain number, with no et or moins: dix-neuf heures quarante. 19 h is not neuf (9).

questions.stem: Complete: "Il est ___ heure."
questions.explanation: Heure is feminine, so one o'clock is une heure. The same goes for vingt et une heures (21 h).

questions.stem: What does "Le samedi, je vais au marché" mean?
choices: This Saturday I'm going to the market.
Last Saturday I went to the market.
Next Saturday I'm going to the market.
On Saturdays I go to the market.
questions.explanation: Le + day means every week: on Saturdays. Without the article, samedi means this (coming) Saturday. Last and next Saturday are samedi dernier and samedi prochain.

questions.stem: Which means "next week"?
questions.explanation: For next week, prochain comes after semaine and agrees with it (feminine): la semaine prochaine. La semaine dernière is last week; prochain without -e doesn't agree with semaine.

questions.stem: Read the sign: "PHARMACIE CENTRALE — Ouvert du lundi au samedi : 9 h – 19 h 30. Fermé le dimanche." Can you buy medicine there on Sunday at 10 a.m.?
choices: No, it is closed on Sundays.
questions.explanation: Fermé le dimanche means closed every Sunday. The hours 9 h – 19 h 30 are for Monday to Saturday (du lundi au samedi).

questions.stem: "Je travaille de neuf heures à dix-sept heures." When do you finish?
questions.explanation: De … à means from … to. Dix-sept heures (17 h) is 5 p.m. on the 24-hour clock. Don't confuse dix-sept (17) with sept (7).

questions.stem: Choose the right word: "J'arrive ___ huit heures, ou huit heures dix."
questions.explanation: Vers + time means at about: the speaker isn't sure of the exact time. Jusqu'à means until, and à l'heure means on time.

questions.stem: "À quelle heure commence le film ?" What is a good answer?
questions.explanation: À quelle heure asks at what time, so answer with à + time. "Il est vingt heures" answers "What time is it?"; "Il dure deux heures" tells how long it lasts.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Heure(s) is always said with the hour: il est cinq heures. Midi and minuit are the exceptions: they stand alone.

questions.stem: The class starts at 10:00. You arrive at 9:50. You are…
questions.explanation: Arriving before the time is en avance (early). En retard is late, à l'heure is on time, and tard is late in the day.

questions.stem: Write the day that comes after "mardi".
questions.explanation: The week runs lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. Days are written with a small letter.

questions.stem: It is 4:30. Complete in everyday French: "Il est quatre heures ___."
questions.explanation: Half past is et demie, with -e because heure is feminine: quatre heures et demie. (With midi and minuit it is et demi.) Quatre heures trente, read like the 24-hour clock, is also correct.

questions.stem: Put the days of the week in order, starting with the first day of the French week.
questions.explanation: In France the week, and the calendar, starts on Monday: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche.

questions.stem: Match each 24-hour time to the everyday way of saying it.
questions.explanation: Subtract 12 from afternoon hours: 14 h = 2, 21 h = 9. 18 h 45 is a quarter to 19 h, so sept heures moins le quart. 12 h 30 is midi et demi and 0 h 15 is minuit et quart.

questions.stem: What time does each numbered clock show?

image.alt: Six numbered clock faces. They show 3:00, 3:15, 3:30, 3:45, 3:50 and 12:30.

questions.explanation: Read the short hand for the hour and the long hand for the minutes. 3:15 is et quart, 3:30 et demie. From half past on, count back from the next hour: 3:45 is quatre heures moins le quart and 3:50 quatre heures moins dix. 12:30 is midi et demi.

questions.stem: Which mean "on Mondays (every Monday)"? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Le lundi and tous les lundis both describe a weekly habit. Lundi alone is one Monday (usually the coming one); lundi prochain is next Monday and lundi dernier last Monday.

questions.stem: How do you say "the 1st of May"?
questions.explanation: The first of the month is the only date with an ordinal: le premier mai (written le 1er mai). Le comes first, then the number, then the month.

questions.stem: How is "le 21 juin" said?
questions.explanation: Only the 1st uses premier. Every other date uses the plain number, including 21 and 31: le vingt et un juin. Juin is masculine, so un, not une.

questions.stem: In France, a form says "10/11/2026". What date is it?
questions.explanation: French writes the day first, then the month: 10/11/2026 is le 10 novembre 2026. Reading it the US way (month first) gives 11 October, a common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Tu ___ venir samedi ?" (want)
questions.explanation: Vouloir with tu is tu veux. Je veux and tu veux end in -x; il veut ends in -t. Voulez goes with vous and voulons with nous.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ils ___ travailler demain." (must)
questions.explanation: Devoir with ils is ils doivent, with a new stem, like veulent and peuvent. Doit is the il form and devons the nous form; devent doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je ne ___ pas venir, je suis malade."
questions.explanation: Je peux ends in -x (like je veux). Il peut ends in -t. The infinitive pouvoir can't follow je; peus is not a French form.

questions.stem: In a café, which is the most polite way to ask for a coffee?
choices: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite form for ordering. Je veux sounds demanding, "Donne" is a blunt tu command, and je dois un café means "I owe a coffee".

questions.stem: Read: "Salut Tom ! Samedi 6 juin, c'est mon anniversaire. Je fais une fête chez moi à partir de 19 h. Tu veux venir ? Réponds-moi avant mercredi ! Lina" What does Lina ask Tom to do?
questions.explanation: Réponds-moi avant mercredi means "answer me before Wednesday". The party starts at 19 h, which is 7 p.m., not 7 a.m.; she says nothing about a present or a call.

questions.stem: "Tu veux venir au cinéma ce soir ?" You want to say yes. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Avec plaisir (with pleasure) accepts. "Désolé, je ne peux pas" and "Je dois travailler" decline; Joyeux anniversaire is happy birthday.

questions.stem: Which is a polite way to decline an invitation?
choices: Désolée, je ne peux pas : je dois travailler.
questions.explanation: A polite no says sorry (désolé/désolée), je ne peux pas, and gives a reason with devoir. "Non, je ne veux pas" is a blunt "I don't want to"; the other two accept.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Vouloir, pouvoir and devoir are followed directly by an infinitive, with no de or à: nous voulons partir. In "Vous pouvez venez" the second verb must be the infinitive: venir.

questions.stem: "Mon anniversaire est en août." What does "en août" mean?
questions.explanation: En + month means in that month: en août, in August. A precise day needs le + number: le 1er août.

questions.stem: Which date is written correctly in French?
questions.explanation: Months are written with a small letter, the day comes before the month, and only the 1st is an ordinal: le 3 mars.

questions.stem: Write the month that comes after "juillet".
questions.explanation: After juillet comes août (August). Since the 1990 spelling reform, aout without the circumflex is also correct. Months take a small letter.

questions.stem: Write the right form of devoir: "Nous ___ partir à huit heures."
questions.explanation: Nous and vous keep the infinitive stem: nous devons, vous devez. The new stem doiv- is only for ils/elles: ils doivent.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I can't come."
questions.explanation: Ne … pas goes around the conjugated verb (peux), and the infinitive venir comes after: Je ne peux pas venir.

questions.stem: Match each subject and verb to the right present-tense form.
questions.explanation: Je veux, il peut, ils doivent, nous voulons, vous pouvez. Nous and vous keep the infinitive stem (voul-, pouv-), so veulons and peuvez are wrong.

questions.stem: Say each circled date in May.

image.alt: A calendar page for May 2026, with the week starting on Monday. Six dates are circled and numbered: the 1st, 2nd, 8th, 14th, 21st and 31st.

questions.explanation: Only the 1st of the month is an ordinal: le premier mai. All the others use plain numbers: le deux, le huit, le quatorze, le vingt et un, le trente et un mai.

questions.stem: Which are good ways to accept an invitation? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Avec plaisir, Oui, je veux bien and Super, merci ! À samedi ! all say yes. Désolé, je ne peux pas and Je dois travailler are how you decline.

questions.stem: Tell a friend "Turn left!"
questions.explanation: The tu imperative is the tu present without tu, and -er verbs drop the -s: tu tournes → Tourne ! The imperative has no subject pronoun.

questions.stem: Tell a stranger, politely: "Take the second street on the right."
choices: Prends la deuxième rue à droite.
Prenez la deux rue à droite.
Prendre la deuxième rue à droit.
Prenez la deuxième rue à droite.
questions.explanation: With a stranger use the vous form: Prenez. Which street needs the ordinal deuxième, and "on the right" is à droite with -e. Prends is the tu form, too familiar here.

questions.stem: What is the tu imperative of aller?
questions.explanation: Aller follows the -er rule: tu vas loses its -s, giving Va ! (Va tout droit !). Allez is the vous form and aller the infinitive.

questions.stem: What does "Ne traversez pas !" mean?
questions.explanation: Ne … pas around the imperative makes it negative: Don't cross! Let's cross would be Traversons ! and keep going Continuez !

questions.stem: Complete: "La banque est à côté ___ parc."
questions.explanation: De + le always contracts to du: à côté du parc. Parc is masculine and singular, so de la (feminine) and des (plural) don't fit.

questions.stem: Complete: "L'hôtel est en face ___ gare."
questions.explanation: Gare is feminine, and de + la doesn't contract: en face de la gare. Du is for masculine nouns; en face always takes de, not à.

questions.stem: Tell a child "Get up!"
questions.explanation: In a positive imperative, the pronoun goes after the verb with a hyphen, and te becomes toi: Lève-toi ! Only in the negative does it stay in front: Ne te lève pas !

questions.stem: What does "tout droit" mean?
questions.explanation: Tout droit means straight ahead. On the right is à droite, with -e and a pronounced t; in tout droit the t is silent.

questions.stem: Marseille is on the Mediterranean coast. Complete: "Marseille est ___ de la France."
questions.explanation: Marseille is in the south: dans le sud de la France (inside the country). Au nord de would mean north of a place, outside it.

questions.stem: Read: "Allez tout droit, puis prenez la troisième rue à gauche. Le musée est au coin, à côté de la poste." Which is true?
choices: You turn right at the third street.
The museum is next to the post office.
The museum is opposite the post office.
You turn left at the second street.
questions.explanation: À côté de means next to (opposite is en face de). The directions say the third street (la troisième) on the left (à gauche).

questions.stem: "Pardon, où sont les toilettes ?" Which answer is correct?
choices: Elles sont à droite, à côté de la sortie.
Il est à droite, à côté de la sortie.
Je suis à côté de la sortie.
questions.explanation: Les toilettes is feminine plural, so the answer uses elles sont. Il est doesn't agree, and the other two don't answer "where are they?"

questions.stem: Which is the "nous" imperative ("Let's cross")?
questions.explanation: The nous imperative is the nous present without nous: Traversons ! With the pronoun it is a statement (we cross); Traverse is the tu form.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Traverser is an -er verb, so its tu imperative drops the -s: Traverse la rue ! The other three are correct imperatives.

questions.stem: Write the tu imperative of continuer: "___ tout droit !"
questions.explanation: Tu continues loses tu and, as with every -er verb, the -s: Continue tout droit !

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Don't turn right!"
questions.explanation: In a negative imperative, ne … pas goes around the verb, as in a statement without the subject: Ne tournez pas à droite !

questions.stem: Match each French expression to its meaning.
questions.explanation: À droite is on the right, à gauche on the left, tout droit straight ahead, en face de opposite and à côté de next to. Far from is loin de and between is entre.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on the town map.

image.alt: A town map with a dashed route from a star at the bottom, up a street, right along a main street over a river and left up to a building marked GARE. A hotel stands next to the station. Five places are numbered: the point where two streets cross, a traffic light, the road over the river, a signpost with an arrow and a park with trees.

questions.explanation: Where the two streets cross is le carrefour; the traffic light is le feu; the road over the river is le pont; the signpost with an arrow is le panneau; the green area with trees is le parc. There is no exit or square marked.

questions.stem: Name the four numbered points of the compass.

image.alt: A compass rose with four numbered arms, pointing up, right, down and left, with Paris in the middle. Lille is near the top arm, Strasbourg near the right arm, Marseille near the bottom arm and Brest near the left arm.

questions.explanation: Up is le nord (Lille), right is l'est (Strasbourg), down is le sud (Marseille) and left is l'ouest (Brest). On French maps west is O for ouest.

questions.stem: Which are correct imperatives? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Tourne and Va drop the -s of the tu form (an -er verb and aller); Dépêche-toi puts the pronoun after the verb as toi. Tournes keeps the -s it should drop, and Te lève puts the pronoun in front: Lève-toi !

questions.stem: You have a ticket for the TGV 6603. Which platform does it leave from?

image.alt: An invented departure board headed Départs, time 14:00. 14 h 04, TGV 6603, Lyon Part-Dieu, voie 9, à l'heure. 14 h 12, TER 17721, Dijon Ville, voie 3, retard 15 min. 14 h 20, TGV 6115, Marseille St-Charles, no platform yet, à l'heure. 14 h 31, TER 17725, Montereau, voie 5, supprimé. 14 h 46, Intercités 5953, Nevers, no platform yet, à l'heure.

questions.explanation: Find the train number in the Train column: TGV 6603, to Lyon Part-Dieu, leaves at 14 h 04 from voie 9, on time.

questions.stem: What does the board say about the TER 17721 to Dijon?

image.alt: An invented departure board headed Départs, time 14:00. 14 h 04, TGV 6603, Lyon Part-Dieu, voie 9, à l'heure. 14 h 12, TER 17721, Dijon Ville, voie 3, retard 15 min. 14 h 20, TGV 6115, Marseille St-Charles, no platform yet, à l'heure. 14 h 31, TER 17725, Montereau, voie 5, supprimé. 14 h 46, Intercités 5953, Nevers, no platform yet, à l'heure.

questions.explanation: Retard 15 min means about 15 minutes late (le retard, the delay). It still has a platform: voie 3.

questions.stem: Which train will not run at all?

image.alt: An invented departure board headed Départs, time 14:00. 14 h 04, TGV 6603, Lyon Part-Dieu, voie 9, à l'heure. 14 h 12, TER 17721, Dijon Ville, voie 3, retard 15 min. 14 h 20, TGV 6115, Marseille St-Charles, no platform yet, à l'heure. 14 h 31, TER 17725, Montereau, voie 5, supprimé. 14 h 46, Intercités 5953, Nevers, no platform yet, à l'heure.

questions.explanation: Supprimé means cancelled: the 14 h 31 TER to Montereau won't run. The TER to Dijon is only late (retard 15 min).

questions.stem: The TGV to Marseille has no voie yet. What should you do?

image.alt: An invented departure board headed Départs, time 14:00. 14 h 04, TGV 6603, Lyon Part-Dieu, voie 9, à l'heure. 14 h 12, TER 17721, Dijon Ville, voie 3, retard 15 min. 14 h 20, TGV 6115, Marseille St-Charles, no platform yet, à l'heure. 14 h 31, TER 17725, Montereau, voie 5, supprimé. 14 h 46, Intercités 5953, Nevers, no platform yet, à l'heure.

choices: Wait in the hall and watch the board.
Go to the ticket office: it is cancelled.
questions.explanation: An empty Voie column is normal: in big stations the platform often appears only about 20 minutes before departure. The train is à l'heure, not supprimé.

questions.stem: What does "Le train part dans dix minutes" mean?
choices: The train left ten minutes ago.
The train leaves ten minutes from now.
The train is ten minutes late.
questions.explanation: Dans + time looks forward from now. En dix minutes would be how long the trip takes, il y a dix minutes would be ten minutes ago, and a delay is un retard de dix minutes.

questions.stem: The trip takes two hours. Complete: "On va de Paris à Lyon ___ deux heures."
questions.explanation: En + time measures how long something takes: en deux heures. Dans deux heures would mean two hours from now, and il y a deux heures two hours ago.

questions.stem: How is "21 h 34" said in an announcement?
questions.explanation: Heure is feminine, so 21 is vingt et une before heures, and heures takes -s. The 24-hour clock gives the minutes as a plain number: trente-quatre.

questions.stem: You hear: "Le TER numéro 3112, en provenance de Rouen, arrive voie 2." What do you learn about Rouen?
choices: The train is going to Rouen.
The train to Rouen is late.
The train is coming from Rouen.
questions.explanation: En provenance de means arriving from. A train going to Rouen would be à destination de Rouen.

questions.stem: At the ticket office you want a one-way ticket to Bordeaux, second class. What do you say?
choices: Un aller-retour pour Bordeaux, en première, s'il vous plaît.
Un aller simple pour Bordeaux, en seconde, s'il vous plaît.
Un simple pour Bordeaux, deuxième, s'il vous plaît.
Une voie pour Bordeaux, en seconde, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: A one-way ticket is un aller simple (a return is un aller-retour), and second class is en seconde (classe). La voie is a platform, not a ticket.

questions.stem: An announcement says: "… est annoncé avec un retard de vingt minutes environ." What is the news?
choices: The train will be about twenty minutes late.
The train leaves in twenty minutes.
The platform changes in twenty minutes.
questions.explanation: Annoncé avec un retard de means expected with a delay of; environ means about. A cancelled train would be supprimé.

questions.stem: A train will not run at all. Write the word you see in the Informations column: "TER 17725 — ___"
questions.explanation: Supprimé means cancelled. Retardé means delayed: the train still runs.

questions.stem: The trip takes three hours. Complete: "Paris–Marseille ___ trois heures."
questions.explanation: En + length of time says how long something takes. Dans would mean three hours from now.

questions.stem: Match each expression to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Dans looks forward, en measures how long something takes, and il y a looks back. Ten minutes late is dix minutes de retard.

questions.stem: Put the parts of this announcement in order.
questions.explanation: Announcements open with Votre attention, name the train (kind and number), then where it is going (à destination de), and end with the news: here the platform (partira, will leave).

questions.stem: Which notes on a departure board mean there is a problem? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Retardé (delayed), supprimé (cancelled) and retard 15 min (15 minutes late) all signal a problem. À l'heure means on time, and direct means with no change of train.

questions.stem: How many public holidays (jours fériés) does France have by law?
questions.explanation: The Code du travail lists eleven: le jour de l'an, Easter Monday, 1 May, 8 May, Ascension, Whit Monday, 14 July, 15 August, la Toussaint, 11 November and Christmas. Alsace and Moselle add two more locally.

questions.stem: Which holiday is a day off by law for almost every employee?
questions.explanation: Only le 1er mai (la fête du Travail) is a compulsory day off for almost all employees. For the other holidays it depends on the job and the contract, even though many places close.

questions.stem: "Jeudi, c'est l'Ascension. Je fais le pont." What does the speaker do?
questions.explanation: Faire le pont means taking the day between a holiday and the weekend off. With a Thursday holiday that is Friday, giving four days off.

questions.stem: In 2026, le 14 juillet is a Tuesday. Which day do people take off to faire le pont?
questions.explanation: The pont links the holiday to the weekend. With a Tuesday holiday, the gap is Monday: Saturday to Tuesday makes four days off.

questions.stem: What is hidden in a galette des rois?
questions.explanation: La fève, once a real bean and now usually a small porcelain figure. Whoever finds it is king or queen. Paper fish belong to 1 April, and muguet to 1 May.

questions.stem: On le 1er avril, what do children traditionally do?
choices: stick paper fish on people's backs
questions.explanation: 1 April is the day of the poisson d'avril: paper fish and jokes. Lily of the valley is for 1 May, the galette for January and the parade for 14 July.

questions.stem: What does le 14 juillet remember?
choices: the end of the First World War
the storming of the Bastille (1789) and the Fête de la Fédération (1790)
the end of the Second World War in Europe
questions.explanation: La fête nationale recalls 14 July 1789 and 14 July 1790; a law of 1880 made it the national holiday. The First World War is 11 November and the Second World War in Europe 8 May; France has no independence day.

questions.stem: Which date heading is correct for a letter written in Lyon?
questions.explanation: The pattern is place, comma, le + day + month + year: Lyon, le 3 mars 2026. The month is lower case and comes after the day, with no comma before the year.

questions.stem: Which flowers are best avoided as a dinner gift in France?
questions.explanation: Chrysanthemums are the flowers people take to cemeteries for la Toussaint, so most French hosts wouldn't expect them as a gift. This is a general custom, not a rule.

questions.stem: Why is "joyeuses" feminine plural in "Joyeuses Pâques !"?
choices: It agrees with les œufs (the eggs).
With an adjective, Pâques is treated as feminine plural.
questions.explanation: Pâques on its own is masculine singular (Pâques tombe tôt cette année) and has no article: à Pâques. With an adjective in front, it is feminine plural: Joyeuses Pâques ! It has nothing to do with œufs, which is masculine anyway.

questions.stem: Complete the wish for 1 January: "Bonne ___ !"
questions.explanation: Bonne année ! means Happy New Year! People often add et bonne santé ! (and good health).

questions.stem: Write the date heading for a letter from Nantes on 1 June 2026: "Nantes, le ___ juin 2026"
questions.explanation: The first of the month is an ordinal, written 1er (or premier in full): Nantes, le 1er juin 2026. Every other day uses a plain number.

questions.stem: Match each date to its holiday.
questions.explanation: 1 May is Labour Day, 14 July the national holiday, 1 November All Saints' Day, 11 November the 1918 Armistice and 25 December Christmas. L'Ascension moves with Easter, and le jour de l'an is 1 January.

questions.stem: Put these holidays in calendar order, starting in January.
questions.explanation: 1 January (le jour de l'an), 1 May (la fête du Travail), 14 July (la fête nationale), 1 November (la Toussaint), 25 December (Noël).

questions.stem: Which of these dates are public holidays in France? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 1 May (la fête du Travail), 8 May (Victoire 1945) and 15 August (l'Assomption) are public holidays. 1 April (poisson d'avril) and 6 January (Epiphany, the galette des rois) are traditions, not days off.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hier soir, nous ___ un film."
questions.explanation: "Regarder" takes avoir, and the subject is "nous", so "avons" + the participle "regardé" (-er → -é). "Avons regarder" uses the infinitive, which sounds the same but is wrong after avoir. "Sommes regardés" uses être, which is only for the small group of être verbs.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "finir"?
questions.explanation: Finir-type -ir verbs drop -r: "fini" (j'ai fini). "Finit" is the il form of the present (il finit), not the participle; "finé" and "finu" use the -er and -re patterns.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "prendre"?
questions.explanation: "Prendre" is irregular: "pris" (j'ai pris le train). The same goes for comprendre → compris and apprendre → appris. "Prendu" wrongly applies the -re → -u rule; the final s of "pris" is silent, but it is written.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I didn't eat"?
questions.explanation: Ne … pas goes around the auxiliary "ai", and the participle stays outside: "Je n'ai pas mangé." Putting "pas" after the participle is English word order, "je ne mangé" has no auxiliary, and "manger" is the infinitive.

questions.stem: What does "J'ai déjà fini." mean?
questions.explanation: "Déjà" means "already", and it sits between "ai" and the participle. "I haven't finished yet" would be "Je n'ai pas encore fini"; "I'm going to finish" is the near future "Je vais finir".

questions.stem: Complete so that it means "She didn't say anything": "Elle n'a ___ dit."
questions.explanation: "Ne … rien" means "nothing, not anything" and wraps the auxiliary like ne … pas: "Elle n'a rien dit." "Pas" would give "She didn't say" (incomplete), "jamais" means "never".

questions.stem: What does "il y a deux jours" mean?
questions.explanation: "Il y a" + a length of time means "ago", and it comes before the time: "il y a deux jours" = two days ago. "In two days" is "dans deux jours"; "for two days" (how long) is "pendant deux jours".

questions.stem: Complete: "Vous ___ la porte ?" (Did you close the door?)
questions.explanation: "Fermer" is a regular -er verb with avoir: "vous avez fermé". "Avez fermer" uses the infinitive; "êtes fermé" would mean "you are closed".

questions.stem: Which is the correct present-tense form: "Qu'est-ce que vous ___ ?" (dire)
questions.explanation: "Dire" is irregular: vous dites, like vous êtes and vous faites. "Disez" follows the regular -ez pattern, which "dire" doesn't use.

questions.stem: Read the message. "Salut ! Hier, j'ai vu un spectacle au théâtre avec Julie. C'était génial ! Après, nous avons mangé une pizza. Je n'ai pas encore vu ton nouvel appartement : je passe samedi ? Tom" What hasn't Tom done yet?
questions.explanation: "Je n'ai pas encore vu ton nouvel appartement" = I haven't seen your new flat yet. He saw a show (j'ai vu un spectacle) and ate a pizza (nous avons mangé une pizza) with Julie yesterday.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "ouvrir"?
questions.explanation: "Ouvrir" is irregular: "ouvert" (j'ai ouvert la fenêtre). It is also the adjective "open": la porte est ouverte.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "Le concert, c'était comment ?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: "C'était comment ?" asks how it was, so answer with "c'était" + an adjective: "C'était super !" The other answers give a time or answer a yes/no question.

questions.stem: Write the passé composé of "prendre" (to take): "Ce matin, j'___ ___ le bus de 8 heures."
questions.explanation: "Prendre" takes avoir (j'ai) and has the irregular participle "pris": "Ce matin, j'ai pris le bus de 8 heures." — This morning I took the 8 o'clock bus.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "I haven't eaten yet."
questions.explanation: "Je n'ai pas encore mangé." Ne … pas wraps the auxiliary, "encore" follows "pas", and the participle comes last.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its past participle.
questions.explanation: All four are irregular: faire → fait, voir → vu, mettre → mis, écrire → écrit. "Bu" belongs to boire and "pris" to prendre.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Fait" and "lu" are the right participles of faire and lire. "Prendu" should be "pris" and "ouvri" should be "ouvert": irregular verbs don't follow the -é/-i/-u rules.

questions.stem: Name each part of the sentence "Je n'ai pas mangé."

image.alt: The passé composé building blocks: avoir in the present plus a past participle, with three example sentences. At the bottom, the negative sentence Je n'ai pas mangé is split into five boxes, Je, n', ai, pas and mangé, with a numbered marker under each.

questions.explanation: "Je" is the subject, "n'" is ne (elided before a vowel), "ai" is the auxiliary avoir, "pas" closes the negative, and "mangé" is the past participle. There is no infinitive or article in this sentence.

questions.stem: Today is Friday (vendredi). Name the numbered days and times.

image.alt: A strip of thirteen days in French: last week from Monday to Sunday under a bracket, then this week from Monday to Saturday, with Friday shaded as today. Numbers mark the bracket over last week, Wednesday, Thursday, a moon on Thursday evening, Friday and Saturday.

questions.explanation: Today is Friday, so Thursday is "hier" and Thursday evening "hier soir". Wednesday is "il y a deux jours" (two days ago). The whole week before is "la semaine dernière". Saturday is "demain".

questions.stem: Complete: "Hier, je ___ allé au cinéma."
questions.explanation: "Aller" is one of the verbs that take être, and the subject is "je": "je suis allé". "J'ai allé" is the most common mistake: aller never takes avoir.

questions.stem: Which verb takes être in the passé composé?
questions.explanation: "Arriver" is a verb of movement in the house of être: "je suis arrivé". Manger, finir and prendre take avoir: j'ai mangé, j'ai fini, j'ai pris.

questions.stem: Complete: "Marie est ___ à 8 heures." (partir)
questions.explanation: With être the participle agrees with the subject. Marie is one woman: feminine singular, add -e: "partie". "Partis" and "parties" are plural.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mes deux sœurs sont ___ en Italie." (aller)
questions.explanation: "Mes deux sœurs" is feminine plural, so add -es: "allées". "Allés" would be for a masculine or mixed group.

questions.stem: Complete: "Samedi, nous ___ restés à la maison."
questions.explanation: "Rester" takes être; with "nous" the form is "sommes": "nous sommes restés". "Avons" is avoir; "êtes" and "sont" are for vous and ils.

questions.stem: What does "Elle est née en 1990." mean?
questions.explanation: "Naître" (to be born) takes être, and the participle "née" agrees with "elle". English says "was born", French uses the passé composé. "She died" would be "Elle est morte".

questions.stem: Complete: "J'ai habité à Rome ___ trois ans." (for three years, now finished)
questions.explanation: "Pendant" + a length of time says how long something lasted: "pendant trois ans". "Pour" is for a purpose or a plan, and "il y a" means "ago".

questions.stem: Complete so that it means "Last night I got home at midnight": "Hier soir, je suis ___ chez moi à minuit."
questions.explanation: "Rentrer" means to go (back) home: "je suis rentré chez moi à minuit" = I got home at midnight. The other verbs also take être, but "monté" (went up), "tombé" (fell) and "né" (was born) don't mean "got home".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ce matin, Léa s'___ levée à 7 heures."
questions.explanation: Pronominal verbs always take être, and the pronoun goes before it: "elle s'est levée". "S'a" would use avoir, which pronominal verbs never do.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "They (men) didn't come"?
questions.explanation: Ne … pas goes around the auxiliary "sont"; the participle "venus" stays outside and agrees with "ils". "Venir" takes être, so "ils n'ont pas venus" is wrong.

questions.stem: In Inès's postcard from Annecy (in this lesson), why is she alone today?
choices: Her sister went back to Paris this morning.
Her sister fell off her bike and is in hospital.
Her sister stayed at the campsite.
Her sister went up the mountain.
questions.explanation: "Je suis seule aujourd'hui : elle est rentrée à Paris ce matin." Her sister did fall off her bike, but "ce n'est pas grave" (it's not serious).

questions.stem: What does "Elle travaille à l'étranger." mean?
questions.explanation: "À l'étranger" means "abroad". On its own, "un étranger" is a foreigner. The countryside is "la campagne", the seaside "la mer".

questions.stem: Write the passé composé of "tomber" with the subject Léa: "Léa ___ ___ dans la rue."
questions.explanation: "Tomber" takes être, so "est"; the participle agrees with Léa (feminine): "tombée". "Léa est tombée dans la rue." — Léa fell in the street.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "She didn't get up early."
questions.explanation: "Elle ne s'est pas levée tôt." With a pronominal verb, ne … pas wraps the pronoun and the auxiliary together (ne s'est pas); the participle agrees with "elle", and the time word comes last.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its past participle.
questions.explanation: naître → né, mourir → mort, venir → venu (revenir → revenu), and descendre, a regular -re verb, → descendu. "Sorti" goes with sortir and "pris" with prendre.

questions.stem: Which verbs take être in the passé composé? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Rester" and "tomber" are in the house of être, and every pronominal verb (se coucher) takes être. "Regarder" and "prendre" take avoir: j'ai regardé, j'ai pris.

questions.stem: Which être verb does each numbered arrow or scene show?

image.alt: A two-storey house without labels. Numbered: an arrow going in at the front door, an arrow coming out of the door, an arrow going up the stairs, a dashed arrow coming down the stairs, a person sitting in an armchair upstairs, and a flowerpot falling from the balcony.

questions.explanation: Into the door: entrer. Out of it: sortir. Up the stairs: monter; down them: descendre. Sitting in the armchair: rester (to stay). The falling pot: tomber. All of them take être in the passé composé.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places in this landscape.

image.alt: A landscape without labels: snowy mountains, pine trees at their foot, a lake, a few houses with a church, fields, a strip of sand along the sea, a sailing boat, and a small island with a palm tree. Six places are numbered.

questions.explanation: The mountains are "la montagne" and the trees at their foot "la forêt". The water surrounded by land is a lake, "le lac", not the sea. The houses and church are "le village", the sand "la plage", and the land in the sea "l'île".

questions.stem: Complete: "Tu veux du thé ___ du café ?"
questions.explanation: "Ou" (no accent) means "or". "Où" with an accent means "where". "Et" (and) doesn't make sense in a choice between two drinks.

questions.stem: Complete: "Il pleut, ___ je prends mon parapluie."
questions.explanation: The second part is the result of the first, so use "donc" (so): it's raining, so I'm taking my umbrella. "Parce que" would give a reason, which would need the clauses the other way round: "Je prends mon parapluie parce qu'il pleut."

questions.stem: You write an e-mail that ends "Cordialement, Paul Martin". Which opening matches it?
questions.explanation: "Cordialement" is a closing for vous, so the opening must be formal too: "Madame, Monsieur,". Salut, Coucou and Chère Mamie are for friends and family.

questions.stem: Who would you end a message with "Bises" to?
questions.explanation: "Bises" (kisses, love) is informal and goes with tu: friends and family only.

questions.stem: Complete the opening of a letter to a man called Paul: "___ Paul,"
questions.explanation: "Cher" agrees like an adjective: "Cher Paul" for a man, "Chère Léa" for a woman, "Chers amis" for a group.

questions.stem: Which is the nous form of "écrire"?
questions.explanation: "Écrire" adds a v in the plural: nous écrivons, vous écrivez, ils écrivent. "Écrivez" is the vous form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Tu as ___ mon message ?" (received)
questions.explanation: The participle of "recevoir" is "reçu", with ç so that c sounds like s before u. "Reçois" is the present (je reçois).

questions.stem: Ana was born on 5 April 1990. What does she write after "Date de naissance" on a French form?
questions.explanation: French dates go day/month/year: 05/04/1990. "04/05/1990" is the American order and would be read as 4 May.

questions.stem: Which spelling is correct?
questions.explanation: "Envoyer" changes y to i in je, tu, il and ils, and only the i spelling is correct: j'envoie, tu envoies, il envoie. "J'envoies" has the tu ending.

questions.stem: Read the text: "Salut Hugo ! Je suis à la gare mais mon train est en retard, donc je vais arriver vers 20 h. Tu peux venir me chercher ? Léa" Why will Léa arrive at about 8 pm?
choices: Hugo can't pick her up earlier.
questions.explanation: "Mon train est en retard, donc je vais arriver vers 20 h": the late train is the reason, and "donc" introduces the result.

questions.stem: What does "Quand je suis arrivé, il est parti." mean?
choices: If I arrive, he will leave.
