questions.explanation: "Quand" here links two events in time: "when". "Because" would be "parce que", "so" would be "donc" or "alors", and "if" is "si".

questions.stem: What does "J'ai une bonne nouvelle !" mean?
questions.explanation: "La nouvelle" is a piece of news. Don't confuse it with the adjective "nouveau, nouvelle" (new). A novel is "un roman".

questions.stem: You are writing an e-mail to your bank, with vous. Write the usual one-word closing: "___, Paul Martin"
questions.explanation: "Cordialement" (or "Bien cordialement") is the everyday closing for e-mails with vous. "Bises" and "À plus" are for friends.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "It's raining, so we're staying at home."
questions.explanation: "Il pleut, donc nous restons à la maison." The cause comes first, then "donc" and the result.

questions.stem: Ana is filling in a form. Match each field to what she writes in it.
questions.explanation: Nom is the surname, often in capitals (GARCIA). The date of birth is day/month/year. The nationality is the adjective with no capital (espagnole). The French postcode has five figures. "Toulouse" goes under Ville and "infirmière" under Profession.

questions.stem: Which closings can end an e-mail written with vous? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Cordialement" and "Bien cordialement" are the usual closings with vous, and "Bonne journée" suits someone you know a little. "Bises" and "Grosses bises" are only for friends and family.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of Lucie's postcard.

image.alt: Lucie's postcard from Biarritz without the part names. Numbers mark the place and date at the top of the message, the opening Chère Mamie, the closing Bises, the name Lucie, the stamp, and the address on the right.

questions.explanation: "Biarritz, le 12 août" is the place and date; "Chère Mamie," the opening; "Bises," the closing; "Lucie" the name. On the right, the stamp at the top and the address below it. A postcard has no subject line.

questions.stem: Six field names are missing from Ana's form. Name each numbered field.

image.alt: Ana's enrolment form for the École de langues du Parc. Six field names are blank and numbered; their answers are GARCIA, 14/03/1998, Séville (Espagne), espagnole, infirmière and 31000. The fields Prénom (Ana), Adresse, Ville (Toulouse) and Signature are still named.

questions.explanation: GARCIA in capitals is the surname (Nom). 14/03/1998 is the date of birth, Séville the place of birth, "espagnole" the nationality, "infirmière" the occupation (Profession) and 31000 the postcode.

questions.stem: How many points is each of the four parts of the DELF A1 worth?
questions.explanation: Each part (listening, reading, writing, speaking) is marked out of 25, for a total of 100.

questions.stem: What do you need to pass the DELF A1?
choices: 50/100 overall, whatever the mark in each part
50/100 overall and at least 5/25 in every part
questions.explanation: The pass mark is 50 out of 100, and a mark below 5 out of 25 in any part means you fail, even with 50 overall.

questions.stem: Which part of the DELF A1 gives you time to prepare before you start?
questions.explanation: For the speaking test you get about 10 minutes of preparation, then 5–7 minutes with the examiner. The three written parts are taken together in 1 h 20.

questions.stem: Complete: "Tu ___ Marc ? C'est mon frère."
questions.explanation: For a person, use "connaître": "Tu connais Marc ?" "Savoir" is for facts and skills. "Connaissez" is the vous form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Je ___ nager." (I can swim / I know how to swim)
questions.explanation: "Savoir" + infinitive means to know how to do something: "Je sais nager." "Connaître" is followed by a noun, not a verb.

questions.stem: What does the instruction "Cochez la bonne réponse." mean?
questions.explanation: "Cocher" means to tick (a box). "Complétez" = complete, "répétez" = repeat, "expliquez" = explain.

questions.stem: What does "Il a réussi son examen." mean?
questions.explanation: "Réussir un examen" is to pass it. Be careful: "passer un examen" means to take (sit) it, not to pass.

questions.stem: Complete: "J'ai travaillé ___ la journée."
questions.explanation: "Tout" agrees with the noun: "la journée" is feminine singular, so "toute la journée" (all day). Compare "tout le texte, tous les jours, toutes les questions".

questions.stem: Which of these can a learner at CEFR level A1 do?
choices: follow a fast film without subtitles
introduce themselves and ask simple personal questions
questions.explanation: A1 is the first level: simple everyday expressions, introducing yourself, simple questions, and a slow, helped conversation. The others are much higher levels.

questions.stem: In the listening part you hear: "Le rendez-vous est à 15 heures… non, pardon, à 16 heures." When is the appointment?
questions.explanation: The speaker corrects himself ("non, pardon"), so the second time is the right one: 16 heures. Corrections like this are common in listening tasks.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: "Aller" takes être, and the participle agrees with "elle": "Elle est allée". This combines lessons 12 and 22.

questions.stem: Someone asks: "Comment dit-on « holiday » en français ?" Which is a good answer?
questions.explanation: "Comment dit-on … en français ?" asks for a word, so answer "On dit …": "les vacances". The other answers don't give the word.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: French gives age with avoir and "ans": "J'ai 30 ans" (lesson 4). "Je suis 30 ans" copies English.

questions.stem: Complete with "savoir" or "connaître" in the present: "Vous ___ où est la poste ?"
questions.explanation: A question word (où) follows, so use "savoir": "Vous savez où est la poste ?" — Do you know where the post office is?

questions.stem: Complete: "Il y a ___ à la porte." (someone)
questions.explanation: "Quelqu'un" means someone. It goes with "quelque chose" (something) and "rien" (nothing).

questions.stem: Match each exam instruction to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These are vous imperatives: cochez (tick), complétez (fill in, complete), lisez (read), répondez (answer). "Listen" would be "écoutez" and "write" "écrivez".

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask "Could you repeat, please?"
questions.explanation: "Est-ce que vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?" Est-ce que + subject + pouvoir + infinitive, with s'il vous plaît at the end.

questions.stem: Which statements about the DELF A1 are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The three written parts take 1 h 20 in total.
You need at least 5/25 in each part.
The speaking test lasts about an hour.
Each part is marked out of 25.
questions.explanation: Listening, reading and writing are taken together in 1 h 20. Each part is out of 25, and you need 50/100 with at least 5/25 in every part. The speaking test lasts 5–7 minutes after about 10 minutes of preparation.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I slept well"?
questions.explanation: Short adverbs such as "bien" go between the auxiliary and the participle: "J'ai bien dormi." "J'ai dormi bien" follows English word order.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Time words such as "hier" don't go in the adverb slot: they go at the end or at the start (Hier, je suis arrivé). "Arriver" takes être.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ce matin, Julie s'est ___ tard." (se réveiller)
questions.explanation: Pronominal verbs take être, and the participle agrees with the subject. Julie is feminine singular: "réveillée".

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul et Léa se sont ___ au bord du lac." (se promener)
questions.explanation: A mixed group counts as masculine plural, so add -s: "promenés".

questions.stem: What does "tout à coup" mean?
questions.explanation: "Tout à coup" marks a sudden event in a story. "Finally" is "enfin", "first of all" is "d'abord", "luckily" is "heureusement".

questions.stem: Which sentence describes the background of a story rather than an event?
choices: Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
questions.explanation: "Il y avait beaucoup de monde" (there were lots of people) describes the scene, using the imparfait chunk "il y avait". The others are events in the passé composé.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "He didn't sleep well"?
questions.explanation: Ne goes before the auxiliary, then "pas", then "bien", then the participle: "Il n'a pas bien dormi."

questions.stem: In Emma's diary, why did Emma and Chloé go into a café?
choices: They were hungry after the dune.
It started to rain and Emma had no umbrella.
questions.explanation: "Tout à coup … la pluie est arrivée. Malheureusement, je n'avais pas de parapluie ! … nous sommes entrées dans un café." They had already eaten oysters at the harbour.

questions.stem: "Elle s'est lavé les mains" has no -e on "lavé". Why?
choices: A body part (the object) follows the verb.
It is in the present tense.
questions.explanation: This is the preview rule beyond A1: when an object such as "les mains" follows, se means "for herself" and the participle doesn't agree. "Elle s'est lavée" (she washed) does agree.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "She has never seen the sea."
questions.explanation: "Elle n'a jamais vu la mer." Ne … jamais wraps the auxiliary, like ne … pas, and the participle follows "jamais".

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Yesterday I (a woman) got up early."
questions.explanation: "Hier, je me suis levée tôt." The reflexive pronoun comes before être, the participle agrees with a woman speaker, and "tôt" goes after the participle.

questions.stem: Rewrite "Je me suis levé à 8 heures" about Léa: "Léa ___ ___ à 8 heures."
questions.explanation: Je me suis → elle s'est, and the participle agrees with Léa (feminine): "Léa s'est levée à 8 heures."

questions.stem: Write the French for "suddenly": "___, il a commencé à pleuvoir."
questions.explanation: "Tout à coup" (or "soudain") introduces a sudden event: "Tout à coup, il a commencé à pleuvoir." — Suddenly it started to rain.

questions.stem: Which words go between the auxiliary and the participle in the passé composé? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Short adverbs (bien, déjà) and negative words (jamais) go in the slot: j'ai bien dormi, j'ai déjà vu, je n'ai jamais vu. Time words (hier, tôt) go after the participle (hier can also start the sentence).

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Heureusement = fortunately, malheureusement = unfortunately, tout à coup = suddenly, il y avait = there was / there were. "Finally" is enfin and "first" is d'abord.

questions.stem: You write to a company and don't know who will read your letter. Which opening is right?
questions.explanation: "Madame, Monsieur," is the standard opening when you don't know the reader. "Cher Monsieur Dupont" sounds over-familiar to a stranger, and salut and coucou are for friends.

questions.stem: In a French formal letter, where does the recipient's address usually go?
choices: at the bottom, under the signature
on the right, below the sender's
questions.explanation: The sender goes top left; the recipient goes on the right, lower down, where it shows through a window envelope.

questions.stem: What is "l'objet" in a formal letter or e-mail?
questions.explanation: "Objet :" introduces a few words saying what the letter is about, like a subject line. In an e-mail, l'objet is the subject field.

questions.stem: Which address is written the French way?
questions.explanation: Number first with no comma, then the street; on the last line the postcode, then the town in capitals, with no punctuation.

questions.stem: What does "mdr" mean in a text message?
questions.explanation: "Mdr" stands for "mort de rire" (dying of laughter), the French LOL. Sorry is "dsl", see you later "a+", I don't know "jsp".

questions.stem: What does "tkt" mean in a text message?
questions.explanation: "Tkt" is "t'inquiète (pas)", don't worry. Please is "stp" or "svp".

questions.stem: Which closing is the most formal?
choices: Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
questions.explanation: The long formula "Je vous prie d'agréer … salutations distinguées" is for official letters. Cordialement and Bien à vous are e-mail closings, and Bises is for friends.

questions.stem: Your formal letter opens with "Madame,". How should the closing formula read?
choices: Je vous prie d'agréer, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
Je vous prie d'agréer, chère amie, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
questions.explanation: The formula repeats the opening exactly: you opened with Madame, so the formula says Madame.

questions.stem: Your classmate Inès wrote to you with tu. Which reply is consistent?
choices: Salut Inès, merci pour votre message ! Tu veux aller au cinéma ? Bises
Madame, merci pour ton message. Vous voulez aller au cinéma ? Cordialement
Salut Inès, merci pour ton message ! Tu veux aller au cinéma samedi ? À samedi !
Bonjour Inès, merci pour votre message. Vous voulez aller au cinéma ? Bises
questions.explanation: Keep one form from opening to closing. Only the reply with "ton message" and "À samedi !" uses tu everywhere: salut, ton message, tu veux, À samedi. The others mix votre/vous with tu, Bises or Madame.

questions.stem: What does "en pièce jointe" mean in an e-mail?
questions.explanation: "La pièce jointe" is an attachment: "Vous trouverez le formulaire en pièce jointe" = please find the form attached.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of Thomas's formal letter.

image.alt: Thomas Bernard's formal letter without the part names. Numbers mark his own address at the top left, the school's address on the right, the place and date line, the Objet line, the closing formula, and the signature.

questions.explanation: Top left is the sender (l'expéditeur), on the right the recipient (le destinataire), then the place and date. "Objet :" is the subject line. The long sentence before the signature is la formule de politesse, and at the bottom la signature. A letter has no stamp; that goes on the envelope.

questions.stem: Write the text-message abbreviation for "s'il te plaît": ___
questions.explanation: "Stp" is "s'il te plaît" and "svp" is "s'il vous plaît". Both are informal in texts; write the full words in an e-mail.

questions.stem: Put the lines of this address on an envelope going to France in order, from top to bottom.
questions.explanation: The order goes from the person down to the place: name, number and street, postcode and town, and, for a letter from abroad, the country last.

questions.stem: Match each text-message abbreviation to its meaning.
questions.explanation: slt = salut (hi), dsl = désolé (sorry), bcp = beaucoup (a lot), rdv = rendez-vous. "Why" is pk (pourquoi) and "don't worry" is tkt.

questions.stem: Which of these belong in a formal e-mail to a company? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A formal e-mail has a subject (Objet), a formal opening (Madame, Monsieur,) and a matching closing (Cordialement). Salut and mdr are informal and don't belong there.

cards.front: T2 / F2 in a flat ad
cards.back: Two main rooms (pièces principales): a living room + one bedroom. Kitchen, bathroom, toilet and hall don't count. A T3 usually has two bedrooms.
la pièce = any main room of a home (counted in T2, T3); la chambre = a bedroom only.
Ground floor / one floor up (US: second floor). In ads: RDC, 1er ét.
charges comprises (service charges included) / hors charges (not included). Total per month = loyer + charges.
avec ascenseur (with a lift), cuisine équipée (fitted kitchen), salle de bains (bathroom), meublé (furnished; non meublé = unfurnished).
Both ways: the owner (le propriétaire) lets the flat, the tenant (le locataire) rents it. À louer = for rent. Une location = a rental (not "a location").
The lease (plural les baux): usually 3 years unfurnished (private landlord), 1 year furnished, 9 months for a student.
1. Everyday: the deposit (officially le dépôt de garantie). 2. Legal: the guarantee given by a guarantor (le garant).
One month of rent without charges for an unfurnished flat; two months for a furnished one. Returned within 1 month after you leave, or 2 if there is damage.
The written check of every room when you move in and again when you leave. It decides whether you get your deposit back.
To move (house): je déménage, nous déménageons (like manger). To move in = emménager.
13 in metropolitan France since 1 January 2016 (12 on the mainland + Corse), plus 5 overseas regions: 18 in all. 101 departments, numbered (75 = Paris).
Nickname for mainland France, from its roughly six-sided shape. With Corse: la France métropolitaine.
In Normandie (on the border with Bretagne).
Bretagne: crêpes and galettes. Normandie: camembert, cidre. Grand Est: choucroute, champagne. Occitanie: cassoulet. Provence: bouillabaisse.
un fleuve reaches the sea (la Loire, la Seine, le Rhône, la Garonne); une rivière flows into another river.
en + feminine region: en Bretagne, en Normandie. dans le Grand Est, dans les Hauts-de-France. Islands vary: à La Réunion, à Mayotte, but en Corse, en Martinique.
Guadeloupe and Martinique (Caribbean), Guyane (South America), La Réunion and Mayotte (Indian Ocean). Departments 971–976; euro; part of the EU.
French Guiana, in South America: part of France, with Europe's space centre at Kourou. Not Guyana.

cards.front: Travel story in the passé composé
cards.back: Movement verbs take être and agree: je suis allée, je suis montée (Sofia). Others take avoir: j'ai goûté, j'ai découvert (découvrir → découvert).
1621–1695. First Fables in 1668 (books I–VI), about 240 fables in 12 books in all, many retold from Aesop and Phaedrus.

cards.front: La Cigale et la Fourmi: the story
cards.back: The cicada sings all summer and has nothing in winter. She asks her neighbour the ant to lend her grain. "What did you do in the warm weather?" "I sang." "Then dance now."

cards.front: Why every French pupil knows it
cards.back: It's fable 1 of book 1, and French children have learned it by heart in primary school for generations.
A cicada (not a grasshopper, which is une sauterelle).
prêter = to lend (give for a time); emprunter = to borrow (take for a time). Tu peux me prêter ton stylo ? J'emprunte un livre.

cards.front: Vous chantiez, j'en suis fort aise ! Eh bien, dansez maintenant.
cards.back: "You were singing! I'm delighted. Well then, dance now." fort = very (literary use); the ant's delight is ironic. Many editions print Vous chantiez ? (a question).

cards.front: The passé simple: what and when
cards.back: The tense of written stories, = passé composé in meaning: elle alla = elle est allée. Recognise it; don't use it in speech.
-er: il chanta, ils chantèrent. Others: il finit, il dit, il fit; il fut (être), il eut (avoir), il vint (venir).
Present participles (-ant, from the nous form): priant = begging; ayant chanté = having sung.

cards.front: le vers / le ver / vert / le verre
cards.back: line of poetry / worm / green / glass: all pronounced "vair".
Bonjour, madame / Bonjour, monsieur before anything else. Leaving: Merci, au revoir, bonne journée !
Say tu / say vous: je tutoie, nous tutoyons; je vouvoie, nous vouvoyons. On se tutoie ? = Shall we say tu?
Usually the older person or the one with more status. Once you've switched, don't go back to vous. Two people are always vous.
Cheeks touch, kiss in the air. Two in most of France; one in north Finistère, three in parts of the south, four in parts of the north and west. Let the other person lead.

cards.front: Arriving for dinner at someone's home
cards.back: About 15 minutes after the time given (le quart d'heure de politesse), never early. Bring wine, flowers (not chrysanthemums) or a dessert.
Drinks and small things to eat before the meal. Wait until every glass is full, then Santé ! and look each other in the eye.
apporter = bring a thing (j'apporte du vin); amener = bring a person (j'amène mon ami).

cards.front: Setting a French table (mettre la table)
cards.back: Fork on the left, knife on the right (blade towards the plate), spoon right of the knife, glass above the knife, bread on the tablecloth.
Not straight after dessert. Merci pour cette excellente soirée ! A short thank-you message the next day.

cards.front: Letter names that trap English speakers
cards.back: E = "uh", I = "ee", G = "zhay", J = "zhee". Comment ça s'écrit ? = How do you spell that?
é (aigu), è à ù (grave), â ê î ô û (circonflexe), ë ï (tréma), ç (cédille). They are part of the spelling.
Final c, r, f, l are usually said (avec, bonjour, neuf, il); most other final consonants are silent. Verbs in -er end in "ay".
u (tu): say "ee" with rounded lips, tongue forward. ou (tout): "oo" as in food, tongue back.
an/en (France), in/ain (vin, pain), on (bon), un (un). Not nasal when a vowel or a second n/m follows: bonne, fine.
je, le, la, de, ne, que drop their vowel before a vowel or mute h: j'habite, l'accent, d'accord, n'est, qu'il. Compulsory.
On the last syllable of each group of words: merCI, merci beauCOUP.

cards.front: I don't understand. / Can you repeat that? / Slowly, please.
cards.back: Je ne comprends pas. / Vous pouvez répéter ? / Lentement, s'il vous plaît.
bonjour until the evening; bonsoir from about 6 p.m.; bonne nuit only when someone goes to bed.
au revoir; bonne journée (day), bonne soirée (evening); à bientôt, à demain, à plus tard; salut among friends.
tu: family, friends, children. vous: strangers, staff, older people, your boss, and ANY group. When in doubt: vous.
Ça va ? (casual) · Comment vas-tu ? (informal) · Comment allez-vous ? (formal). Answer: Très bien / Bien / Pas mal, merci. Et toi / et vous ?

cards.front: What's your name? My name is…
cards.back: Comment tu t'appelles ? (informal) · Comment vous appelez-vous ? (formal) — Je m'appelle Léa. Enchanté(e) !
Bonjour, monsieur / madame (M., Mme). Madame is the safe form for any adult woman; mademoiselle left official forms in 2012.
je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont
Usually "we" in speech, with the il form: on est. Also "people" in general.
elles only for an all-female (or all-feminine) group; ils for any group with a man or masculine noun in it.

As an adjective, use lowercase and agree with the person: Elle est canadienne. As a noun naming a person, use a capital: une Canadienne. After être, Elle est Canadienne is also possible with the noun reading.
C'est + name or un/une + noun (C'est Marc, c'est un ami). Il/elle est + adjective (Il est canadien).
à + city (à Paris) · en + feminine country (en France) · au + masculine country (au Canada) · aux + plural (aux États-Unis)
soixante-dix (60 + 10), quatre-vingts (4 × 20), quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10)
soixante et onze (with et), quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze (no et)
With s only when nothing follows: quatre-vingts, but quatre-vingt-trois.
Alone "sees, weet, dees"; before a consonant "see, wee, dee"; before a vowel "seez, weet, deez".
J'ai trente ans (avoir + ans). Quel âge avez-vous ? Never "je suis trente".
Read in pairs: 06 12 45 78 97 = zéro six, douze, quarante-cinq, soixante-dix-huit, quatre-vingt-dix-sept. @ = arobase, . = point.
Determiner + noun (les_amis), pronoun + verb (nous_avons, sont-ils), short adjective + noun (petit_ami), short prepositions (chez_elle), fixed phrases (les États_Unis).
After et; after a singular noun (étudiant | anglais); before aspirated h (les | héros), onze, oui, huit.
After verbs (c'est_un), plural nouns, pas (pas_encore). More in careful speech; when unsure, leave it out.
s, x, z → "z"; d → "t" (grand_homme); f → "v" in neuf ans, neuf heures.
A consonant that is always said slides into the next vowel: il est = "ee-LEH", une amie = "ü-na-MEE".
Often dropped in speech (p'tit, sam'di, j'sais pas), kept when three consonants would meet (vendredi). Always written.
Silent but blocks elision and liaison: le haricot, les | héros, la hauteur. Mute h: l'homme, les_hommes.
Closed é (et, été) vs open è (est, très); closed o (beau, mot) vs open o (porte, bonne).
Statements fall at the end; yes/no questions rise (Tu es français ?); question-word questions usually fall (Où habitez-vous ?).
No liaison before aspirated h: "lay ay-ROH". With a liaison it would sound like les zéros (the zeros).
Small f: the French-speaking world. Capital F: the OIF, an organization of states and governments sharing French.
France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Monaco, Canada, Haiti, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, DR Congo, Madagascar…
au Québec = in the province; à Québec = in Québec City. Same with au Luxembourg / à Luxembourg.

cards.front: au Sénégal, en Côte d'Ivoire, en Haïti
cards.back: Masculine country → au; feminine → en; Haiti: en Haïti is usual (à Haïti also correct).
70 and 90 in Belgium and Switzerland; huitante (80) in Vaud, Valais, Fribourg. Belgium says quatre-vingts.
déjeuner = breakfast, dîner = lunch, souper = dinner. France: petit-déjeuner, déjeuner, dîner.
la fin de semaine (weekend), le courriel (e-mail); tu is used more widely than in France.
France: un portable · Belgium: un GSM · Switzerland: un natel
+ plus ("plüss"), − moins, × fois, ÷ divisé par, = égale (or font, ça fait)
A trace of medieval counting in twenties (deux vins = 40; the Quinze-Vingts hospital: 15 × 20 = 300). Standard forms fixed in the 17th century.
Out of 20. 10 = la moyenne (pass mark). Bac: 12 assez bien, 14 bien, 16 très bien.
French 1 has a long upstroke; so the 7 gets a bar across the middle.
le chiffre = a digit (0–9); le nombre = a quantity; le numéro = a label (phone, house, room).

cards.front: Catching a phone number at speed
cards.back: Wait for the whole pair: soixante… could be 60–79, quatre-vingt… 80–99. soixante-quatorze = 74.
once, twice. In sums fois = times: trois fois quatre = 3 × 4.
to get the pass mark, at least 10 out of 20. J'ai quinze sur vingt = I got 15/20 (good).
le (masculine), la (feminine), l' (before a vowel or mute h), les (plural): le lit, la table, l'ordinateur, les livres.
un (masculine), une (feminine); plural des: un sac, une clé, des clés. English often says nothing where French needs des: There are books = Il y a des livres.

cards.front: How do you hear that a noun is plural?
cards.back: From the article: le (luh) vs les (lay), un vs des. The plural -s of the noun is silent.
-eau adds -x (le bureau → les bureaux); -al → -aux (le journal → les journaux); -s, -x, -z don't change (le cours → les cours).
c'est + one thing or person (C'est une chaise.); ce sont + several (Ce sont des clés.). In speech you'll also hear c'est with a plural.
il for a masculine noun, elle for a feminine one: Où est la clé ? — Elle est sur la table.
there is / there are (never changes): Il y a deux chambres. With a time: ago (il y a deux ans).
on, under, in (inside), in front of, behind: Le chat est sous la table.
là (accent) = there (often "here" in speech); la (no accent) = the (feminine).
j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
ils ont (z sound: eel-ZON) = they have; ils sont (s sound: eel-SON) = they are.
avoir + number + ans: J'ai trente ans. Never je suis trente.
mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses; then notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs. Owner picks the word, noun picks the form.
Either his or her. The possessive agrees with the noun (père masculine, mère feminine), not with the owner.
No: mon amie. Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or mute h, ma/ta/sa become mon/ton/son (mon_amie).
leur + one thing (leur fils), leurs + several (leurs enfants). Both mean "their".
la fille = daughter or girl; la femme = wife or woman; l'enfant = child, masculine or feminine (un enfant, une enfant).
Who is it? Who's that? — C'est ma sœur. / Ce sont mes parents.
stem + -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.
je, tu, il and ils: parle, parles, parle, parlent are all "parl". Only nous (-ons) and vous (-ez) have endings you hear.
j': j'aime, j'étudie, j'écoute, j'habite. Liaison after nous/vous/ils: nous_aimons, ils_écoutent.
to listen to, to watch / look at, to look for. No extra word: J'écoute la radio. Je cherche ma clé.

cards.front: Elle est médecin vs C'est un médecin
cards.back: After être, a job takes no article (Elle est médecin). After c'est, it does (C'est un médecin).
Masculine, small letter: le français, l'anglais. Parler français (usually no article), but étudier le français, aimer l'espagnol.
+ le/la/les + noun (J'aime le café) or + infinitive (J'aime danser).

cards.front: J'aime Paul vs J'aime bien Paul
cards.back: J'aime Paul = I love Paul. J'aime bien Paul = I like Paul.
+ e (feminine), + s (plural), + es (feminine plural): un sac noir, une porte noire, des sacs noirs, des portes noires. Adjectives in -e don't add another e.
bon → bonne, gentil → gentille, blanc → blanche, heureux → heureuse, long → longue.
Usually after the noun (colours, nationalities, most others). BAGS before: beau, joli; jeune, vieux, nouveau; bon, mauvais; grand, petit.
un beau livre, un bel appartement (before a vowel), une belle maison. Likewise vieux / vieil / vieille and nouveau / nouvel / nouvelle.
In careful writing: de beaux livres, de petites chambres. In speech also des. After the noun, des stays: des chambres bleues.
marron never changes: des sacs marron. But rose agrees: des portes roses.
very, quite (also: enough), too. Trop is a complaint: trop petit = too small.

cards.front: A man and a woman: adjective?
cards.back: Masculine plural: Paul et Julie sont gentils.
-tion, -té, -ette, -ure, -ée: la solution, la liberté, la baguette, la voiture, l'idée.
-ment, -age, -eau, -isme: le bâtiment, le fromage, le bureau, le tourisme.
la page, la plage, l'image, la cage, la nage.
l'eau is feminine (exception to -eau); le musée and le lycée are masculine (exception to -ée); l'été is masculine (exception to -té).
Only a weak hint: le livre, le téléphone, le problème are masculine.
From a verb: -euse (chanteur → chanteuse). -teur: -trice (acteur → actrice, directeur → directrice). No verb behind it: -eure (professeur → professeure, ingénieur → ingénieure).
le/la journaliste, le/la dentiste, le/la ministre: only the article changes.
Both are used for a woman author. Auteure was more frequent in 2019; autrice is gaining ground. Usage varies.
Québec 1979; France: circulars 1986 and 1998, guide 1999; Académie française accepts them 28 February 2019.
Middle-dot forms showing both genders. Debated; kept out of official texts (2017) and schools (2021). Safe form: les étudiants et les étudiantes.
avoir + les + noun + adjective: Elle a les cheveux longs. Il a les yeux bleus. Masculine plural adjectives.
blond, brun (dark), roux/rousse (red, ginger, never rouge), gris, blanc. Elle est rousse = she has red hair.
Il a une barbe (a beard). Elle a des lunettes (glasses; plural only).
-if → -ive (sportive), -er → -ère (chère), -on → -onne (mignonne), -el → -elle (naturelle), -en → -enne (ancienne), -eux → -euse (sérieuse).

cards.front: un grand homme / un homme grand
cards.back: a great man / a tall man. Before the noun: figurative; after: literal.

cards.front: mon ancien prof / une maison ancienne
cards.back: my former teacher / an old (antique) house.

cards.front: mon cher ami / un restaurant cher
cards.back: my dear friend / an expensive restaurant.
gentil (kind), sympa (nice), drôle (funny), timide (shy), sportif (sporty), mignon (cute). Le caractère = personality.
du (masc.), de la (fem.), de l' (before a vowel), des (plural): "some", an amount you don't count. Je mange du pain. Elle boit de l'eau.
Liking verbs → le/la/les (J'aime le café). Counting → un/une/des (un café = one cup). An amount → du/de la/de l' (Je bois du café).
de + le (always joined). de la and de l' never join.
nous mangeons (the e keeps the g soft)
je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent
Je voudrais … : Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. (Je veux sounds blunt.)
le petit-déjeuner (breakfast), le déjeuner (lunch), le dîner (dinner)

cards.front: Meal words in Belgium, Switzerland, Québec
cards.back: le déjeuner = breakfast, le dîner = lunch, le souper = evening meal
The f is said in un œuf, silent in des œufs ("day-ZUH").
ne + verb + pas: Je ne mange pas. n' before a vowel: Il n'aime pas. ne … jamais = never.

cards.front: un / du / des after a negative
cards.back: become de / d': Je n'ai pas de lait. Il n'y a pas d'œufs.

cards.front: What does NOT change after a negative?
cards.back: le, la, les (Je n'aime pas le lait) and anything after être (Ce n'est pas un livre).
s when multiplied and no number follows: deux cents (euros). No s when a number follows: deux cent un.
Never takes s, no un before it: mille, deux mille, dix mille.
trois euros cinquante (comma for decimals; at the till often just "trois cinquante")
un kilo de tomates, une bouteille d'eau, un paquet de pâtes, beaucoup de sucre (de, never du/des)
j'achète, tu achètes, il achète, nous achetons, vous achetez, ils achètent

cards.back: Et avec ça ? (Anything else?) — C'est tout. (That's all.) C'est combien ? (How much is it?)

cards.back: Vous avez une table ? (intonation) / Est-ce que vous avez une table ? / Avez-vous une table ? (inversion)
Between a vowel and il/elle/on in inversion: A-t-il faim ? Parle-t-elle anglais ?
Si ! Tu n'as pas faim ? — Si, j'ai faim.
which / what + noun, agrees with it: Quelle boisson ? Quel est le plat du jour ?
qui = who (people); qu'est-ce que = what (things): Qu'est-ce que tu manges ?
parce que (because); parce qu' before a vowel
la carte = the menu card (all dishes); le menu = a set menu at a fixed price
starter, main course, dessert (l'entrée is NOT the main course)
J'ai faim. / J'ai soif. (avoir, no article)
je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont
au / aux: au cinéma, aux toilettes. à la and à l' don't change.
at / to someone's place or shop: chez Paul, chez moi, chez le médecin (people, not places)
moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles: avec lui, pour eux, chez moi
aller + infinitive: Je vais visiter le musée. Negative: Je ne vais pas travailler.
je vois, tu vois, il voit, nous voyons, vous voyez, ils voient
visiter = a place (visiter Paris); aller voir = a person (aller voir ma grand-mère)
library / bookshop

cards.back: entrée → plat → fromage → dessert → café (cheese before dessert)

a small black espresso. un déca = decaf; un allongé = with extra water
espresso with a dash of milk / large coffee with hot milk
boulangerie (bread), pâtisserie (cakes), boucherie (meat), charcuterie (ham, sausage), fromagerie (cheese), épicerie (groceries)

noun + verb-pronoun: Votre fils parle-t-il anglais ? Les enfants ont-ils faim ?
after où, quand, comment, combien, que: Où habite votre fils ? Not after pourquoi.
quel + noun; qu'est-ce que (standard); que + inversion (formal); quoi (casual, at the end)

n'est-ce pas ? (neutral, formal) / hein ? (very casual)
Y a-t-il … ? (inversion of il y a)
est-ce que with vous: Est-ce que vous avez … ?
Text: intonation, quoi, où at the end. E-mail to a hotel: Avez-vous … ? Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ?
fais, fais, fait, faisons, faites, font. Vous faites, never "vous faisez".

cards.front: faire de, jouer à or jouer de?
cards.back: faire du / de la + activity (faire du vélo); jouer au / aux + game (jouer au tennis); jouer du / de la + instrument (jouer de la guitare).

cards.front: Negative of faire du vélo and jouer au tennis
cards.back: Je ne fais pas de vélo (du becomes de). Je ne joue pas au tennis (au stays).
Il fait beau / mauvais / chaud / froid. Il pleut. Il neige. Il y a du soleil. Quel temps fait-il ?
A person: j'ai chaud (never je suis chaud). The weather: il fait chaud. A thing: c'est chaud.
au printemps, en été, en automne, en hiver. Only spring takes au.
prends, prends, prend, prenons, prenez, prennent. Comprendre and apprendre are the same.
viens, viens, vient, venons, venez, viennent. pars, pars, part, partons, partez, partent.
en + a vehicle you sit in: en bus, en train, en voiture, en avion. à pied, à vélo. With prendre: je prends le bus.
la gare = train station; la station = metro station; l'arrêt (m.) = bus or tram stop.
le billet: train or plane ticket (also a banknote). le ticket: metro or bus ticket. un aller-retour = a return ticket.
à l'heure / en retard. Le train est en retard. (tard = late in the day)
Stem-changing -er verbs change in je, tu, il, ils (silent endings), not in nous, vous: j'achète / nous achetons; je préfère / nous préférons.
j'appelle, nous appelons; je paie (or paye), nous payons; j'essaie (or essaye), nous essayons.
nous commençons (ç before o), nous mangeons (e after g). In the present, only the nous form changes.
ce pull (m.), cet homme / cet été (m. before vowel or mute h), cette robe (f.), ces chaussures (plural).
porter = to wear (have on), to carry. mettre = to put, to put on: Il fait froid, je mets mon manteau.
Quelle taille faites-vous ? — Je fais du 40. (un pantalon, un jean: singular in French)
finis, finis, finit, finissons, finissez, finissent. Also choisir, réfléchir.
vends, vends, vend, vendons, vendez, vendent. No ending in the il form. Also attendre, répondre, entendre, perdre.
dors, dors, dort, dormons, dormez, dorment. Not a finir verb: no -iss-.
avoir mal à + article: j'ai mal à la tête, à l'oreille, au dos, aux dents. Never "à ma tête".
les yeux. Le bras, le dos, le nez, le corps don't change in the plural.

It suits you! (Ça vous va bien.) C'est trop serré / large / grand / petit. Je le prends / Je la prends.
